components.name: AI Agent Activity Log
components.description: 4 variants: `feed` (filterable event feed with opt-in step replay), `timeline`, `compact` (dense table with expandable rows) and `trace` (span waterfall with a step-detail panel). Tracks agent runs, tool calls, LLM steps and retrieval operations. Events are shown in arrival order, clock skew is reported rather than re-sorted, and every variant caps its rows and says when it has.
whenToUse: Tracing an AI agent's execution: tool calls, LLM steps, retrieval and timing.
Debugging multi-step agents or showing users what the agent did.
For non-agent activity history, use the Timeline.
customization: Feed, timeline, compact and trace views.
Per-step status, duration and tokens.
Expandable step details.
Set `replayable` (feed view) to play the run back step-by-step — play/pause, step, restart, tunable `replaySpeed`, with a `stepChange` output.
Emits `traceSelect` with the clicked run/trace id.

A scale ceiling in every variant: `[maxEvents]` (500) is how many rows a view renders at once — `timeline` and `compact` keep the newest events, `trace` keeps the first spans (cutting a flattened tree from the top would orphan child spans), and each says what it left out. In the feed it is windowed over what the FILTER left rather than the raw run, and keeping the newest — a retry loop emits thousands of events in minutes, and the feed would get slower exactly as the run got more interesting. What is missing is disclosed at the top, the counters keep reporting the whole run, and step replay is exempt: replay walks the run from its first event forward, so a window keeping the newest would show an empty feed at step one. Set `0` if you virtualize the feed yourself.

`[replayOnChange]` decides what an arriving event does to a replay already running: `hold` (the default — keep walking the events it started with, and **count** the ones waiting, which join the feed when the reader leaves the replay), `cancel` (leave the replay the moment an event it did not start with arrives, stop the auto-play timer and return to the live feed — right for a monitoring wall) or `extend` (append, which is only honest for a run still in progress). Without a rule, the feed would re-slice against whatever had arrived, so 'step 4 of 20' would quietly become step 4 of a different list, mid-sentence, with no signal at all.

A **filter change is the reader’s own action**, not the run moving under them, so it takes effect immediately whatever `replayOnChange` says. The snapshot is of the *filtered* list — taking it earlier would let a filter change mid-replay reveal events the reader had deliberately hidden.

On a phone the `trace` view stacks the waterfall above the step detail, and each span row narrows to a 7rem label and its duration so the bar keeps its width; self time, tokens and cost stay in the row’s accessible name and in the step detail, and return as columns from `sm` up.

Events are rendered in the order they arrived and **never re-sorted by timestamp**. Two agents on two machines produce clocks that disagree, and sorting by them would put a tool result before the call that produced it. An event whose time runs backwards against the one before it is flagged instead, compared against its predecessor rather than the maximum so far — otherwise one machine an hour ahead would report the entire remainder of the run as out of order and tell the reader nothing.
accessibility: Steps expose status and timing as text.
Type filter reports aria-pressed; expandable rows expose aria-expanded.
Replay transport buttons are labelled and keyboard-operable.
Keyboard expand/collapse of details.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the data is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Which view: `feed`, `timeline`, `compact` or `trace`.

inputs.name: run
inputs.description: The agent run to visualize (steps, tool calls, timings). Events are shown in the order they arrived, never re-sorted by time. Two agents on two machines produce timestamps that disagree, and sorting by a skewed clock would put a tool result before the call that produced it. When an event's `elapsedMs` is earlier than the one before it, `feed`, `timeline` and `compact` say so in a notice instead — each event compared with its predecessor, so one skewed event flags itself rather than everything after it. A late event is appended where it arrives, whether through a new `run` or `appendEvent()`; re-delivering an id patches that event in place. What a late event does to a replay in progress is `replayOnChange`.

inputs.name: trace
inputs.description: The tree shown by the `trace` variant. Leave `null` to walk `run.events` (they already nest through `children`); supply a tree when your trace endpoint returns a different shape from the flat feed.

inputs.name: connection
inputs.description: State of your `EventSource` / WebSocket. A run that stops growing looks the same whether the agent is thinking or the socket died, so the component cannot infer this — only you know.

inputs.name: reconnectable
inputs.description: Offer a manual reconnect while the feed is down.

inputs.name: replayable
inputs.description: Enables step-replay controls in the feed view: play/pause, step and restart to walk the run one event at a time.

inputs.name: replaySpeed
inputs.description: Playback speed multiplier applied to the run's inter-step timings.

inputs.name: replayOnChange
inputs.description: What an incoming event does to a replay already running. Without a rule, the feed would re-slice against whatever had arrived, so "step 4 of 20" would quietly become step 4 of a different list — the same index over different events, mid-sentence, with no signal at all. `'hold'` (the default) keeps walking the events the replay started with and counts the ones waiting, which join the feed when the reader leaves the replay; `'cancel'` leaves the replay as soon as a new event arrives and returns to the live feed, which is right for a monitoring wall; `'extend'` appends, which is only honest for a run still in progress.

inputs.name: expandedIds
inputs.description: IDs of events whose detail panel is expanded (two-way). A `model` so a host can open the event a deep link names — the case this log exists for, since an agent trace is usually shared by pointing at one step — and so the open set survives a route change. It was a plain signal, readable only from inside the template.

inputs.name: maxEvents
inputs.description: How many events (or, in `trace`, spans) a variant renders at once. `0` = no ceiling. Applies to every variant, each with its own notice. An agent run is the list-shaped surface that grows while you watch it. A retry loop emits thousands of events in minutes, and a feed that renders every one of them gets slower exactly as the run gets more interesting — the operator is watching an incident through a page that is failing for a second, unrelated reason. The window keeps the newest. A run's latest events are the ones being read; the beginning is history, and history is what a filter and a search are for. Replay is exempt, and that is deliberate — see visibleEvents. `trace` keeps the FIRST spans instead — see spanWindow.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load.

outputs.name: reconnect
outputs.description: The user asked to re-open the feed.

outputs.name: stepChange
outputs.description: Emitted on each replay step with the revealed event and its index.

outputs.name: traceSelect
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of the trace/run the user clicks.

outputs.name: expandedIdsChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `expandedIds` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(expandedIds)]`.

components.name: AI Chat Interface
components.description: 4 chat variants: fullscreen assistant, floating widget, embedded panel and compact sidebar — with streaming indicators, tool/function-call cards, file attachments, copyable code blocks and markdown-ready messages.
whenToUse: Adding a conversational AI surface: assistant, support bot, copilot panel.
You want streaming indicators, tool-call chips and markdown/code rendering ready-made.
Pick the variant that fits placement — floating for apps, embedded for a page section.

examples.title: Checkpoints — rewind to a turn
examples.code:
<sv-ai-chat
  [branching]="true"
  [checkpoints]="checkpoints()"
  [(messages)]="messages"
  (checkpointRestore)="agent.restore($event.checkpoint.messageId)" />

// A restore point after every finished answer.
readonly checkpoints = computed(() => svChatTurnCheckpoints(this.messages()));

examples.title: Wired to a streaming API
examples.code:
<sv-ai-chat
  #chat
  variant="copilot"
  [models]="models"
  [messages]="messages()"
  [loading]="loadingHistory()"
  [error]="error()"
  [(activeSessionId)]="sessionId"
  (messageSent)="ask($event)"
  (stopRequest)="abort()"
  (resendRequest)="ask($event.content)"
  (retry)="loadHistory()" />

// The four streaming methods are imperative on purpose: an SSE reader pushes
// tokens as they arrive, and rebuilding the transcript per token would be both
// awkward and slow.
ask(text: string): void {
  const userId = this.chat().messages().at(-1)!.id;
  const replyId = this.chat().beginAssistantMessage();
  this.controller = new AbortController();

  this.api.stream(text, this.controller.signal).subscribe({
    next: (token) => {
      this.chat().acknowledgeMessage(userId);   // the send got through
      this.chat().appendToken(token, replyId);
    },
    error: (e) => {
      this.chat().failMessage(userId, 'Could not send.');
      this.chat().failAssistantMessage(String(e), replyId);
    },
    complete: () => this.chat().completeAssistantMessage(replyId),
  });
}

abort(): void { this.controller?.abort(); }

examples.title: Demo with no backend
examples.code:
// demoMode fakes a reply token by token. For demos and screenshots only —
// left on, a chat wired to a real API would answer itself.
<sv-ai-chat
  [demoMode]="true"
  [models]="DEMO_MODELS"
  [suggestedPrompts]="DEMO_PROMPTS"
  [sessions]="DEMO_SESSIONS"
  [account]="{ name: 'Riley M.', plan: 'Pro plan' }" />

customization: Checkpoints (`ChatCheckpoint`: `{ id, messageId, label?, timestamp? }`) render as a marker after their message with a Restore button; `svChatTurnCheckpoints(messages)` makes one after every complete answer. `restoreCheckpoint(id)` and `undoRestore()` are public. With `branching` the path is cut after the checkpoint and nothing is removed — the next message starts a sibling of the old continuation; without it `messages` is truncated and Undo puts the tail back until the transcript changes. `checkpointRestore` reports `{ checkpoint, mode: 'branch' | 'truncate', later }`.

With `branching` on, a message the chat appends (a send, `beginAssistantMessage`, a regenerate) attaches to the message on screen, not to the end of the array — a follow-up after switching back to an earlier version stays on that version. Messages a host appends without `parentId` still link in list order.

Built from parts you can use on their own: the composer is `sv-prompt-input`, the full-page history is `sv-thread-list`, starter prompts are `sv-suggestions` and the per-reply row is `sv-message-actions` (both free, in `@styloviz/ai`), and `[selectionActions]` turns on `sv-selection-toolbar` over replies.

The model picker lives in the composer’s toolbar (copilot and full-page layouts), portalled to `<body>` so an `overflow: hidden` panel cannot clip it; the header keeps the model’s name. `modelChange` and `[(selectedModel)]` report the choice.

Composer options pass through: `[slashCommands]`, `[attachable]` with `[attachmentLimits]`, `[voice]` with `[listening]`; outputs `promptSubmit` (text, accepted attachments and the `/` command), `filesPicked`, `slashCommand` and `micToggle`. An attachment-only message is allowed.

The full-page history searches (`sessionSearch` is the debounced term for server search) and, with `[sessionActions]`, offers rename / pin / delete through `sessionRename`, `sessionPin` and `sessionDelete`.
`copyMessage(id, text)` resolves `true` or `false`; the row’s copied / failed state lives in `sv-message-actions`.

Every content set is an input and every one defaults to empty — `messages` (two-way), `models`, `selectedModel` (two-way, nullable), `suggestedPrompts`, `sessions` and `activeSessionId` (two-way, nullable). The component ships no sample data; import `DEMO_MODELS` / `DEMO_PROMPTS` / `DEMO_SESSIONS` for a demo.

The full-page sidebar’s account footer is the `account` input (`ChatAccount`: `{ name, plan? }`, default `null`). The kit does not invent a user: with `null` the footer is not rendered, so bind the signed-in account — `[account]="{ name: user.name, plan: user.plan }"` — where you want it shown.

Stream a real reply with `beginAssistantMessage()` → `appendToken()` → `completeAssistantMessage()` / `failAssistantMessage()`. A failed stream keeps whatever text arrived and offers a resend. Acknowledge a delivered user message with `acknowledgeMessage()`, or reveal its resend control with `failMessage()`.
While a reply is streaming the send button becomes a stop control, which emits `stopRequest` — abort your request there.
Set `demoMode` to fake replies with no backend; it is off by default.
Use `loading` / `error` / `retry` for fetching the transcript or the session list; `busy` for your own in-flight state.
Four layouts, set with `variant`: `copilot` (docked side panel), `fullscreen`, `inline` (embedded in a page) and `bubble` (floating launcher).
Streaming indicators; assistant messages render `toolCalls` (running/success/error cards with args + result) and `attachments` (file chips).
Markdown + code-block rendering with copy.

Every variant exposes working per-message copy, like and dislike actions (like/dislike are mutually exclusive) via a shared action row. Copy confirms only once the clipboard write resolves — the clipboard is unavailable over plain HTTP and can reject — and emits `copyFailed` with the message id when it does not, so a host can offer the text another way.
Emits `messageSent` (the sent text) and `modelChange` so a host can wire it to a real backend.
Responsive: in the fullscreen layout the session sidebar is hidden on phones (chat takes the full width) and returns from `md` up.

One privacy policy for the whole pack: `provideSvAiPrivacy({ patterns, reveal, copy, telemetry })` in `@styloviz/core` configures masking once instead of eight times. Message content is masked at RENDER — your `messages` are never edited — and `copy: false` hides the copy control AND refuses `copyMessage()`, because a hidden button is a styling decision and the method is public API. With no policy provided nothing is masked and every message can be copied.

A scale ceiling on the transcript: `[maxMessages]` (300) is how many messages the thread renders at once, and the window keeps the NEWEST — a conversation cut at its first hundred messages would hide the part the user is having right now. What is missing is disclosed at the top of the thread, where it was, and `messages` itself stays complete: the ceiling is a rendering decision, not an edit to your data. Set `0` if you virtualize the thread yourself.

Attachment limits are a policy the kit owns and the host enforces: `svCheckAttachments(list, { maxCount, maxBytes, accept })` returns what is accepted and what is refused, each refusal carrying a reason in `ChatAttachment.rejected`. The count limit **refuses the overflow rather than truncating it**, and a refused attachment stays in the transcript, struck through with its reason — one that disappears is indistinguishable from one that uploaded, and the user sends 'here’s the recording' to a model that never saw it.

An unknown size or MIME type is accepted rather than refused: the host may not have either until the upload finishes, and a limit that rejects everything is indistinguishable from a broken picker. A non-positive `maxCount` or `maxBytes` falls back to the default (10 files, 25 MB) rather than meaning 'nothing allowed'.
Attachments render on **user** messages as well as assistant ones, so a file the user attached — and any refusal of it — shows on the message that carried it.

When the clipboard refuses — plain HTTP, a denied permission, an unfocused document — the component **selects the message text** and says which keys to press, naming ⌘C or Ctrl+C for the platform the reader is actually on. Telling somebody 'copying failed' leaves them to select three paragraphs by hand, which is the moment they give up and retype it.

Streaming is a **separate package**: `@styloviz-pro/ai-chat-transport`. Nothing in this component imports it, and that is the point — a transport baked into the UI is a UI that has picked your backend for you, and a provider renaming a field would ship as a new version of the chat. It carries `svSseReader` (SSE framing that survives a chunk boundary, which is the bug that makes a hand-rolled loop drop one token in a few hundred), `svFrameGate` (duplicate, late and missing WebSocket frames), `svDecodePart` (an AI-SDK-style part decoder that tells an incremental delta from a cumulative snapshot — confuse them and the reply either repeats itself or loses all but its last token), and `svStreamStart` / `svApplyParts` / `svStreamEnd` / `svToChatMessage` to reduce the lot into one of these messages.

A stream that stops arriving without a terminal event is `interrupted`, not `complete`, and `svToChatMessage` renders it as an `error` message so the reader gets the reason and a resend control beside the half answer. Flipping it to complete — tempting, because there IS text to show — tells them the half answer is the whole answer, which is the one lie in a chat UI they will act on.

A part of a kind the decoder does not model is counted, not dropped: `svStreamNotice` then says that something which arrived is not shown. Providers add part types constantly, and ignoring the unknown ones produces a transcript missing content that looks whole.

The AI SDK is decoded in both of its wire formats: the **v5 UI message stream** (text, reasoning, tool input/output, sources, errors; `start` / `start-step` / `text-start` lifecycle markers are understood rather than counted as unknown; `finish-step` separates the steps of a tool → answer run with a paragraph break and only `finish` ends the reply; `abort` ends it as interrupted) and the **v4 data stream protocol** (`0:` text, `9:` / `a:` tool call and result, `e:` / `d:` step and finish, `3:` error), which arrives as a plain line-per-part body and is read with `svDataStreamReader`. **OpenAI Responses** function calls are assembled from `output_item.added` and `function_call_arguments.delta` addressed by `output_index`.

The transport also decodes the two provider formats most hosts actually hold: **Anthropic Messages streaming** (`content_block_delta` text and thinking deltas, `tool_use` arguments assembled from `input_json_delta` fragments addressed by `index`, `message_delta` stop reasons, `ping` ignored) and **OpenAI Chat Completions** (`chat.completion.chunk` — `choices[].delta.content`, index-addressed `tool_calls`, `finish_reason`, and the usage chunk that arrives after the finish). `svFinishReason` maps both vocabularies onto one, so an Anthropic reply cut off at `max_tokens` reads as truncated rather than finished. Use `svDecodeParts` — one Chat Completions chunk can carry several parts, and `svDecodePart` returns such a chunk as `unknown` rather than keeping only the first.

A reply the provider’s **content-safety filter** stopped (`finish_reason: content_filter`, or a refusal) is its own message state, `filtered` — not an ordinary complete answer. It renders a notice (“The provider’s safety filter stopped this reply”), keeps whatever text arrived, shows the provider’s own reason from `error` when there is one, and gets no copy / rating row and no resend, because the same prompt meets the same filter. The transition is announced once through `SvLiveAnnouncer`. Set it with `filterAssistantMessage(reason?, id?)`; `svToChatMessage` maps a content-filter finish to it, and `svStreamNotice` / `svIsContentFiltered` give a host its own wording.

Per-message provenance: `ChatMessage.model` and `modelVersion` render in the message’s meta line (“Model: gpt-4o (2024-08-06)”), so a thread that switches model — or regenerates a reply on a different one — says which model wrote which answer. `beginAssistantMessage(id, { model, modelVersion })` stamps them; `svToChatMessage` takes them in its options. Unset renders nothing.

Auto-scroll follows the conversation only while the reader is at the bottom (within `stickToBottomThreshold`, default 48px) or has just sent a message. Scrolled up to re-read an answer, their position is kept while tokens stream in, and a **Jump to latest** control — with a count of new messages — appears instead of the view being pulled out from under them.
accessibility: A checkpoint marker is a named separator; its Restore button sits beside it ("Restore checkpoint: {label}"), the restore is announced once, focus moves to the composer, and Undo is a real button in the status bar.
Message log uses a live region for streaming; user text is bound safely and all assistant HTML — including tool-call and attachment markup — is escaped.
Model picker exposes aria-haspopup/aria-expanded; feedback buttons report aria-pressed.
Input and actions are labelled and keyboard reachable.

The Jump to latest control is a real button outside the message live region, so Tab reaches it and it is not announced as a message; activating it moves focus to the transcript rather than dropping it to the page.
variants: AI Chat — Checkpoints, Rewind to a Turn

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Chat layout: fullscreen, floating, embedded or sidebar/copilot.

inputs.name: branching
inputs.description: Keep every regeneration as a version instead of replacing the answer. Off by default because it changes what regenerate does. With it off, `regenerate()` deletes the last assistant message and asks for another. With it on, the old answer survives as a sibling and the row grows a "2 / 3" switcher. The reason to turn it on: a user presses regenerate when they are unsatisfied, and "unsatisfied" is not "this is worse than whatever comes next". The destructive version throws away a good answer with no undo and no warning, routinely.

inputs.name: models
inputs.description: Models offered by the picker.

inputs.name: suggestedPrompts
inputs.description: Starter prompts shown on an empty thread.

inputs.name: sessions
inputs.description: Past conversations, for the fullscreen variant's rail.

inputs.name: agents
inputs.description: The agents that can speak in this thread. Empty — the default — is a single-model chat: messages render under one sparkle avatar. Supply a roster and every assistant message that names an `agentId` is attributed to it by name.

inputs.name: handoffs
inputs.description: Control moving between agents. Their own entries, not inferred from `agentId` changing. A handoff can produce no reply at all — the specialist has nothing to add and hands straight back — and inference shows nothing at all in that case: the user sees an unexplained pause and the trail of who was consulted is gone.

inputs.name: checkpoints
inputs.description: Points the user can rewind the conversation to — `svChatTurnCheckpoints(messages)` gives one per finished reply. Each renders a marker after its message with a Restore button. Empty — the default — renders nothing. What restore does depends on `branching`. On, nothing is deleted: the transcript is cut after the checkpoint and the next message starts a new branch beside the old continuation. Off, `messages` is truncated (two-way, so the host sees it) and the tail is kept for Undo.

inputs.name: demoMode
inputs.description: Fake an assistant reply, token by token, with no backend. For demos and screenshots only. Off by default; left on, a chat wired to a real API would answer itself as well.

inputs.name: account
inputs.description: The signed-in account shown at the foot of the full-page sidebar. The kit does not invent one: with `null` the footer is not rendered.

inputs.name: busy
inputs.description: A reply is in flight. Ignored while `demoMode` is on, which drives its own.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the session list or a transcript is being fetched. Shows a placeholder in place of the message list.

inputs.name: connection
inputs.description: State of your streaming transport. `isStreaming` says a reply is in progress; this says whether the pipe carrying it is still up. A reply that stops mid-sentence is the single most confusing failure in a chat UI — without this the user cannot tell it from the model pausing to think.

inputs.name: reconnectable
inputs.description: Offer a manual reconnect while the transport is down.

inputs.name: slashCommands
inputs.description: Commands offered when a message starts with `/`. Empty turns the menu off.

inputs.name: attachable
inputs.description: Show the composer's attach button. You upload what `filesPicked` hands you.

inputs.name: attachmentLimits
inputs.description: Count, size and type limits for composer attachments. `null` uses the defaults.

inputs.name: voice
inputs.description: Show the composer's mic toggle; wire `micToggle` to your recorder.

inputs.name: listening
inputs.description: Your recorder is listening — the mic shows pressed.

inputs.name: sessionActions
inputs.description: Row actions in the fullscreen history. Empty shows none.

inputs.name: selectionActions
inputs.description: Actions offered over text selected in an assistant reply. Empty — the default — turns the toolbar off. An action with id `quote` also puts the selection into the composer as a quote.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Failure loading the conversation. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`. A failed *message* is different: set that message's `status` to `'error'` and the row offers its own resend.

inputs.name: messages
inputs.description: The transcript. Two-way — append the model's reply, and mutate the tail message's `content` to stream it in.

inputs.name: activeSessionId
inputs.description: Id of the conversation highlighted in the fullscreen rail and titled in the header. Two-way: picking a session in the rail writes its id and clears the transcript so the host can load it.

inputs.name: maxMessages
inputs.description: How many messages the transcript holds at once. `0` = no ceiling. A transcript is the list-shaped surface most likely to get long, and an agent conversation with tool calls woven in reaches four figures inside an afternoon. Rendering every one of them is a page that slows down until the user reloads it — and reloading a chat is how a support transcript gets lost. The window keeps the newest, which is the only correct direction and the opposite of `slice(0, n)`: a conversation cut at its first hundred messages hides the part the user is having right now. Set `0` if the host virtualizes the thread itself.

inputs.name: stickToBottomThreshold
inputs.description: How close to the bottom of the transcript, in pixels, still counts as "following the conversation". Appending must not fight a reader who has scrolled up. A new message or a streamed token scrolls the transcript only when the reader was already within this distance of the bottom — or when they just sent a message themselves. Anyone further up keeps their place, and a "Jump to latest" control appears instead of the view being yanked out from under the paragraph they were reading. A few lines of slack, not zero: sub-pixel layout and a token that wraps onto a new line both leave a reader who IS following a few pixels short. Negative or non-finite values are treated as `0`.

inputs.name: selectedModel
inputs.description: The chosen model. Two-way, so a host can drive it from its own state.

outputs.name: messageSent
outputs.description: Emitted with the trimmed text whenever the user sends a message.

outputs.name: modelChange
outputs.description: Emitted with the newly selected model.

outputs.name: stopRequest
outputs.description: The user asked to stop the reply in progress. Abort your request here — the component has already marked the streaming message complete.

outputs.name: resendRequest
outputs.description: The user asked to resend a message that failed. The payload is the original text; the message is back in `sending` state.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed conversation load.

outputs.name: branchChange
outputs.description: The user moved to a different version of a message. The payload is the message now shown at that point in the thread — which is also the root of the subtree that came with it, since switching a version switches everything after it.

outputs.name: checkpointRestore
outputs.description: A checkpoint was restored — what was set aside or removed, and how.

outputs.name: reconnect
outputs.description: The user asked to re-open the transport.

outputs.name: copyFailed
outputs.description: Copying a message to the clipboard failed — the payload is that message's id. The clipboard is unavailable over plain HTTP and `writeText` rejects when the permission is denied, so the button stays silent rather than claiming a copy that did not happen. Surface the text some other way.

outputs.name: promptSubmit
outputs.description: The whole composer payload on send: text, accepted attachments and the `/` command.

outputs.name: filesPicked
outputs.description: Files picked in the composer that passed `attachmentLimits` — upload these.

outputs.name: slashCommand
outputs.description: A `/` command was chosen in the composer.

outputs.name: micToggle
outputs.description: The mic was pressed. `true` asks to start listening.

outputs.name: sessionSearch
outputs.description: The debounced history search term — for searching sessions on the server.

outputs.name: sessionRename
outputs.description: The user renamed a session. Persist it and bind `sessions` back.

outputs.name: sessionPin
outputs.description: The user pinned or unpinned a session.

outputs.name: sessionDelete
outputs.description: The user confirmed deleting a session. The payload is its id.

outputs.name: selectionAction
outputs.description: An action was pressed over a selection; `messageId` is the reply it came from.

outputs.name: messagesChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `messages` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(messages)]`.

outputs.name: activeSessionIdChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `activeSessionId` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(activeSessionId)]`.

outputs.name: selectedModelChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `selectedModel` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(selectedModel)]`.

components.name: AI Insight Cards
components.description: 5 variants: `feed` (priority-ordered list), `grid` (confidence-ring cards), `inline` (single featured insight), `panel` (detailed insight with evidence) and `anomaly` (the baseline behind each claim) — with confidence provenance, evidence links, trend arrows, sparklines and action buttons.
whenToUse: Surfacing AI-generated insights with confidence, trend and supporting actions.
Analytics summaries, anomaly callouts, recommendation feeds.
For raw metrics without AI framing, use Stat Cards or a Widget Grid.

examples.title: An anomaly scale that fits the domain
examples.code:
<!-- The defaults are 14 observations, 3 sigma and 5 sigma. They are
     reasonable for a DAILY business metric and wrong nearly everywhere
     else: a fortnight of hourly data is 336 observations, a fortnight of
     monthly data is not a baseline at all. The floor the component
     applies is also the number the card SHOWS when it refuses to judge,
     so moving it moves the explanation with it. -->
<sv-ai-insight-cards
  variant="anomaly"
  [baselines]="hourlyMetrics()"
  [anomalyMinSamples]="336"
  [anomalyNotable]="2.5"
  [anomalySevere]="4" />

customization: `insights` defaults to an empty list, so the board renders nothing it was not given; the exported `DEMO_INSIGHTS` are for showcases, and each carries `sample: true` so the card says so on screen. Accept and dismiss are layered locally and reported as outputs — the array you pass is never mutated.
`simulate` is off by default, so Refresh only emits `refreshRequested` and `busy` drives the loading state. Set it to true only in a showcase, where a fabricated reload is the point.
Feed, grid, inline, panel and anomaly layouts.
Confidence scores and trend indicators.
Inline sparklines and actions.
Emits `insightAccept` / `insightDismiss` with the insight id.

The anomaly scale is host policy, not arithmetic: `[anomalyMinSamples]`, `[anomalyNotable]` and `[anomalySevere]` default to the exported `SV_ANOMALY_MIN_SAMPLES` (14), `SV_ANOMALY_NOTABLE` (3σ) and `SV_ANOMALY_SEVERE` (5σ), which are still exported for callers using `svAnomaly` directly. A figure that is not a positive finite number falls back to the default rather than being clamped near it, and `svResolveAnomalyThresholds` is exported so a host can see what the component settled on.

`evidenceUrl` is where a reader goes to check a claim, and an insight without one **renders as an assertion** rather than as a finding. The field is optional and visible rather than required, because a required field is satisfied by `''` and buys nothing the reader can see, whereas 'No evidence linked — this is an assertion' cannot be satisfied by typing quotes. A non-http(s) scheme is refused rather than rendered as a dead `unsafe:` link, which would teach the reader that evidence links do not work rather than that this one is wrong. The evidence link, the assertion label and the confidence basis render in **every** variant that shows a confidence — `feed`, `grid`, `inline` and `panel` — sized for each, not in the feed alone.

`confidenceBasis`, `model` and `modelVersion` travel with the percentage, and the figure still renders when they are missing — saying 'no method or model recorded' rather than hiding a number the host already shows. '87%' reads as calibrated when it is usually a model rating its own certainty.

`sample: true` marks the kit’s own demo insights, and every entry in `DEMO_INSIGHTS` carries it. The card says so on screen. A board rendering believable insights with no data wired is indistinguishable from one rendering real ones, and that array is one copy-paste from a host’s fixture and one deploy from a board somebody trusts — so the label travels with the **data**, not with the component’s mode, because that is the path it actually takes.
accessibility: Confidence and trends conveyed as text.
Priority filter chips report aria-pressed.
Action buttons are labelled.

A finding with too little history behind it says so in words, and says the floor it was judged against — the number travels with the finding, so the sentence cannot state a threshold that had nothing to do with the verdict.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the data is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Presentation: `'feed'`, `'grid'`, `'inline'`, `'panel'` or `'anomaly'`.

inputs.name: insights
inputs.description: The insights to show. Decisions are layered locally, never written back.

inputs.name: baselines
inputs.description: The series behind each claim, for the `anomaly` variant. One entry per metric: its recent history and its current reading. The deviation is computed here rather than taken from the host because the arithmetic is where the mistakes are.

inputs.name: busy
inputs.description: A fetch is in flight.

inputs.name: simulate
inputs.description: Reload with the bundled sample when Refresh is pressed. **Off by default.** Refresh emits `refreshRequested` and waits for a new `insights` — production behaviour must not depend on an integrator remembering to turn a demo switch off. Set it explicitly to `true` in a showcase, where a fabricated reload is the point.

inputs.name: anomalyMinSamples
inputs.description: Observations required before any severity is claimed. The default is a policy about somebody else's domain. Fourteen is right for a daily business metric and wrong almost everywhere else: a fortnight of hourly data is 336 observations, a fortnight of monthly data is not a baseline at all, and a seasonal series needs a season. The figure was well reasoned and still a guess, so it is a default and not a rule — and it is the number the card SHOWS when it refuses to judge, so moving it moves the explanation with it.

inputs.name: anomalyNotable
inputs.description: Sigma at which a finding is worth a look. Also the line the anomaly variant's "a mean-and-sigma detector would have missed this" note judges by and quotes.

inputs.name: anomalySevere
inputs.description: Sigma at which it is worth waking somebody.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load.

outputs.name: insightAccept
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of an insight the user accepts.

outputs.name: insightDismiss
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of an insight the user dismisses.

outputs.name: refreshRequested
outputs.description: Emitted when the user asks for fresh insights.

components.name: AI Model Selector
components.description: 5 variants: dropdown picker, card grid, side-by-side comparison, settings panel and routing policy — with provider badges, capability tags and latency/cost/context indicators.
whenToUse: Letting users choose an LLM with provider, capability, latency, cost and context info.
AI products that expose multiple models or providers.
For a generic single-choice list, a Select Dropdown is simpler.
customization: A retired model cannot be selected by any path. Clicks and keys are refused; a `[selectedId]` or `[config].modelId` bound to a retired id is replaced with the first selectable model, written back through the two-way binding, and named on screen ("X is retired and cannot be selected, so Y is selected instead") — `modelChange` does not fire, because the reader chose nothing. The `routing` variant shows the same lifecycle and region marks, faults a retired or out-of-region step (so a chain containing one does not read as sound) and warns on a deprecated one.

`models` is an input that starts empty, so an unwired selector offers no invented catalogue; pass the exported `DEMO_MODELS` for a demo. The selection is moved onto the offered list if it is not already on it.
`selectedId`, `config` and `compareIds` are two-way, so the chosen model, the tuned generation settings and the comparison set can each be driven from — and restored into — your own state.
Dropdown, grid, comparison, settings and routing layouts.
Provider badges and capability tags.
Latency, cost and context indicators.
Emits `modelChange` with the selected model id.

`[budgetWarningPct]` (80, from the still-exported `SV_BUDGET_WARNING_PCT`) is the share of a routing cap at which the budget reads `warning`. Eighty per cent is early enough to act on for a steady burn; a fleet whose traffic triples at month end wants it earlier and a prepaid credit later. It must stay below 100 — at 100 the warning band vanishes and every state is either ok or exceeded — so a figure at or above the cap is refused with a dev warning.

`[catalogueAsOf]` is when the figures were true, rendered as an 'as of' line under every variant and marked stale past `[staleAfterDays]` (30 — prices and context windows change monthly). Supply nothing and nothing is rendered, plus a dev warning: a banner on an unmigrated host is noise the reader cannot act on, and the person who can act on it is reading the console.

`isFeatured` has to answer for itself. `featuredReason` on the model, or `[recommendationPolicy]` for the catalogue, is rendered beside the star; with neither, the card says plainly that no reason was recorded and the console says so too. 'Recommended' with no visible policy reads as authority and cannot be told apart from a vendor placement.

`lifecycle: 'preview' | 'ga' | 'deprecated' | 'retired'` plus `retiresAt` and `regions`, with `[region]` for the deployment. A deprecated or out-of-region model stays **visible and marked** rather than silently absent — dropping it is how a team finds out about a retirement from a 404 in production. Only `retired` is refused, because calling it cannot succeed. The lifecycle badge, the retirement date and a 'Not in <region>' mark render in **every** variant — dropdown options and trigger, cards, the comparison header and the settings list — and `retiresAt` shows on a deprecated model that is still available, because the date is the planning fact. A retired model is refused on every path — pointer, Enter and Space, and a programmatic `selectModel()` / `selectConfigModel()` — is marked `aria-disabled` (not `disabled`, so it stays focusable and its reason readable), and is skipped when the component picks a default.

`[overlayContainer]` and `[overlayZIndex]` (9999, from the exported `SV_MODEL_OVERLAY_Z_INDEX`) hand the dropdown panel to an app that owns the top of its own page. The default appends to `<body>`, which is outside a host overlay stack's ordering rules and lands under or over the wrong layer depending on document order — something no z-index on this side can fix, because stacking contexts do not compare across them. Give it your overlay root instead, and raise the index above your modal layer if the panel has to open from inside a dialog.

A container brings a browser subtlety with it and the component handles it: a `transform`, `filter`, `perspective`, `will-change` or `contain: paint` on **any ancestor** of that container makes the ancestor the containing block for `position: fixed`, so viewport coordinates are silently re-based on its box and the panel appears offset by wherever the overlay root sits — the properties an app puts on an overlay root for compositing and modal animations are exactly these. The panel finds that ancestor and converts into its space, and a container that is not yet in the document falls back to `<body>` with a dev warning rather than rendering nowhere at all.
accessibility: The scrolling list of models is the `listbox`, named, with the options as its own children — the search box and the footer sit outside it, because a listbox may own only options.
The trigger is `aria-haspopup="listbox"` with `aria-expanded`, and `aria-controls` the list while it is open.
Options expose full model metadata as text.
Search inputs are labelled; parameter sliders carry aria-label (and aria-valuetext for temperature).
Keyboard selection with clear focus.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the data is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`.

inputs.name: emptyMessage
inputs.description: Shown when no models are on offer.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP 47 locale for dates and numbers.

inputs.name: overlayContainer
inputs.description: Where the dropdown panel is mounted while it is open. `null` — the default and the supported path — means `document.body`. An app-wide overlay stack is a real thing and it owns the top of the page. A host with a modal layer, a toast layer and a command palette has one element every overlay must live inside so that its own ordering rules hold; a component that appends to `<body>` regardless is outside those rules, and lands under or over the wrong thing depending on document order — which no z-index on our side can fix, because stacking contexts do not compare across them. And it changes what `position: fixed` means, which is the part that bites. A `transform`, `filter`, `perspective`, `will-change: transform` or `contain: paint` on ANY ancestor of the container makes that ancestor the containing block for fixed descendants, so viewport coordinates are silently re-based on its box and the panel appears offset by wherever that ancestor happens to sit — a bug that looks like "the dropdown is in the wrong place on one page". The panel finds that ancestor and positions itself in its space, so it lands where it should either way.

inputs.name: overlayZIndex
inputs.description: The panel's `z-index` within its container. The default is a guess about somebody else's page, so it has to be overridable. `9999` wins against most things and loses against a host whose modal layer sits higher, and a dropdown rendered UNDER the dialog that opened it is unusable rather than merely ugly.

inputs.name: catalogueAsOf
inputs.description: When the figures in `models` were true. Every number here goes stale on its own. Context windows, prices and availability change monthly, and this component renders them in the present tense. A price with no date is a claim about the past presented as the present, and the reader who budgets against it is comparing spend with a figure that moved three weeks ago. Supply nothing and nothing is rendered — plus a dev warning to the integrator. A banner on every host that has not migrated yet is noise the reader cannot act on, and the person who can act on it is the one reading the console.

inputs.name: recommendationPolicy

inputs.description: The chosen model's id. Two-way, so it can be driven from your own state. Empty until a catalogue arrives — the first offered model is selected automatically if you do not pick one. inputs.name: compareIds
inputs.description: Ids shown side by side in the `comparison` variant (two-way). Seeded from the first three offered models the first time a catalogue arrives — unless the host has bound a set, which wins — and owned by the user's toggles after that. A `model` rather than a signal plus a `compareChange` output: that pairing let a host persist the comparison but never restore it, which is the half of the job that matters after a reload.

inputs.name: budgetWarningPct
inputs.description: Share of the cap at which the budget reads `warning`. Eighty per cent is a statement about how fast the budget is spent. A team burning a monthly cap evenly wants the warning with a fifth of the money left; a team whose traffic triples at month end wants it far earlier. It must stay below 100 — at 100 the warning band vanishes and every state is either `ok` or `exceeded`, with nothing left of the stage that exists to be acted on.

components.name: AI Data & Privacy Inspector
components.description: The AI pack's privacy contract, on screen: what is masked, what is deliberately not, which rules do not compile, whether content can be unmasked, copied or sent to analytics — and what a policy let through when run against real prompts, transcripts and tool arguments. 4 variants: policy, scan, retention and surfaces.
whenToUse: Answering "what do you redact, can it be unmasked, and does content reach analytics" without reading a TypeScript file.
Checking a policy against real prompts and tool arguments before deciding it is finished.
A settings or admin screen where the person configuring the AI pack should see what their configuration actually does.
Not for end users mid-conversation: this is a review surface, and the masking itself happens in the components that render the content.

examples.title: Run it against your own content
examples.code:
<sv-ai-privacy-inspector
  variant="scan"
  [samples]="[
    { id: 'p', label: 'System prompt', kind: 'prompt', text: systemPrompt },
    { id: 't', label: 'Last turn', kind: 'transcript', text: lastTurn },
  ]" />

examples.title: Compare two policies
examples.code:
<!-- The one in force, from provideSvAiPrivacy() -->
<sv-ai-privacy-inspector />

<!-- And the one staging is on, to see whether they agree -->
<sv-ai-privacy-inspector [policy]="stagingPolicy" />

customization: Four variants via `variant`: `policy` (the contract, its rules, its switches and what is wrong with it), `scan` (the contract run against bound samples), `retention` (how long content is kept, on what basis, who else receives it) and `surfaces` (which components read the shared policy).

Reads the policy from `provideSvAiPrivacy()` by default — the question is always "what is THIS app doing", and a component you had to pass the answer to could be handed a policy nothing is using. `[policy]` overrides it, for holding two side by side.
`[samples]` are host-bound: a prompt, a transcript turn, a tool argument, a retrieved chunk. Four is usually enough to learn something and few enough that a reader reads them.
`openSampleIds` is two-way, so a reviewer who opened the one row that matters can be put back on it.

No score, no percentage, no green tick. You cannot know what share of the secrets in arbitrary text a pattern set catches, and one invented number spends the panel's credibility for good — so it states what is looked for and what is not, by name, and refuses to add them up.

A rule that does not compile is reported as a hole, not a warning: `svAiMask` reports it with one console line in a dev build and then masks nothing for the life of the app, which on screen is indistinguishable from a rule that matched nothing.

A miss is reported by its SHAPE — length and last two characters — never its value. The panel exists to say a card number got through; printing the card number to make that point would be the leak it is warning about.
A category the policy has a rule for that got through anyway is reported separately from one nothing looks for. The first is a rule that does not work; the second is a decision to review.

`svPolicyRules`, `svPolicyRisks`, `svCoverageStatement`, `svPolicyFingerprint`, `svScanSample` and `svScanSummary` are exported, so a host can put the same findings in its own admin UI or assert them in a test.
Nothing leaves the browser. There is no fetch, no telemetry and no output carrying sample text anywhere in this component, and the panel says so rather than leaving it in a README.

`[retention]`, `[consent]` and `[destinations]` are host declarations, because no component can detect a deletion job or a consent record — and each row says which it is. A retention window with nothing showing the deletion happening renders as a stated policy, not a verified one; evidence older than `SV_VERIFICATION_STALE_DAYS` (90) is reported as too old to stand for anything, because a deletion report from last year is not evidence that deletion ran last night.

An expired grant is not consent, and the `retention` variant will not render it as one. Withdrawal beats a live grant whatever the dates say, and `unknown` is kept apart from `declined`: treating “nobody asked” as a refusal looks safe and hides the actual finding.

`[destinations]` is where the sharpest thing in this component gets said: `svAiMask` runs in the RENDERER, so the model call, the log line and the analytics event all receive the original. A team that sees masked transcripts on screen will tell an auditor their data is redacted — so a content destination marked unmasked produces the sentence “masking applies to what these components render” in as many words.

`[surfaces]` defaults to the kit’s own audit of the AI pack (`SV_AI_PACK_SURFACES`) and is labelled a declaration rather than a detection, because Angular gives a component no way to ask which others injected a token. An exemption with no reason recorded is named as an omission wearing the word.
`[now]` pins the clock for a screenshot or a test; `Date.now()` otherwise.
accessibility: Findings are ordered so that everything which leaks content comes first. A panel that opened with "copy enabled — worth knowing" while content was flowing to analytics further down would be worse than no panel, because the reader would believe they had read it.

Each switch states On or Off in words as well as colour, and the sentence beside it describes the state the policy is in rather than naming the flag — "reveal: false" tells a reader nothing they can act on.
Sample rows are real buttons with `aria-expanded`, and the masked text sits in a focusable `<pre>` so a keyboard reader can scroll it.
Every risk row is activatable and emits `riskSelect`, so a host can link a finding to its own policy documentation.
Consent state, retention staleness and adoption status are each rendered as a WORD as well as a colour — the difference between granted and expired is the whole row, and a hue cannot carry it.

The empty state names the variant’s own subject: one message about “samples” on the retention view reads as a broken panel rather than as nothing declared, and “nothing declared” is said in those words rather than as a clean bill.
variants: Policy — The Contract, and What Is Wrong With It
Retention — A Promise Is Not a Control
Surfaces — A Declaration, Not a Detection

components.name: AI Token Dashboard
components.description: 5 variants: overview KPI grid, timeline (cost trend), per-model breakdown (donut + bars), budgets, and tenant / key / user attribution — for LLM usage and cost analysis.
whenToUse: Monitoring LLM token usage and cost across models and time.
FinOps and engineering dashboards that track AI spend.
For general (non-token) analytics, use the Charts components.
customization: `cachedInputTokens` and `reasoningTokens` are subsets of input and output, shown as notes rather than added to the total: per model in `breakdown`, and summed across models on the `overview` Token Distribution card. Beside the quality-adjusted multiple, `breakdown` shows the amount — cost per passing result against cost per request — in the display currency.
`daily`, `models` and `budgets` are inputs that start empty, so an unwired dashboard reports no invented spend; pass the exported `DEMO_DAILY_USAGE`, `DEMO_MODEL_USAGE` and `DEMO_BUDGETS` for a demo.
`period` is two-way, so the reporting window can be driven from your own state and drive a refetch.
KPI, breakdown, trend and comparison views.
Per-model cost and token tracking.
Configurable currency and period.
Emits `periodChange` when the usage period changes.

The cost-efficiency verdict is host policy: `[efficiencyMinRequests]` (25) is the traffic a row needs before it is compared with the fleet at all — without a floor the anomaly column is permanently topped by a tenant who made two calls, one of them a long document — and `[efficiencyBand]` (0.5) is how far from the fleet rate reads expensive or cheap. Both default to the still-exported `SV_EFFICIENCY_MIN_REQUESTS` / `SV_EFFICIENCY_BAND`, and `svAttribute` takes them as an optional last argument. A band at or above 1 is refused, because "cheap" would then ask for a non-positive cost per request and no row could ever reach it.

`[billing]` — currency, rate, tax, discount, and how far the provider has settled — drives both the figures and a note that says **which gaps this page cannot account for**. Every displayed cost — totals, per-model, per-request, per-1M, budgets and attribution — goes through `svDisplayCost`, so the discount, tax and conversion the note claims are the ones the numbers carry, and the note renders under every variant that shows a cost, not only the breakdown. `rateAsOf` names the day the conversion rate was taken; a converted figure with no rate date says so, because an invoice converted on a different day will differ. A non-USD `currency` with no usable `rate` stays in USD and the note names the missing conversion — labelling unconverted dollars in another currency would be a claim about money nobody has. Budgets are compared with usage at list price, so they are displayed on the same basis as the spend they cap. A cost dashboard that disagrees with the invoice destroys trust in one billing cycle, and it will disagree: list prices, in USD, before tax, before whatever the contract discount is, over a window nobody has settled. A dashboard that says 'estimated' and stops has not helped — the reader needs to know which direction it is wrong in before taking it to finance.

`cachedInputTokens` and `reasoningTokens` are **subsets** of the input and output figures, never additions, so nothing on the page moves when a host adopts them. Cached input bills at a fraction, so counting it with fresh input overstates spend on exactly the workload somebody optimised; reasoning output is billed and never shown, so a reader who counts the words they got back and a bill that counts the tokens produced disagree by a factor — and the reader concludes the provider is overcharging.

`[passRates]` (model id → 0–1, from your eval suite) turns spend into **cost per result that passed**, rendered as a multiple of the sticker price because that survives a currency change and a period change. A model at a third of the price that passes two thirds as often is not cheaper, and every dashboard in this category ranks by raw spend and calls the cheap one a saving. At a zero pass rate the figure is refused rather than rendered as infinity — which would put a number in a column somebody will sort — or as the raw cost, which would say the failures were free. A pass rate outside 0–1 is labelled out of range (above 1 it reads as a percentage passed by mistake) rather than 'not recorded', and a model with no spend reads 'no spend recorded' rather than NaN×.
accessibility: Chart values are surfaced as text/tables.
Period and sort segmented controls are labelled and report aria-pressed.
Color-coded series paired with labels.

Without a floor the anomaly column is permanently topped by noise: one tenant makes two calls, one of them a 200k-token document, and their rate is forty times the fleet's — so the column that exists to find the runaway agent spends every month pointing at somebody who owes eleven cents. WHERE the floor sits is traffic-shaped, though: 25 requests is a month for one tenant and a minute for another.

inputs.name: efficiencyBand

The cheap test is `ratio <= 1 - band`, so at 1 it asks for a non-positive cost per request and above 1 for a negative one: no row could ever be cheap, and the column would lose half its vocabulary while still rendering the legend for it.

inputs.name: billing
inputs.description: What the invoice will do to these numbers. A cost dashboard's figures differ from the invoice's: list prices, in USD, before tax, before whatever discount the contract carries, over a window the provider has not finished settling. Every one of those gaps is ordinary; this context lets the dashboard state each one, so the figures can be reconciled with the invoice.
