components.name: AI Workflow Builder
components.description: 5 variants: canvas node graph, list step editor, template gallery, run history and run debugger — with a column-layout DAG, enable/disable toggles, category filter and execution logs. Sized for up to about 50 nodes across about 10 columns (not enforced, not virtualised); chains, fan-out, fan-in and loops are supported, nesting is not — a subworkflow node is one opaque step.
whenToUse: Building and reviewing multi-step AI automations as a DAG or step list.
Products that let users compose chains of LLM/tool steps.
For visualizing a finished run rather than editing, use the AI Agent Activity Log.

examples.title: Run on your backend
examples.code:
<!-- Run emits runStart; pass back a workflow whose nodes carry the real status. -->
<sv-ai-workflow-builder variant="canvas" [workflow]="workflow()" (runStart)="startRun($event)" />

customization: Canvas DAG or list step editor.

**Run is the host’s.** `simulate` is off by default: Run emits `runStart` with the workflow id and changes nothing else. Start the execution on your backend and pass a new `workflow` as node states change — the button is busy while any node is `running`. `[simulate]="true"` animates an invented run (made-up durations, then `runComplete`) for a showcase.

**Graph size — stated, not enforced.** Sized for up to about 50 nodes across about 10 columns. Nothing is virtualised: every node is one 176px card and one Tab stop, and each column with its connector is about 216px wide, so ten columns are ~2,160px and a full-width canvas at 1280px scrolls sideways past about five columns (about four with the detail panel open). Larger graphs still render; split them into `subworkflow` nodes or edit them in the `list` variant.

**Supported topologies.** Chains; fan-out (several nodes in the next column, and the branch outputs of `condition`, `loop` and `human`); fan-in (several edges into one input); loops (a `loop` node or a back edge — never refused, with a warning when no node is left without a predecessor). Not supported: nesting — a `subworkflow` node is one opaque step whose inner graph is not drawn, expanded or validated. Nodes sit on a whole-number grid (`x` column, `y` order in it); edges are not drawn as lines — the canvas shows column order and each node's connections are listed in its panel with `[editable]`.

**Validation panel** (canvas variant): `svValidateWorkflow(nodes, edges, labels)` reports orphan nodes, nodes no trigger can reach, a missing trigger, edges naming a node or port that does not exist (errors), and branch outputs that lead nowhere (warnings) — one finding per node, errors first. It is listed under the canvas whenever there is a finding, and always with `[editable]` (where "no problems found" is itself the answer); each finding is a button that selects the node and moves focus to its card. `validation()` is public, and the function is exported so a host can run the same check before saving.
Template gallery and run history.
Token/cost tracking per run.
With `[simulate]="true"`, Run animates an invented run — nodes and steps go running → success in sequence, disabled steps are skipped, and re-running resets the state.
Emits `nodeSelect` and `runSelect` with the chosen node/run id.

`[editable]` (off) turns the canvas from a viewer into an editor: a node palette, a connections panel and the keyboard shortcuts. Off by default because hosts put the canvas variant on dashboards to show a pipeline, and a Delete button appearing on one of those tells the reader something false about what they are looking at.

`[nodeTypes]` (all nine, from `SV_NODE_TYPES`) is the palette. Offer only what the runtime accepts: a node type the engine will reject is a failure the reader discovers at run time, which is the most expensive place to discover it.

Edits are applied to the component's own copy and emitted: `(nodeCreate)`, `(edgeCreate)`, `(nodeDelete)` with the edge ids that went with the node, `(edgeDelete)`, and `(workflowEdit)` with the whole definition. Named `workflowEdit` rather than `workflowChange` because `[workflow]` is a plain input — `[(workflow)]` is not a binding this component offers, and a `Change` output beside an input would imply it is.

The editing operations are exported as pure functions — `svCreateNode`, `svPlaceAfter`, `svCheckConnect`, `svConnect`, `svDeleteNode` — so a host that keeps the workflow in its own store can run the same rules against it (`svCreateNode`, `svCheckConnect` and `svConnect` take the labels last, for the default node names and refusal reasons: pass `SV_AI_WORKFLOW_BUILDER_PRO_LABELS` or your translation).

A connection is refused in four cases and only four: a node feeding itself, a duplicate of an existing edge, a source with no output port, and a target that accepts none (a trigger). A cycle is not one of them — a loop node is a cycle by design — but an edge that leaves no node without a predecessor is reported, because the debug trace measures depth from those and with none of them every node reads at the same level.

Undo and redo are a command stack, not a stack of snapshots: `[historyCeiling]` (50, from `SV_HISTORY_CEILING`) edits are remembered, the oldest is dropped rather than the newest refused, and a new edit after an undo clears the redo branch — those commands describe a graph that is gone. Exported as `svRecord` / `svUndo` / `svRedo` / `svApply` / `svInvert` for a host that owns the workflow.

Undoing a delete puts the node, its edges AND the list variant's matching step back at the indexes they were at. Membership alone is not enough: the debug trace maps nodes in array order, so an undo that appends reshuffles the whole trace for an edit that changed nothing.
A fresh `[workflow]` clears the history. The stack belongs to the workflow it was recorded against, and a command naming a node from the previous graph is one `undo` that appears to do nothing.

Not offered, and deliberately not faked: collaborative editing and schema migration. The command stack is the shape collaboration needs — a stack of snapshots can only say mine or theirs, where a stack of commands can say what each person did — but there is no presence, no merge and no conflict resolution here, so two editors on one workflow will overwrite each other. Version the `WorkflowDefinition` yourself; `(workflowEdit)` is the hook for both.
accessibility: Nodes and steps are keyboard reachable; step enable toggles use role="switch".
Category filter reports aria-pressed; log toggles expose aria-expanded.
Run status surfaced as text; the Run button disables while executing.

With `[editable]`, the canvas can be built without a pointer: on a node, `n` adds one after it, `c` starts a connection and `c` on a second node completes it, `Delete` removes it and `Escape` cancels a pending connection. The shortcuts are written on the canvas, because a single letter nobody can discover is not a feature.
Connecting is two discrete steps rather than one continuous gesture, which is what makes it announceable at all: a drag has no moment to report.

Every edit — and every refusal — goes into a `role="status"` live region. An edit a screen reader cannot hear did not happen, and a silently dropped connection is how a reader presses the same two keys four times believing it worked.

The connection control offers only the nodes that can be connected and writes the reason beside the one on offer, rather than presenting a disabled button that tells the reader something is wrong with them.
The Add control says where the node will go before it goes there — column and row — because the reader cannot watch it appear.

Undo and redo take Ctrl/Cmd+Z and Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Z on a node card, and their buttons are named after the edit they will reverse — `Undo deleting Classify and 3 connections`, not `Undo`. A reader who pressed the wrong key by accident is the least able to remember what it was.

Undo and redo announcements name a connection by its nodes’ labels (“Undid connecting Classify to Route”), not their ids — pass the nodes and `SV_AI_WORKFLOW_BUILDER_PRO_LABELS` (or your translated labels) to `svCommandLabel` / `svUndoLabel` / `svRedoLabel` to get the same sentence in a host-owned stack. Tested in a real browser: Tab order in and out of the canvas, refusals announced, and undo/redo on Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z and Ctrl+Y.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the data is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: View: canvas DAG, list editor, template gallery, run history or run debugger.

inputs.name: workflow
inputs.description: The workflow being edited, the templates on offer, and the run history. All three come from the host. The bundled `DEMO_WORKFLOW*` fixtures are exported for showcases and demos. The `workflow` input is copied into a local signal because the canvas edits it: the host owns what arrives, the component owns what the user does to it next, and a fresh input replaces both. Sized for up to about 50 nodes across about 10 columns (not enforced, not virtualised — every node is a rendered card and a Tab stop). Chains, fan-out, fan-in and loops are supported; nesting is not — a `subworkflow` node is one opaque step. `x`/`y` are whole-number grid positions. The canvas lists `svValidateWorkflow` findings (orphans, unreachable nodes, dangling edges/ports, branches leading nowhere) under the graph.

inputs.name: templates
inputs.description: Starter templates for the template-gallery variant, filterable by category and search.

inputs.name: runs
inputs.description: Past executions for the run-history variant, listed with status, cost and duration and summarised in the stats header.

inputs.name: simulate
inputs.description: Animate Run with an invented execution: every node turns `running`, then `success` with a made-up duration, and `runComplete` follows. **Off by default.** Run emits `runStart` with the workflow id and waits for the host: start the run on your backend, then pass a new `workflow` whose nodes carry the real `status` and `durationMs` as they change; the button is busy while any node is `running`. Production behaviour must not depend on an integrator remembering to turn a demo switch off — set it to `true` only in a showcase, where a fabricated run is the point.

inputs.name: editable
inputs.description: Whether the canvas offers the editing controls at all. Off by default, and not because editing is dangerous. This component shipped as a viewer: hosts put the canvas variant on dashboards to show a pipeline. Adding an Add-node control and a Delete button to every one of those on upgrade would be a change to a screen nobody asked to change, and the reader who finds a Delete button on a read-only dashboard has been told something false about what they are looking at.

inputs.name: nodeTypes
inputs.description: The node types the palette offers. A host running a workflow engine without human-review steps should not offer a node type its runtime will reject — the reader finds out when the run fails, which is the most expensive place to find out.

inputs.name: historyCeiling
inputs.description: How many edits `undo` can walk back. Fifty is past what anybody undoes in one sitting and nowhere near a memory problem, because a command is a node or an edge rather than a copy of the workflow. Undo and redo are a command stack, not a stack of snapshots: past the ceiling the oldest edit is dropped rather than the newest refused, and a new edit after an undo clears the redo branch. Undoing a delete puts the node, its edges and the list variant's matching step back at the indexes they were at — not appended, which would reshuffle the debug trace. A fresh `[workflow]` clears the history. Exported as `svRecord` / `svUndo` / `svRedo` / `svApply` / `svInvert` for a host that owns the workflow.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load.

outputs.name: nodeCreate
outputs.description: A node was created.

outputs.name: nodeDelete
outputs.description: A node was removed, with the edges that went with it.

outputs.name: edgeCreate
outputs.description: Two nodes were connected. A connection is refused in four cases and only four: a node feeding itself, a duplicate of an existing edge, a source with no output port, and a target that accepts none (a trigger). A cycle is not one of them — a loop node is a cycle by design — but an edge that leaves no node without a predecessor is reported, because the debug trace measures depth from those. The same rules are exported as `svCheckConnect`.

outputs.name: edgeDelete
outputs.description: A connection was removed.

outputs.name: workflowEdit
outputs.description: The whole workflow after an edit. Named `workflowEdit`, not `workflowChange`: `[workflow]` is a plain input, and `(workflowChange)` beside it would read as a two-way binding that does not exist — a host would write `[(workflow)]` and Angular would silently not write back. Not offered, and deliberately not faked: collaborative editing and schema migration. There is no presence, no merge and no conflict resolution, so two editors on one workflow overwrite each other, and `WorkflowDefinition` is unversioned. This output is the hook for both.

outputs.name: nodeSelect
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of the workflow node the user selects.

outputs.name: runSelect
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of the run the user selects from history.

outputs.name: runStart
outputs.description: Emitted with the workflow id when Run is pressed. Without `simulate` this is the whole of Run: start the execution and report node states back through `workflow`.

outputs.name: runComplete
outputs.description: Emitted when a simulated run finishes (`simulate`) — every node has resolved to `success` or `skipped`. A host running the workflow itself knows when it finished; this output is not emitted for a real run.

components.name: AI Writing Assistant
components.description: 5 variants: toolbar (actions + readability stats + live editor), tone picker with preview, suggestions (accept/reject rewrite cards), history (revision timeline with diff) and inline (a toolbar anchored to the selection).
whenToUse: Augmenting a writing surface with AI: rewrites, tone changes, readability stats.
Wiring a real model needs no flag: `simulate` is off by default, so handle `actionRun` / `toneChange` and write the result back through `text` — the component renders, it does not call anything.
Editors where the assistant should follow the selection rather than sit in a sidebar — the `inline` variant.
Editors where users want inline suggestions they can accept or reject.
For plain rich-text editing without AI, use the Rich Text Editor.

examples.title: Wire it to a real model
examples.description: The default already: handle actionRun, then write the answer back through text.

examples.title: Inline — anchored to the selection
examples.description: Select text and the toolbar appears over it. Portaled to <body> and clamped on both axes.

customization: Toolbar, tone, suggestions, history and inline views.

Every content set is an input that starts EMPTY — `text` (two-way), `actions`, `tones`, `suggestions` and `history` — so an unwired assistant shows no invented text or history; demos pass the exported `DEMO_EDITOR_TEXT`, `DEMO_ACTIONS`, `DEMO_TONES`, `DEMO_SUGGESTIONS` and `DEMO_HISTORY`.

`inline` anchors a floating toolbar to the current text selection: three quick actions plus a free-text prompt. It portals to `<body>` so an overflow, transform or backdrop-filter ancestor cannot clip it, prefers to sit above the selection, and flips or slides when the viewport edge is close.
Readability stats and before/after diffs.
Accept/reject rewrite cards.
Emits `actionRun`, `toneChange` and `suggestionAccepted` for host integration.
Responsive: the diff stats strip stacks two-up on phones (`grid-cols-2 sm:grid-cols-4`) so the numbers stay readable.

`[protectedRanges]` marks stretches of the original — quotations, legal clauses, code, names — that must survive a rewrite untouched, and the component **checks the result** rather than asking the model nicely. A protected range in a prompt is a request; a model asked to 'make this clearer' will reword a quotation, tidy a license clause or correct somebody’s surname while doing exactly what it was told, and the only enforcement a UI can actually offer is on what came back. Every write the component makes itself — a simulated action or tone, an inline rewrite, a history restore — is **refused** when it would change a protected range: the text stays as it was, a dismissible alert names the range, and `protectedRefused` fires. A suggestion whose `originalText` overlaps a range cannot be accepted (`acceptAll` skips it). Offsets are into the current `text()`; a history entry can carry its own `protectedRanges`, because one set of offsets cannot describe every revision; an entry without them is checked against `protectedRanges`.
With `simulate` off, pressing a tone or an inline action says **requested**, not applied, until the host writes the rewrite back through `text` — the component never reports a rewrite it did not see.

Protection is about **containment, not position**: a rewrite that shortens the paragraph above a quotation has not touched the quotation, and reporting it as a violation because its offsets moved would make the check useless on exactly the rewrites it exists for. A breach renders as a `role='alert'` above the diff, naming what was changed.

Past `SV_PROSE_DIFF_MAX_TOKENS` (2,000 words) the word-by-word comparison is abandoned, and the panel says so in a `role='status'` notice. One enormous red block beside one enormous green block is what the reader gets when a model rewrites a document from scratch — a real and alarming outcome — and it is also what they get when the comparison simply gave up. The colours cannot tell those apart, and only one of them is a finding.

`[proseDiffMaxTokens]` (default `SV_PROSE_DIFF_MAX_TOKENS`, 2,000, still exported) sets that ceiling per host; the notice quotes the value in force. The comparison is O(n·m), so raise it only within the budget of the slowest device you support; a non-positive value falls back to the default.

Readability (Flesch reading ease and the grade band) is an **English** formula with an English syllable count, so it is shown only when the text is English: `[textLanguage]` (falling back to `locale`) decides, and any other language renders “Readability not available for <language>” instead of a number that is noise presented as a metric. The grade text comes from the `gradeLevel` label (“Grade {grade}”).
accessibility: Suggestions are reachable and dismissible.
The inline toolbar is `role="toolbar"` with a label naming what it acts on, and is dismissible by Escape, an outside click or a scroll — never a mouse-only affordance.
Category/tone/history/diff toggles report aria-pressed; action feedback uses polite live regions.
Diff changes conveyed beyond color.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the data is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: View: toolbar editor, tone picker, suggestions, history or inline.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP 47 locale for dates and numbers.

inputs.name: textLanguage
inputs.description: BCP 47 language of the TEXT being edited, when it differs from the UI `locale`. Readability (Flesch reading ease and the grade band) is an English formula, so it is shown only when this language is English; any other language renders "Readability not available for <language>".

inputs.name: proseDiffMaxTokens
inputs.description: Above this many words on either side of a revision, the word-by-word diff is not run and the passage is shown as replaced, with a notice quoting this number. The comparison is O(n·m); raise it only within the budget of the slowest device you support. Non-positive or non-finite values fall back to the default.

inputs.name: text
inputs.description: The text being edited. Two-way: write a rewrite back through it.

inputs.name: actions
inputs.description: Quick actions offered in the rail and the inline toolbar.

inputs.name: tones
inputs.description: Tones offered by the tone picker.

inputs.name: suggestions
inputs.description: Proposed rewrites awaiting a decision.

inputs.name: history
inputs.description: Past revisions.

inputs.name: busy
inputs.description: The host has a request in flight — shows the busy state without owning a timer.

inputs.name: simulate
inputs.description: Apply the bundled sample rewrites when an action runs. **Off by default.** The component emits `actionRun` / `toneChange` and waits for you to set `text` — reporting a rewrite the document never received is the worst thing this component can do, so it cannot happen by omission. Set it explicitly to `true` in a showcase.

inputs.name: protectedRanges
inputs.description: Stretches of the original that must survive a rewrite untouched. Offsets are half-open `[start, end)` into the CURRENT `text()`; when the text changes, send ranges for the new text. Enforced where this component writes `text`, not by asking the model nicely. A protected range in a prompt is a request; a model asked to "make this clearer" will reword a quotation, tidy a license clause or correct somebody's surname while doing exactly what it was told. So every write the component makes — a simulated action or tone, `applyInlineResult`, restoring a revision — is checked first and REFUSED if a protected stretch would not survive: the text stays as it was, a `role="alert"` says why, and `protectedRefused` fires. Accepting a suggestion is refused the same way when its `originalText` is found in `text()`. What the component cannot check is a rewrite the host writes into `text` directly — that write never passes through here.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load.

outputs.name: actionRun
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of the writing action the user runs (rewrite, summarise …).

outputs.name: toneChange
outputs.description: Emitted with the tone the user applies.

outputs.name: suggestionAccepted
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of a suggestion the user accepts.

outputs.name: suggestionRejected
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of a suggestion the user rejects.

outputs.name: protectedRefused
outputs.description: Emitted when a write was refused because it would alter a protected range.

outputs.name: textChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `text` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(text)]`.

components.name: Alert Banner
components.description: Dismissible alert banners in 5 semantic variants and multiple display styles.
whenToUse: Communicating a persistent, page-level status or message (info, success, warning, error).
You need an inline banner the user can act on or dismiss.
For transient confirmations, use a Toast; for blocking decisions, a Confirm Dialog.

Not sure this is the right outcome surface? Compare toast, banner, result, empty state, notification center and modal by severity, persistence and whether the user can correct it in the “Choosing a feedback pattern” guide under Guides.
components.usage: <sv-alert-banner variant="warning" title="Heads up" message="Your trial ends in 3 days." [dismissible]="true" />

examples.title: With actions
examples.code:
<!-- No autoDismissMs here, and it would be ignored if there were:
     a banner with actions must not remove itself while the user is
     aiming at one of them. Same for variant="danger". -->
<sv-alert-banner
  variant="success"
  message="Changes published."
  [actions]="bannerActions"
  (actionClick)="onAction($event)" />

examples.title: Auto-dismiss, where it is allowed
examples.code:
<!-- Allowed: no actions, and not a danger banner. The countdown
     pauses while the pointer or the keyboard focus is over the
     banner (WCAG 2.2.1). -->
<sv-alert-banner
  variant="success"
  message="Saved."
  [autoDismissMs]="5000" />

examples.title: Two pinned banners that do not know about each other
examples.code:
<!-- The shell renders one, the route renders the other. Without
     coordination both would pin to the same edge and one would hide
     the other; the higher priority takes the edge and the other is
     stacked below it. -->
<sv-alert-banner
  position="top-fixed"
  [priority]="10"
  variant="danger"
  message="Read-only until 21:00 UTC" />

<sv-alert-banner
  position="top-fixed"
  variant="info"
  message="Your trial ends in 3 days" />

<!-- And two copies of the SAME notice are one notice: the later
     registration renders nothing. Give it a key when the wording
     differs but the subject does not. -->
<sv-alert-banner
  position="top-fixed"
  dedupeKey="maintenance"
  message="Maintenance in progress" />

examples.title: Announcement bar (full-bleed top strip)
examples.description: alertStyle="announcement" with position="top-fixed" renders a centered, edge-to-edge promo bar with an inline CTA and dismiss.
examples.code:
<sv-alert-banner
  alertStyle="announcement"
  position="top-fixed"
  variant="info"
  title="New:"
  message="Styloviz 2.0 is here."
  [actions]="[{ id: 'learn', label: 'Learn more' }]" />

customization: Five semantic variants.
Soft, solid, outline, left-accent, top-accent and announcement styles.
Optional icon and action buttons.

Priority stacking for pinned banners: `[priority]` decides which gets the edge and the rest are offset by the measured height of the ones above them — `top` for a top-pinned banner, `bottom` for a bottom-pinned one, and `top-sticky` is a stack of its own because it scrolls with its container. Coordinated through a root service, because the banners on a page do not share a parent.
Duplicate suppression: a pinned banner identical to one already on screen renders nothing. Key it with `dedupeKey`, or `null` to opt out.

Auto-dismiss is REFUSED for a `danger` banner and for any banner with `actions`: a state the user has to know about does not stop being true after a few seconds, and a control cannot be used if it disappears while being aimed at. Everything else keeps its countdown, paused while the pointer is over it OR focus is inside it. The rule, stated: only a short, informational message the user needs to do nothing about may time out. The component enforces it three ways — the countdown is refused when projected content holds a link, button or field (not only for `actions`), and it is never shorter than the text takes to read (`readingTimeMs`: title + message length × `SV_ALERT_READING_MS_PER_CHAR`, 60 ms per character), so `effectiveAutoDismissMs` reports what actually runs.
A full-bleed `announcement` style: a centered, gradient top bar with an inline CTA and dismiss — pair with `position="top-fixed"`.

Remembered dismissal: `persistKey="acme/maintenance"` stores a user dismissal (through `svPersistedStore` — versioned envelope, SSR- and storage-failure-safe) and the banner renders nothing on later visits: no strip, no announcement, no slot in the pinned stack. `persistVersion` is dismissed-until-version — raise it when the message is new and the banner shows again. Only the dismiss button is remembered, never an auto-dismiss. Default off.
accessibility: Announces through the kit's single live region (`SvLiveAnnouncer`), assertively for `danger` and politely for everything else — including `warning`, because `assertive` cuts a screen reader off mid-word and a warning you are not blocked by does not earn that.

The banner itself is not a live region: a region inserted complete, with its text already inside it, is the arrangement assistive technology is least likely to announce, because AT watches an existing region for changes. The visible root keeps `role="status"` so you can still find it and reach its actions.
The same message is not repeated when the host re-renders the banner, which is what the shared announcer's deduplication is for.

Dismiss control is a labelled button, the auto-dismiss timer pauses on hover/focus (WCAG 2.2.1), and dismissing with the close button leaves focus in the region the banner was removed from rather than on `<body>`.

Motion: the banner fades and slides 4px in and out on `opacity` + `translate` only. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` both are dropped — the banner appears and is removed at once, with no invisible 300 ms gap where it was.

inputs.name: title
inputs.description: Bold heading line. Leave empty to render body-only.

inputs.name: message
inputs.description: Main alert message text.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Semantic color.

inputs.name: alertStyle
inputs.description: Visual treatment.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Size controls padding and text scale.

inputs.name: position
inputs.description: Positioning mode. - `inline` — block element in document flow (default) - `top-fixed` — fixed to viewport top, full width - `bottom-fixed` — fixed to viewport bottom, full width - `top-sticky` — sticky inside its scroll container

inputs.name: showIcon
inputs.description: Show the leading icon.

inputs.name: icon
inputs.description: Icon-library NAME overriding the default variant icon — e.g. `'bell'`. Leave empty to use the built-in icon for the current variant.

inputs.name: actions
inputs.description: Up to 2 action buttons rendered inline. Each button emits its `id` via `actionClick`.

inputs.name: dismissible
inputs.description: Show the × close button.

inputs.name: autoDismissMs
inputs.description: Auto-dismiss after N milliseconds. Set to 0 to disable auto-dismiss.

inputs.name: priority
inputs.description: Stack weight for a pinned banner: higher sits against the edge.

inputs.name: dedupeKey
inputs.description: Identity for suppressing a duplicate pinned banner. Omitted, it is derived from variant + style + title + message; a string suppresses on that, whatever the text; `null` never suppresses. A suppressed banner renders nothing — no count, unlike a deduplicated toast. A toast reports an event, so "it happened eleven times" is information; a banner reports a state, and "your trial expires ×2" is not a thing that can be true.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Additional CSS classes merged on the root element.

inputs.name: persistKey
inputs.description: Storage key that remembers a dismissal, or `null` to forget it on the next render.

inputs.name: persistVersion
inputs.description: Which edition of the message a remembered dismissal covers. Raise it when the message is new — "dismissed until version": a user who closed version 2 sees version 3.

outputs.name: dismissed
outputs.description: Emitted after the alert finishes its close animation.

outputs.name: actionClick
outputs.description: Emitted when an action button is clicked, carrying the action `id`.

components.name: Anchor
components.description: An "on this page" navigation list that tracks scroll position with an IntersectionObserver and smooth-scrolls to a section on click. Vertical (side-rail) and horizontal (pill-row) layouts, nested and collapsible sections, outline numbers, a sliding marker and reading progress. Pro adds a sticky underline bar and an outline written from the article's headings.
whenToUse: Job: document position — renders real hash links and reports where the reader is via `activeIdChange` (compare all seven in the “Choosing a navigation pattern” guide under Guides).
A long docs or article page where readers benefit from a persistent "on this page" outline.
You want the outline to highlight itself as the reader scrolls, without wiring up scroll listeners by hand.
For a fixed set of in-page tabs that switch content rather than scroll to it, use Tabs instead.
customization: Vertical (bordered side-rail) or horizontal (pill-row) orientation.
`offset` shifts the smooth-scroll landing position, e.g. to clear a sticky header.
`root` scopes both the IntersectionObserver and the scroll-to call to a custom scrollable container instead of the window.
`activeIdChange` emits whenever the active section changes, for syncing external UI.
`AnchorItem.children` (or a flat `level`) nests sections; `collapsible` shows sub-sections only under the one being read, with `[(expandedIds)]` for the ones the reader opened.
`appearance` (`rail`, `compact`, `minimal`, `card`), `marker` (`slide` or `border`), `numbered`, and per-item `icon` and `meta`.

`progress` + `progressChange` for reading progress; `activationOffset` moves where a section counts as read apart from the jump `offset`; `hashSync="auto"` mirrors the section into the hash with no app provider.
Pro: `sv-anchor-bar` (a sticky tab bar with a sliding underline) and `sv-anchor-outline` (generated from headings, with `affix`), both in `@styloviz-pro/layout`.
accessibility: Rendered as a labelled `nav` landmark ("On this page").
The active link is marked with `aria-current="true"`; ancestors on its trail are styled but not marked current.
Up/Down (Left/Right when horizontal, mirrored in RTL), Home and End move focus between the links; collapse toggles expose `aria-expanded` and a translatable name.
Respects `prefers-reduced-motion`: falls back to an instant jump instead of a smooth scroll.
Links are real anchors with real `href`s (`#section-id`), so they work without JavaScript and are keyboard-focusable in document order.
variants: Nested, Collapsible, Numbered — with Reading Progress
Hash Sync — the Address Follows the Reader

inputs.name: items
inputs.description: The sections to list and track, in document order.

inputs.name: root
inputs.description: Scroll container the sections live in. `null` = the window/viewport.

inputs.name: orientation
inputs.description: Layout axis.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible name of the `<nav>` landmark. Two rails on one page need two names, or a screen reader's landmark list shows "On this page" twice.

inputs.name: offset
inputs.description: Extra pixels kept between a jumped-to section and the top of the scroll container — room for a sticky header the section would otherwise land underneath.

inputs.name: offsetFrom
inputs.description: A sticky header to measure instead of using a fixed `offset` — its current height becomes the offset, and follows it as it changes.

inputs.name: activation
inputs.description: Which reading of "current" to highlight: `'last-passed'` (the last heading scrolled past), `'first-visible'`, `'most-visible'`, or `'nearest-offset'` (the heading closest to the sticky-header line).

inputs.name: urlKey
inputs.description: Reflect the section being read into the URL under this key — pair it with `svHashNavLocation('section')` for `#installation`. Needs `provideSvNavLocation()` at the app root.

inputs.name: urlWriteMode
inputs.description: What a CLICK on a nav link does to history — `'push'` makes back return to the section the reader came from. Scrolling always replaces, whatever this says.

inputs.name: appearance
inputs.description: The list's look. Vertical: `'rail'`, `'compact'`, `'minimal'`, `'card'`. Horizontal: `'minimal'` draws plain text tabs instead of pills.

inputs.name: marker
inputs.description: How the rail marks the active item.

inputs.name: numbered

components.name: Animated Icons
components.description: Motion for any glyph in the kit — 27 presets plus a curated default per icon, driven by the Web Animations API with no CSS file and no animation library. Five triggers (hover, click, in-view, mount, manual) and `prefers-reduced-motion` honoured before anything plays.
whenToUse: Giving one icon a moment of motion: a bell on a new notification, a spinner during a sync, a check when something saved.
You want the motion that suits each glyph without choosing one per icon — `default` already resolves it.
For a page-wide loading state use a Spinner or Skeleton; an animated icon draws the eye to one spot, which is wasted on a whole screen.

examples.title: The curated motion, per glyph
examples.description: `animation` defaults to `default`, which resolves the motion chosen for that specific glyph — a bell rings, a trash lid tips, a check draws itself on. That is the reason to reach for this component over the directive: you get the right motion without picking one for all 687 glyphs.

examples.title: A named preset, looping
examples.description: Name a preset to override the curated choice. `loop` repeats until something stops it, which is what a spinner wants and what a hover affordance does not.
examples.code:
<sv-animated-icon-pro name="refresh-cw" animation="spin" trigger="mount" loop />
<sv-animated-icon-pro name="heart" animation="beat" trigger="hover" />
<sv-animated-icon-pro name="star" animation="tada" trigger="click" persist />

examples.title: Driven by your own state
examples.description: `trigger="manual"` hands control over. Bind `play` for a declarative state, or call `start()` / `stop()` on the component when the moment comes from an event rather than a signal.
examples.code:
<sv-animated-icon-pro
  #sync
  name="refresh-cw"
  animation="spin"
  trigger="manual"
  [play]="syncing()"
  loop
  title="Syncing" />

<sv-button label="Retry" (clicked)="sync.start()" />

examples.title: On scroll, once
examples.description: `in-view` plays when the icon enters the viewport, via IntersectionObserver. `viewOnce` is on by default — an icon that re-animates every time it scrolls back into view is the thing people disable animation over. `viewMargin` starts it early.

examples.title: The directive, on an icon you already have
examples.description: The component is `sv-icon-pro` with the directive applied and the name forwarded. Use `svAnimate` directly to animate an icon that is already placed — including a per-icon component, which has no `name` for the resolver to read, so pass `svAnimateFor` to get that glyph's curated motion.

examples.title: Timing overrides
examples.description: `speed` scales the preset; `duration` and `easing` replace what it declares. Prefer `speed` — a preset's duration is tuned to its own keyframes, and a flat override is what makes a draw finish before the stroke has arrived.

customization: Pick the motion with `animation` — `default` for the glyph's curated choice, or one of 27 presets (`draw`, `draw-loop`, `pulse`, `spin`, `spin-ccw`, `spin-slow`, `beat`, `ring`, `swing`, `wobble`, `jello`, `tada`, `shake`, `flash`, `blink`, `pop`, `bounce`, `float`, `flip`, `sweep`, `fly`, `hinge`, `rotate-in`, `nudge-right`, `nudge-left`, `nudge-up`, `nudge-down`).
Choose what starts it with `trigger` (hover · click · in-view · mount · manual); with `manual`, bind `play` or call `start()` / `stop()`.
Shape the timing with `delay`, `speed`, `duration` and `easing`; `loop` repeats and `persist` keeps the end state instead of resetting.
Tune `in-view` with `viewOnce` and `viewMargin` (an IntersectionObserver root margin).
Everything `sv-icon-pro` takes is forwarded: `name`, `size`, `weight`, `strokeWidth`, `title`, `flip`, `rotate` and `cssClass`.
React to `animationStart` / `animationDone` — both emit the RESOLVED motion key, so a handler can tell which motion `default` picked.
Apply `svAnimate` directly to any icon you have already placed; pass `svAnimateFor` when the icon is a per-icon component with no `name` for the resolver to read.
accessibility: `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` suppresses playback entirely — the icon renders in its resting state rather than playing a shortened version, because a smaller amount of the thing that triggers vestibular symptoms is still that thing.
Motion never carries meaning on its own. Set `title` when the animation IS the status: it names the glyph `role="img"`, which is the only part of a spinning icon that reaches a screen reader.
Playback is Web Animations API only, with no CSS keyframes and no library, so it degrades to a static icon under SSR and on any runtime without WAAPI instead of throwing.
The animation runs on transforms and stroke properties, so it never moves the glyph out of its box and never reflows the text beside it.
`animationDone` fires with the resolved motion key on non-looping playback, so a host can wait for the motion to finish before moving focus rather than guessing at a duration.

components.name: App Shell
components.description: The frame of a dashboard: a collapsible sidebar, a top bar, the page and a footer — slot-based, with the collapsed and mobile-overlay state shared by the parts without a single binding.
whenToUse: The outer frame of an admin panel, a SaaS dashboard or an internal tool: navigation on the side, actions on top, the page in between.
You want the collapsed rail and the small-screen overlay handled once, for every page, instead of per page.
Use `sv-page-header` at the top of each routed page for its title, subtitle and primary actions.
Sidebar (shell) · Sidebar Nav (tree): `sv-sidebar` is the collapsible container, and Sidebar Nav (`sv-sidebar-nav`, a variant of this family) is the navigation tree you put inside it.
Compare with Site Footer: `sv-footer` is the one-line bar inside the shell; `sv-site-footer` is the multi-column marketing footer.

customization: Slots: `[svShellSidebar]`, `[svShellTopbar]`, the default slot (the page), `[svShellFooter]`. A shell with no sidebar takes no left offset.

`sv-sidebar`: `[svSidebarBrand]` (the 64 px brand row), the default slot (navigation) and `[svSidebarFooter]` (pinned to the bottom); `w-64` expanded, a `w-20` rail collapsed from `lg` up, an overlay below it.

`sv-topbar`: the sidebar toggles, then `[topbar-start]`, `[topbar-search]` (the flexible middle), `[topbar-actions]`, then the theme toggle. `showSidebarToggle` and `showThemeToggle` turn the built-in controls off.
`sv-footer`: the default slot (start) and `[svFooterEnd]` (end); stacked on small screens.
Every surface uses the theme tokens with a `dark:` counterpart; the sidebar and topbar are glass because the page scrolls beneath them.

`sv-page-header`: `title` and `subtitle`; slots `[svPageHeaderBack]` and `[svPageHeaderBreadcrumb]` above the title, `[svPageHeaderMeta]` beside it, `[svPageHeaderTabs]` along the bottom edge, the default slot for actions; `actions` (+ `actionClick`, `actionsLabel`) for a responsive actions row that folds into the toolbar's overflow menu. Import the slot directives (`SvPageHeaderBreadcrumbDirective`, …) so the header knows it holds page navigation.
accessibility: Landmarks: the sidebar is a `complementary` region named by `label` (default "Main navigation"), the topbar a `banner`, the page `main`, the footer `contentinfo`. Put a named `<nav>` inside the sidebar.

The desktop toggle reports `aria-pressed` and is named for what it will do ("Collapse sidebar" / "Expand sidebar"); the hamburger and the theme toggle are named too, and every name is an input for translation.
The small-screen overlay closes on Escape, on its backdrop (hidden from assistive technology) and when a link inside the sidebar is followed.
Collapsed, the navigation is the nav component's job: `sv-sidebar-nav` keeps every item named in its rail.

Skip link (WCAG 2.4.1): the shell's first focusable element is a "Skip to main content" link, visually hidden until it takes focus. Activating it moves focus to `<main>` (which has `tabindex="-1"`), so the next Tab continues inside the page instead of walking the sidebar and topbar again. Its text comes from the `layout` label pack (`skipToMainContent`, all 12 languages); `skipLinkLabel` overrides it, `skipLink` turns it off, and `focusMain()` lets a host shortcut do the same move.

RTL: the sidebar is pinned to the inline start (`start-0`, border on the inline end) and the content is offset with `margin-inline-start`, so under `dir="rtl"` the sidebar is on the right and the page makes room on the right; the small-screen overlay slides off to the right.

`sv-page-header`: the title is the page `<h1>`. With a breadcrumb, back/up or tabs slot in use the header is one `region` landmark named by that title, so the page's own navigation sits in one place; a plain header adds no landmark. The actions row is a named `toolbar` ("Page actions") whose overflow is the kit's keyboard-operable "More actions" menu.

components.name: Artifact Panel
components.description: Conversation and generated document side by side, with a revision history that records why each version says what it says. 3 variants: split, focus and history.
whenToUse: An assistant that produces a document rather than a reply — a policy, a spec, a component, a query.
Any surface where somebody will later ask "why does it say this", which is every document an assistant edits more than once.
For a plain chat with no artifact, use the AI Chat Interface.
customization: `artifact` and `messages` are inputs; import `DEMO_ARTIFACT` / `DEMO_MESSAGES` for a demo.
Three layouts via `variant`: `split` (conversation and document), `focus` (document alone) and `history` (every revision with what it changed and why).
`selectedVersionId` and `showDiff` are two-way. Activating a conversation turn moves the document to the revision that turn caused.
A `kind: 'code'` artifact renders through `sv-code-block` with its language; prose renders as text. The diff renders by line in both cases.

`SV_DIFF_LINE_CAP` (2000) is the point past which an exact LCS diff is not computed — the counts still are, from a line-multiset comparison, and the result is labelled `approximate` rather than silently degraded.

`[diffLineCap]` (default `SV_DIFF_LINE_CAP`, still exported) moves that point per host; the approximate-diff notice quotes the cap that produced the verdict (`SvDiffSummary.cap`). The diff is O(n·m) per version switch, so raise it only within the budget of the slowest device you support.

Past that cap the diff surface itself carries the reason it is empty: pressing 'What changed' shows a notice naming the cap, the counts it does know, and the fact that the positions are not known — never a blank box, which reads as 'nothing changed' on the largest documents.

`saveState` is the host's: `saved` / `saving` / `unsaved` / `conflict`, each with its own sentence, and the last two styled as needing attention. The component never infers it from a changed input — only the host knows whether its write landed — and it does not resolve a conflict, it states one.
A staleness banner appears when the reader is behind, and offers the jump rather than taking it.

Copy and Export act on the revision **on screen**, not silently the newest. Copy confirms only after the browser accepted the write: `(copied)` then, `(copyFailed)` and a select-the-text fallback when the clipboard is unavailable. Export downloads `<title>-v<n>.<ext>` (extension from `kind` and `language`) and emits `(exportRequested)` with `{ filename, content, mimeType, version }`, so a host can upload it instead. `svArtifactExport()` builds the same payload outside the component. Both controls are withdrawn when the AI privacy policy sets `copy: false` (`provideSvAiPrivacy`).
accessibility: Each revision row carries its change summary, its cause and the scope warning in its accessible name.
The diff marks additions and removals with a sign character as well as colour.
The diff toggle is hidden on the first revision rather than present and dead — there is nothing to compare it against.
The copy outcome is announced through a `role="status"` region that is always present, and the Copy and Export buttons name the version (and the file) they act on.
variants: Split — And Why the Document Says What It Says
History — The Revision That Did More Than It Was Asked
Focus — Behind the Conversation, and Told So

The diff is O(n·m) per version switch; raise it only within the budget of the slowest device you support. Non-positive or non-finite values fall back to the default.

inputs.name: saveState

Only the host knows whether its write landed, and a canvas that infers "saved" from "the content input changed" reports success for an edit that never left the browser. Left at `'saved'` the indicator is a quiet confirmation; a host that never sets it is making the same claim every other canvas makes silently. `conflict` is not resolved here either — the component says so, loudly and persistently, and the merge is the host's.

components.name: Audio Device Select
components.description: Choose a microphone and, where the browser can route sound, a speaker. The permission states are said in words — checking, not asked yet (with the button that asks), blocked (with how to re-allow it and Check again), an insecure page, an unsupported browser — and a Web Audio level meter tests the input. Device lists follow `devicechange` live, and a chosen device that is unplugged falls back to the system default. It never opens the microphone on render, is SSR-safe, and feature-detects everything.
whenToUse: Call, meeting, dictation and voice-assistant settings; a pre-call "check your mic" step.
Anywhere a voice feature should explain a blocked microphone instead of failing silently.
For a plain list of options, use the Select Dropdown.

examples.title: Remember the microphone
examples.description: `deviceId` is two-way and `''` is the system default. Device ids are stable per origin, so they can be saved.

examples.title: Route a player to the chosen speaker
examples.description: The speaker list appears only where `HTMLMediaElement.setSinkId` exists. Bind its id to `sv-media-player`'s `sinkId`.

examples.title: Stand in for the browser
examples.description: `SV_AUDIO_DEVICES` is the seam to `navigator.mediaDevices`, the Permissions API and Web Audio. Provide an `SvAudioDeviceBackend` for a test, a demo or a native shell.

customization: `showOutput` adds the speaker list; `meter` hides the test and the level meter; `size` sizes both lists; `disabled` locks it.
`requestAccess()`, `startTest()`, `stopTest()` and `refresh()` drive it from code; `svAudioLevel` and `svMicErrorCode` are exported for your own call UI.
Every string comes from the `display` labels (`audioDevice*` keys) in 12 language packs, or the per-instance `labels` input.
accessibility: A labelled group. The lists are the kit's Select Dropdown (labelled combobox, full keyboard, body-portal panel).
The level is a `role="meter"` with a spoken value refreshed a few times a second; the bar is a `scaleX` transform, so it never causes layout, and it stops with the test.
The test toggle is a button with `aria-pressed`; access errors are a `role="alert"` in words; granting access and a device being unplugged are announced politely.
Built without `@angular/aria`, which the kit does not depend on in 2.0.

components.name: Audit Log
components.description: An audit / activity log: who changed what, when, and from what to what. The events are an interactive `sv-timeline`, newest first; the open one shows its facts (when, actor, action, resource, request context) as `sv-descriptions`, its field changes as a before → after table, each long, multi-line or structured value as an `sv-diff-viewer` line diff, and the raw record in a collapsed `sv-json-viewer`. A sensitive field is listed as changed and never printed. Filters by actor, action, resource and changed field use the shipped `sv-select-dropdown`, client-side or reported to your API; the filtered list downloads as CSV or JSON, built in the browser.
whenToUse: The "History" or "Activity" tab of a record — an invoice, a customer, a member — where people need to see who changed which field.
A workspace security or compliance log: permission changes, sign-ins, exports, rotated secrets.
Use `sv-timeline` on its own for a feed with no field-level changes, and `sv-diff-viewer` on its own to compare two versions of one document.

examples.title: An event with field-level changes
examples.description: Each change names the field and its two sides. `undefined` means the field did not exist on that side (shown "Not set"), `null` or `''` that it was empty. A string longer than 80 characters, one with a line break, or an object or array is compared as a line diff; anything else is a table row.

examples.title: Filtering and paging on the server
examples.description: Set `serverSide`: `entries` is shown as given and the filters only report `filtersChange`. Pass `filterOptions` from your API so a filter can offer values that are not loaded yet, and `hasMore` / `loadingMore` / `(loadMore)` to append older pages.

examples.title: Export
examples.description: CSV and JSON of the events currently listed (after the filters), built in the browser with no request. The CSV has one row per field change and machine column names (`event_id`, `time`, `actor`, … `field`, `before`, `after`), the spreadsheet formula guard and a BOM for Excel; sensitive values are written `[redacted]`. The JSON leaves out `raw` and keeps a sensitive change as `{ field, label, sensitive: true }`. For a full server-side export, set `[exportFormats]="[]"` and add your own button.
examples.code:
<sv-audit-log [entries]="events" [exportFormats]="['csv']" exportFileName="invoice-audit"
  (exported)="track($event.format, $event.count)" />

// The same text without the component, e.g. for a scheduled e-mail:
import { svAuditEntriesToCsv, svAuditFilterEntries } from '@styloviz-pro/display';
const csv = svAuditEntriesToCsv(svAuditFilterEntries(events, { action: 'permission' }));

examples.title: Your own actions
examples.description: Eight actions have their own words and colours: create, update, delete, restore, permission, access, login, export. Any other `action` string works too — give its past tense as `actionLabel` and the summary reads "Billing job archived Invoice INV-1990".

customization: Colours: create / restore paint `accent`, update `info`, delete and failures `danger`, permission changes `warning`, export the brand accent, access and sign-in `gray` — the timeline's tokens, so a theme that remaps them recolours the dots.
`filterKeys` chooses which of the four filters show and in what order (`[]` hides the bar); `filterOptions` replaces the derived choices per filter.
`diffView` (`unified` / `split`) sets the layout of the line diffs; `showRaw` hides the raw record; `collapseAfter` folds a long list behind "Show N more".
The list and the details sit side by side once the component is about 48rem wide (a container query, not the viewport), and stack below that — so it fits a drawer as well as a page.

Every string comes from the `displayPro` labels (`audit*` keys) in 12 language packs — `provideSvLabels(SV_DISPLAY_PRO_LABELS_DE)` or the per-instance `labels` input. CSV column names stay machine names in every language.
`svAuditFilterEntries`, `svAuditFilterOptions`, `svAuditChangeKind`, `svAuditEntriesToCsv`, `svAuditEntriesToJson` and `svAuditStableJson` are exported for a server, a digest or a test.
accessibility: Events are the shipped interactive timeline: each is a focusable button with `aria-pressed` for the open one, Enter / Space opens it, and the list is named ("Audit events"). Action and failure are words in a badge, never colour alone.
The open event is a labelled region with a real heading at `headingLevel + 1`; its facts are a description list (`<dl>`), and its time is a `<time datetime>`.

Field changes are a `<table>` with a caption and `scope="col"` / `scope="row"` headers; before and after are `<del>` / `<ins>` under "Before" / "After" column headers, and missing, empty and hidden values are words ("Not set", "Empty", "Hidden"), not blank cells. The table scrolls inside a focusable, named region on a narrow screen and prints in full.

Filters are the shipped `sv-select-dropdown` combobox, each with a visible label, grouped and named ("Filter audit events"). An export is announced in a polite status region ("Exported 6 events as CSV.").
Loading, error and both empties use the kit's shells: the error is a `role="alert"` with Try again, and "No matching events" offers Clear filters.
variants: Security Trail — Permissions, Failed Sign-in, Rotated Secret

components.name: Autocomplete
components.description: Searchable dropdown with grouping, sublabels, icons, disabled options, custom option rows, async search, keyboard navigation and query highlighting.
whenToUse: Typing to filter and pick a single value from a large or remote dataset.
You want query highlighting, grouping and async-friendly inputChange.
For multiple selections use Tag Input; for a fixed short list use Select Dropdown.

examples.title: Accent-insensitive and prefix matching
examples.description: Matching folds accents and case in `locale` — `jose` finds and highlights José. `match` is `substring` (default), `prefix` (word starts) or your own `(option, query) => boolean`. Select Dropdown's search and Search Bar's highlight fold the same way (`svTextMatches` / `svHighlightSegments` in `@styloviz/core`).

examples.title: Create new entry
examples.description: With `creatable`, a query no option is labelled gets an explicit Create row (an option, reached by ↓/End/Enter). It emits a typed `SvCreateRequest` — label, value, idempotency `requestKey`, `resolve()` / `reject()`. `awaitCreate` shows the entry as pending until the host settles. The same contract ships on Select Dropdown Pro and Tag Input Pro.
examples.code:
<sv-autocomplete
  [options]="people()"
  [creatable]="true"
  [awaitCreate]="true"
  [(value)]="assignee"
  (createRequest)="save($event)" />

// save(req: SvCreateRequest) → POST, then req.resolve({ value: saved.id }) or req.reject(message)

examples.title: Grouped sections
examples.description: Give options a `group` and set `grouped` to render labelled sections.

examples.title: Search an endpoint with svSuggestController
examples.description: The controller from `@styloviz/core` debounces, aborts superseded requests, keeps stale results visible and honours `minChars`. Turn the field's own debounce off and mark the options as the server's answer.
examples.code:
readonly airports = svSuggestController<AutocompleteOption>(
  (term, signal) => fetch(`/api/airports?q=${encodeURIComponent(term)}`, { signal }).then((r) => r.json()),
  { minChars: 2 },
);

<sv-autocomplete [serverSide]="true" [debounceMs]="0" [minChars]="2"
  [options]="airports.options()" [loading]="airports.loading()"
  [stale]="airports.stale()" [error]="airports.error()"
  (inputChange)="airports.search($event)" (retry)="airports.reload()" />

examples.title: Custom option rows
examples.description: An `svAutocompleteOption` template replaces what each row shows; the row itself — `role="option"`, its active-descendant id, highlight and click — stays the component's. Context: the option, `active`, `selected`, `query`.
examples.code: {{ opt.label }}

customization: `maxItems` (default 8) is a hard boundary, and the panel discloses it: a query matching 500 options shows eight and says so (“Showing 8 of 500 — keep typing to narrow”) as a `role="presentation"` footer row plus a `role="status"` announcement outside the listbox, so a user whose entry is 300th knows to keep typing. Deliberately not `aria-setsize`: the unrendered options are genuinely unreachable, so declaring 500 would promise items no key can get to — worse than saying nothing.

With `serverSide`, pass `totalCount` so the disclosure reads “8 of 4,312” rather than counting the one page you handed over; the “keep typing” advice is dropped there, because what a narrower query returns is the host’s endpoint to promise, not this component’s.
Options with sublabels, icons and disabled state; query highlighting and a configurable no-results message.
Set `grouped` to render results in labelled sections by each option's `group` (keyboard nav and active-descendant stay correct across sections).
Clearable, loading state, `maxItems` cap and three sizes; named via `label`.
Two-way bind `[(value)]` or a reactive control (CVA); listen to `selected`, `cleared`, `inputChange`.

`creatable` + `awaitCreate` + `(createRequest)`: the shared create-new flow — an explicit Create row, a typed request with an idempotency key, and the pending entry while the host saves. A rejection is announced through the live announcer and shown under the field.

Custom rows: an `svAutocompleteOption` template (`SvAutocompleteOptionDirective`) replaces each row's content and gets the option, `active`, `selected` and the typed `query`; the default label highlighting is yours to redo if you want it.
Recent searches: offer them from the host — when the query is empty, pass the recent options with `group: 'Recent'` (and `grouped`), and update the list on `(selected)`.

`match`: `substring` | `prefix` | `(option, query) => boolean`; the built-in modes are accent- and case-folded in `locale` (NFD fold + locale lower-casing), and the highlight keeps the label's own spelling.
accessibility: Proper ARIA combobox on the `<input>`: `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls` and `aria-activedescendant` track the highlighted option (options carry per-instance ids).
Arrow keys move, Home/End jump, Enter selects, Esc closes; the input is named by `label` or `placeholder`.
Implements ControlValueAccessor — works with `[(ngModel)]`, `[formControl]` and `formControlName`.

inputs.name: options
inputs.description: Options to filter and choose from (supports groups, sublabels, icons).

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: Selected value (two-way).

inputs.name: placeholder
inputs.description: Placeholder shown when empty.

inputs.description: Field size: sm, md or lg.

inputs.description: Visual variant.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disable the field.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Accessible label for the field.

inputs.name: clearable
inputs.description: Show a clear (×) button when a value is selected.

inputs.name: maxItems
inputs.description: Maximum suggestions rendered at once. A hard boundary, and a disclosed one: a query matching 500 options shows eight and says how many more there are, so a user whose entry is 300th in the list knows to keep typing; see `truncationNote`.

inputs.name: totalCount
inputs.description: How many results exist in total, when the component cannot know. With `serverSide` the supplied `options` are already one page of a larger answer, so counting the array understates it. A host that knows the real total passes it here and the disclosure reads "8 of 4,312" instead of "8 of 20". Ignored without `serverSide`, where the array IS everything.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP 47 locale for dates and numbers.

inputs.name: match
inputs.description: How the query matches an option: `'substring'` — anywhere in the label, sublabel or value; `'prefix'` — at the start of one of their words; or a function `(option, query) => boolean` for your own rule (it gets the raw trimmed query). Built-in modes fold accents and case in `locale`, so `jose` finds José. Ignored with `serverSide`.

inputs.name: grouped
inputs.description: Render results in labelled sections using each option's `group`.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: Show a loading state (e.g. while fetching async results).

inputs.name: stale
inputs.description: The options on screen answer an **older** query — a newer request is still in flight. Distinct from `loading`, which cannot separate the two cases it covers: the first fetch (nothing on screen — show a skeleton) and a refinement of results already visible (keep them, and say they are provisional). Blanking the panel on the second is the most jarring thing a combobox can do; showing the old list with no indication is a quiet lie. Bind `svSuggestController(...).stale` from `@styloviz/data`, or `createRequestGuard().stale` from `@styloviz/core`. The results dim and report `aria-busy` while staying fully interactive.

inputs.name: noResultsLabel
inputs.description: Text shown when no options match.

inputs.name: serverSide
inputs.description: Let the server do the matching. The supplied `options` are shown exactly as given — filtering them again hides entries the server matched on fields the component cannot see.

inputs.name: debounceMs
inputs.description: Delay before `inputChange` fires, in ms. `0` emits immediately.

inputs.name: minChars
inputs.description: Characters required before a lookup is sent. Below this the panel says so instead of showing a misleading "No results found".

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Failure loading the options, rendered inside the panel.

inputs.name: icon
inputs.description: Name of an icon in `@styloviz/icons`, e.g. `'search'`. A name, not a raw `<path d="…">` string: the library supplies the sizing, stroke and dark-mode handling.

inputs.name: creatable
inputs.description: Offer an explicit "Create ‹query›" row when what the user typed matches no option's label. Activating it emits `createRequest`.

inputs.name: awaitCreate
inputs.description: Keep a created entry PENDING — shown in the field, marked busy, not yet the value — until the host settles `createRequest`. Off, the entry becomes the value at once and `reject()` takes it back out.

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: Client-side validation message.

inputs.name: serverError
inputs.description: A rejection reported by the server about this value. Self-expiring.

outputs.name: selected
outputs.description: Emitted with the chosen option.

outputs.name: createRequest
outputs.description: The user activated "Create ‹query›": persist it, then `resolve()` (with the server's id) or `reject()`. Shared with select-dropdown-pro and tag-input-pro.

outputs.name: cleared
outputs.description: Emitted when the selection is cleared.

outputs.name: inputChange
outputs.description: Emitted on every query change (debounce upstream for async sources).

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed lookup.

outputs.name: valueChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `value` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(value)]`.

components.name: Avatar
components.description: User avatar with initials fallback, status indicator, size and shape variants.
whenToUse: Representing a user or entity by image, with a reliable initials fallback.
You want a status dot, verified mark or notification badge on the avatar.
For several people, use Avatar Group (`sv-avatar-group`) — a limited, named stack with a counted "+N".

examples.title: Presence, said in more than one way
examples.description: Green, grey, amber and red at ten pixels across is a colour code with no second channel — deuteranopia alone makes the green and the amber the same mark, and online/away is exactly the pair a reader has to tell apart before sending a message. Each state has a form as well: online is solid, busy carries the do-not-disturb bar, away is a crescent, offline is a hollow ring (a grey fill on a white card is nearly the card, so "offline" and "no dot" looked the same). statusLabel replaces the wording, and showStatusText puts it beside the avatar wherever there is room for three words.
examples.code: <sv-avatar name="Ada Lovelace" status="busy" statusLabel="In a meeting until 3" [showStatusText]="true" />

examples.title: The fallback is a layer, not a replacement
examples.description: The initials are what the image sits on top of, and the image fades in once it has decoded — so a slow image shows initials rather than an empty hole, and a broken one never flashes from a hole to initials. While both layers are present the img alt carries the name and the initials underneath are hidden from assistive tech, so nothing is announced twice.

customization: Image with graceful initials fallback — the initials are the layer underneath, so a slow image never leaves a blank square and a broken one never flashes.
Online/away/busy/offline status dot with a distinct shape per state, plus size and shape options; `statusLabel` and `showStatusText` add words.
Stack several with `sv-avatar-group`.
accessibility: Alt text derived from the name; broken images fall back to initials/icon.
A `clickable` avatar exposes `role="button"`, is focusable, and activates on Enter/Space (Space is prevented from scrolling).
Status dot and notification badge are individually labelled; decorative initials/icon are hidden from assistive tech.

Presence is never colour alone: online is solid, busy carries a bar, away is a crescent and offline is a hollow ring — all four readable in greyscale. The dot is announced in words ("Status: In a meeting until 3"), not the raw enum value.
While an image is still loading, the `alt` carries the name and the initials underneath are `aria-hidden`, so the same person is not announced twice.
variants: Presence, Said in More Than One Way

components.name: Back / Up
components.description: Back and Up as two different controls, because they are two different promises: back is history and may leave the site, up is hierarchy and is always defined. A back control with nothing behind it goes up rather than dead-ending, and says which it did.
whenToUse: A detail page that people arrive at by deep link — from an email, a chat, a notification — and need a reliable way out of.
The mobile form of a breadcrumb: one control pointing at the one crumb that matters.
When you need to know afterwards whether "back" actually went back. `(navigated)` carries `reason`, and a fallback is otherwise indistinguishable from a working back button.
For a full trail, use Breadcrumb; for moving between peers, use Tabs or Jump Menu. This is for moving out and up.

examples.title: Back, with somewhere safe to land
A breadcrumb's mobile form
examples.code:
<!-- A breadcrumb knows the "up" target; a back button does not. Below the
     breakpoint, the trail collapses to the one crumb that matters. -->
@if (narrow()) {
  <sv-back-up mode="up" [up]="parentPath()" [upLabel]="parentLabel()" />
} @else {
  <sv-breadcrumb [items]="crumbs" />
}

customization: Three variants: ghost, outline, link. Three sizes: sm, md, lg.
`iconOnly` for a dense toolbar — the text stays as the accessible name.
`label` overrides the composed text entirely; `upLabel` alone composes "Back to X" / "Up to X".
The up target routes through `SvLinkAdapter`, so no router dependency — with none wired up the anchor is simply followed.
accessibility: Up renders a real `<a href>` and back renders a `<button>`, chosen by what each can promise: only one of them has a destination a browser could open in a new tab.
A modified click (⌘, middle, Shift) on the up control is never intercepted — that gesture means "open this somewhere else".
Icon-only keeps the composed text as `aria-label`, so the control is never announced as a bare graphic.
Disabled is `disabled` on the button and `aria-disabled` on the anchor, which cannot take the former.
variants: Back and Up are different promises

inputs.name: mode
inputs.description: What this control promises. `back` returns through history and falls back to up; `up` always goes to up.

inputs.name: up
inputs.description: The hierarchical parent — where "up" goes, and where "back" lands when there is no history. **Required in practice**: without it a `back` control has no fallback and can dead-end on a deep-linked page. Warns once in dev when it is missing.

inputs.name: upLabel
inputs.description: Name of the up destination, used in the visible text and the accessible name — "Back to Orders", "Up to Orders". Without it the control reads as a bare "Back", which tells a screen-reader user nothing about where they will end up.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Override the whole visible text. Leave unset to compose it from mode and upLabel.

inputs.name: stayInSite
inputs.description: Only use history when the previous entry is provably this app's — otherwise go up. Off by default, and that is the right default for a *BACK* CONTROL. Back meaning "the browser's back", including off the site, is what the word has always meant and what the hardware button does. Turn this on for a control that is really *"return to where you were in this app"* — a wizard's escape hatch, a detail page's return-to-list — where leaving the site is never the intended answer. "Provably ours" means: this control has observed at least one in-app navigation since it was created, **or** `document.referrer` is same-origin. Anything else is treated as not ours, because the failure modes are not symmetric — going up when back would have worked is a mild surprise; leaving the site when the user expected to stay is a lost session. In a single-page app both signals are weaker: a router's `pushState` is not observed, a control inside a routed page starts counting from zero on each route, and `document.referrer` describes how the reader entered the app, not the entry behind this one. So it errs towards going up.

whenToUse: Labelling status, category or counts inline with other content.
You need a small, color-coded indicator next to titles, rows or icons.

customization: Eight tones with published meanings — see the meanings under Best practices; the meaning is the contract, and the colour is downstream of it.

Readable contrast for every variant in both themes.
Conveys meaning with text, not just color; the dot/icon are decorative.
Static badges carry no ARIA live region by default — opt in with `live` only for values that update in place, so screen readers are not spammed.

components.name: Bar Chart
components.description: Pure-SVG grouped bar chart with vertical/horizontal orientation and animated bars.
whenToUse: Comparing a value across discrete categories (revenue by month, sales by region).
You want grouped or stacked series for category comparisons.
For trends over a continuous axis, use the Line Chart.

examples.title: Live leaderboard — sorted, sliding
examples.code:
<!-- sort orders the categories by their total; when values change the bars
     slide to their new places. Table, Tab order and (barSelect) keep the input order. -->
<sv-bar-chart-pro [categories]="regions" [datasets]="datasets()" sort="descending" />

customization: Vertical or horizontal orientation.
Grouped, stacked and 100%-stacked modes, with each category's absolute total drawn beside its bar on the normalised ones (`showCategoryTotals`, on by default).
Animated entrance with configurable colors.
Handle `barSelect` for drill-down or selection.

`valuePolicy` decides what happens to a bar this chart cannot draw — a negative, `NaN` or `Infinity`. `clamp` (default) draws it as a marked 3px stub at the baseline; `reject` refuses the dataset and shows the error state. `omit` is not offered: a bar's position is its index within its group, so dropping one would slide every later bar out from under its own category label. The cylindrical, placement and drilldown columns take the same `clamp`/`reject` choice. The stacked and range variants default to `omit` instead — a segment or a range keeps its own slot, so leaving one out moves nothing else — and count what they left out under the plot. For data that genuinely goes below zero use `<sv-negative-stack-chart>`.

Pro (`sv-bar-chart-pro`): error bars — `errors` on a dataset, a ± per value or `{ minus, plus }` — and `barStyle="lollipop"`, a stem and a dot per value. The range charts take `rangeStyle="dumbbell"`.
accessibility: The SVG is a `role="group"` with an auto-generated data summary as its name (override via `ariaLabel`) — `group`, not `img`, because focusable bars inside an `img` are invisible to a screen reader, which prunes its subtree.

A bar's height is its value, so `sv-data-summary-table` publishes the numbers beside it: one row per category, one column per series, captioned with the chart title. There is deliberately no overview line above it — the SVG's own name already states the series and the category count, and repeating it is the same sentence twice.
Numeric value labels accompany bars; respects reduced-motion for animations.

A clamped bar is disclosed three ways, because the stub alone is only visual: a sentence under the plot naming how many bars and their real values, "not drawn to scale" appended to the bar's own `aria-label`, and the same phrase in its table cell. The table keeps the REAL number — it is the data, not a transcript of the drawing.

A blank source cell reads as "no value", not `NaN`. `Math.max(10, NaN)` is `NaN`, so a blank read as `NaN` would take the axis, every bar height and every grid tick with it — and SVG drops a `NaN` dimension silently, blanking the plot with no error anywhere.

On a 100 %-stacked chart the absolute total is drawn beside every bar, so the magnitude that normalising removes is present as text rather than only in a tooltip. A negative contribution is excluded from the total exactly as it is from the segments, so the caption always equals the sum of what is actually drawn.

The Gradient Bar variant publishes the same table. Its bars are not focusable, so a per-bar `aria-label` had nothing to attach to and the SVG's name says only how many series there are — every number on it reached the page as a gradient length and nothing else.

The chart accessibility module puts the same table on screen: `svChartDataTable` on the chart, or `provideSvChartA11y({ dataTable: 'toggle' })` for the app, adds a “Show data table” button under the plot (`aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`; the visible table is a named, focusable scroll region). Every chart in the kit supports it.
An error range is spoken, not only drawn: “60 (−4, +12)” in the bar's name, its tooltip and its table cell; the whisker itself is `aria-hidden`.
