inputs.name: pasteToUpload
inputs.description: Accept files pasted from the clipboard. The default is `'off'`, and `'page'` is the one to think about before turning on. A document-level paste listener is what makes "just paste a screenshot" work, and it is also how an upload zone steals a paste intended for the comment box next to it. `'page'` therefore ignores any paste whose target is an editable element — an input, a textarea, a contenteditable — because in that case the user was demonstrably typing somewhere else. `'zone'` is the conservative option: the paste only counts when focus is inside the dropzone.

inputs.name: directory
inputs.description: Let the user pick a whole folder, and expand folders that are dropped. Sets `webkitdirectory` on the picker. Folder DROPS are expanded whichever way this is set — see `onDrop` for why that is not a choice.

inputs.name: maxScannedFiles
inputs.description: Cap on how many files one folder drop may add, before `maxFiles` applies. A separate, much larger number than `maxFiles` on purpose. This one exists to stop a home directory dropped by accident from locking the tab while it walks a hundred thousand entries; `maxFiles` is a product rule about how many the user may submit. Conflating them means the walk keeps going long after the answer stopped mattering.

inputs.name: cropImages
inputs.description: Hold croppable images back so the user can crop them before they upload. This component does not render a cropper, and will not. `file-upload` takes no dependency on `@styloviz-pro/image-editor`: a host that wants inline crop composes `<sv-image-cropper>` itself against `cropQueue()` and calls `applyCrop()` with the blob, and a host that does not should not ship a canvas cropper it never renders. The seam is a `Blob`, which is all an uploader ever needed. Only types a canvas can actually round-trip are held — see `svIsCroppableImage`, where every exclusion is a different silent failure. Anything else queues normally, so turning this on can never strand a file.

inputs.name: cropType
inputs.description: The type crops are written as. `'auto'` follows the source, which is the only setting that neither inflates a photo into a lossless PNG nor composites a transparent logo onto black. See `svCropOutputType`.

inputs.name: listType
inputs.description: Rows, or a grid of picture cards.

inputs.name: reorderable
inputs.description: Let the user put the files in order — a grip to drag (mouse, touch, pen) that also moves with the arrow keys, announced. The order is the order of `files()`, the form value and `filesChange`.

inputs.name: rowActions
inputs.description: Preview opens the file in a dialog (image, video, PDF); download saves it.

inputs.name: transferDetails
inputs.description: Bytes sent, speed and time left under the overall bar.

inputs.name: pausable
inputs.description: A pause button on uploading rows; a paused row resumes on demand.

inputs.name: resumeStore
inputs.description: Bookmark uploads as they go, and offer interrupted ones back on the next visit — pair with `svChunkedUploader`'s `probe` so a re-added file carries on from the server's offset. Use `svLocalResumeStore({ scope: userId })`.

inputs.name: dropOnPage
inputs.description: While files are dragged anywhere over the page, a full-screen drop target appears, and a drop anywhere adds them.

inputs.name: beforeRemove
inputs.description: Asked before a file is removed; resolve `false` to keep it.

inputs.name: metadataFields
inputs.description: Details the user fills in per file. A `required` field holds the file back from upload and makes the control invalid until it is filled.

inputs.name: addFrom
inputs.description: Where files can be added from, besides the picker and a drop.

inputs.name: demoFailureRate
inputs.description: In `demoMode`, the share of files that fail — chosen by hashing the file, so the same files fail on every run.

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: Client-side validation message.

inputs.name: serverError
inputs.description: A rejection reported by the server about this value. Self-expiring.

outputs.name: filesChange
outputs.description: Files were added, removed or cleared, or one finished uploading, was cropped or got a scan verdict. Carries every entry, including scan-blocked ones.

outputs.name: fileAdded
outputs.description: A file was added to the queue. Fires once per file, including files that failed validation.

outputs.name: fileRemoved
outputs.description: A file was removed from the queue. Carries the removed entry's `id`.

outputs.name: uploadComplete
outputs.description: The run has settled: every file finished uploading or failed and, under `scanPolicy="required"`, every uploaded file has a verdict (`'clean'` or `'flagged'`). Fires once per run with the full list — read each entry's `status` and `scan`, since a flagged file is in it.

outputs.name: uploadError
outputs.description: A file failed: too large, rejected by `accept`, or its upload errored. Carries the entry with `errorMsg` set.

outputs.name: uploadCancelled
outputs.description: A file's upload was cancelled by the user.

outputs.name: scanChange
outputs.description: A file's malware-scan verdict changed. Carries the whole entry. Fires for every transition the host drives, `'pending'` included, so a toast or an audit line can be written at the moment it happens rather than by diffing `files()`.

outputs.name: intakeSkipped
outputs.description: Files an intake left behind, and why — junk metadata, the `accept` filter, or the scan limit; a full queue (`reason: 'max-files'`); or a file already queued under `duplicates="skip"` (`reason: 'duplicate'`). A folder drop that quietly loses files is the worst outcome. Dropping 250 photos and seeing 180 queue up, with nothing saying which 70 went or why, is indistinguishable from a broken component. This fires once per cause per intake so the host can say so.

outputs.name: cropRequested
outputs.description: A file is waiting to be cropped. Fires once per held file, as it is added. The entry is emitted before its `preview` exists. The thumbnail is read asynchronously by a `FileReader`, so the entry handed over here has no `preview` yet — a host that pins this object as its cropper's `src` gets an empty string forever. Bind to `cropQueue()` instead, which is a signal over the live entries; this event is a notification, not a snapshot to hold on to.

outputs.name: cropApplied
outputs.description: A crop was applied, with whatever the round trip cost.

outputs.name: reordered
outputs.description: The user put the files in a new order.

outputs.name: metaChange
outputs.description: A row's `metadataFields` values changed.

outputs.name: removeRefused
outputs.description: `beforeRemove` kept a file.

outputs.name: uploadPaused
outputs.description: The user paused an upload.

components.name: Filter Panel
components.description: A faceted filter panel for product listings: collapsible groups for checkbox lists, color swatches, star ratings and a price range, with per-option counts, a live active-filter chip row and a one-click clear-all. Selection is exposed through two-way selected / price models and a consolidated change output.
whenToUse: The sidebar of a product-listing or search-results page.
A filter drawer on mobile, paired with sv-drawer.
Any catalog view that needs faceted refinement with a live count.

examples.title: Long facets: limit, search, named colours and a stated currency
examples.code:
<sv-filter-panel
  [groups]="groups"
  [maxVisibleOptions]="8"
  [searchableAfter]="12"
  [showColorNames]="true"
  [(selected)]="selected" />

// groups: { id: 'price', label: 'Price', type: 'price', min: 0, max: 500, currency: 'USD' }

examples.title: Stale counts and zero-result facets
examples.code:
<!-- countsStale while the server recomputes; zero-count options are disabled -->
<sv-filter-panel [groups]="groups" [(selected)]="selected"
  [countsStale]="facetsLoading()" [disableEmptyFacets]="true"
  (filterChange)="refetch($event)" />

examples.title: URL sync

customization: `maxVisibleOptions` (or a group's `maxVisible`) shows the first N options of a long facet behind "Show N more"; selected options are always shown. `searchableAfter` (or a group's `searchable`) adds a search box that matches case- and accent-insensitively, and the limit then applies to the matches.
Price groups take an ISO 4217 `currency` for the accessible names and the default symbol; `prefix` still overrides the symbol.
Four facet types: checkbox, color, rating and price.
Collapsible groups with a per-group override and remembered state.
Toggle counts, active chips, clear-all and an Apply footer.
countsStale dims counts during recalculation; disableEmptyFacets (default true) disables zero-count options.
urlParamPrefix namespaces the query parameters serializeToUrl / restoreFromUrl own — override it when two panels share a page.
Card or plain variant to match the surrounding layout.
accessibility: Colour facets can print their names (`[showColorNames]="true"`) beside a decorative swatch, so a colour is never told by colour alone; by default the name is still the swatch's accessible name and tooltip.
A price group with an ISO `currency` names it in both inputs ("Price minimum, in US Dollar") — a bare "$" is five currencies — and shows its symbol when `prefix` is unset.
"Show N more" is a real `<button>` with `aria-expanded`/`aria-controls` over the same list, so focus stays put; the facet search box is named "Search <group>" and announces its match count politely.
Group headers are buttons with aria-expanded; options use real checkboxes and pressed-state buttons.
Color swatches and rating rows expose descriptive labels and aria-pressed.
Zero-count options are disabled with an sr-only ", no results"; stale counts carry an sr-only ", recalculating".
All controls have visible focus rings in light and dark mode.
variants: Stale counts, empty facets & URL sync

inputs.name: groups
inputs.description: Facet groups to render.

inputs.name: heading
inputs.description: Panel heading.

inputs.name: showClearAll
inputs.description: Show the "Clear all" control when filters are active.

inputs.name: showCounts
inputs.description: Show per-option result counts.

inputs.name: showActiveChips
inputs.description: Show the active-filter chip row.

inputs.name: showApply
inputs.description: Batch the selection and emit only when Apply is pressed. On, `filterChange` does not fire per toggle: the selection is a draft until Apply, so on mobile each tap costs no request. Off, every toggle emits.

inputs.name: countsStale
inputs.description: True while the server is recomputing the facet counts. A facet count that does not reflect the current selection is worse than no count. It is a number, so the reader trusts it, and it is wrong — it describes the results of the PREVIOUS query. Counts are dimmed and announced as recalculating rather than left standing as fact.

inputs.name: disableEmptyFacets
inputs.description: Disable facets whose count is zero, so a dead end cannot be selected. A zero-result combination is reachable in one tap and escapable only by guessing which facet caused it. Preventing it is far kinder than the empty state afterwards. An already-SELECTED facet is never disabled, whatever its count says: deselecting has to stay possible, and a selected facet reading zero is usually how the user got into the dead end in the first place.

inputs.name: applyLabel
inputs.description: Apply button label.

inputs.name: clearLabel
inputs.description: Clear-all label.

inputs.name: collapsible
inputs.description: Whether groups can collapse (per-group `collapsible` overrides).

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Visual style.

inputs.name: showColorNames
inputs.description: Print each colour swatch's name beside it, instead of only in its accessible name and tooltip. Colour alone does not say "navy" vs "black" to anyone who cannot tell them apart (WCAG 1.4.1).

inputs.name: maxVisibleOptions
inputs.description: Options a checkbox / colour / rating group shows before a "Show N more" button; `0` shows them all. A group's own `maxVisible` wins. Selected options are always shown, wherever they sit in the list.

inputs.name: searchableAfter
inputs.description: Offer a search box on any option group with at least this many options; `0` never does. A group's own `searchable` wins. Matching ignores case and accents, and the number of matches is announced politely.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP 47 locale for currency names and search matching.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the facets are being fetched. Replaces the groups with a placeholder rather than showing an empty panel.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Failure loading the facets. Showing an empty filter panel instead would tell the user there is nothing to filter by.

inputs.name: selected
inputs.description: Selected values per group id (two-way: `[(selected)]`).

inputs.name: price
inputs.description: Chosen price range per price-group id (two-way: `[(price)]`).

inputs.name: expandedGroups
inputs.description: Ids of option groups opened past their limit with "Show N more". Two-way, so a host can restore it with the rest of the filter state.

inputs.name: urlParamPrefix
inputs.description: Namespace for the query parameters this panel owns. Override when two panels share one page; anything outside the prefix is left alone, so the host's own `?page=2&q=shoes` survives every facet change.

inputs.name: debounceMs
inputs.description: Debounce delay for `filterChange`, in ms. `0` emits immediately.

outputs.name: filterChange
outputs.description: The filter selection changed — refetch. Debounced by `debounceMs`. Distinct from `selectedChange`, which is the output half of the `selected` model.

outputs.name: apply
outputs.description: Emitted when the Apply button is pressed.

outputs.name: clear
outputs.description: Emitted when everything is cleared.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed facet load.

outputs.name: selectedChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `selected` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(selected)]`.

outputs.name: priceChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `price` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(price)]`.

outputs.name: expandedGroupsChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `expandedGroups` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(expandedGroups)]`.

components.name: Form Builder
components.description: Renders a form from a JSON schema — conditional visibility, per-field validation, and a payload with hidden fields pruned out. The three things it exists for are the three a schema form silently gets wrong: a hidden field whose value is still submitted, a required field in a hidden branch that blocks the form with nothing on screen to fix, and a schema whose own mistakes never surface because it came from a database rather than a compiler.
whenToUse: The form’s shape is data — an admin builder, a per-tenant intake form, a survey.
Fields appear and disappear based on other answers, and what is submitted has to match what was on screen.
You need the same visibility and pruning rules on the server: the engine is exported separately from the component.

examples.title: Let a browser agent drive it (WebMCP)
examples.code:
<!-- svWebMcp from @styloviz/core registers signup_describe, signup_… — see /docs/webmcp -->
<sv-form-builder svWebMcp="signup" [schema]="schema" />
<!-- tools: describe, list_fields, set_field, submit, get_payload, get_schema -->

examples.title: Conditional visibility, and what gets submitted
examples.description: A field inside a hidden group is hidden whatever its own condition says, and its value never reaches `submitted`. The component keeps it in memory, so ticking the box back restores what the user typed — destroying it on hide loses the typing of anyone who unticked a box just to read what was underneath.

examples.title: Validation ignores what is not on screen
examples.description: A required field in a hidden branch would otherwise keep the form invalid forever: submit disabled, every visible field green, and the thing blocking the user not rendered at all. A field that is not shown is not asked, so it cannot be unanswered.

examples.title: The schema’s own mistakes
examples.description: A schema arrives from a database or a CMS, so its author has no compiler and often no console — and every one of these is silent. The component renders them rather than logging them.

examples.title: A field kind the builder does not know
examples.description: A schema form’s premise is that the form’s shape is data, so the field kinds are open too: any control the builder does not draw itself is one registered renderer away.
examples.code:
<!-- A template renderer: nothing to import, nothing to inject. -->
<ng-template #rating let-ctx>
  <sv-rating [value]="$any(ctx.value)" (valueChange)="ctx.set($event)" />
</ng-template>

<sv-form-builder [schema]="schema" [(value)]="value" [renderers]="{ rating }" />

<!-- Or a component, registered once and used by every form in the app: -->
<sv-form-builder [renderers]="{ rating: RatingFieldComponent }" ... />

// export class RatingFieldComponent {
//   readonly ctx = inject(SV_FIELD_CONTEXT);
// }

// The context is LIVE — ctx.value, ctx.error, ctx.disabled and
// ctx.asyncStatus are accessors over the component's signals. Read them in a
// template or a computed; copying one into a field freezes it.

// A custom kind is a full citizen: showIf hides it, svPruneHidden prunes it,
// required/minLength/pattern validate it, asyncChecks can check it.
// It coerces as TEXT — see SvFieldKind for when that is the wrong answer.

examples.title: Rules only the server knows
examples.description: The bug this closes is not the request — it is that a form with an unanswered check LOOKS VALID. Press Submit before the check lands and every schema rule passes, so the form submits a value whose server-side guarantee was never established. Invisible in development, where the check answers in 4ms.
examples.code:
<sv-form-builder [schema]="schema" [(value)]="value" [asyncChecks]="checks" />

checks = {
  // Resolve null to accept, or with the message to show.
  username: async (value, ctx) => {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/free?u=${value}`, { signal: ctx.signal });
    return (await res.json()).taken ? 'That username is taken.' : null;
  },
  // A question about TWO fields has to say so, or changing the country
  // leaves the old verdict standing for a combination nobody has checked.
  'company.vat': {
    check: (v, ctx) => verifyVat(v, ctx.form['country'], ctx.signal),
    dependsOn: ['country'],
  },
};

// Validity is three-valued, and submit() waits.
builder.awaitingChecks();  // true — neither valid nor invalid
builder.valid();           // false
await builder.submit();    // runs what has not run, then decides

// REJECTING the promise means the check could not RUN. That blocks the
// submit and says so — reporting a 503 as "that username is taken" sends
// the user off to invent a new name that will be refused the same way.

customization: **Not a `ControlValueAccessor`, and there is no single value for one to carry.** This component has two: `value()` is the working state including hidden fields, and `payload()` is what may be submitted, with those pruned. A CVA exposes one — pick `value` and every host silently submits answers the user could not see; pick `payload` and a user who unticks a box to read what is underneath loses their typing the moment they tick it back.

The contract instead: `[(value)]` is the working state, `payload()` is what to send, and **`await submit()`** returns a promise — it runs any server check that has not run, then emits `submitted` or `rejected`. `valid()` means *established as valid* (no schema errors, no rejected checks, nothing outstanding); `awaitingChecks()` is the middle state Angular's `PENDING` does not cover, because it also includes a check that has not been REQUESTED yet — the debounce window, which is exactly where a user pressing Enter lands.

Field kinds: `text`, `textarea`, `number`, `checkbox`, `select`, `radio`, `date` and `group`. Each renders through the kit’s own control, so a schema form looks like the rest of the app rather than like a form generator.

Constrain each field with `min` / `max` / `minLength` / `maxLength` / `pattern` — the pattern is anchored for you, because an unanchored one matches a substring and quietly accepts anything containing a match.
`showIf` takes three narrow predicates (`equals`, `in`, `truthy`) rather than an expression language, so a schema stays serialisable, diffable in review, and reasonable about visibility.
`eagerErrors` shows every problem immediately; the default reveals them on blur and all at once on a refused submit, because a form that is red before it is touched teaches the user to ignore red.

Layout: `columns="2"` pairs fields side by side once the form's container is about 28rem wide (one column below that, on any screen), a field's `span: 2` takes the whole row, and a group always heads its own; `density` (`comfortable` · `compact`) sets how tightly fields and sections stack. A nested group is a section inside its parent, and the submit row sits apart from the fields.

Every control id is scoped to the form instance (`sv-fb-<n>-<path>`), so two forms built from one schema on one page never share an id. Do not hard-code a control's id: read answers from `value()` and find a section by its `data-sv-fb-group` path.
Call `reset(partial)` to go back to `svSchemaDefaults` merged per level — a spread would lose half of every group.

**Schema evolution.** Store submissions as `{ schemaVersion, value }` and load them through `svMigrateValue(stored, migrations, currentVersion, schema)` before binding. Migrations are yours — one pure `SvSchemaMigration` step per version, because only you know `dept` became `team` rather than being deleted — and a missing step stops the chain (`incomplete: true`) rather than running a later one on input it was not written for. The result also lists `orphaned` keys the current schema does not have: `payload()` prunes those, so a renamed field without a migration is otherwise silently dropped on the next save. `svCoerceToSchema` fixes values that kept their old type (a v1 string in a now-`number` field) on load rather than on first touch.

`renderers` maps a field kind to a `TemplateRef` or a component `Type`, so a schema can use controls this package does not ship. A key matching a built-in kind overrides it — a host that wants its own date control everywhere registers `date`, rather than forking the schema’s vocabulary into "my-date". `SvFieldKind` is open, so a custom kind typechecks while the built-ins still autocomplete.

`asyncChecks` gives a field a server-side rule, keyed by path, with `asyncDebounceMs` for the quiet period. The verdict belongs to a VALUE, not to a field — edit the box and the previous answer is gone rather than stale, which is what stops a form reading green for something nobody checked. Declare `dependsOn` when the answer turns on another field too.

Validity is three-valued: `valid()`, the errors, and `awaitingChecks()` for the state that is neither. `submit()` returns a promise, runs any check that has not run (cutting a counting-down debounce short) and refuses if the value moved while it waited. `busy()` and each row’s `asyncStatus` drive the in-progress copy.
accessibility: Each control is the kit’s own accessible component, so labels, descriptions, required marking and error wiring come from there rather than being re-implemented.
A group renders as a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` that CONTAINS its fields (nested groups nest), so a screen reader announces which section a field belongs to.
Schema problems are rendered in a `role="alert"` region rather than logged, because the person who authored the schema is working in a CMS and has no console.

The submit button is deliberately never disabled: a disabled submit refuses silently, and pressing it is what reveals the form’s objections — which matters most when the offending field is scrolled off screen.

A check in progress is announced with `role="status"`, not `role="alert"`: a field being checked is not something the user got wrong, and an assertive announcement per keystroke-pause would make a form with two checked fields unusable with a screen reader.
variants: Schema-Driven Form — The Three Things It Silently Gets Wrong
A Schema With Mistakes In It

inputs.name: schema
inputs.description: Field definitions to render — each `SvFormField` sets its key, kind, label, validation rules, `showIf` condition and nested `fields`; defaults, errors and the submitted payload derive from it.

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: The working value, including fields that are currently hidden. Two-way bindable. A host that wants what is *submittable* wants `payload()`.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disables every field and the submit button; edits and submits are ignored while true.

inputs.name: submitLabel
inputs.description: Text of the submit button.

inputs.name: density
inputs.description: Spacing between fields and sections — `'compact'` for a dense settings panel, `'comfortable'` for a page-level form.

inputs.name: columns
inputs.description: Lay fields out in two columns once the form's own width allows (a container query, so a form in a narrow side panel stays single-column on any screen). A field's `span: 2` takes the whole row; groups always do.

inputs.name: eagerErrors
inputs.description: Show every error immediately rather than after the field is left. The default is `false` because a form that is red before it is touched teaches the user to ignore red. Errors appear on blur, and all at once on a failed submit — which is the moment they are actually useful.

inputs.name: asyncChecks
inputs.description: Server-side rules, by field path. ```ts checks = { username: async (value, ctx) => { const res = await fetch(`/api/free?u=${value}`, { signal: ctx.signal }); return (await res.json()).taken ? 'That username is taken.': null; }, }; ``` Resolve with `null` to accept and with the message to show. **Rejecting means the check could not run**, which blocks the submit and says so — reporting a 503 as "That username is taken" is a lie the user cannot act on, and treating it as a pass submits the thing the check was guarding.

inputs.name: asyncDebounceMs
inputs.description: Quiet period before a check fires, in milliseconds. A check runs per *value*, not per keystroke, so the debounce is about request volume rather than correctness — pressing Submit cuts a counting-down debounce short rather than waiting it out.

inputs.name: renderers
inputs.description: Draw a field kind this package does not know. Keys are field kinds; values are a `TemplateRef` or a component `Type`. A key matching a built-in kind overrides it. ```html <ng-template #rating let-ctx> <sv-rating [value]="$any(ctx.value)" (valueChange)="ctx.set($event)" /> </ng-template> <sv-form-builder [schema]="schema" [renderers]="{ rating }" /> ``` A component renderer reads `SV_FIELD_CONTEXT` instead. Either way the context is LIVE — `value`, `error`, `disabled` and `asyncStatus` are accessors over the component's signals, so reading one in a template or a `computed` tracks it. Copying it into a field does not. Everything else still applies to a custom kind: `showIf` hides it, `svPruneHidden` prunes it, `required` / `minLength` / `pattern` validate it, and `asyncChecks` can check it. It coerces as TEXT — see `SvFieldKind` for when that is the wrong answer.

outputs.name: submitted
outputs.description: The pruned value, once the form is valid.

outputs.name: rejected
outputs.description: A submit that was refused, with the errors that refused it.

outputs.name: valueChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `value` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(value)]`.

components.name: Form Error Summary
components.description: The list of what is wrong at the top of a long form, with a way into each field — including the ones a collapsed group or a wizard step is currently hiding.
whenToUse: Any form long enough that an invalid field can be off-screen — which in practice is most forms past about six fields.
Any form with collapsible groups, wizard steps or tabs, where a field can be invalid AND not rendered. This is the case a per-field message alone cannot cover.
A short, always-visible form does not need one. Two fields both on screen with their own messages are already reachable, and a summary above them is a second copy of what is already said.

examples.title: The field the form is hiding
examples.description: A long form fails validation, the invalid field is inside a collapsed accordion group or on a wizard step the user has moved past, and so nothing on screen looks wrong — the form simply refuses to go, with no way to find out why. Activating an entry emits `(errorActivated)` FIRST, which is the host's chance to open the group, and focus lands on the field a frame later.

examples.title: Errors in reading order, and only after a submit
examples.description: The list is a map of the page. One whose entries follow whatever order the validators happened to run in is a map nobody can follow — so order them as they appear. And keep it empty until the user has attempted something: a summary on a pristine form tells them they have made mistakes they have not yet had the chance to make.

examples.title: A server rejection, and the recheck it arrives from
examples.description: Not every problem is a field's. "Your card was declined" and "your session expired" reject the SUBMISSION, so they have no control to focus — omit `fieldId` and the entry is listed as text rather than as a link that could only report that it went nowhere. It still counts, because the form is refusing to submit over it. While the answer is being recomputed, `busy` marks the list as the last attempt's verdict (`aria-busy` plus a note) and HOLDS the announcement, so the reader hears the outcome instead of a count that was obsolete when it was spoken.
examples.code:
<sv-form-error-summary [errors]="errors()" [busy]="submitting()" />

async submit(): Promise<void> {
  this.submitting.set(true);
  const rejected = await this.api.pay(this.form.value);   // 402
  this.serverErrors.set(
    rejected ? [{ label: 'Payment', message: 'Your card was declined' }] : [],
  );
  this.submitting.set(false);   // the summary speaks now, once
}

examples.title: The second failed submit
examples.description: `autoFocus` moves focus here when the summary appears — that is, when the list goes from empty to non-empty. A repeat submit with the same errors is not a transition, so nothing moves and the user is left wondering whether the button worked. `focusSummary()` is the reliable half of the pair; call it from the submit handler.

customization: `heading` overrides the wording, with `{n}` substituted for the count; the default pluralises between "There is a problem" and "There are N problems".
`headingLevel` (2–4) places it in the page outline — it renders a real heading element, not a styled div.
`autoFocus` (on by default) moves focus here when the summary appears; `focusSummary()` does it on demand for a repeat submit.
`customClass` adds classes to the region.
`busy` marks the list as being rechecked: `aria-busy` on the region, a `busyMessage` note (default "Rechecking…"), and every announcement held until the recheck lands.
An entry with no `fieldId` is a submission-level problem — rendered as text, counted in the heading, and never a jump that could fail.
accessibility: A documented WCAG technique (G139, and the error-identification half of 3.3.1) rather than an invention: the list at the top of the form, each entry linking to its field.

It is a focusable region (`tabindex="-1"`) named by its own heading, NOT a `role="alert"`. An alert interrupts, and this list changes on every submit — the reader would get the whole thing re-announced over the top of the field they had just reached. Focus arrives once instead, announcing the heading and the count, and the reader moves through at their own pace.

Entries are buttons, not anchors, because the fields worth linking to are the ones not currently in the DOM. `(errorActivated)` fires first so the host can reveal the field, and focus is attempted on the next frame.

A target that is not itself focusable — a `<fieldset>` holding a required radio group, say — falls through to the first focusable control inside it. Sending the user to the group and leaving focus on `<body>` would be the same silent nothing the component exists to prevent.
Focus uses `preventScroll` and then centres the field deliberately, so it arrives with its label and its message both visible rather than scrolled twice to the nearest edge.

A list that CHANGES while the reader is elsewhere on the page is announced politely through the kit's one announcer — a server error joining a list already on screen was otherwise known only to someone looking at it. The announcement and the focus move are exclusive (focusing the region already reads the heading and the count), a burst of async validators supersedes itself under one key rather than queueing counts the user has passed, and a change that does not change the count says nothing.

An entry whose field could not be reached says so, and emits `(reachFailed)`. Silence there is worse than no summary: the user has been told where the problem is and that they cannot go to it, with no way to tell a broken link from a field that is merely off-screen.
variants: A field the form is hiding
Form Error Summary — No Errors, One, Several, Server & Rechecking
Form Error Summary — A Checkout That Focuses the Summary

inputs.name: errors
inputs.description: Every invalid field, in the order they appear in the form. Reading order, not validation order. The list is a map of the page, and a map whose entries are in the order the validators happened to run is a map the reader cannot follow. Pass an empty array while the form is untouched: a summary that appears before the user has attempted anything tells them they have made mistakes they have not yet had the chance to make.

inputs.name: heading
inputs.description: The heading above the list. `{n}` is replaced with the number of problems.

inputs.name: headingLevel
inputs.description: Heading level, so the summary sits correctly in the page outline. It renders a real `<h2>`–`<h4>`, not a styled `<div>`. A screen-reader user navigating by heading is the reader most likely to be looking for this, and a `<div>` with big text is invisible to that.

inputs.name: autoFocus
inputs.description: Move focus here when the summary appears — that is, when the error list goes from empty to non-empty. **A second failed submit with the same errors is not a transition**, so this will not fire for it, and the user is left where they were with no indication anything happened. Call focusSummary from your submit handler for that case; it is the reliable half of this pair, and `autoFocus` is the one that means you usually do not have to remember.

inputs.name: busy
inputs.description: The list is being rechecked — an async validator or a server round-trip is in flight. What is on screen during a server submit is the last attempt's verdict, and a summary that asserts it while the answer is being recomputed is stating something it does not currently know. This marks it as such: `aria-busy`, a visible note, and — the part that matters most — every announcement is HELD rather than skipped, so the reader hears the outcome of the recheck instead of a count that was already obsolete when it was spoken.

inputs.description: The note shown while busy.

inputs.description: Extra classes on the root region.

outputs.description: An entry was activated. Emitted **before** the focus attempt, so a host can open the accordion group, switch the wizard step or select the tab that contains the field.

outputs.name: reachFailed
outputs.description: The field could not be reached even after `(errorActivated)` had a frame to reveal it — `'not-found'` when nothing has that id, `'not-focusable'` when something does but neither it nor anything inside it can take focus. Almost always a wrong `fieldId`. Worth logging.

components.name: Gantt Chart
components.description: Portfolio roadmaps with command bus, undo/redo, drag & drop, dependency engine, a computed critical path (real forward/backward pass, total float in days, all four link types with lag), baselines, resource leveling, MS Project XML import/export and row virtualization.
whenToUse: Planning and tracking project schedules with dependencies and resourcing.
You need critical path, baselines, or resource leveling on a roadmap.
For a simple status board without dates, use the Kanban Board.

examples.title: Let a browser agent drive it (WebMCP)
examples.code:
<!-- svWebMcp from @styloviz/core registers plan_describe, plan_… — see /docs/webmcp -->
<sv-gantt-chart svWebMcp="plan" [tasks]="tasks" />
<!-- tools: describe, list_tasks, update_task, set_zoom, scroll_to_date, level_resources -->

examples.title: Lag on a link
examples.description: A link carries the gap, so it follows when the predecessor slips. Typing the gap into the successor's dates instead looks identical on the chart and does not.

examples.title: Read the float, not just the flag
examples.description: `taskFloat()` is how many days each task can slip before the project finish moves — the question a planner asks far more often than "is this critical".
examples.code:
<sv-gantt-chart #gantt [tasks]="tasks" [highlightCritical]="true" />

// days of room on a given task, and the sentence for a tooltip
gantt.taskFloat().get('design');   // → 3
gantt.floatLabel('design');        // → '3 days of float.'

examples.title: Surface a dependency cycle
examples.description: Two tasks each waiting for the other can never be scheduled. They are named rather than quietly drawn.
examples.code:
@if (gantt.scheduleCycles().length) {

These tasks depend on each other and cannot be scheduled: {{ gantt.scheduleCycles()[0].join(', ') }}

}

customization: Zoom from quarter-hours to decades: `scale` takes `minute` (15-minute columns), `hour`, `day`, `week`, `month`, `quarter`, `year` and `decade`. A task given a time (`2026-03-04T07:30`) draws at that time, and Zoom to fit picks the finest scale whose columns fit the view.

Resource load and levelling: `sv-gantt-resource-histogram` draws each person's load against capacity, and `svGanttLevelResources` moves tasks later, never earlier, until nobody is over capacity. It reports every move with its reason, plus anything it could not resolve.

Rollups, S-curve and progress line: `svGanttRollup` gives summary dates, planned dates and working-day-weighted progress; `sv-gantt-s-curve` / `svGanttSCurve` plot planned against earned work; and `progressLineDate` draws the progress line through every task.
PNG and PDF export: `exportPng()` and `exportPdf()` (also in the Export menu) snapshot the chart through `@styloviz-pro/export`.
Configurable columns, holidays and work week.

**The scheduling invariants, as guarantees rather than current behaviour.** Links: `fs` starts the successor no earlier than the predecessor finishes, `ss` no earlier than it starts, `ff` finishes no earlier than it finishes, `sf` finishes no earlier than it starts — each plus `lag`, in whole days, negative for a lead, defaulting to `fs` when no type is given. Every one is a floor and never a ceiling: a task is never pulled earlier than the date you gave it, so hand-typed dates survive. `sf` is the one that surprises — "may not finish before the other starts" is satisfied by being early, so an `sf` successor can legitimately land entirely before its predecessor.

**Pinned, unschedulable and derived.** A `scheduleMode: 'manual'` task keeps its dates whatever its predecessors require, and still constrains its own successors. A task in a cycle keeps the dates it was given, is named in `scheduleCycles()`, and is never critical — a plan that cannot be executed has no critical path. A dependency naming an absent task is ignored and reported. `projectFinish` is the latest early finish; `totalFloat` is late start minus early start in whole days; a task is critical exactly when its float is zero and it is not in a cycle. Spans are whole calendar days, so a DST transition inside one changes nothing.

**Resource leveling.** Only ever moves a task later, never earlier; preserves every duration in calendar days; leaves no two tasks of one assignee sharing a day, including the handover day; is idempotent, so a second pass moves nothing; touches only leaf tasks that have an assignee; and costs one undoable command however many tasks move.

**MS Project XML fidelity, field by field.** Carried unchanged: title, start, end, progress, `scheduleMode`, `baselineStart` / `baselineEnd`, assignee, group, lane, priority, status, tags, summary, colour, WBS, split `segments`, and all four `constraints` bounds. Carried in meaning but re-keyed: `id`, `parentId`, `children` (flattened to `parentId`) and `dependencies[].taskId`, because MSPDI identifies tasks by integer `UID`. Not carried, deliberately: `ownerId` (re-derived from the file's assignments, so writing it too would give one fact two sources of truth), `reallocated` (computed by the levelling pass, never authored) and `milestone: false` (absent and false say the same thing).

**Where the fidelity comes from, and what MS Project itself will honour.** Link `lag` is written as MSPDI `LinkLag` in days, and baselines and `scheduleMode` as `<Baseline>` and `<Manual>` — all native fields, so MS Project schedules against them. The fields MS Project has no column for — group, colour, lane, status, tags, `segments` and `constraints` — travel in `<Notes>` as bracketed markers, so this kit round-trips them while MS Project shows them as text. `constraints` is the one place its model is genuinely narrower: it holds one constraint per task where this kit holds up to four bounds, so its own scheduler will not enforce them on a file it opens.

An imported colour is validated before it is used: `color` reaches the DOM as a class list, so a file may only name colour utilities (`bg-`, `text-`, `border-`, `ring-`, `from-`, `via-`, `to-`, optionally `dark:`-qualified) and only a few of them. A file that tries to hand a bar layout classes gets the default colour instead of painting over your page. One consequence for your own data: an arbitrary-value class such as `bg-[#ff0000]` does not survive a round trip — brackets are what delimits a marker — so use palette utilities on `color` if the plan will be exported.

`maxTimelineColumns` (default 480) caps the time axis. Rows are virtualized on height; columns are bounded by coarsening the scale, so a plan whose span grows over time cannot silently turn into thousands of columns. Raise it when rendering to paper or a very wide screen, lower it for embedded and mobile hosts.
Scheduling modes, baselines and dependency links, each with optional `lag` in days (negative for a lead).

A real critical path method: forward and backward pass, `taskFloat()` in whole days, `scheduleCycles()` for unschedulable data, and all four link types honoured in both directions. Manually scheduled tasks stay put and still constrain what follows them.
`tasksChangeRequest` (with `rollback()`), `rangeChange`, `loading` / `error` / `retry` and `pendingTaskIds` make it wireable to a real planner API; `tasksChange` remains for hosts that only persist.
accessibility: The resource histogram and the S-curve each carry a hidden table of their figures. Over-capacity bars are hatched as well as red, and the S-curve says the latest variance in words.

A bar's position IS its dates, so the chart publishes a table alongside it — task, start, end, progress, status and assignee, one row per visible row and in the same order. Nothing else on the page carries those dates. It mirrors what is drawn: collapsed children are absent, a nested chart gains a Parent column so the hierarchy is not left to the indent, and a milestone reads "Milestone" rather than a second identical date.
A one-line overview above the table gives the row count, the span the schedule covers and how many rows are critical or at risk — the shape of the picture, which the rows can only imply.
A resource-view header names its own task count and reads its number as "% utilised", because that column means utilisation there and a listener has no indent to tell them the row is a grouping.
The chart is a focusable region with a labelled toolbar; toolbar actions expose disabled state via `aria-disabled`.
Keyboard task selection and movement; command notices use polite live regions and loading sets `aria-busy`.
Row headers and dates are screen-reader friendly.

inputs.description: The most time columns the timeline will draw. Past this, `scale` coarsens a step at a time — day → week → month → quarter — until it fits. This is the render-side limit on the time axis (rows are virtualised; time columns are not). Every column becomes two DOM elements, in the header and in the grid backdrop, and render time grows faster than the column count: a ten-year plan left at `day` is 3661 columns and 14851 nodes, a forty-year plan 14619 columns and 58683 nodes, and the second takes about twenty times as long to render. It protects a plan whose `scale` was set to `'day'` and that later grows to span years. The default is generous — 480 columns is over a year of days, or nine years of weeks — so ordinary plans never notice it. outputs.name: tasksChange
outputs.description: Emitted whenever the working task set changes through user interaction (add / edit / delete / indent / move / bar drag / undo / redo / reset). Payload is the full, current task list — persist it to your backend.

outputs.name: selectionChange
outputs.description: Emitted when the selected task changes. Payload is the selected task, or `null` when the selection is cleared.

outputs.name: tasksChangeRequest
outputs.description: The same change as `tasksChange`, with a way to undo it.
