components.name: Gauge / Speedometer
components.description: Half-circle gauge with colored range bands, animated progress arc, needle, tick marks, an optional target notch and configurable min/max. The active band and the distance to the target are written out, not left to colour. Pure SVG.
whenToUse: Showing a single value against a range with a "good/warning/critical" feel.
KPIs like utilization, score, speed or health where thresholds matter.
For a plain percentage with no bands, a Progress Ring is simpler.

When the reading has to be compared precisely — against a target, against last period, or across several KPIs side by side — use the Bullet Chart. A gauge spends a whole dial on one number and its arc is hard to read to the unit; a bullet chart is the linear gauge: the same bands and target notch on a straight bar that takes a fraction of the space and stacks into a column of comparable rows.
customization: Colored range bands and thresholds, with the active band named in text under the reading.

An optional `target` notch on the scale, with the distance to it stated in words and `targetLabel` for the wording. Every variant draws the marker. A target outside the scale is still measured against as bound — 40 against 500 on a 0–100 scale is "460% below target", not "60% below" a pinned 100 — while its marker is pinned to the end of the scale and a line under the reading, repeated in the accessible name, says the target is off the scale.
Needle and tick customization.
Animated arc with reduced-motion fallback.
Responsive: all three variants scale down to fit narrow containers (`max-w-full h-auto`) while keeping their aspect ratio, instead of overflowing at their fixed `size`.
accessibility: An unusable scale is said, never drawn silently: `max <= min` or a non-finite bound leaves the dial empty — no bands, no target notch, no band status — and the frame notice and the accessible name state the bounds and why the reading cannot be placed. An empty or full arc would look like a real reading at the end of its scale. `sv-radial-bar-chart` does the same for a chart-wide `max` that is not above zero.
The gauge is `role="img"` with a generated value/range summary (override via `ariaLabel`), and is keyboard-focusable.
Animations honour `prefers-reduced-motion`; Enter/Space (or click) emits `selected` with the current value, the active range and the target. Range thresholds are described, not color-only.

The active band is written out under the reading, and so is the distance to the target. The band colours carry their whole meaning in hue, which is nothing to a screen reader, unreliable for a reader with a colour-vision deficiency, and gone in print; the target notch is a mark on an arc and has nothing to say either, so both travel in the accessible name as well.
variants: Read Against a Target, and Say So in Words
Radial Bar — Values the Rings Cannot Hold

inputs.name: value
inputs.description: The current reading, or `null` when the metric has none — which is what the gauge's empty state means. Defaults to `null`, not to a number, so a dashboard that failed to load its metric shows the empty state rather than a reading.

inputs.name: min
inputs.description: Minimum value of the scale.

inputs.name: max
inputs.description: Maximum value of the scale.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Caption shown under the value.

inputs.name: suffix
inputs.description: Unit appended to the value (e.g. %).

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Gauge style variant.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Overall diameter in pixels.

inputs.name: thickness
inputs.description: Arc thickness in pixels.

inputs.name: ranges
inputs.description: Colored threshold bands along the scale.

inputs.name: target
inputs.description: A target or reference the reading is meant to be measured against. A gauge without one shows a number and a colour, and the reader has to already know what good looks like. The target is drawn as a notch on the scale and stated in words beside the reading, with the distance to it — "8 below target" is the sentence a dashboard is usually being read for. `null` (the default) draws nothing at all: an invented target would be worse than none. A target off the scale is still measured against as bound; its marker is pinned to the end of the scale and a line under the reading says so. Every variant draws the marker.

inputs.name: targetLabel
inputs.description: Wording for the reference marker.

inputs.name: showNeedle
inputs.description: Show the value needle.

inputs.name: animated
inputs.description: Animate the arc/needle on value change.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible name override. Falls back to a generated value/range summary.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Extra CSS classes applied to the root wrapper.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the reading is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. A bare string is accepted; use `toSvDataError()` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse` and get sensible retry behaviour.

inputs.name: emptyMessage
inputs.description: Copy for the empty state.

inputs.name: filtered
inputs.description: Distinguishes "no reading at all" from "nothing matched the current filters".

outputs.name: selected
outputs.description: Emitted when the gauge is clicked or activated via keyboard (Enter/Space). Named `selected` rather than `select`, which is a native DOM event name.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load.

components.name: Gift Card
components.description: A gift-card / e-gift visual: a locale-formatted denomination or remaining balance, a redeemable code that is masked, gated behind the host's own authorization and re-hidden on a timer, plus redeemed / void / expired states, a zone-aware expiry, recipient, sender and an optional greeting. Five gradient themes with a decorative ribbon and shimmer.
whenToUse: A live preview beside a gift-card purchase or gifting form.
An e-gift confirmation email or order receipt.
The account wallet, showing a redeemable balance and code.
A support console, where the last four identifies the card and nobody needs the code.

examples.title: Answer the reveal gate with your own step-up
examples.code:
<!-- Pressing Reveal emits revealRequest instead of showing the code. -->
<sv-gift-card
  [amount]="100"
  code="STZ 4H9K 22QX 8PLM"
  [revealAuthorized]="verified()"
  (revealRequest)="verify()" />

async verify(): Promise<void> {
  this.verified.set(await this.auth.stepUp('reveal-gift-code'));
}

examples.title: Audit a copy without logging the code
examples.code:
<sv-gift-card [amount]="50" [code]="card.code" (codeCopied)="audit.record('gift_card.copied', $event)" />

// $event is { last4: 'EFGH', at: Date, viaReveal: true } — the code is not in it.

examples.title: Remaining balance and a zone-aware expiry
examples.code:
<!-- 12.40 becomes the large figure, 50.00 sits beside it with a bar.
     '2028-12-31' means the END of 31 December in Europe/Berlin. -->
<sv-gift-card
  [amount]="50"
  [balance]="12.4"
  expiresAt="2028-12-31"
  timeZone="Europe/Berlin" />

examples.title: A spent or cancelled card
examples.code:
<sv-gift-card [amount]="50" [code]="card.code" status="redeemed" />
<!-- Drains to grey, shows a Redeemed chip and withdraws the reveal control.
     A balance of 0 does the same without being told. -->

customization: Five gradient themes (aurora, gold, rose, midnight, mint).
Toggle the amount, redeem-code row, code masking and the copy button.
Reveal gate: requireAuthorization, revealAuthorized, revealRequest, and revealTimeout for the auto-hide (0 disables it).
balance renders what is left against the face value, with a bar; 0 reads as redeemed.
status of active / redeemed / void, plus expired derived from expiresAt and timeZone.
now injects the clock, for tests or for a card that should flip while it is open.
Every label is an input: redeemedLabel, expiredLabel, voidLabel, remainingLabel, revealLabel, hideLabel, verifyLabel, copyLabel, copiedLabel, copyFailedLabel.
Recipient, sender, greeting and a validity line.
Custom brand name and amount caption.
accessibility: The reveal control is a real button whose label says what pressing it will do — verify, reveal, or hide — and it activates on Enter and Space.
The copy button is a real button with its own label; the outcome is announced once through a status region, not on every tick.
The auto-hide countdown is hidden from assistive tech, since the button label already carries the fact and a per-second live figure would repeat itself.
The state chip is text, not a colour: Redeemed, Void and Expired are read out, and the chip declares its own background and ink so the pair is contrast-checkable on all five gradients.
A spent card is desaturated with a luminance-preserving grayscale filter rather than dimmed with opacity, so the measured ink still clears AA.
The ribbon, gift mark, shimmer and balance bar are decorative and hidden from assistive tech.
Each theme carries the one ink measured against all three of its own gradient stops, so contrast holds in light and dark mode.

inputs.name: brand
inputs.description: Brand / store name shown top-left.

inputs.name: amount
inputs.description: Gift-card value.

inputs.name: currency
inputs.description: ISO 4217 currency code.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP 47 locale for number formatting.

inputs.name: code
inputs.description: Redeemable code. Grouped into blocks of 4 when it has no separators of its own; a punctuated code like `FRESH-GIFT-2K` is printed as written.

inputs.name: recipient
inputs.description: Recipient name (To).

inputs.name: sender
inputs.description: Sender name (From).

inputs.name: message
inputs.description: Optional greeting / message.

inputs.name: expiry
inputs.description: Validity line as free text, e.g. "Valid through 12/28". Display only: it carries no expiry logic, so a card whose text has gone stale still reads as active. Pass `expiresAt` to have the card actually expire, and this is used only as the fallback when `expiresAt` is null.

inputs.name: expiresAt
inputs.description: When the card stops being redeemable. A `Date`, or an ISO string. A string with `Z` or an offset names an instant and is taken as-is; a bare `2028-12-31` or an offsetless `2028-12-31T18:00` is read as wall-clock time in `timeZone`, and a bare date means the END of that day there. See `wallClockToInstant`.

inputs.name: timeZone
inputs.description: The zone `expiresAt` is written in — the merchant's, normally, since that is whose midnight the terms mean. IANA name, e.g. `'Europe/Berlin'`. Falls back to UTC, never to the reader's own zone: a card must not expire at a different moment for each customer.

inputs.name: now
inputs.description: The clock expiry is measured against — for tests, and for a host that wants the card to flip while it is on screen by feeding its own tick. Left null it reads `Date.now()` when the inputs change, which is right for a card the reader opens and closes; it does NOT tick on its own, because a permanent interval in a display component costs more than it buys.

inputs.name: status
inputs.description: What the host knows about the card. `expired` is not accepted here — it is derived from `expiresAt` — and a declared status wins over both expiry and a zero balance, because "redeemed" says more than "expired" about a card that is both.

inputs.name: balance
inputs.description: Amount still on the card, when it differs from the face value. Null means the card is worth its face value — not that the balance is unknown, which is indistinguishable to a reader and so is not offered.

inputs.name: requireAuthorization
inputs.description: Whether pressing Reveal needs the host's say-so. On by default: the caller who has already re-authenticated the user says so by setting `revealAuthorized`, and the caller who has not gets an event to act on instead of a code on screen.

inputs.name: revealAuthorized
inputs.description: The host has verified the person in front of the screen recently enough to show them the code. Set it after a password prompt, a step-up, a fresh login.

inputs.name: revealTimeout
inputs.description: How long a revealed code stays on screen, in ms. 0 disables the auto-hide. A code revealed on a screen someone else can see is a code spent by whoever is behind you, and the reader who reveals it has no reason to remember to hide it again. 20 seconds is long enough to read twelve characters aloud.

inputs.name: allowCopy
inputs.description: Offer a copy button once the code is actually visible.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Gradient theme.

inputs.name: showCode
inputs.description: Show the redeem-code row.

inputs.name: maskCode
inputs.description: Mask all but the last four of the code until revealed.

inputs.name: privacy
inputs.description: Declare that this session is recorded, screen-shared or replayed. While set, the code stays masked to its last four whatever `maskCode` or `revealed` say, the reveal and copy controls go away, and the card says why. An app-wide `provideSvSensitivePrivacy()` does the same while this is left unset. A declaration, not a detection — a page cannot observe a capture it did not start itself.

inputs.name: withheldLabel
inputs.default: 'Hidden while this screen may be shared'
inputs.description: Shown in place of the reveal control while `privacy` withholds the code.

inputs.name: showAmount
inputs.description: Show the denomination.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Small caption above the amount.

inputs.name: redeemedLabel
inputs.description: State chip for a spent card.

inputs.name: expiredLabel
inputs.description: State chip for a card past its expiry.

inputs.name: voidLabel
inputs.description: State chip for a cancelled card.

inputs.name: remainingLabel
inputs.description: Caption on the remaining balance.

inputs.name: revealLabel
inputs.description: Reveal button, when the code is hidden.

inputs.name: hideLabel
inputs.description: Reveal button, when the code is on screen.

inputs.name: verifyLabel
inputs.description: Reveal button, when the host has still to authorize.

inputs.name: copyLabel
inputs.description: Copy button.

inputs.name: copiedLabel
inputs.description: Confirmation after a copy.

inputs.name: copyFailedLabel
inputs.description: Shown when the clipboard is unavailable or refused.

inputs.name: revealed
inputs.description: Whether the masked code is revealed (two-way: `[(revealed)]`). A host writing this is authorization by definition — it is the host's own code making the decision — so the gate applies only to the user-initiated path.

outputs.name: revealRequest
outputs.description: The user asked to see the code while `requireAuthorization` was on and `revealAuthorized` was off. Step up, then set `revealAuthorized` — or set `revealed` directly once the challenge passes.

outputs.name: codeCopied
outputs.description: The code was copied. Log it: see `GiftCardCopyEvent` for what it carries.

outputs.name: revealedChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `revealed` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(revealed)]`.

components.name: Input Group
components.description: Semantic fieldset wrapper for grouping related form fields, with vertical/horizontal layout, bordered or filled variants, fused edges and an optional collapsible toggle.
whenToUse: Grouping related fields into a labelled section within a larger form.
You want a semantic fieldset/legend with consistent spacing and optional collapse.
For unrelated page regions use a Card or layout container instead.
components.usage:
<sv-group label="Address" description="Where should we ship?" variant="bordered">
  <sv-input-field label="Street" />
  <sv-input-field label="City" />
</sv-group>

examples.title: Named without a visible label
examples.description: A group is exposed as `role="group"` only with a name — `label` or `ariaLabel`. Unnamed, it is a plain wrapper (no `role`, no `aria-invalid`), and one that carries an error or a collapse warns in dev.

customization: Set `orientation` (vertical/horizontal) and `gap`, then pick a `variant` (default, bordered, filled, card).
Use `fused` to merge adjacent control edges or `divide` to add separators between fields.
Make the section `collapsible` with a two-way `[(collapsed)]` state and a heading `label` / `description`.
accessibility: Renders a `role="group"` named via `aria-labelledby` → the heading `label`, so the group is announced for its controls.
Collapsible groups expose `aria-expanded` / `aria-controls` on the toggle and hide the content region when collapsed.

Group-level validation ("Select at least one") goes in `errorMessage`: a `role="alert"` slot, with `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` on the group container, which also becomes programmatically focusable (`tabindex="-1"`) while invalid so an error summary can reach it.

Pass `errorCount` (the number of invalid fields inside). While the group is collapsed it shows as a badge with a full sr-only sentence ("3 fields need attention"), named by both the container and the collapse toggle. With `expandOnError` (default on) a programmatic collapse over an error is refused and a collapsed group re-opens when an error appears; a collapse the user asks for is still honoured.
Projected fields keep their own native labels and focus order; ids are generated per instance.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Section label shown above children.

inputs.name: description
inputs.description: Optional description text below the label.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible name for a group with no visible `label`. The group is only exposed as `role="group"` when it has a name — `label` or this — because an unnamed group is announced as "group" and nothing else, which is worse than no group at all. A layout-only wrapper (Split Button's two halves) stays role-less.

inputs.name: orientation
inputs.description: Layout direction of children.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Visual style variant.

inputs.name: gap
inputs.description: Gap between children (ignored when fused=true).

inputs.name: fused
inputs.description: Fuse children edge-to-edge — removes gap and unifies border-radius. Use for button groups, input addons and toolbars.

inputs.name: divide
inputs.description: Add dividing lines between children. Direction matches orientation (divide-y vertical, divide-x horizontal).

inputs.name: collapsible
inputs.description: Whether the group is collapsible.

inputs.name: collapsed
inputs.description: Desired collapsed state (requires `collapsible=true`).

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: A validation message about the group as a whole — "Select at least one option", "These dates overlap". Rendered in an `role="alert"` slot, pointed at by the container's `aria-describedby`, and paired with `aria-invalid` on the `role="group"`. **There is deliberately no `serverError` here**, unlike every field control in the kit. `createFieldError` self-expires a server rejection against the value it was reported about; a group owns no value and cannot see its children change, so the anchor could never move. A self-expiring error that never expires is worse than not offering one — a group-level rejection from the server goes here, and the host clears it when it re-validates.

inputs.name: errorCount
inputs.description: How many fields inside this group are currently invalid. Rendered as a badge on the header **while the group is collapsed**, which is the only time it tells the user something they cannot already see. Expanded, the errors are on screen and a second count beside the legend is noise. The host owns this number: the group projects arbitrary content and has no business reaching into it to count `aria-invalid`.

inputs.name: expandOnError
inputs.description: Never leave an error hidden behind a collapsed header.

outputs.name: collapsedChange
outputs.description: The group's collapsed state changed. Always carries the **real** state, including when that is not the state that was asked for: a refused collapse emits `false`, and an auto-expand emits `false` too, so a host mirroring `collapsed` is never left out of sync with what is on screen.

components.name: Guardrail Panel
components.description: Safety policy as an operating surface: the rules, what they caught, and the answer the policy actually produced. 3 variants: rules, feed and redaction preview.
whenToUse: Tuning a safety policy, where the question is not how many things it caught but what it did to the output.
Reviewing PII redaction before it ships, so an over-redacted answer is caught by a human rather than by a customer.
Auditing which rules earn their latency — a policy grows rules and never loses them.

examples.title: A policy tuned to your own traffic
examples.code:
<!-- Every one of these four is a policy question wearing a number, and
     every default is about somebody else's traffic. lowConfidenceMatch
     is a PROBABILITY (0-1): passing 70 would mean "70% confidence" and
     make every match a guess, so the component refuses it, keeps the
     documented default, and says so once in a dev warning. -->
<sv-guardrail-panel
  [rules]="rules()"
  [events]="events()"
  [lowConfidenceMatch]="0.85"
  [overRedactionPct]="50"
  [destructiveRunChars]="400"
  [dormantMinEvents]="40" />

customization: `[revealScope]` decides who sees the original text behind a redaction: `on-request` (the default — the role allows it and the reader asks for that one event), `all` (a role whose job is reading raw matches all day, because a reviewer told to check two hundred matches cannot click two hundred times) or `none`. The feed masks **by span**, using the ranges the policy itself found, so it is offset-exact — which is why it does not hit the objection that keeps the pack-wide pattern policy out of this component. Every reveal fires `(revealRequested)` so the host can log who looked at what; hiding it again does not, because nobody needs an audit trail of somebody closing a panel. The redaction preview's **As generated** view is the same reveal under the same scope: under `none` the control is absent and the preview stays on the delivered text; under `on-request` showing the original adds the event to the shared `[(revealedEventIds)]` and fires the same `(revealRequested)`, so one audit log covers both surfaces; under `all` it is a plain view switch. The preview opens masked in every scope, including for an event already revealed in the feed.

`[editable]` false shows every rule and its state with no controls — a guardrail toggle is an authorization decision and the component does not know the role, and a policy nobody can see is a policy nobody revisits. The handler refuses as well as the control disappearing, so a host calling it directly cannot change a policy either.

`(ruleToggle)` carries `{ rule, enabled, observedEnabled, at }`. Two operators disabling the same rule during an incident is the ordinary case: the second toggle is a **no-op, not a second change**, and an audit log that records it as one describes an event that never happened. `svRuleToggleIsStale(toggle, current)` is the comparison. `[pendingRuleIds]` disables a rule while its change is in flight, so one click cannot fire the same privileged change twice.

`[policyVersion]` and `[policyHistory]` (newest first, in the host’s own order — parsing '2 Sept' and 'yesterday' to sort would invent an ordering) render the version and the last change with its author, because 'who turned this off, and when' is the first question asked after an incident.

The pack-wide privacy policy deliberately does NOT apply to this panel. Every span here is a pair of offsets into the event text, so masking that text first would shift every offset after it and the highlighting would colour the wrong characters; and this is the surface where an operator reads what their own redaction policy did, so a second invisible layer would hide the over-redaction evidence the panel exists to show.
`rules` and `events` are inputs and both default to empty; import `DEMO_RULES` / `DEMO_EVENTS` for a demo.
Three layouts via `variant`: `rules` (the policy in review order), `feed` (what it saw, newest first) and `redaction` (one event before and after).

Overlapping spans are merged before anything is masked. Two rules matching the same address produce overlapping ranges, and splicing them one at a time shifts every offset after the first replacement.
A merged run keeps the LOWEST confidence and the STRONGEST action of its contributors: a run containing a guess is a guess, and a `block` overlapping a `redact` is a block.
`[overRedactionPct]` (30) and `[destructiveRunChars]` (120) each independently flag a redaction that probably destroyed the answer — they catch different failures, one scattered and one contiguous.
`[dormantMinEvents]` (200) is the traffic needed before "this rule never fired" means anything. Disabled rules are never called dormant: they cost nothing.

All four thresholds are inputs defaulting to the exported `SV_LOW_CONFIDENCE_MATCH`, `SV_OVER_REDACTION_PCT`, `SV_DESTRUCTIVE_RUN_CHARS` and `SV_DORMANT_MIN_EVENTS`, which are also exported for direct callers of `svRuleStats` / `svRedactionImpact` / `svIsUncertainMatch` — each of those takes the thresholds as an optional last argument. `thresholds()` reports what the component settled on, and `svResolveGuardrailThresholds` is exported so a host can compute the same answer.
Emits `ruleToggle` and `eventSelect`; `selectedEventId` is two-way, so a feed row moves the preview.
accessibility: Each rule row states its action, hits and the dormancy caveat in its accessible name, not only in a badge.
Blocked and redacted are given visibly different colours as well as different words, because one of them is a user who got nothing.
The redaction toggle reports `aria-pressed`; masked runs carry a title naming the rule and its confidence.
variants: Redaction — The View Every Guardrail Product Omits
Rules — The Dead One Is at the Top

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the policy is being fetched; shows a skeleton in place of the panel.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure, shown as an error panel in place of the content. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Presentation: the policy, the feed, or one event's text.

inputs.name: rules
inputs.description: The policy.

inputs.name: events
inputs.description: What the policy has seen.

inputs.name: selectedEventId
inputs.description: The event whose text the `redaction` variant shows. Two-way, because selecting a row in the feed should move it. Falls back to the first event that actually had something masked — a redaction preview opening on an untouched answer teaches nothing.

inputs.name: mask
inputs.description: What a masked run is replaced with.

inputs.name: revealScope
inputs.description: Who may see the original text behind a redaction. The redaction reviewer sees exactly what the redaction exists to hide. Unavoidable for the person judging whether a rule fired correctly — and not a reason to render every event's raw text to everyone who opens the panel, on a surface that gets screenshotted into tickets and shared over calls. `'on-request'` needs the role *and* a click on that event; `'all'` is for a role whose job is reading raw matches all day, because a reviewer who clicks reflexively two hundred times is not consenting to anything.

inputs.name: editable
inputs.description: Whether the reader may change the policy. A guardrail toggle is an authorization decision, and the component does not know the role. Set it false and the rules stay listed and readable with no controls — a policy a reader cannot see is a policy nobody revisits, so read-only is the right shape rather than an empty panel.

inputs.name: pendingRuleIds
inputs.description: Ids of rules with a toggle in flight. Their controls disable, so a second click cannot fire the same privileged change twice.

inputs.name: policyVersion
inputs.description: The policy's version, as the host's system of record names it.

inputs.name: policyHistory
inputs.description: Recorded changes, newest first. Ordered by the host, not sorted here. These are display strings from whatever keeps the audit log, and parsing them to sort would invent an ordering out of "2 Sept" and "yesterday".

inputs.name: now
inputs.description: Clock for the toggle payload, injectable so a test is not at the mercy of the wall clock.

inputs.name: lowConfidenceMatch
inputs.description: Confidence below which a match counts as a guess, `0`–`1`. Every threshold on this component is a policy question wearing a number, and every default is about somebody else's traffic. 0.7 is where a classifier's guess stops being trusted — a team matching medical identifiers wants it higher than a team filtering profanity.

inputs.name: overRedactionPct
inputs.description: Share of an answer past which the policy has probably destroyed it, `0`–`100`. 30 assumes an answer of a few hundred characters. On an SMS reply it fires constantly; on a ten-page report it never does.

inputs.name: destructiveRunChars
inputs.description: A single masked run this long means a claim went, not a phone number. 120 characters is a paragraph in prose and three lines of a table.

inputs.name: dormantMinEvents
inputs.description: Events needed before "this rule never fired" means anything. On forty requests a zero-hit rule has not had the chance. Calling it dormant there teaches the reader to ignore the label, and then the genuinely dead rule goes unread with the rest — which is the failure the dormant badge exists to prevent.

inputs.name: revealedEventIds
inputs.description: Event ids the reader has explicitly asked to see in the clear. A `model()`, not a private signal. Keyed state a host cannot reach is state that cannot be restored after a route change, and on *this* surface it is worse than inconvenient: a host logging reveals through `(revealRequested)` needs to be able to put the same set back, or its own audit trail and what the panel shows disagree after every navigation.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: Emitted when the user presses the error panel's "Try again" button (retryable errors only); the host should re-run the failed load.

outputs.name: ruleToggle
outputs.description: The reader asked to enable or disable a rule. Carries the state the reader saw. Disabling a guardrail is a privileged, logged act, and a payload of just the rule says which rule was clicked without saying what the reader believed they were changing. Two operators disabling the same rule during an incident is the ordinary case: the second toggle is a no-op, not a second change, and an audit log that records it as one describes an event that never happened. `svRuleToggleIsStale()` is the comparison. **Breaking:** the payload was `PolicyRule`. Migration is `$event` → `$event.rule`.

outputs.name: revealRequested
outputs.description: The reader asked to see one event's original text. Log it.

outputs.name: eventSelect
outputs.description: The reader activated an event.

outputs.name: selectedEventIdChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `selectedEventId` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(selectedEventId)]`.

outputs.name: revealedEventIdsChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `revealedEventIds` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(revealedEventIds)]`.

components.name: Heatmap Calendar
components.description: 8 color-palette variants with interactive tooltips, shape options, stats badges and full dark-mode support.
whenToUse: Visualizing daily activity/intensity over weeks or a year (contributions, usage).
You want a GitHub-style calendar with a color scale and tooltips.
For arbitrary X/Y matrices use the Heatmap Chart instead.
customization: Columns start on the locale's first weekday (Sunday for `en-US`, Monday for most of Europe, Saturday for much of the Middle East); `weekStart` (0–6) pins one, and the row labels follow it.
Eight palettes (GitHub, GitLab, fire, ocean…).
Square or rounded cells with configurable scale.
Optional stats badges and tooltips.
accessibility: The active days are ONE tab stop (the last one focused, else the most recent): ↑/↓ move to the previous/next active day, ←/→ to the same weekday a week away (mirrored right-to-left), Home/End to the first/last, PageUp/PageDown four weeks; Enter or Space activates. The keys are named once on the group.

The value reaches the page as a colour step and nothing else (WCAG 1.4.1), so the calendar publishes a table beside it — one row per MONTH, not per day, with the total, the active-day count and the busiest day. A day's own value is already reachable through its cell button; what is not reachable is the SHAPE, which is the only thing 371 squares say and is said entirely by their arrangement. A 371-row table would restate what is already there and still not answer it.
Empty months stay in the table. A gap is a fact about the year — the pale band the picture shows as a quiet stretch — and dropping those rows would hide exactly what the shape is for.
The table describes the window that is drawn, and the streak/total figures above it are counted over the same window, so scrolling to a different year cannot leave the numbers describing the old one.
Active days are focusable buttons that expose their date and value, and activate on Enter/Space.
Tooltips appear on hover and on keyboard focus; the grid is a labelled group and empty days are hidden from assistive tech.
Color scale is paired with text values in the tooltip, so meaning is not conveyed by color alone.

components.name: Heatmap Chart
components.description: Row × column heatmap with 4 variants (default, calendar, blocks, glow), 9 color schemes (viridis, magma and cividis sampled from the published colormaps, plus six single-hue ramps), a no-jump tooltip and ambient hover glow. Pure CSS.
whenToUse: Showing intensity across two categorical dimensions (hour × day, region × metric).
You want to spot hot/cold patterns in a matrix at a glance.
For date-based daily activity, use the Heatmap Calendar.
customization: Four variants and nine colour schemes: three perceptually uniform ramps (viridis, magma, cividis) and six single-hue ones. The uniform three run dark-to-bright already, so they are not re-picked for the dark glow variant — doing that would break the very uniformity they are chosen for.
Configurable cell shape and scale.
Ambient glow on hover.

`valuePolicy` decides what happens to a square whose reading this chart cannot plot — `NaN` from a blank source cell, `Infinity` from a division by zero. A negative is not one of these: this is a colour ramp, so −12 °C sits on it perfectly well. `render` (default) draws the square as missing — a hatch, plus a key for the hatch in the legend — which is the honest answer a pie cannot offer, because a matrix already has a way to say "this square has no colour". `omit` leaves a hole and discloses the count; `reject` refuses the matrix. `clamp` is not offered: a missing reading pushed to 0 lands on a real point of the ramp and looks like a measurement.
accessibility: The matrix is an ARIA `role="grid"`: real `columnheader` and `rowheader` cells (an unlabelled one is named by position — "Column 3"), and every square a `gridcell` whose `aria-label` carries row, column and value. That grid is the chart's non-visual alternative, so it does not also render a summary table that would read every value twice.

One tab stop for the whole matrix. Tab lands on the active square; the arrow keys move in two dimensions (skipping holes in a sparse matrix), Home/End go to the ends of the row, Ctrl+Home/Ctrl+End to the first and last square, Page Up/Page Down five rows, and Tab leaves the grid in one press. An off-screen hint describing the keys is attached with `aria-describedby`.
Tooltip content is available on focus and Enter/Space emits `cellSelect`; moving to a square emits `cellHover` with its row and column labels.

A missing square announces "no reading" rather than a number, and is reachable like any other — the hatch is the visual half of the same fact, and the legend key names it in words so it is not colour-only.

Whatever `valuePolicy` did is stated under the grid, not only in `console.warn`. A `NaN` that reached the ramp interpolator would come back as the literal `#NaNNaNNaN`, which browsers discard — blanking the entire matrix with no error anywhere.

Past `cellCeiling` squares (2,500 — a 50 × 50 grid) a note under the grid names the real count: the matrix renders slowly and neighbouring colours become hard to tell apart. The chart still draws every square — aggregate or split a matrix whose individual squares have to be read.

The six named hues are single-hue lightness ramps: better than a rainbow, but their steps are not evenly spaced perceptually, so the middle of the scale compresses. The default stays `blue` rather than moving to `viridis`, because a default is the one thing a host cannot opt out of having already shipped: changing it would restyle every existing dashboard without anybody asking. Reach for `viridis` on anything where the reader has to judge magnitude from colour rather than just spot the hot corner.

components.name: Histogram & Density
components.description: Distribution of a sample: five bin-width rules, count / density / cumulative measures, an optional kernel density curve, a rug, and mean / median / quantile markers. The rule that shaped the picture is always stated. Pure SVG.
whenToUse: Seeing the SHAPE of one numeric variable — where the mass sits, whether it is skewed, whether it has two modes.
Answering "what share came in under X" with the cumulative measure.
For comparing distributions across several groups, a Box Plot puts them side by side; for individual points, a Scatter Plot.
customization: Five bin-width rules, or explicit edges of your own — an edge is widened rather than lose a sample outside it, because a count that does not add up is the one thing a histogram must never do. Repeated edges are merged; an edge list with fewer than two distinct numbers falls back to the bin rule, and the note under the plot says so rather than showing an empty chart.
Count, density or cumulative measures.
Optional kernel density overlay with a bandwidth override — weighted the same way as the bars when the samples carry weights — and an optional rug of individual readings.
Statistical annotation: `showMean`, `showMedian` and `quantiles` (probabilities, e.g. `[0.9, 0.99]`) draw labelled reference lines, weighted like the bars. Off by default.
Bar colour, plot size, and a unit label carried into the axis and the table.
accessibility: Every bar is a focusable `role="button"` named with its range, count and share. Bar height is the only place a count exists in the drawing and no axis is precise enough to read one off, so those figures are in the name rather than left to be estimated.

The plot is ONE tab stop: Tab lands on a bar, the arrow keys walk the others (Home / End jump to the ends, no wrap), Enter or Space selects. A tab stop per bar was up to 200 Tab presses to get past one chart.
Mean, median and quantile markers are told apart by dash pattern and label, never by colour alone, and every marked figure is stated in the chart's accessible name.
`sv-data-summary-table` publishes every bin's range, count, share and running total — the last of which the plain measure never draws at all.
The rug is deliberately not focusable: every reading it marks is already counted in a bar that is, so making each tick a tab stop would add hundreds of stops that say nothing new.

What shaped the picture is stated in the rendered output: the bin rule that actually ran (including a fallback, or your own edges), the sample count, unequal widths drawn at count, the density bandwidth, and any reading that could not be binned or whose weight could not be used.
variants: A Distribution, and the Rule That Shaped It
Unequal Bins, and Why They Need Density
Cumulative, and Readings It Could Not Use

inputs.name: binRule
inputs.description: How the bin width is chosen. Freedman–Diaconis is the default because it is the most robust to outliers: it scales with the interquartile range rather than the full spread, so one extreme reading does not widen every bin. The rule is always named under the plot — a histogram's shape is a function of its bin width as much as of its data, so an unstated rule leaves the picture unfalsifiable.

components.name: Icon Library
components.description: 185 original glyphs on a 24px grid, drawn by name through one component once registered, or imported per icon. Only the glyphs you register or import ship. currentColor throughout, so an icon inherits its text colour in light and dark mode. Pro adds 514 more glyphs and the `sharp` and `duotone` weights.
whenToUse: Any icon in the kit — every component that takes an `icon` input resolves the name through this registry, so register the glyphs you hand it.
You want one component that renders any glyph by name, with no sprite sheet, no icon font and no build step.
Reach for the per-icon components when a page draws a few fixed icons and you would rather not register anything.

examples.title: Register the glyphs you name
examples.description: A name is a string, and a bundler cannot see a string — so nothing is bundled by name. Import each glyph you draw by its subpath and register it once; the kit's own components register theirs. `provideSvIcons(svAllIcons)` (from `@styloviz/icons/registry`) is the explicit opt-in to every glyph, for an icon picker or a prototype. An unregistered name renders nothing and warns once in development.

examples.title: Size and colour
examples.description: `size` takes a token (sm · md · lg) or a number of pixels. Colour comes from the surrounding text — every glyph is stroked in `currentColor` — so a Tailwind `text-*` class on the icon or any ancestor is the whole styling story.
examples.code: Payment failed

examples.title: Decorative or meaningful — the `title` decides
examples.description: An icon beside its own label is decoration and must not be announced twice; an icon that IS the label needs a name. Setting `title` switches the glyph from `aria-hidden` to `role="img"`, which is why there is no separate `ariaLabel` input to get out of step with it.
examples.code: hello@example.com

examples.title: Per-icon imports, for bundle-critical apps
examples.description: A per-icon component carries its glyph with it, so there is nothing to register — the shortest path for a page that draws a handful of icons. The glyph-by-name component is the better fit where names come from data (a nav menu, a status map).

examples.title: Your own glyphs, resolved by the same component
examples.description: `provideSvIcons` also takes a map of your own glyphs. They are consulted before the built-in ones, so a brand mark can be added without a second component and a built-in name can be overridden in one place rather than at every call site.

examples.title: Flip and rotate, instead of a second glyph
examples.description: A chevron pointing the other way is the same path mirrored. `flip` and `rotate` are applied around the centre of the viewBox, so the glyph stays on the grid and no extra bytes ship.

examples.title: Pro weights
examples.description: `sv-icon-pro` resolves your own glyphs first, then the Pro set, then the free set — every registered glyph in the kit through one tag (`provideSvIcons([brainProIcon])`, glyphs from `@styloviz-pro/icons/glyph/*`). It adds `sharp` (1.5 stroke, mitre joins, butt caps) and `duotone` (a stroked outline over a low-opacity `currentColor` fill) to the free `line` and `solid`.
examples.code:
<!-- provideSvIcons([brainProIcon, settings2ProIcon, checkIcon]) -->
<sv-icon-pro name="brain" weight="duotone" size="lg" />
<sv-icon-pro name="settings-2" weight="sharp" />
<sv-icon-pro name="check" />   <!-- free glyphs resolve here too -->

customization: Resolve any glyph with `name`; size with `size` (sm · md · lg, or a number of pixels) and tune the stroke with `strokeWidth` (line weight only).
Pick a `weight` — `line` or `solid` free; Pro adds `sharp` and `duotone` on `sv-icon-pro`.
Orient with `flip` (horizontal · vertical) and `rotate` (degrees clockwise around the centre).
Style the root `<svg>` through `cssClass` — a Tailwind `text-*` class is all a colour change takes, in either theme.
Register glyphs with `provideSvIcons([...])` or `registerSvIcons([...])`; add or override with a map of your own, which is consulted before the built-in glyphs.
Import per-icon components (`SvArrowRightIcon` from `@styloviz/icons/glyph/arrow-right`) for a fixed icon with nothing to register.
accessibility: An icon with no `title` is `aria-hidden` — the correct default, because most icons in a UI sit beside a label that already says what they mean, and announcing both reads the same word twice.
Setting `title` promotes the glyph to `role="img"` with that string as its accessible name. One input drives both, so the role and the name can never disagree.
Every glyph is stroked in `currentColor`, so contrast is inherited from the text colour that surrounds it and is fixed once for both themes rather than per icon.
The glyphs sit on a 24px grid with consistent optical weight, so a row of icons stays legible at `sm` instead of one turning to mush.

A name nobody registered renders nothing at all rather than a broken-image box, and warns once in development with the line to add. The kit's own build refuses a template of its own that names a glyph it does not register.

components.name: Image Compare
components.description: A before/after wipe that admits when it is not one: it measures both images' intrinsic sizes and says so when their aspect ratios disagree, because then part of what the reader sees as "the change" is the crop. Operated as a real ARIA slider — arrows, page keys, Home and End.
whenToUse: Showing a retouch, a restoration, a render change or a before/after of the same frame.
The two images are the same scene at the same framing — that is the only case a wipe means anything.
For two genuinely different pictures, put them side by side; a wipe would imply a correspondence that is not there.

examples.title: Alignment landmarks — the check the component cannot make
examples.description: It compares DIMENSIONS, never content. Two files of identical size can still be different crops of the same scene — a tighter lens, a nudged horizon — and no measurement available to a browser will tell. Landmarks give the reader the thing the component cannot compute: a fixed line drawn once over the whole box, above both layers, that does not move with the wipe. A feature sitting on the line in one image and beside it in the other proves the frames do not match. crosshair is the centre, thirds is the rule-of-thirds grid, grid is quarters.

examples.title: A quarter turn is not a reframing
examples.description: "Different shapes" is a symptom, not a diagnosis. A pair whose ratios are reciprocal — 4000×3000 against 3000×4000 — is one file carrying an EXIF orientation tag the other does not, and the fix is to re-export, not to re-crop. The warning names which of the four cases it is: identical, scaled (the wipe is honest, but the smaller one is being upscaled and will look softer), rotated, or genuinely reshaped.
examples.code:
<sv-image-compare variant="inspect" [beforeSrc]="a" [afterSrc]="b" />
<!-- the inspect read-out carries the verdict as data-sv-verdict -->

customization: Three variants: `slider`, `bare` (no handle drawn; keyboard and drag still work) and `inspect`.
Two-way `position`, 0–1.
Corner captions, alt text and an accessible name for the slider.
`mismatch` fires once with the size of the difference; `allowMismatch` suppresses the on-screen warning for a deliberately letterboxed pair.
`landmarks` (`none` / `crosshair` / `thirds` / `grid`) draws a fixed reference over both images at once. Two-tone strokes, so the line survives both a white sky and a black shadow.
`svFrames()` is exported and classifies a pair without rendering anything: `identical`, `scaled`, `rotated`, `reshaped` or `unknown`, each with the sentence that fits it.
accessibility: Until both images have loaded the wipe is covered by a status ("Loading the images to compare…", `aria-busy` on the box, `data-sv-media-state="loading"`) and the slider is `aria-disabled` — a wipe over half a pair compares a picture with a blank. A failed image says which one (`data-sv-media-state="error"`) and emits `(loadError)` with `'before'` or `'after'`.

On touch the box is `touch-pan-y touch-pinch-zoom`: a horizontal drag moves the wipe, a vertical swipe still scrolls the page and pinch still zooms it. The pair is `w-full` and reflows with its container.
A real `role="slider"` with `aria-valuenow` and an `aria-valuetext` naming the two images, so a screen reader announces what is showing rather than a bare percentage.
Arrows nudge by 1%, Page keys by 10%, Home and End go to the extremes — and every other key is left alone, so Tab still moves on rather than being trapped.
The stacked copy is `aria-hidden`, so the pair is announced once instead of as two pictures.

The aspect warning is rendered above the images as a `role="status"`, because the failure it describes is invisible: the widget looks right and the difference it shows is real, just the wrong difference.
The landmark overlay is `aria-hidden` and `pointer-events-none` — it is a visual aid for a check the component cannot make, and it must neither be read out as content nor eat the drag.
variants: Mismatch — Two Images That Cannot Be Wiped Between
Inspect — Where the Ratios Came From
The Check the Component Cannot Make

inputs.description: Presentation: `'slider'` (draggable handle), `'bare'` (no handle; keyboard and drag still work) or `'inspect'` (adds the measured ratios).

inputs.name: beforeSrc
inputs.description: The image revealed on the left of the wipe.

inputs.name: afterSrc
inputs.description: The image revealed on the right of the wipe.

inputs.name: beforeAlt
inputs.description: Alt text, used in the slider's spoken value as well as on the images. "Before" and "after" are what the CONTROL does, not what the images are. A screen reader user hearing "50% after" learns nothing; "50% retouched" is the sentence a sighted reader gets from looking.

inputs.name: afterAlt
inputs.description: Alt text for the after image, also used as its name in the slider's spoken value.

inputs.name: beforeLabel
inputs.description: Corner captions. Empty hides them.

inputs.name: afterLabel
