components.name: Kbd
components.description: A native `<kbd>` wrapper for rendering keyboard shortcuts and hint keys, with three visual variants and two sizes so every shortcut hint in the kit shares one styled source instead of one-off utility classes.
whenToUse: Hinting a keyboard shortcut next to a command, menu item or search input.
Labelling a hotkey in a tooltip, palette footer, or empty-state hint.
Not for standalone body copy — `<kbd>` communicates "a key you press," not general emphasis.

examples.title: A shortcut you can hear
examples.description: ⌘ is U+2318 PLACE OF INTEREST SIGN. A screen reader says "place of interest sign", or nothing at all — and the entire content of a shortcut hint is which keys to press, so a hint made of projected glyphs is documentation nobody can hear. It is unreadable to a sighted Windows or Linux user too, who has never been taught the symbol. Give the component the key and it draws the glyph, knows what it is called, and hides the symbol from assistive tech behind the word. Glyphs work as tokens do, because hosts already have ⌘ hard-coded everywhere and a fix that needs a rewrite first never gets adopted.
examples.code:
<sv-kbd key="cmd" />      <!-- draws ⌘, announces "Command" -->
<sv-kbd key="⌘" />        <!-- the same, from the glyph you already had -->
<sv-kbd key="esc" />      <!-- draws Esc, announces "Escape" -->

examples.title: A chord is one thing, and breaks like one
examples.description: "Ctrl +" at the end of a line and "C" at the start of the next is not a shortcut, it is two. chord renders the whole thing as one non-breaking group — nested <kbd> is the HTML spec's own idiom for it — and announces it once, in order, rather than reading three symbols nobody named. A literal plus is written ++.
examples.code:
<sv-kbd chord="cmd+shift+K" />   <!-- announces "Command Shift K" -->
<sv-kbd chord="ctrl+++" />      <!-- Control and the plus key -->

examples.title: A shortcut combo, laid out yourself

customization: A SEQUENCE — chords pressed one after another — is `sequence="g i"` or `sequence="mod+k mod+s"`: steps are separated by spaces, each step is a chord in `chord` syntax, each is drawn as its own unbreakable group with "then" between (from the label pack), and the whole is announced once — "G then I". `sequence` wins over `chord`, which wins over `key`.

`platform` (`auto` | `apple` | `other`) decides what `mod` draws. `auto` reads the browser; on the server there is no navigator, so a prerendered `mod` reads "Ctrl" and becomes ⌘ on an Apple device at hydration — pass `platform` when you know better.
Three variants: solid (bordered, filled), ghost (bordered, transparent) and plain (no chrome, inherits surrounding text color).
Two sizes: sm (default) and md.
`customClass` appends extra utility classes for one-off placement (e.g. margins) without a wrapper element.

`key` takes a token or a glyph — `cmd`, `shift`, `esc`, `⌘`, `K` — and supplies both what is drawn and what is said. `SV_KBD_KEYS`, `svKbdKey(token, labels)`, `svKbdChord(chord, labels)` and `svKbdSpoken()` are exported for building the same mapping elsewhere — pass `SV_KBD_LABELS` for the English names, or the labels `injectSvKbdLabels()` returns so the spoken names follow `provideSvLabels`.
`chord` takes a whole combo (`"cmd+shift+K"`) and renders it as one unbreakable group.
`alt` and `option` are separate entries on purpose: the same physical key, and not the same word. A macOS user reads ⌥ and hears "Option"; a Windows user reads Alt and hears "Alt".
accessibility: Renders a semantic native `<kbd>` element; a chord nests one `<kbd>` per key inside an outer one, which is the HTML spec's own idiom for a chord.

When the component drew the glyph — `key` or `chord` — the symbol is `aria-hidden` and the spoken name is given as visually-hidden text, so a screen reader says "Command Shift K" rather than reading three symbols nobody named. `ariaLabel` replaces that wording.
When the host projects content instead, the component cannot read it and `ariaLabel` becomes an attribute on the element — the only thing available for that case.
A chord never wraps mid-shortcut.
Purely presentational otherwise — carries no interactive role or focus state of its own.

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: The key, by name or by glyph — `cmd`, `shift`, `esc`, `⌘`, `K`. The point of this input is the spoken name. `⌘` is U+2318 place of interest sign and a screen reader says "place of interest sign", or nothing at all; `⇧` is upwards white arrow; `↵` is downwards arrow with corner leftwards. None of those is the name of a key, and the entire content of a shortcut hint is which keys to press — so a hint made of projected glyphs is documentation nobody can hear. Given the key, the component draws the glyph AND knows what it is called, so the symbol is hidden from assistive tech behind the word. Glyphs are accepted as well as tokens because hosts already have `⌘` hard-coded in a hundred templates, and a fix that requires rewriting all of them first is a fix that never gets adopted.

inputs.name: chord
inputs.description: A whole chord — `"cmd+shift+K"` — rendered as one unbreakable group. "Ctrl +" at the end of a line and "C" at the start of the next is not a shortcut, it is two. A literal `+` is written `++`.

inputs.name: sequence
inputs.description: A SEQUENCE — chords pressed one after another — separated by spaces: `"g i"` (Gmail's "go to inbox"), `"mod+k mod+s"`. Each step is drawn as its own unbreakable chord with "then" between them, and announced as "G then I". Takes precedence over `chord` and `key`.

inputs.name: platform
inputs.description: Which keyboard to draw for, which is what the `mod` token resolves by — Command (⌘) on `apple`, Control on `other`. `auto` reads the platform in the browser; on the server it answers `other`, so a prerendered `mod` reads "Ctrl" until hydration (see `svKbdPlatform`).

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Visual weight.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Chip size.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible label when the projected content is a symbol a screen reader won't say usefully on its own (e.g. `↵`, `⌘`) — announced instead of the glyph. Leave unset for plain text keys (`Esc`, `Tab`), which already read fine.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Extra classes appended after the resolved variant/size classes.

components.name: Like / Reaction Button
components.description: Reaction button with 4 icon variants (heart, thumbs-up, star, clap), burst particle animation on toggle, and an optimistic count that rolls back when the write fails. 3 sizes.
whenToUse: Adding a lightweight reaction/like affordance to posts, comments or cards.
You want an optimistic count with a burst animation on toggle.
For multi-emoji reactions on a thread, use the Comment component's reactions.
components.usage:
<!-- Heart (default) -->
<sv-like [count]="24" />

<!-- Persisted: both are two-way, and the event carries the way back -->
<sv-like
  variant="thumbs-up"
  [(count)]="count"
  [(liked)]="liked"
  [pending]="saving()"
  [error]="failure()"
  (likeChange)="onLike($event)" />

<!-- Star, large -->
<sv-like variant="star" [count]="12" size="lg" />

<!-- Clap, small, count hidden -->
<sv-like variant="clap" [count]="7" size="sm" [showCount]="false" />
customization: `countNotation="standard"` writes the full grouped count ("12,345") instead of the compact default; `locale` overrides the kit locale.
Switch icon with `variant`: `heart`, `thumbs-up`, `star` or `clap`.
Control size with `size` (sm, md, lg).
Hide the counter by setting `[showCount]="false"`.
Seed initial state with `[liked]="true"`; bind both `[(liked)]` and `[(count)]` two-way so the server's numbers win over the optimistic guess.

`[error]` accepts a string or an `SvDataError` — the message renders as visible "Not saved: …" text under the button, announced through a polite live region and linked to the button with `aria-describedby`.
accessibility: The visible count is compact ("1.2K", "12K", "1.2万") in the kit locale, but the button's accessible name carries the full, locale-grouped number ("Like, 1,234"), so the rounding never reaches a screen reader.
A native `<button>` with `aria-pressed` reflecting the toggled state, and an accessible name that carries the count and "not saved" after a failed write.
A failed write is a danger ring, a triangle glyph and visible message text — the button's `aria-describedby` points at that text, so the reason is read once as its description — never colour alone.
While `[pending]`, the button sets `aria-busy` and stops responding.

The burst is `motion-safe:` only and is not rendered at all under `prefers-reduced-motion` (with `motion-reduce:hidden` covering a preference that changes mid-burst), so reduced motion gets no particles rather than four dots parked on the button.
Disabled state sets `aria-disabled` and blocks interaction.

inputs.name: count
inputs.description: The reaction count (two-way). A `model`, because the count is the thing the toggle changes: it moves the instant the button is clicked, and the host's next value — the number the server actually recorded — wins over whatever was shown optimistically.

inputs.name: liked
inputs.description: Whether the current user has reacted (two-way: `[(liked)]`). Bind it two-way, not one-way. The button flips the state itself, and being a `model` is what pushes that back into your signal, so the two never drift and a later correction is always a real change. With a one-way `[liked]`, a host undoing a rejected like by re-asserting `[liked]="false"` changes nothing — Angular skips a binding whose expression has not changed — and the like stays on screen.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Icon variant.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Size.

inputs.name: showCount
inputs.description: Show the count next to the icon.

inputs.name: countNotation
inputs.description: How the visible count is written: `'compact'` — "1.2K", "12K", "1.2M" in the locale's own compact form — or `'standard'` — "1,234". The accessible name always carries the FULL number, grouped for the locale, so "1.2K" never reaches a screen reader as the count. Under 1,000 both read the same.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP 47 locale for the count.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disabled state.

inputs.name: pending
inputs.description: True while the toggle is being written. The button stops responding, which is what keeps `rollback()` unambiguous — and it is also the answer to a double-tap producing two requests.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: The last write failed. Rendered as a danger ring, a triangle glyph and the message as visible text under the button — tied to it with `aria-describedby` — so the state is not conveyed by colour alone. Roll the value back as well — this input reports the failure, it does not undo it.

inputs.name: signedIn
inputs.description: Whether the viewer is signed in. When false the button does not toggle; it emits `authRequired` so the host can prompt for sign-in. A reaction control shown to a signed-out user had no defined behaviour: it toggled, looked saved, and the write it reported could not succeed.

outputs.name: likeChange
outputs.description: The user toggled the reaction.

outputs.name: authRequired
outputs.description: A signed-out viewer tried to react.

outputs.name: countChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `count` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(count)]`.

outputs.name: likedChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `liked` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(liked)]`.

components.name: Line Chart
components.description: 12 variants: line, spline, step, dashed, custom animation, inversed, zones, multi-colored, stacked and 100% stacked, plus trend lines and strip lines (free and Pro). A missing reading is drawn as a break in the line, not as a zero. Pure SVG.
whenToUse: Showing a trend or change over a continuous/ordered axis (time series).
You want multi-series comparison with zones, trend lines or markers.
For category comparisons rather than trends, use the Bar Chart.
A series of thousands of readings: `renderer="large-data"` draws its outline instead of one vertex per reading.
A live feed: `[live]="true"` with `liveWindow` follows the newest readings as you append them (Pro); `sv-live-stream-chart` scrolls a pushed stream. See the Live data guide.

examples.title: A reading that was never taken
examples.code:
// null is a gap: the line breaks there rather than joining across it.
series = [{ label: 'Sensor', data: [12, 14, null, 19, 21] }];

examples.title: Preset — time series with zoom
Preset — annotated analytical
Large data — thousands of points
examples.code:
<!-- Each horizontal unit of the plot keeps its lowest and highest reading, so
     every peak and trough is drawn; markers are off and the note under the plot
     says how many points were drawn. Hover reads the exact value. -->
<sv-line-chart renderer="large-data" [categories]="timestamps" [series]="readings" />

examples.title: Export to PNG, SVG or PDF
Preset — compact sparkline

customization: Interactive legend (both tiers): hover or keyboard-focus an entry and every other series fades; Enter, Space or a click hides or shows it. The hidden set is `[(hiddenSeries)]`, two-way bound so a host can persist it; the last visible series cannot be hidden, and the value axis keeps its scale. `[interactiveLegend]="false"` keeps the static key.
Line, spline or step interpolation.
Zones, trend lines and strip bands.
Multi-series with custom colors and markers.

`null` in a series is a gap: the line breaks, no marker is drawn, the filled area stops at the break rather than painting under readings nobody took, and the axis scales to the values that exist. `NaN` and `Infinity` are treated the same way — a chart cannot tell a sensor fault from a `parseFloat('n/a')`.

Synchronised groups: `svChartSync="ops"` (from `@styloviz/core`) on several charts shares the hovered category and — from a `zoomable` Pro line chart — the brush window. Matched by category LABEL, so charts with different ranges still line up; a remote change is never re-published. Line and bar charts (both tiers) take part; `injectSvChartSync()` joins your own chart to a group.
accessibility: The legend is a `role="toolbar"` of `aria-pressed` toggle buttons with ONE tab stop — the keyboard path between series: the arrow keys (and Home/End) move from series to series, each one put in front as focus lands on it, and Enter or Space shows or hides it. Showing and hiding are announced through the live region, and a hidden series stays in the summary table (hiding is a view, not a deletion).

The SVG is `role="img"` with an auto-generated data summary (override via `ariaLabel`), backed by an `sv-data-summary-table` of every point and series value — one row per point, one column per series.

When `zoomable` is on, the table follows the brush window instead of the full dataset, and adds a line saying which window it is ("Showing points 6–15 of 40."). A table that listed all forty points beside a chart brushed down to ten described points that are not on screen, with no way to tell which ten were — and an alternative that contradicts the picture is worse than none. The free Line Chart has no brush, so it has neither.
Series legend is keyboard reachable; reduced-motion disables the draw-on animation.

A break in a line is ambiguous on sight — "nothing was recorded here" to one reader, a rendering glitch to another, and easy to miss entirely at one missing point in a dense series. The count of missing readings is stated in text under the plot, so it does not depend on noticing a gap in a drawing.

In a sync group, another chart's hover shows here as a tooltip and crosshair at the same category — a pointer convenience; every value stays reachable through the data table, which `svChartDataTable` can also put on screen.

components.name: Line Clamp
components.description: Text truncation using CSS line-clamp with ResizeObserver overflow detection, an optional gradient fade and an animated Show more / Show less toggle.
whenToUse: Truncating long text to a fixed number of lines with an optional expand toggle.
Card descriptions, comments, table cells where vertical space is constrained.
For collapsing arbitrary content (not just text), use Expand / Collapse.

examples.title: Links inside clamped text
examples.description: line-clamp CLIPS; it does not remove. A link on line eight of a three-line clamp is still in the tab order and drawn nowhere the user can see, so tabbing through the page appears to swallow focus. Focus landing below the clamp line opens the block, and leaving it closes it again — unless the reader took it over by pressing the toggle. Not inert: there is no element boundary between the shown lines and the clipped ones, so inert on the box would take the visible text out of the accessibility tree as well.
examples.code: Read the full policy before continuing. {{ plainText }}

examples.title: Printing
examples.description: Paper has no "Show more". A printed clause that stops mid-sentence is indistinguishable from one that ended there, so the component unclamps under @media print and hides the fade and the toggle. Nothing to configure; it is in the component stylesheet.
examples.code:
<!-- Prints in full, expanded or not. -->
<sv-line-clamp [lines]="3">{{ incidentNote }}</sv-line-clamp>

customization: Overflow is re-measured when the box resizes AND when web fonts finish loading (`document.fonts.ready` and every later `loadingdone`) — a font swap changes where the text wraps without resizing the clamped box, so a ResizeObserver alone would leave the toggle as the fallback font measured it.
Set the visible line count with `lines` and add a `fadeOut` gradient.
Toggle expansion with `showToggle` and relabel via `expandLabel` / `collapseLabel`.
Two-way bind `[(expanded)]` to control or read the state, or listen to `expandedChange`.

`expandOnFocus` (on by default) opens the block when focus reaches something clipped out of view, and closes it again when focus leaves — unless the reader pressed the toggle themselves, which takes ownership.
Printing unclamps the text and drops the fade and the toggle. It lives in the component stylesheet under `@media print`, so there is nothing to bind.
accessibility: The toggle is a labelled button that reflects expanded state via `aria-expanded` and points at the text region with `aria-controls`.
Full text remains in the DOM for screen readers and search.
Overflow is detected so the toggle only appears when needed.

A focusable element clipped by the clamp is not left as an invisible tab stop: focus landing below the clamp line expands the block, so the focus ring is always drawn somewhere the user can see. `inert` was rejected — there is no element boundary between the shown and clipped lines, so it would remove the visible text from the accessibility tree too.
Printed output is unclamped, and the fade and toggle are hidden — a printed page cannot follow a "Show more".

components.name: List View
components.description: List patterns: default, checklist, nested tree, virtualized, grouped, template cards, call history and infinite scrolling — and swipe actions on rows, with an Actions button that reaches them without a swipe.
whenToUse: Rendering feeds, checklists, contacts or any vertical collection of items.
You need grouping, quick/bulk actions, or virtualization for long lists.
For tabular, column-aligned data use Data Table.

examples.title: Cursor and scroll position that survive a route change
Swipe actions on rows
examples.code:
<!-- Swipe toward the end for Read, toward the start for Archive / Delete.
     A full swipe runs the edge action (Delete); every row's ⋯ button opens the same actions. -->
<sv-list-view
  [items]="messages()"
  [swipeStartActions]="[{ id: 'read', label: 'Read', icon: 'mail', tone: 'primary' }]"
  [swipeEndActions]="[
    { id: 'delete', label: 'Delete', icon: 'trash', tone: 'danger' },
    { id: 'archive', label: 'Archive', icon: 'archive', tone: 'success' }
  ]"
  (swipeAction)="onSwipe($event)" />

customization: Swap between flat, grouped, checklist and card layouts.
Virtualization keeps long lists fast.
Quick actions and bulk actions per row.
Every mode renders the same row: avatar, badge, trailing amount, quick actions and the selection control are present under `virtualized` and `grouped` too, not only on a flat list.

`[(activeItemId)]` is the keyboard cursor and `[(scrollOffset)]` the scroll position — both two-way, so a host can deep-link to a row, restore either after a route change, or read back where the user left off.

**Feature compatibility.** Row presets (`default`, `checklist`, `template`, `call-history`) compose with everything. The structural ones do not: `virtualization` windows flat lists only, `grouped` renders every section in full, and `nested` renders the tree in full and beats `grouped`.

Under `virtualized`, a row's height is computed from `itemHeight` plus a line for a `subtitle`/`description` and a strip for `tags`, and the row is then sized to that number — so the scrollbar and the rows always agree.

Swipe actions: `swipeStartActions` behind the start edge, `swipeEndActions` behind the end edge, each `{ id, label, icon?, tone? }` (neutral · primary · success · warning · danger); a swipe past half a tray opens it, past 60% of the width runs the edge action unless `[fullSwipe]="false"`; `(swipeAction)` reports `{ item, action, side, trigger }` with trigger tap · full-swipe · menu, and `closeSwipe()` folds an open row away. Flat and grouped rows, windowed or not; nested rows do not swipe.
accessibility: Keyboard at scale: the list is ONE tab stop however many rows it holds — the region around the rows is not a second one. ↑/↓ move a row and stop at the ends, Home/End jump to them, PageUp/PageDown move one viewport of rows and clamp (they never wrap), and typing a few letters moves to the next row whose title starts with them. Documented ceiling: 2,000 rendered rows (`SV_UNVIRTUALIZED_ROW_CEILING`) — above it, turn on `virtualized` (flat lists); a nested or grouped list past it warns once in dev mode.
Rows are keyboard navigable (roving focus with arrow keys, Home/End) and have clear focus.

Under `virtualized` the cursor walks the whole list, not the rendered window: ArrowDown past the last visible row scrolls the next one in, and End reaches the true last row. Exactly one row is a tab stop, so Tab enters and leaves the list once.
Scrolling the focused row out of the window moves focus to the scroller rather than losing it to the page, and the next arrow key carries on from the row the cursor was on.

Each row declares `aria-posinset`/`aria-setsize` — against the whole list when windowed, against its own section when grouped — so a screen reader announces "row 140 of 241" rather than the size of the window.
A grouped, checkable list gives each section header a checkbox that reports `indeterminate` as "mixed" while the section is partly checked; disabled rows are left out of it.

A nested list publishes its shape rather than drawing it: depth is not `padding-left` alone, which would read every branch as one flat pile. Each row is a `listitem` carrying `aria-level` and an `aria-posinset`/`aria-setsize` counted against its own siblings, and each expander carries `aria-expanded` plus a label naming the branch ("Collapse src"), not a generic "Expand node".

A paged list says where it ends. On the last page the footer holds an end marker naming the total, so "the data ends here" and "the next page is slow" look different, and the live region speaks each page arriving ("Loaded 20 more items.") and the list running out ("End of list. All 241 items loaded."). A list that arrives already complete stays silent — nothing happened.
Quick/bulk action buttons and per-row selection controls are individually labelled.
The search field is labelled; selection changes are announced via a polite live region.

Swipe actions never depend on the swipe: every row gets an Actions button (⋯, named "Actions for <title>", `aria-expanded`) that opens the same actions as buttons over the row — ←/→ between them (mirrored in right-to-left), Escape closes and returns focus to the button. It shares the row's roving tab stop, so the list is still one stop. The trays behind a closed row are `inert` and hidden from assistive technology. The swipe is touch and pen only, locks onto the horizontal axis after 8 px, and leaves vertical scrolling to the browser (`touch-pan-y`); right-to-left reverses which way each side opens.
