inputs.name: trigger
inputs.description: What triggers opening: click, hover, or manual (programmatic only).

inputs.name: title
inputs.description: Optional header title for the popover panel.

inputs.name: subtitle
inputs.description: Optional secondary header line (also wired to `aria-describedby`).

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Color / semantic variant.

inputs.name: minWidth
inputs.description: Minimum width of the popover panel (px).

inputs.name: maxWidth
inputs.description: Maximum width of the popover panel (px). 0 = unconstrained.

inputs.name: offset
inputs.description: Gap between the trigger and the panel (px).

inputs.name: flip
inputs.description: Flip to the opposite side when there isn't room on the requested side.

inputs.name: showArrow
inputs.description: Render a pointer arrow that tracks the trigger.

inputs.name: showIcon
inputs.description: Show the built-in variant icon badge in the header.

inputs.name: showClose
inputs.description: Show a close (×) button in the header.

inputs.name: closeOnOutsideClick
inputs.description: Close when clicking outside the trigger and panel.

inputs.name: closeOnEsc
inputs.description: Close on the ESC key.

inputs.name: closeOnContentClick
inputs.description: Close when any content inside the panel is clicked (menu behaviour).

inputs.name: hoverOpenDelay
inputs.description: Delay before opening on hover (ms).

inputs.name: hoverCloseDelay
inputs.description: Delay before closing after the pointer leaves (ms).

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Prevent the popover from opening.

inputs.name: autoFocus
inputs.description: Move focus into the panel when opened via click/manual (keyboard a11y).

inputs.name: interactive
inputs.description: Passive or interactive. One input moves role, focus and Tab behaviour together, and it is orthogonal to `trigger` (how it opens, never what it is). - `false` — a passive callout. The panel is `role="tooltip"` and the trigger is `aria-describedby` it while open instead of announcing a dialog popup; focus never moves in, `autoFocus` is ignored. Escape, outside click and anchor loss still dismiss it. - `true` — an interactive surface such as a mini form. `role="dialog"`, focus moves to the first focusable element (or the panel itself) on a click/manual open, and Tab / Shift+Tab cycle inside the panel instead of walking out of it. A hover open never moves focus — that is a hover card, and pulling focus to wherever the pointer drifts is not an open. - unset — `role="dialog"`, no Tab containment, focus moved only under `[autoFocus]`.

inputs.name: align
inputs.description: Cross-axis alignment folded into `position`'s side: `position="left" align="start"` is the `left-start` placement, which `position` alone cannot spell. Unset leaves `position` exactly as written.

inputs.name: padding
inputs.description: Padding around the projected body; `none` gives the content the whole panel.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible label used when no `title` is provided.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Extra CSS classes merged onto the popover panel surface.

inputs.name: sheetOnNarrow
inputs.description: Become a bottom sheet on a narrow viewport (640px and below).

outputs.name: opened
outputs.description: Emitted after the popover opens (by any means, including `[(open)]`).

outputs.name: closedEvent
outputs.description: Emitted after the popover closes (by any means, including `[(open)]`).

outputs.name: openChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `open` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(open)]`.

components.name: Price
components.description: Locale-aware money formatting with an optional compare-at price and an auto-calculated discount, shown as a badge or inline text. Minor units are scaled by the currency rather than by a hardcoded 100, the rounding rule is stated rather than implied, and ranges, credits and a stated tax basis are first-class.
whenToUse: Rendering any product / cart / order price consistently across the app.
You want a strikethrough original price with an automatic saving badge.
Prices are stored in minor units and need locale-aware formatting.
A product is priced by variant or configuration and needs a range or a "from".
The figure is a refund, credit or adjustment rather than something owed to you.
You sell where the tax basis has to be printed beside the price.

examples.title: Minor units + currency
examples.description: Store prices in cents and format for any locale.

examples.title: Minor units are not always hundredths
examples.description: All three of these hold the integer `1000`. The currency decides what it is worth: USD has two decimals, JPY none, KWD three. The scale is read back from `Intl` for the currency in play, so `1000` prints as $10.00, ¥1,000 and 1.000 KWD — dividing by 100 regardless would show a tenth of a thousand yen and ten dinars instead of one.
examples.code:
<sv-price [amount]="1000" [minorUnits]="true" currency="USD" locale="en-US" />
<sv-price [amount]="1000" [minorUnits]="true" currency="JPY" locale="ja-JP" />
<sv-price [amount]="1000" [minorUnits]="true" currency="KWD" locale="en-US" />

examples.title: Rounding you can audit
examples.description: `roundingMode` defaults to `halfExpand`, which is also what `Intl` applies when nothing is said — so setting nothing changes no output. It exists because a rule chosen implicitly is a rule nobody can reconcile against: two systems that agree on the amount and disagree on the mode disagree by a cent.
examples.code:
<!-- bankers' rounding, for a figure that has to match the ledger -->
<sv-price [amount]="1.005" roundingMode="halfEven" />

<!-- never quote below the real price -->
<sv-price [amount]="1.001" roundingMode="ceil" />

examples.title: A range, and an open-ended one
examples.description: A product whose variants are not all one price does not have a price. `amountTo` prints both ends and reads the dash as the word "to"; `from` prints a lower bound alone. An `amountTo` at or below `amount` is dropped rather than printed backwards, and a range suppresses `compareAt` — a percentage off a span is not one number.

examples.title: Money owed the other way
examples.description: A negative amount is a refund or a credit, and the minus glyph in front of it is not read out — so the figure is announced as a credit. A figure that rounds away to nothing loses the sign, because "-$0.00" reads as a refund that is not happening. Under `floor`, -0.001 legitimately is -$0.01 and keeps it.

examples.title: Stating the tax basis
examples.description: A consumer-facing price with no stated basis is not compliant in the EU, the UK or Australia. The component cannot know the jurisdiction or the buyer, so `unstated` is the default and stating it is one input; the note prints as text under the price, never as a colour or a tooltip. The rate goes in the label.
examples.code:
<sv-price [amount]="49.99" taxMode="inclusive" taxLabel="20% VAT" />
<sv-price [amount]="49.99" taxMode="exclusive" taxLabel="sales tax" />

examples.title: Naming the currency for a screen reader
examples.description: "$" and "£" are shared by several currencies, so heard alone they do not say which one the shopper is charged in. With `currencyName="auto"` (the default) a shared symbol is spoken as the currency's name — "49.99 US dollars" — while the symbol stays on screen; "€" and "CA$" already say it and are left alone. `always` names every figure; `never` keeps the symbol only.

customization: Four sizes (sm/md/lg/xl) and three alignments — alignment drives both axes, so the tax note lines up with the price.
Discount as a badge, inline text, or hidden.
Any ISO 4217 currency + BCP-47 locale; a code `Intl` rejects falls back to "CODE 49.99" instead of throwing and blanking the grid.
Nine rounding modes, named exactly as `Intl` names them.
Optional Free label for zero amounts (ignored on a range — "Free – $79.99" is a lie about every variant but one).
Range wording via `fromLabel`; tax wording and rate via `taxLabel`.
accessibility: Prices are real text (tabular-nums), not images.
The original price uses a semantic `<s>` element.
Sufficient contrast for the sale and discount colours in light and dark mode.

A sale price is prefixed "Sale price" and the struck figure "Regular price", because a strike-through conveys nothing to a screen reader — without them the pair reads as two numbers with no way to tell which is charged.
A range reads "$49.99 to $79.99": the en dash is `aria-hidden` and the word carries it, since some screen readers read the glyph as nothing and others as "dash".
A negative amount is prefixed "Credit", because the minus sign in front of a figure is not announced.
The discount badge is a `role="img"` with an `aria-label` of "N% off", so the U+2212 glyph is replaced by words.
The tax basis is text in the accessibility tree, not a title attribute — so it is read, translated and findable.

A currency symbol shared with other currencies ("$", "£", "¥") is spoken as the currency's name ("49.99 British pounds") through an sr-only figure, and the visible symbol is `aria-hidden` so the price is read once (`currencyName`).
variants: Minor units are not always hundredths

inputs.name: amount
inputs.description: Current price. Interpreted as minor units (cents) when `minorUnits` is true.

inputs.name: compareAt
inputs.description: Original / "compare-at" price for a discount. `null` hides it.

inputs.name: currency
inputs.description: ISO 4217 currency code.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP-47 locale for formatting.

inputs.name: minorUnits
inputs.description: Treat `amount` / `compareAt` / `amountTo` as minor units. Minor units are not always hundredths: the scale is read from `Intl` for the currency in play, so `1000` is ¥1,000 in JPY, $10.00 in USD and 1.000 KWD in KWD.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Text size.

inputs.name: align
inputs.description: Horizontal alignment of the price block.

inputs.name: discount
inputs.description: How to present the saving when `compareAt` is set.

inputs.name: freeLabel
inputs.description: Label shown when the amount is 0 (e.g. "Free"). Empty renders a formatted 0.

inputs.name: fractionDigits
inputs.description: Decimal places, or `null` for the currency's own convention. `null` is the default and it is the right one for a shop. USD wants two places, JPY wants none, and `Intl` already knows which — hard-coding a number would print `¥1,200.00`, a figure that does not exist. It exists because a whole class of prices are never quoted to the cent: a house at `$1,180,000.00` reads as a rounding error, and every property portal, car listing and B2B quote drops the decimals. Setting `0` is the caller saying "this is that kind of price", which is a judgement the component cannot make from the amount alone. It changes only how the figure is *printed*. It says nothing about how the host *stored* it, so it never moves the `minorUnits` scale: a house price held in cents and shown without decimals is still cents.

inputs.name: roundingMode
inputs.description: How a figure with more precision than the printed decimals is resolved. A rounding rule chosen implicitly is a rounding rule nobody can audit. Two systems that agree on the amount and disagree on the mode disagree by a cent, which is a reconciliation task rather than a display bug. The default is `halfExpand` — the same rule `Intl` applies when nothing is said — so this input changes no existing output; it only makes the rule visible and overridable. Finance systems that use bankers' rounding want `halfEven`; a shop that must never quote below the real price wants `ceil`.

inputs.name: amountTo
inputs.description: Upper bound of a price range — "$49.99 – $79.99" for a product whose variants are not all one price. Ignored unless it is above `amount`, on the same rule as `compareAt`: a range that runs backwards is bad data, and printing it as given would tell a shopper the cheapest option costs more than the dearest. A range suppresses `compareAt` and the saving, because a percentage off a span is not one number.

inputs.name: from
inputs.description: Print `amount` as the start of an open-ended range — "From $49.99" — for a product priced by configuration. Ignored when `amountTo` is set, since a closed range already says it.

inputs.name: fromLabel
inputs.description: Wording for the open-ended range.

inputs.name: taxMode
inputs.description: Whether the printed figure includes tax. `unstated` is the default only because this component cannot know. Whether a price must be shown with tax included is a property of the jurisdiction and the buyer, not of the number — and in the EU, the UK and Australia a consumer-facing price with no stated basis is not compliant. There is deliberately no way to state a basis *wrongly* cheaply: pick `inclusive` or `exclusive` and the component prints it beneath the price, as text, every time.

inputs.name: taxLabel
inputs.description: What the tax is called — 'VAT', 'GST', 'sales tax'. Also the place to put a rate: `'20% VAT'` prints "incl. 20% VAT".

inputs.name: currencyName
inputs.description: Give assistive tech the currency's full name ("49.99 US dollars") in place of the visible symbol. The symbol stays on screen; the named figure is sr-only and the symbol is hidden from the accessibility tree, so the price is read once. - `auto` — only when the symbol is shared with another currency: "$" in a store that also sells in CAD, "£" next to EGP. "€" and "CA$" are left as is. - `always` — every figure, e.g. a multi-currency comparison table. - `never` — the symbol only.

components.name: Pricing Table
components.description: Subscription plans as cards or a feature-by-plan comparison table, with a monthly / annual toggle. Each plan carries one monthly figure: the annual price, the invoice actually charged, the cash saved and the "save at least N %" are derived from it and one discount, so the page can never advertise a saving it does not give. The highlighted plan is badged in text, quote-only and free plans are first-class, and CTA links are checked for a safe scheme.
whenToUse: The pricing page of a SaaS product or a marketing site, with two to four plans.
An upgrade screen inside the app, where `selectedPlanId` marks the plan the account is on or is about to choose.
A feature-by-plan comparison under the plan cards (`layout="table"`).
Use `sv-price` instead for a single amount on a product, cart line or invoice.

examples.title: Three tiers with an annual discount
examples.description: One monthly figure per plan. `[annualDiscount]="0.2"` derives every annual figure, rounded to the precision the monthly price is quoted in — whole units for $149, cents for $9.99.

examples.title: Comparison table
examples.description: Rows are keyed by plan id: `true`, `false` (or missing) or a text. Rows with a `group` sit under one group heading.

examples.title: A plan you quote, with a link
examples.code:
{ id: 'enterprise', name: 'Enterprise', price: 'Contact sales',
  cta: { label: 'Talk to sales', href: 'mailto:sales@example.com' } }

examples.title: The same arithmetic elsewhere
examples.description: The helpers the table uses are exported, so a checkout summary or an upgrade dialog quotes the same figures rather than computing them a second way.
examples.code:
import { svAnnualMonthly, svAnnualTotal, svAnnualSaving, svAnnualSavingPercent } from '@styloviz/commerce';

svAnnualMonthly({ monthly: 149 }, 0.2);       // 119
svAnnualTotal({ monthly: 149 }, 0.2);         // 1428
svAnnualSaving({ monthly: 149 }, 0.2);        // 360
svAnnualSavingPercent({ monthly: 149 }, 0.2); // 20

customization: Two layouts: `cards` (one card per plan, stacked on a phone, sized to the number of plans) and `table` (a comparison table that scrolls sideways on a phone with the feature column pinned).

Currency per table (`currency`) or per plan (`plan.currency`), formatted with `Intl.NumberFormat` in `locale`: whole amounts print without decimals ($149), others with the currency's own ($9.99, ¥1,200).
The highlighted plan, the toggle and the CTAs paint from the `primary-*` tokens, so a template that remaps primary recolours the table.

`caption`, `headingLevel`, `showBillingToggle` and `selectedPlanId` shape the output; every string comes from the `commerce` labels (`pricing*` keys) — `provideSvLabels(SV_COMMERCE_LABELS_DE)` or the per-instance `labels` input.
`svAnnualMonthly`, `svAnnualTotal`, `svAnnualSaving`, `svAnnualSavingPercent`, `svPricingHeadlineSaving` and `svFormatPlanPrice` are exported for use elsewhere.
accessibility: The billing toggle is two native radio inputs in a `<fieldset>` with a "Billing period" legend — arrow keys move between them, no ARIA widget roles. The "save at least N %" is linked to the Annual radio with `aria-describedby`.

The highlighted plan is emphasised by a border and ring **and** a text badge ("Most popular"). In the cards it is read with the plan's heading; in the table it sits inside the plan's `<th scope="col">`, so it is announced with every cell of that column.

The comparison is a real `<table>` with a `<caption>`, `<th scope="col">` per plan, `<th scope="row">` per feature and `<th scope="rowgroup">` per group. Its scroll container is a focusable region named by the caption, so a keyboard can scroll it.
Included and not-included cells draw an icon and carry "Included" / "Not included" as screen-reader text — never an icon alone.

The visible "/ month" is hidden from screen readers and "per month" is read instead. Each CTA is described by its plan's name, so "Selected" or "Talk to sales" is never heard out of context; targets are at least 44 px tall with a visible focus ring.

inputs.name: plans
inputs.description: The plans, cheapest first. Plans with an empty or duplicate `id` are skipped.

inputs.name: features
inputs.description: The comparison rows, shown as the table in the `table` layout and as each card's bullet list when a plan has no `features` of its own.

inputs.name: billing
inputs.description: Which period the prices are shown for. Two-way: `[(billing)]`; emits `billingChange`.

inputs.name: annualDiscount
inputs.description: The annual discount as a fraction (`0.2` = 20 % off), used for every plan whose price has no `annual`. Outside `[0, 1)` it counts as none.

inputs.name: showBillingToggle
inputs.description: Show the monthly / annual toggle. It is hidden anyway when no plan has a price.

inputs.name: currency
inputs.description: ISO 4217 currency code, unless a plan sets its own.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP-47 locale for prices and numbers.

inputs.name: layout
inputs.description: `cards` — one card per plan, stacked on phones — or a `table` comparing features.

inputs.name: selectedPlanId
inputs.description: The plan whose CTA reads "Selected" — the one your sign-up form is set to.

inputs.name: caption
inputs.description: The comparison table's `<caption>`. Null uses the `pricingCaption` label ("Compare plans").

inputs.name: headingLevel
inputs.description: Heading level for each plan's name in the cards layout — match the page outline.

inputs.name: labels
inputs.description: Per-instance text, merged over the registry's `commerce` labels.

outputs.name: planSelect
outputs.description: A plan's call to action was activated — its button, or its link (which also navigates).

outputs.name: billingChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `billing` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(billing)]`.

components.name: Product Card
components.description: Commerce product card composing price and rating with a wishlist toggle, badge, colour swatches, add-to-cart and an out-of-stock state. Grid and list layouts.
whenToUse: Product listing grids, search results, wishlists, related-product rails and comparison pickers.
You want price, rating and a wishlist affordance in one consistent card.
For dense non-visual rows, prefer a List View instead.

examples.title: Persisting the heart, and putting it back
examples.description: The heart flips the instant it is pressed — a heart that waits for a round trip reads as a broken button. `rollback()` is on the event because the code that learns the write failed is the code handling it. It refuses once the heart has been toggled again, so keep `wishlistPending` bound.

examples.title: Adding the right variant, once
examples.description: There is no `rollback()` on `addToCart` and inventing one would be a lie — the card holds no cart, so it changes nothing optimistically. What it gives you instead is the swatch in effect and a `requestKey`: bind `addingToCart` so one press cannot become two, and de-duplicate on the key so a retry cannot either.

customization: Grid and list layouts.
Corner badge with five colours.
Colour swatches with a selection output.
Toggle the wishlist, add-to-cart and out-of-stock affordances.
`error` renders next to the price rather than over the image, which already carries the badge, the heart and the out-of-stock banner.
accessibility: Wishlist toggle exposes `aria-pressed` and a descriptive label.
Stretched title link keeps the whole card clickable while swatches and buttons stay reachable.
Add-to-cart is disabled and dimmed when out of stock.
Both actions set `aria-busy` while their write is in flight, so the wait is announced rather than only animated.
The failure note is a live `role="alert"`, so a rejected write is read out rather than silently reverting the heart.
The pending pulse is `motion-safe:`, so it is absent under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
variants: Persisting, in flight & a failed write

inputs.description: Product title.

inputs.name: price
inputs.description: Current price (minor units when `minorUnits` is true).

inputs.description: Link target for the product.

inputs.name: brand
inputs.description: Brand / vendor line above the title.

inputs.name: compareAt
inputs.description: Compare-at price for a discount.

inputs.name: currency
inputs.description: ISO 4217 currency code.

inputs.description: BCP-47 locale for prices.

inputs.name: swatches
inputs.description: Optional colour swatches.

inputs.name: showWishlist
inputs.description: Show the wishlist toggle.

inputs.name: showQuickView
inputs.description: Show the quick-view button on hover.

inputs.name: showAddToCart
inputs.description: Show the add-to-cart button.

inputs.name: addToCartLabel
inputs.description: Add-to-cart button label.

inputs.name: quickViewLabel
inputs.description: Quick-view button label.

inputs.name: outOfStockLabel
inputs.description: Label shown when out of stock.

inputs.name: hoverable
inputs.description: Hover elevation.

inputs.name: wishlistPending
inputs.description: A wishlist write for this product is in flight. The heart stops responding, so a second toggle cannot race the first and leave `rollback()` ambiguous.

inputs.name: addingToCart
inputs.description: An add-to-cart write for this product is in flight. The button stops responding — the same shopper pressing it twice is how a cart ends up with two of something.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: The last write for this card failed. Rendered as a danger note by the price. One input covers both actions because the HOST supplies the wording, so "Could not save to your wishlist" already says which one failed. Correcting the heart is `rollback()`'s job, not this input's.

inputs.name: wishlisted
inputs.description: Wishlist state (two-way: `[(wishlisted)]`). Bind it two-way, not one-way. The card flips the heart itself, and being a `model` is what pushes that back into YOUR signal, so the two never drift. Over a plain input it would: Angular skips an input binding whose expression has not changed, so re-asserting `false` against a heart already showing true is ignored and a rejected toggle stays on screen for good.

components.name: Product Tour
components.description: 8 onboarding variants: modal (free) plus slideshow, tooltip, spotlight, beacon, checklist, progress steps and announcement (Pro). Portal-based overlay with keyboard navigation.
whenToUse: Onboarding new users or introducing a new feature with guided steps.
You want spotlight/tooltip/beacon/checklist styles over real UI.

examples.title: A step whose target lives on another page
examples.code:
<!-- The tour never navigates: it asks, and you route. Give the step a
     route and the tour emits (routeRequest) the moment that step
     becomes current, then WAITS for its targetSelector to render on
     the new page and anchors to it. Without the wait the target does
     not exist yet when the step arrives, and the step loses its
     spotlight for the rest of the tour. -->
<sv-product-tour-pro
  variant="spotlight"
  [steps]="steps"
  [(active)]="touring"
  [awaitTargetMs]="3000"
  (routeRequest)="router.navigateByUrl($event.route)"
  (targetMissing)="skipStep($event)" />

examples.title: Resuming a tour after a reload
examples.code:
<!-- The tour stores its progress in a versioned envelope under
     persistKey: the step by ID (never an index - inserting a step
     shifts every index after it), the checklist ticks, and whether
     the user completed or dismissed it.

     It never decides whether to show itself: handle
     (progressRestored) and let your own flag, cohort or "seen" table
     decide what [active] should be. -->
<sv-product-tour-pro
  tourId="onboarding"
  [tourVersion]="2"
  persistKey="sv-tour-onboarding"
  resume="step"
  [(active)]="touring"
  [steps]="steps"
  (progressRestored)="onProgress($event)" />

examples.title: What a restored progress tells you
The steps behind it

customization: Spotlight, tooltip, beacon and checklist styles.
Configurable padding and opacity.
Step progress and skip controls.

Progress that survives a reload: `persistKey` + `tourId` store the step BY ID (never an index — inserting a step shifts every index after it), the checklist ticks and whether the tour was completed or dismissed, inside the same versioned envelope six other families use. `resume` decides what an interrupted tour does — `step`, `restart` or `never` — and `(progressRestored)` reports which happened and why. The tour never opens itself: that stays the host's `[active]`.

Schema staleness: `[tourVersion]` versions the steps and `[expectedVersion]` is what the host says its UI is at — a mismatch emits `(schemaStale)`, because only the host can know a screen was rebuilt.
Responsive: the tooltip / beacon cards cap their width to the viewport, so they stay fully on-screen even on the narrowest phones.

Route-aware orchestration: `TourStep.route` + `(routeRequest)` ask the host to navigate (the tour never routes itself), `[awaitTargetMs]` bounds the wait for the new page to render the step's target, and `(targetMissing)` reports a target that never came. A step with no anchor at all centres its card and drops the arrow rather than pointing at whatever the previous step was on.

Off-screen and hidden targets (Pro anchored variants): a step whose target is below the fold or inside a scroll container is scrolled into view first (`scrollIntoView` with `block: nearest` — smooth, instant under reduced motion — and nothing moves for a target already in view). A target that matches but has no box (`display: none`, a collapsed sidebar, a closed `<details>`) counts as missing: it is waited for like a late target, then reported through `(targetMissing)` and handled by the step `onMissingTarget`.
accessibility: Four variants are modal: **modal, slideshow, spotlight, tooltip**. Each dims the page, is `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal="true"`, moves focus into the card on open, traps Tab, marks the rest of the page `inert`, and restores focus on close.

**checklist, announcement, beacon and progress-steps are ambient** — no backdrop, no trap, no inertness. The page behind them stays usable, which is the point of choosing them, and focus stays where the user left it. checklist, progress-steps and announcement are named `role="region"` landmarks (labelled by `tourTitle`, or the announcement's title) so a screen-reader user can find the surface that appeared, and progress-steps marks the current step `aria-current="step"`.

Arrow keys move between steps, except when focus is in a field that has its own use for them (an input, textarea, select, contenteditable, or a listbox/combobox/menu/slider role) — the caret wins there, not the tour.
Esc skips the tour when `allowSkip` is on, and closes a beacon card when one is open. The tour defers Esc to anything opened OVER it, so a select inside the card closes first.

Reduced motion: beacons do not pulse (a still, faint ring marks them instead), the spotlight ring fades rather than sliding between targets, and progress dots, bars and the checklist ring change without animating.

components.name: Progress Bar
components.description: Linear progress with indeterminate, striped, animated and glow modes across 6 variants and 4 sizes.
whenToUse: Showing determinate progress of a known task (upload, import, multi-step save).
Use indeterminate mode when the duration is unknown.
For a compact circular form, use the Progress Ring.

Not sure this is the right wait? Compare spinner, skeleton, progress bar, ring and the fullscreen spinner by duration, known progress and blocking in the “Choosing a feedback pattern” guide under Guides.
customization: Determinate or indeterminate.
Striped, animated and glow styles.
Six variants and four sizes.
`customClass` to extend the wrapper.
accessibility: Always exposes the `progressbar` role with `aria-valuenow`/`min`/`max` and an `aria-valuetext` when a label is set; supply `ariaLabel` to name a standalone bar.

The reported value is quantized to `announceStep` (default 5). A `role="progressbar"` is a live region in everything but name — screen readers speak its value when `aria-valuenow` changes, NVDA by default — so a bar driven by a real upload would otherwise emit a hundred announcements on the way to done and the user could not hear anything else while it ran. The kit cannot throttle the screen reader, so the only lever is how often the attribute changes. `0` and `100` always pass through exactly, and ONLY a real 0 or 100 reports as such: an in-flight 98% reports the last step below 100 (95), never a "finished" the work has not reached, and 99.6 of 100 draws 99%, not a full bar. `[announceStep]="1"` reports every percent again.
Out-of-range values are clamped and disclosed in dev mode; a `NaN` value renders as 0%, never as `NaN`.
Indeterminate state sets `aria-busy` and drops the now-value. A `completed` output fires once on reaching 100%.

Reduced motion: the fill jumps to each value instead of gliding, animated stripes stand still, and the indeterminate sweep is replaced by a still, half-strength track — `aria-busy` still says it is working.

Non-text contrast: every variant fill clears 3:1 against its track in light and dark (success, warning and info use deeper fills for that), stripes darken the fill on a light track and lighten it on a dark one so they can only raise that contrast, and an `xs` bar draws no stripes. Under forced colours the fill is `Highlight` inside a `CanvasText`-edged track.
variants: Progress Ring — Not Started, In Progress, Complete & Failed
Progress Ring — Storage Quota & Onboarding Cards

components.name: Prompt Template Library
components.description: 5 variants: grid card gallery, list view, template editor, picker modal and playground (two templates side by side on one set of variables) — with variable injection, token counter, usage stats, category filter and version history.
whenToUse: Managing reusable prompt templates with variables, versions and usage stats.
Teams standardizing prompts across an AI product.
For a single inline prompt field, a Text Field or Mention input is enough.
customization: Gallery, list, editor, picker and side-by-side playground presentations.
Variable injection with live token count.
Category filter and version history.
Emits `templateSelect` with the chosen template id.

Secret detection is **on out of the box**, using the pack’s own `SV_AI_COMMON_PATTERNS` rather than a second list that would drift. A prompt library is where API keys get pasted into a system message and shared with a team: somebody drops a working key in to see whether the call goes through, it works, and the template is saved, named and handed to nine colleagues — with no commit and no code review anywhere in the path. `[secretPatterns]` narrows or widens it.

The warning renders in the `editor` variant, where the text is edited, as well as in the `grid` footer, and the scan runs on the prompt **as it stands** — a key pasted into a variable is caught as well as one typed into the template.

**Decision: the component emits, the host blocks.** It has no save action of its own, so it cannot block one. `(secretScanChange)` emits `{ id, scan }` (`PromptSecretScanEvent`) when a template is selected and whenever what the scan found changes — including back to clean, so a host can unblock — but not per keystroke; `selectedSecretScan()` exposes the same result for a host that reads it at save time. Copy is deliberately not blocked: putting a key on your own clipboard to call your own model is ordinary use, sharing it through the library is not.

The warning names the **blast radius, not the rule**: 'matches pattern provider-key' tells the author nothing they can act on. And it is a detector, not a redactor — silently rewriting somebody’s prompt is how a template stops working with no explanation.

`[tokenizer]` drives every token figure — the prompt count in the grid footer, list rows, editor header, picker card and both playground sides — and the basis renders beside each one **as text**, not only as a tooltip. The basis travels with the number (`svPromptTokenCount` returns `{ tokens, basis, estimated }`), so a tokenizer that fails falls back to the estimate *and* to the estimate’s label, marked `~`, rather than naming a tokenizer over a figure it never produced. `tokensEst` is shown as the author’s estimate of **output** tokens and is never presented as the count.

Copy confirms only once the clipboard write resolves (`promptCopy`). When the clipboard refuses — plain HTTP, where `navigator.clipboard` does not exist, or a denied permission — the library takes the same in-surface fallback as `sv-ai-chat`: the **resolved prompt is selected**, a line beside the button names ⌘C or Ctrl+C for the reader’s platform, the button’s accessible name says the same, and the line is announced once through `SvLiveAnnouncer`. `copyFailed` still fires with the template id, and `copyPrompt()` resolves `true` / `false`.

Why the basis matters: a token count is a claim about a tokenizer — four characters per token is an **English-prose** approximation, Chinese runs closer to one character per token and minified JSON lands somewhere else again, so an unlabelled figure is a budget built on somebody else’s language. A tokenizer that throws or returns nonsense falls back to the estimate rather than taking the surface down — these come from a host’s own WASM build as often as not.
accessibility: Editor fields are labelled; search inputs carry an aria-label.

inputs.description: Presentation: gallery, list, editor, picker or side-by-side playground.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP 47 locale for dates and numbers.

inputs.name: templates
inputs.description: The library's templates. Bind it to what the server returns; `DEMO_TEMPLATES` is exported for showcases.

inputs.name: compareAId
inputs.description: Left-hand template of the `playground` comparison.

inputs.name: compareBId
inputs.description: Right-hand template of the `playground` comparison.

inputs.name: pricing
inputs.description: Prices and expected completion length the comparison is costed against.

inputs.name: runsPerMonth
inputs.description: Calls a month, for the compounded figure. The per-run difference between two prompts is a fraction of a cent by construction, which is why nobody ever optimises one. This is the number that turns it into something worth acting on.

inputs.name: tokenizer
inputs.description: The tokenizer behind every token figure here. A token count is a claim about a tokenizer. Four characters to the token is an English-prose approximation: Chinese runs closer to one character per token, and minified JSON lands somewhere else again, so a library whose authors write in any of those is handing them a budget wrong by a factor rather than a percentage. Pass your model's own counter and the figures become exact; leave it and they stay estimates that **say** so.

inputs.name: secretPatterns
inputs.description: Patterns that must not be saved into a template. A prompt library is where API keys get pasted into a system message and shared with a team. Somebody drops a working key in to see if the call goes through, it works, and the template is saved, named and handed to nine colleagues — with no commit and no code review anywhere in the path. Defaults to the pack's own `SV_AI_COMMON_PATTERNS`, so this is on out of the box rather than being a policy somebody has to remember to set.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load.

outputs.name: templateSelect
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of the template the user selects/uses.

outputs.name: promptCopy
outputs.description: The resolved prompt reached the clipboard. Carries the template id and the exact text written, so a host can log usage or feed it straight to a model without re-resolving the variables itself.

outputs.name: copyFailed
outputs.description: The clipboard write was refused — an insecure context, or a denied permission. Emitted with the template id so a host can offer a fallback (a select-all, a toast). The component stays silent on its own: claiming a copy that did not happen is worse than saying nothing.

outputs.name: variablesReady
outputs.description: Emitted the moment every required variable of the selected template has a value — distinct from `promptCopy`, which only fires once the user actually clicks copy. A host can use this to enable a "Run" button or log template completion without requiring a clipboard write at all. Fires again if the user clears a required field and refills it, and whenever a different template becomes ready.

outputs.name: secretScanChange
outputs.description: The secret scan of the selected template changed — including back to clean, so a host can unblock. This component has no save action, so it cannot block one. The host owns saving; this is what it blocks on. Emitted when a template is selected and whenever what the scan found changes, not per keystroke. Also readable at any time as `selectedSecretScan()`.

components.name: Property Card
components.description: Real-estate listing card — pageable photo strip with the real gallery count, status ribbon, price with derived price-per-area, a beds/baths/parking/area row that keeps zero and unknown apart, amenity chips, save and compare toggles and an agent line. Grid, list and wide layouts.
whenToUse: Property search results, saved shortlists, agent portfolios and "similar homes" rails.
Anywhere the price needs a per-unit-area figure beside it to be comparable.
For a generic product with a rating and an add-to-cart, use the Product Card instead.

examples.code: <sv-property-card title="7 Sail Loft Row" [price]="3400" pricePeriod="month" [beds]="1" [baths]="1" [area]="890" status="for-rent" />

examples.description: `0` renders as "Studio"; `null` renders nothing. Never conflate them.

examples.title: Sold — the actions are removed, not disabled

customization: Grid, list and wide layouts.
Seven lifecycle statuses with their own ribbon colours, overridable via `statusLabel`.
Amenity chips capped by `featureLimit` with a "+n more" remainder.
Optional 360°-tour marker, agent line and "listed" label.
accessibility: Photo paging exposes labelled previous/next buttons and a polite live region announcing "Photo 2 of 24" — the visible counter sits inside an aria-hidden cluster.
The stat row is a `<dl>` whose `<dt>` carries the written label ("3 bedrooms"), so the figures mean something without the icons.
Save and compare are toggle buttons with `aria-pressed` and labels naming the property.
Alt text is required on every photo rather than optional.

Property prices are not quoted to the cent in any market: `$1,180,000.00` reads as a spreadsheet export rather than an asking price, and the two trailing zeroes are the widest thing on the card. Pass `null` to get the currency default back.

inputs.name: parking

inputs.name: lotArea
inputs.description: Plot area in the same unit. `null` means there is none, or none recorded. It earns its place on a card that already shows floor area because of land: a building plot has no internal area at all, so without this input the card for one renders a price and an empty stat row. It is also the figure that separates two otherwise identical houses. Shown after the floor area, never instead of it — they are different measurements and a card that silently substituted one for the other would make a 1,200 sq ft house on a 9,000 sq ft plot look enormous.

inputs.name: displayAreaUnit

inputs.name: updatedAt
inputs.description: When this listing was last confirmed with its source, as `YYYY-MM-DD` or an ISO timestamp. A sold listing showing as available is the defining failure of a property card, and a status badge alone cannot prevent it: the badge is only ever as true as the last sync, and it never says when that was. A reader who can see the date can judge the badge; one who cannot has to trust it absolutely.

inputs.name: linkMode
inputs.description: Who handles a plain left-click on the card when `href` is set. `'browser'` follows the link, which is a full page load. `'host'` cancels the plain left-click and emits `open` instead, leaving every modified click and every middle-click to the browser — which is what a router-driven app wants: client-side navigation on a normal click, a real new tab on ⌘-click. inputs.name: compareDisabled
inputs.description: The comparison is full, so this card cannot be added to it. A tray with a limit needs this, and every tray has a limit. Told in advance, the button is properly disabled, says why on hover, and is skipped by the keyboard — which is the difference between a limit and a bug. components.name: Pull to Refresh
components.description: A scrolling region that refreshes when pulled down from the top on a touch screen. The pull starts only at the top and only downward — every other touch stays a native scroll, through passive listeners — with an indicator that moves by transform alone, a Refresh button for the keyboard and screen readers, and "Refreshing…" / "Updated" announced. The bare `svPullToRefresh` directive draws no indicator, for your own.
whenToUse: A feed, inbox or list on a phone whose newest items arrive at the top.
Alongside, never instead of, a visible way to refresh on a desktop page — `refreshButton="always"` gives you one.
Not for loading older items at the bottom (use infinite scroll or a Load more button) and not on a page whose content does not change.

examples.title: Your own indicator, with the directive
examples.code: …

customization: `threshold` (indicator px that arms a refresh, 72) and `resistance` (indicator px per finger px, 0.5) tune the feel.
`refreshButton`: `focus` (visible on keyboard focus, like a skip link — the default), `always` or `none`.
`disabled` turns off the pull and the button.
The disc uses the `primary-*` tokens; strings come from the `layout` labels (`pullRegion`, `pullRefresh`, `pullRefreshing`, `pullUpdated`).
For your own indicator, use `svPullToRefresh` on any scroller and read `distance()`, `progress()`, `state()` and `tracking()`; `trigger()` refreshes from code.
accessibility: The region is a named, focusable `role="region"` (a scrolling area must be reachable by keyboard), with `aria-busy` while refreshing.
A real Refresh button sits first inside it — the keyboard, switch and screen-reader way to refresh (WCAG 2.5.7: the pull has a single-pointer alternative).
"Refreshing…" and "Updated" are announced through a polite status region, whichever way the refresh started.
The indicator is decorative (`aria-hidden`). It moves by transform and fades by opacity only; under reduced motion it settles without a slide and the spinner does not spin.
Every listener is passive and none calls `preventDefault()`, so the gesture never delays or blocks native scrolling.

You want a dependency-free encoder with branding (logo, colors) and PNG export.
For displaying an existing barcode image, a plain is enough.

Set `value`, `size` and `errorCorrection` (L, M, Q, H).
Theme with `foreground` / `background` and a configurable `quietZone`.
Overlay a center `logo` sized with `logoSize`; override the accessible name with `ariaLabel`.

High-contrast defaults keep the code scannable.
No interaction required — purely presentational.

inputs.name: size

inputs.name: errorCorrection

The default was 2, which is not a smaller margin but a code a scanner may be unable to find the edges of against whatever surrounds it. Raised to the specified value; anything lower is still accepted and warned about, because a host may be placing the code on a known blank field.

components.name: Query Builder
components.description: Nested AND/OR condition builder — add/remove rules and groups, typed operators per field (string / number / date / enum / boolean), a serializable JSON expression out and import of a saved one back in, and a debounced queryChange output that pairs with a data-table's server-side filtering.
whenToUse: Letting a user build an arbitrary AND/OR filter — support tooling, saved searches, audience/segment builders.

You need the filter itself to be saved, shared or replayed (`svSerializeQuery()` / `svImportQuery()`), not just applied once — the JSON carries a schema version, so a query saved last release is migrated or refused with a reason rather than read as the current shape.

For a single row of per-column filters ANDed together, a data-table's own column filters or `sv-filter-panel`'s facets are lighter weight — `SvDataQuery.filters` is deliberately flat, which is why this ships its own richer expression type.

examples.title: Pairs with a data table's server-side filtering
The headless engine, outside Angular
Translating to SQL without opening an injection
What a date rule means, in which timezone

customization: One-step undo of a removal is built in; the headless engine exposes the same thing as `svLocateQueryNode()` + an `insertNode` action, so a host with its own history stack can restore a node exactly where it was.
Five field types (string / number / date / enum / boolean), each with its own operator set and value editor (single, range, multi-select, or none for `is true`/`is empty`).
No fixed cap on rules per group — the size guidance below is where a query stops being readable — and groups nest up to `maxDepth`.

`svImportQuery()` degrades gracefully when a saved query's field schema has drifted — an unknown field clears the whole rule, a field whose saved operator does not fit keeps the field and clears only the operator/value — and reports both in `result.report` so the user can be told. `svParseQuery()` is the forgiving form for a caller with nowhere to show a message.

**Operator/type pairing is enforced, not just offered.** `applyQueryAction` enforces it as well as the dropdown, so "age contains 5" never round-trips through export, import and `queryChange` as a real filter. An action that would put a rule in a state no field can hold is a no-op — and a refused action emits nothing, because a query that did not change is not a reason to refetch. `isOperatorValidFor()` and `ruleProblem()` are exported for a host validating a query it built itself.

**A plain-language preview** above the rows: "Reads as: Plan is “Pro” and Signed up after 1 Jun 2026." Enum values read by their label, dates as the day the user picked, a nested group bracketed only when it holds more than one condition, and an unfinished rule named rather than skipped — a preview that reads as a finished sentence while the query cannot run is a worse trap than none.
accessibility: Removing a condition or a non-empty group is undoable for one step: a polite status announces it ("Group with 2 conditions removed."), focus moves to the Undo button instead of being dropped on the page, and Undo puts the node back at its old index and returns focus to it. The next edit forgets the removal.
Every field / operator / value control is a native `<select>`/`<input>`, so keyboard and screen-reader support come for free.
Add/remove rule and group buttons are labelled buttons, not icon-only.
Loading, error and empty states for `[fields]` follow the kit-wide async contract (`data-sv-state`) — the expression itself is always local, synchronous state.

Nested AND/OR is the part of this component a non-technical user cannot check their own work on — the rails and indentation say where a group begins and nothing said what the whole query would *do*. The preview says it, in one sentence.

An unfinished condition says what it needs **on the row**, and the row's field control is `aria-describedby` it, so the reason is read out with the control. The toolbar's "some conditions are incomplete" is true of the query and useless about the rule: in three nested groups it left the user checking every row by eye.
The preview is deliberately not a live region — it restates the whole query, so `aria-live` would re-read every condition on each keystroke of a value.

Leave it unset for the browser's own zone, which is right when the user is reading their own dashboard; set it to the zone the *data* is reckoned in when a report has to agree with a server, since that is the one thing this component cannot work out. `svDateRuleWindow()` takes the same zone and does the conversion.

components.name: Radar / Spider Chart
components.description: Multi-series radar/spider chart with configurable axes, fill/stroke mode, dot markers, level grid and auto-positioned labels. States under the plot when the spokes are on different scales, and that the shape depends on the order of the axes. Pure SVG.
whenToUse: Comparing a few items across several shared dimensions (skills, product specs).
You want a quick visual "shape" of strengths and weaknesses.
For exact values, a grouped Bar Chart is more precise.

examples.title: Mixed units, one spoke at a time

customization: Interactive legend (both tiers): hover or keyboard-focus an entry — or a vertex — and every other polygon fades; Enter, Space or a click hides or shows the series. `[(hiddenSeries)]` is two-way bound so a host can persist it; the last visible series cannot be hidden. `[interactiveLegend]="false"` keeps the static key.
Configurable axes and grid levels.
Per-axis `max` or a global `maxValue` for normalisation, with the differing maxima named under the plot when they disagree.
Fill or stroke-only series with markers.
Auto-positioned axis labels.
Responsive: the SVG scales down to fit narrow containers (`max-w-full h-auto`) while keeping its aspect ratio, instead of overflowing at its fixed `size`.
accessibility: The legend is a `role="toolbar"` of `aria-pressed` toggle buttons with ONE tab stop: the arrow keys move between series and put each in front as it is reached, Enter or Space shows or hides it, and the change is announced. A hidden series stays in the summary table.

The SVG is a `role="group"` with a generated summary as its name (override via `ariaLabel`) — `group`, not `img`, because the vertices are tab stops and an `img`'s subtree is pruned out of the accessibility tree with them in it.

A radar encodes value as distance from the centre, which is the hardest quantity on the chart to read off — and impossible to compare across axes whose maxima differ. `sv-data-summary-table` publishes one row per axis and one column per series, plus an "Axis maximum" column when the axes are on mixed scales: without it a reader is told 80 and 40 with no way to know they are the same share of their own axis.

Both caveats are stated in the rendered output, not only in the table — the reader misled by a mixed scale or by an ordering artefact is the one looking straight at the web, and a table is the alternative for someone who cannot see it. There is no input to hide the line, on the same rule as the bullet chart's scale note.
Each vertex is keyboard-focusable with an `aria-label`; focus/hover shows a tooltip and Enter/Space emits `pointSelect`. Legend distinguishes series beyond color.

components.name: Radial Bar Chart
components.description: Concentric progress rings, one per track, with per-track scales, a configurable sweep and start angle, a centre readout and a legend. States under the plot what concentric arcs cannot be read for, and marks any track past the end of its scale. Pure SVG.

examples.title: React to a track running past its scale

customization: Ring thickness, gap and diameter.
Start angle and sweep (360° ring or a 270° dial).
Per-track scale and colour, rounded or butt caps.
Legend and centre readout each optional.

A track past its maximum draws a full ring with a dashed rim outside it and reports its real percentage; one with a non-finite or negative value leaves its ring empty rather than drawing a zero nobody measured.
accessibility: Each ring’s track is a `role="button"` focus target named with its value, scale and percentage — a 0 % track stays reachable because the focus target is the track, not the value arc.

An inner ring is physically shorter than an outer one at the same percentage, so arc length cannot be compared by eye at all — the encoding misleads even a sighted reader. `sv-data-summary-table` publishes each track's value, share and, on per-track scales, its scale maximum: the pair of numbers the rings themselves cannot convey.

The caveat that arc lengths are not comparable is stated in the rendered output, not only in the table — the reader being misled by unequal baselines is the one looking straight at the rings. It names the differing scale maxima when the tracks disagree, and each over-scale track with how far over it is. There is no input to hide it, on the same rule as the bullet chart's scale note.

An over-scale track says so in its accessible name as well as with the dashed rim, because a rim has nothing to say to a screen reader; a track with no usable value is named as such rather than announced as zero — "no value" in the chart's name, "No value" in the table's Share cell and the legend, and `value: null` / `percent: null` on the emitted event.
Animation is disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

examples.title: The chunk inspector, sized for your own model
examples.code:
<!-- 8,192 tokens is text-embedding-3. On a BERT-family encoder the
     limit is 512, and past the REAL limit the embedding call does not
     fail: it truncates, embeds the head, and returns an ordinary
     vector — so the tail is present, searchable-looking and
     unreachable. Tell the inspector which model it is looking at and
     the flag, its tooltip and the row's accessible name all quote that
     number instead of ours. -->
<sv-rag-knowledge-base
  variant="chunks"
  [chunks]="chunks()"
  [embedTokenLimit]="512"
  [maxChunkTokens]="400"
  [minChunkTokens]="32" />

customization: Who can retrieve a source is on **every row**, not only in the expanded panel: a compact audience chip (Everyone, or the group names) in the overview Source Health strip and on each collapsed row in the sources view, with a roll-up of how many sources are open to everyone. The full sentence stays in the expanded detail.

`KbSource.audience` lists the groups that can retrieve a source, and every row says who that is. An **undeclared audience reads as everyone** and says so — reading silence as 'restricted' would make an unmigrated index look safer than it is, which is the one direction this surface must never round. A roll-up counts the sources open to everyone, because a reviewer scanning forty rows will not notice the one without a lock.

`status: 'deleting'` with `KbSource.deletion` — chunks remaining, embeddings remaining, and **whether it can still be retrieved**. Deletion is a lag, not an event: until the chunks and the embeddings go, the retriever can still return the thing somebody asked to have removed, and a panel that says 'deleted' the moment the button is pressed is making a compliance claim it cannot support. The source stays listed while it happens rather than vanishing from a panel whose answers keep arriving. The retrievability sentence renders as real emphasis from `svDeletionParts()` (structured runs, no Markdown, no `innerHTML`); `svDeletionLabel()` is the same notice as plain text.

The retrievability sentence is never omitted while it is true, including when both counts have reached zero — that is the dangerous middle, where nothing is left to delete and answers are still arriving. The counts are reassuring because they go down, and a reader watching them fall will assume the job is done long before it is.

Redaction, from the pack-wide policy: a chunk preview is masked BEFORE it is truncated. The other order leaves a half-secret whenever the preview boundary falls inside one — `sk-live-abcde…` is not a redaction, it is a shorter version of the key.

Every content set is an input that starts EMPTY — `stats`, `sources`, `pipelineRun`, `pastRuns` and `alerts` — so an unwired host shows no invented index, run or history; showcases pass the exported `DEMO_STATS`, `DEMO_SOURCES`, `DEMO_PIPELINE_RUN`, `DEMO_PAST_RUNS` and `DEMO_ALERTS`. The run titles name the run's own `pipelineRun.id`. Uploads and sync progress are transient local state layered over `sources`; supplying a new list discards that layer, because your data is the truth. Alert resolutions are layered the same way and reported through `alertResolved`.

`simulate` is off by default, so `sourceAdded` fires on upload and you supply the updated `sources`. Set it to true only in a showcase — a progress bar that tracks a timer instead of an indexer is worse than none.
Overview, sources, pipeline, health, chunks and retrieval views.
Index stats and sync progress.
Pipeline stage visualization.

Set `uploadable` (sources view) for a drag-and-drop upload zone that adds files as new sources; constrain types with `accept` and listen to `sourceAdded`. An added source is marked as not yet persisted until your `sources` list contains it.
Also emits `sourceSelect` and `syncTriggered` with the source id.

The retrieval panel's two confidence lines are inputs too: `[spreadFlatPct]` (5) and `[marginDecisive]` (0.5), from the still-exported `SV_SPREAD_FLAT_PCT` and `SV_MARGIN_DECISIVE`. Both describe one retriever's score distribution — cosine similarities between 0.78 and 0.83 are flat at five per cent by definition, and BM25 scores from 40 to 2 are never flat at all. `[marginDecisive]` is a SHARE of the spread, so it lives in 0–1; a figure above 1 is refused with a dev warning rather than making every query read "contested" for ever.

The chunk inspector's three token limits are inputs: `[minChunkTokens]` (48), `[maxChunkTokens]` (512) and `[embedTokenLimit]` (8192), defaulting to the exported `SV_CHUNK_MIN_TOKENS`, `SV_CHUNK_MAX_TOKENS` and `SV_EMBED_TOKEN_LIMIT`, which are still exported — `svChunkRows` takes them as an optional last argument and `svChunkFlagLabel(flag, limits, locale)` as its second (pass `undefined` for the defaults). A target ceiling above the embedding limit is clamped down (it would let a chunk be reported healthy AND truncated at embed time), a floor at or above the ceiling is clamped below it, and each `SvChunkRow` carries the limits it was judged against so the wording can never quote a threshold that had nothing to do with the flag.
accessibility: Status and progress conveyed as text.
The upload zone is a real `<label>`-wrapped file input — keyboard-focusable and screen-reader labelled.
Alerts use appropriate roles.

A flagged chunk states the limit it breached in words — in the badge tooltip and in the row's accessible name — and both quote the limits THAT ROW was judged against rather than whatever the inputs currently say, so a re-render cannot put a fresh threshold into a sentence explaining an old verdict.

inputs.description: How many sources either list renders at once. `0` = no ceiling. A source list is short until a connector enumerates. One Confluence space is one row; one Google Drive connector is one row per shared folder, and a large tenant's Drive has thousands. The component cannot tell those apart — they are the same shape of data — so the ceiling is what stops the second case rendering as a page that never paints.

inputs.name: syncingIds
inputs.description: Ids of the sources currently syncing (two-way). A `model` because a sync outlives the click that started it: `syncTriggered` tells the host a sync was asked for, and this is how the host says which ones are still running — after a route change, or for a job that was already in flight when the panel mounted.

inputs.name: minChunkTokens
inputs.description: Below this many tokens a chunk is too small to answer anything.

inputs.name: maxChunkTokens
inputs.description: The target ceiling past which a chunk crowds the context window. A retrieval-budget choice, not a fact: five chunks at 512 tokens is most of a small context window and a rounding error in a large one.

inputs.name: embedTokenLimit
inputs.description: The embedding model's HARD input limit. The default is a fact about one model. 8,192 is `text-embedding-3`; it is 512 on a BERT-family encoder and far higher on some 2026 models. Past the real limit the embedding call does not fail — it truncates, embeds the head and returns a perfectly ordinary vector, so the tail is present, searchable-looking and unreachable. A default that is too high for the deployment hides exactly that, which is why this is an input and not a constant.

inputs.name: spreadFlatPct
inputs.description: Spread, as a share of the top score, under which the set is called flat. A statement about one retriever's score distribution. Cosine similarities that all land between 0.78 and 0.83 are flat at five per cent by definition; BM25 scores running from 40 to 2 are never flat at all. The default is reasoned for a normalised vector score and is not a fact about anyone else's.

inputs.name: marginDecisive
inputs.description: Share of the spread the first step must take for the set to be decisive. A SHARE, so `0`–`1`. Passing `50` for "half" would demand a first step fifty times the whole spread — no result set can reach it, so every query would read `contested`, permanently and silently.

inputs.name: levelLabels
inputs.description: What each level of the scale MEANS, from level 1 upwards. Only stars are ordinal by convention. Five stars is a quality scale everyone has already agreed on, so "3 of 5 stars" is a complete sentence. Three hearts out of five is not a rating of 3 — it is a like count wearing a rating's clothes, and "3 of 5 hearts" tells a screen-reader user a number and nothing about what they just said. Fire and thumb are worse: nobody has a shared scale for either. So the meaning is declarable instead of assumed. With labels, `aria-valuetext` becomes "4 of 5 — Really like it", which is what `aria-valuetext` is FOR: the number is already in `aria-valuenow`, and a value text that only repeats it earns nothing. Labels are per whole level. A half-step has no name, so `3.5` announces numerically — which is honest, and better than inventing "between Good and Great".

components.name: Reasoning Trace
components.description: Reasoning-summary display for a reasoning model. Streams token by token, stays open while the model thinks, then collapses itself to a summary chip the moment it finishes — the lifecycle that separates it from a timeline. Four variants: inline chip, numbered steps, streaming and nested. Per-step kind, status, latency, tokens and attributed confidence; sub-thoughts render recursively; content goes through sv-streaming-markdown so nothing reaches the DOM as markup. `[disclosure]` governs what a viewer may see, and a step’s verbatim provider reasoning is off unless asked for by name.
whenToUse: Showing a reasoning model's thinking beside its answer, without letting it dominate the thread.
Debugging why an agent chose one path over another — the reflection steps are usually where it went wrong.
Giving a reviewer the model's stated confidence per step before they act on the output.
Rendering a live "thinking" state that resolves into something compact when it completes.

examples.title: Inline in a chat message
examples.description: Resolves to one chip — "Thought for 3.5s · 6 steps" — that expands on demand.

examples.title: Live, then self-collapsing
examples.description: Open with a caret while thinking; collapses itself the moment streaming ends.

examples.title: Reasoning as the subject of the page
examples.description: Turn auto-collapse off when the trace is the content rather than an aside.

examples.title: Sub-thoughts with attributed confidence
examples.description: Nested branches render recursively; the meter says what its figure is, so a self-report does not read as a calibrated probability.

examples.title: A deeply branching trace
examples.description: Sub-thoughts past two levels wait behind a counted "Show N nested steps" button; each further level asks again.

customization: `[disclosure]`: `summary` (chip and step titles), `steps` (the model’s narration — the default) or `full` (also each step’s verbatim `raw` provider reasoning). The dangerous field is `raw`: several providers’ terms prohibit displaying the hidden reasoning their models emit, and it is the text most likely to contain a user’s own words repeated back — so it is a field of its own, separate from `content`, and it renders only at `full`, with a dev warning when it actually does.

The default is `steps`, not `summary`. Defaulting a component whose whole purpose is showing reasoning steps to 'hide the steps' would be a silent breaking change dressed as a safety fix; the thing that needed a safe default was `raw`, which is new and starts hidden.

`[confidenceBasis]` names what the confidence figure is — 'self-reported by the model', 'mean token logprob'. A per-step confidence with no method behind it is a decorative number on an unverifiable claim: '80%' reads as calibrated when it is usually the model rating its own certainty, which is not comparable across models, prompts or runs. With the meter on and no basis the figure still renders and says 'no method recorded', and the console says so too.

The prose here says **reasoning summary**, not 'chain-of-thought', deliberately: the older name invites integrators to pipe a provider’s raw hidden reasoning straight to the DOM. The package name and the `sv-reasoning-trace` selector are unchanged — renaming those would break every host for a wording fix.

Redaction, from the pack-wide policy: a step's title and body are masked per `provideSvAiPrivacy({ patterns })`, with a note on the step saying something is hidden. Reasoning content quotes the prompt, and the prompt is where the secrets are — a trace is also the thing people screenshot into a bug report.
`variant` picks the presentation: `inline` for a chip in a thread, `steps` for a numbered list, `streaming` for live output, `nested` for branch connectors.
`summary` replaces the generated chip text when you want domain wording rather than "Thought for 3.5s · 6 steps".
`showTiming` and `showConfidence` control the per-step chips; `maxHeight` sets where the list starts scrolling.

`[maxDepth]` (default `SV_REASONING_MAX_DEPTH`, 4) caps how many nested levels render without asking. A step's sub-thoughts past it wait behind a "Show N nested steps" disclosure that counts every hidden step, and each further level asks again — nothing is dropped, and a deeply branching trace stays readable and cheap. `0` renders every level.
`headingOffset` (default 3) demotes Markdown headings inside a step so a thought cannot hijack the page outline.
Each step's `kind` selects its glyph — observation, plan, thought, reflection, decision — so the shape of the reasoning is readable at a glance.
The `summariseTrace` and `flattenSteps` helpers are exported for building your own summary UI over the same model.
accessibility: The trace is a real disclosure: a `button` with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` pointing at the step list, and the same wiring again per step.
While the model is thinking the region carries `aria-busy="true"` rather than a live region — announcing every token would read the entire monologue aloud.
Completion is announced once, via a visually-hidden `role="status"` region carrying the summary.
Status is never colour-only: each step's marker is a distinct glyph — clock, spinner, check or warning triangle.

The confidence meter is `role="img"` with a spoken label that carries its basis ("Confidence 82% — self-reported by the model", or "— no method recorded"), so it is neither silent to screen readers nor presented to them as a calibrated probability.
Sub-thought indentation is capped at four levels, so a deep chain stays reachable rather than running off-screen.
Past `maxDepth`, the "Show N nested steps" control is a real `button` with `aria-expanded`, and `aria-controls` pointing at the revealed list once it exists; its name carries the count.

Defaulting a component whose whole purpose is showing reasoning steps to "hide the steps" would be a silent breaking change dressed as a safety fix. components.name: Record Grid
components.description: The data table's `responsive="records"`: a table that becomes a list of records when there is no room to be a table. Below the breakpoint the markup stops claiming to be a table and becomes a list of real <dl> label/value pairs — the structure HTML already has for this — with sorting, selection and row actions rebuilt rather than lost, and nothing dropped.
whenToUse: Any data table that has to work on a phone — which is most of them.
A table embedded in a narrow panel on a wide screen: set `recordView="always"`, because a media query cannot see the panel.
For a compact card per row with every column shown (and windowed under `virtualized` on the Pro table), `responsive="cards"` is the lighter option.
For a genuinely small set of fields per record, a Descriptions list on its own may be all you need.

examples.title: Why not the CSS trick
examples.description: The technique everyone reaches for sets display:block on the table elements and pipes the column header into each cell through a data-label and a ::before. Two things go wrong and both are invisible. The moment those elements stop being display:table-* the browser drops their table roles, so a screen reader is handed a pile of anonymous blocks instead of rows and columns. And generated content from ::before is not text a user can select, search for or copy. The result looks like labelled cards and is less accessible than the table it replaced.
examples.code:
• Ada Lovelace

    Status
    Shipped
    Total
    £42.00

examples.title: Nothing is dropped
examples.description: The other common answer to a table that does not fit is to hide the columns that do not. A table that silently drops three of its eight fields on a phone is not a responsive table, it is a different table, and nobody is told which one they are reading. A column marked priority: 'secondary' moves behind a per-card disclosure that says how many are in it.

examples.title: Sorting has nowhere to live in a card list
examples.description: The table's sort affordance is the header cell, and a card list has no headers — so a table that becomes cards loses sorting unless the control is rebuilt somewhere else. The records view rebuilds it as a labelled select and a named direction button, and both drive the table's own sort: client-side it reorders, server-side it emits, and switching views never loses it.

examples.title: A narrow panel on a wide screen
examples.description: A media query measures the viewport, not the panel the table sits in. Where you know the space is narrow, show the records at any width.
examples.code:
<sv-data-table [columns]="columns" [rows]="rows" responsive="records" recordView="always" />
<!-- or move the switch: [recordBreakpoint]="900" -->

customization: `responsive="records"` with `recordBreakpoint` (default 768) and `recordView` (`auto` / `always`) decides when the records replace the table; `auto` measures the viewport with `matchMedia`, re-measuring when the breakpoint changes, and only while `responsive` is `records`.
`recordTitleKey` promotes one field to the record heading; `priority: 'secondary'` on a column moves it behind the per-record disclosure.
Selection, sort, `actions` (each `handler` runs), paging, loading and the empty message are the table's own, shared by both views.
Two-way `recordExpandedIds` holds which records have their secondary fields open, keyed by `rowKey`, so a host can restore it.
Both tiers: `sv-data-table` (`@styloviz/data-table`) and `sv-data-table-pro` (`@styloviz-pro/data-table`). `responsive="records"` is the record-list layout in both.
accessibility: Keyboard at scale: the records view renders the page the table is on, so the table's paging bounds it.

Below the breakpoint the markup **stops claiming to be a table**. It is a `<ul role="list">` of `<article>` cards, each labelled by its own heading and holding a real `<dl>` of `<dt>`/`<dd>` pairs — which is what a screen reader announces as "Status, definition, Shipped".
The labels are real text, not `::before` generated content, so they can be selected, searched and copied.
Every control names the record it acts on — "Select Grace Hopper", "Refund Grace Hopper", "Show 2 more fields for Ada Lovelace" — because a card list has no row context to fall back on.
The sort control is a labelled `<select>` with a named direction button rather than an icon, since a list of records has no header cell to carry the affordance.
A server render shows the table, because a prerender cannot measure and the table is the view that holds every field and every label.

inputs.name: rows
inputs.description: The rows to render. `readonly` on purpose: the table never mutates this array, and anything that hands it one — a signal, a `computed`, `svDataController.items` — is handing over a value it still owns. A mutable `T[]` here rejected every one of those at the template boundary while promising a write the table does not perform.

inputs.name: virtualized
inputs.description: Windows row rendering to what's scrolled into view, using the same variable-height primitive (`createVariableVirtualizer`, `@styloviz/core`) `list-view` uses — a group header and a data row are different heights, so this table always needs the variable form, never the fixed one. Ignores `paginated`: virtualization and client pagination solve the same problem (a huge row set costing too much DOM), so turning this on reads as opting OUT of pagination rather than stacking both — the same relation `groupBy` has to pagination, and for the same reason.

inputs.name: virtualRowHeight
inputs.description: Approximate pixel height of one data row; the virtualized window is computed from it. Approximate, like `list-view`'s `itemHeight`: measure your own rendered row height for pixel accuracy. A wrong guess still renders every row correctly, with a slightly-off scrollbar length until the next scroll event corrects it.

inputs.name: cardRowHeight

A card is taller than a row and its height depends on how many columns are visible — a two-column grid of label/value pairs, so roughly `ceil(columns / 2) * 46 + 32`. Approximate for the same reason `virtualRowHeight` is: a wrong guess costs scrollbar accuracy, never correctness.

inputs.name: viewportHeight
