components.name: Slot Picker
components.description: An appointment picker: a strip of days, each with how many times are free, the free times of the chosen day, a duration and a time zone. Every time is judged by the scheduler's own `svCheckSlot` with double-booking refused, so a public bookings page and the diary behind it never disagree. Working hours, blocked time (lunch, a ward round), a buffer around each booking, minimum notice, resources and daylight-saving changeovers are all honoured; the value carries the business's wall time and the UTC instants.
whenToUse: A public bookings page: a consultation, a clinic, a salon, a demo call — a customer picks one free time.
A booking form inside an app where staff book on someone's behalf and must not double-book.
Use Calendar / Scheduler to see or edit the whole diary, and Date Picker (with Time Picker) when any date or time will do.

examples.title: Hours, lunch and a buffer
examples.description: Times run from the start of working hours every `stepMinutes` (the duration by default) while the whole appointment fits before the end. A blocked interval is shown, disabled, with its label; `bufferMinutes` keeps a gap either side of every booking.
examples.code:
<sv-slot-picker
  timeZone="Europe/London"
  [workingHours]="{ days: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], start: '09:00', end: '17:30' }"
  [blocked]="[{ id: 'lunch', label: 'Lunch', start: '12:30', end: '13:30', daysOfWeek: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] }]"
  [events]="bookings"
  [stepMinutes]="15"
  [bufferMinutes]="10"
  [minNoticeMinutes]="120"
  [(value)]="picked" />

examples.title: Show the times in the visitor's zone
examples.description: The strip's days, the hours and the value stay in the business's `timeZone`; `displayTimeZone` only changes how the times read. A time that falls on another calendar day there says "+1 day" in words.
examples.code:
<sv-slot-picker
  timeZone="Europe/London"
  [timeZones]="['Europe/London', 'America/New_York', 'Asia/Tokyo']"
  [(displayTimeZone)]="viewerZone"
  [(value)]="picked" />
<!-- picked: { date, startTime, endTime (London), start, end (UTC ISO), durationMinutes, timeZone } -->

examples.title: One diary per practitioner
examples.description: With `resourceIds`, only bookings and blocks for those resources count — a ward round closes one doctor's morning, not the clinic's.

examples.title: The rules without the component
examples.description: The generator is exported — for a server that re-checks a booking before it saves it, or a "next free appointment" line elsewhere on the page.

customization: `durations` (minutes) shows a segmented control when there is more than one; `stepMinutes` sets the gap between starts.
`days` sets how many days the strip shows (7 by default); `startDate`, `minDate` and `maxDate` bound it, and a date picker jumps to any day in range.
`showUnavailable` hides taken, blocked and too-soon times instead of listing them disabled; `groupByPartOfDay` turns the Morning / Afternoon / Evening groups off.
`now` pins the clock, for tests and demos. `locale` sets the day and time format, 12- or 24-hour included.
Every string comes from the `schedulerPro` labels (`slot*` keys) in 12 language packs.
`svGenerateSlots`, `svFirstAvailableDate`, `svDurationParts` and `svSlotZone` are exported.
accessibility: Two WAI-ARIA patterns built on the kit's own primitives (`@angular/aria` is not a dependency in 2.0, as with the import wizard): the day strip is a tablist with automatic activation (←/→ — mirrored in RTL — Home and End), and the times are a single-select listbox inside its tab panel.

In the listbox, arrows only move; Enter or Space picks — choosing a time is a commitment, so selection does not follow focus. Home / End, Page Up / Page Down and typing digits move too. One tab stop for the day strip, one for the times.

A taken, blocked or too-soon time stays focusable with `aria-disabled` and says why in its name ("10:30, taken", "12:30, unavailable: Lunch"). Each day tab says how many times are free, or "Full", or "Closed".

Picking a time is announced in a polite live region with the day, the times and the zone, and repeated in a visible summary. "+1 day" for a time that lands on another day in the display zone is text, not colour.

While bookings load or failed, the panel shows the shared skeleton or a `role="alert"` error with a Retry button; an empty day says whether it is closed or fully booked and offers the next free day as a button.
variants: Book a Consultation — Durations, Lunch & Time Zones
A Clinic Rota — One Diary per Practitioner
Wired to an API — Loading, Error & Retry

components.name: Smart Paste
components.description: A button that fills a form from text on the clipboard — an email signature, a contact card, a support ticket, a `Label: value` list. A resolver maps the text to field values (your AI gateway behind your own endpoint, or the built-in reader that runs on the device), and the answer is checked and typed against your field list before `(filled)` emits it: unknown keys dropped, numbers, booleans and dates coerced, select values held to their options.
whenToUse: People retype details they already have in front of them — a lead from an email signature, a customer from a support ticket, an address from a chat.
You have, or plan, an AI gateway and want its output checked against the form before anything is filled.
For many records at once use the Import Wizard; for one value use the field itself.

examples.title: Signal Forms — one update fills the form
examples.description: Describe the fields once; the result is keyed by `name` and already typed (a number for `number`, `YYYY-MM-DD` for `date`, `true`/`false` for `boolean`), so it spreads straight into the model. `missing` lists required fields nothing filled.

examples.title: Your AI gateway, behind your own endpoint
examples.description: `svSmartPasteFetchResolver` POSTs `{ text, fields }` to the URL you give it (relative or http(s) only), reads `{ values }` back, and passes the abort signal, so Cancel stops the request. Keep the model key on the server.

examples.title: A resolver of your own
examples.description: Any `({ text, fields, signal }) => Promise<Record<string, unknown>>`. Its answer may be sloppy — the component coerces it, and `svSmartPasteCoerce` is exported so a server can reach the same verdict.

customization: `fields` (`{ name, label, type?, description?, options?, required?, aliases? }`; types `text` `email` `phone` `number` `date` `select` `boolean` `textarea`), `resolver`, `confirm`, `maxLength` (default 10,000; longer text fails with `TOO_LONG` and is not sent), `disabled`.
`size` (`sm` / `md` / `lg`) and `variant` (`primary` / `secondary` / `outline` / `ghost`) follow `sv-button`.
Outputs: `filled`, `failed` (an `SvDataError`), `pasting` (true / false). Methods: `pasteText(text)` for a paste source of your own, `cancel()`.
Every visible and spoken string is a `smartPaste…` label in the `formsPro` namespace, in 12 language packs; `labels` overrides them per instance.
accessibility: A native `<button>`; while resolving it carries `aria-busy` and becomes Cancel, so the request can always be stopped from the keyboard.

Where the browser will not share the clipboard, a labelled textarea opens in place (`aria-expanded` / `aria-controls` on the button) and takes focus; pasting into it fills at once, Ctrl/⌘+Enter fills what was typed, Escape closes it and returns focus.
The confirm preview is a labelled section that takes focus, lists values as a description list and skipped values with their reason; Escape discards.
The outcome is spoken through the live announcer — “Filled 4 fields, 1 skipped.” — and failures show in an error shell with Try again.
variants: Contact Form — Paste an Email Signature (Signal Forms)
Support Ticket — Mock AI Resolver with a Confirm Preview
States — Failure & Try Again, Length Limit, Sizes

inputs.name: fields
inputs.description: The fields to fill: `{ name, label, type?, description?, options?, required?, aliases? }`. Entries with an empty or repeated `name` are ignored; with none, the button is disabled.

inputs.name: resolver
inputs.description: Maps the text to values: `({ text, fields, signal }) => Promise<Record<string, unknown>>`. `null` uses the on-device heuristic resolver. The result is validated and coerced before `(filled)`. The text is sent wherever this sends it.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disable the button (and `pasteText()`).

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Button size.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Button treatment.

inputs.name: maxLength
inputs.description: The most characters of pasted text accepted; longer text fails with `TOO_LONG` and is not sent.

inputs.name: confirm
inputs.description: Show the mapped values with Apply / Discard before emitting `(filled)`.

inputs.name: labels
inputs.description: Per-instance text, merged over the registry's `formsPro` labels.

outputs.name: filled
outputs.description: Coerced values to apply: `{ values, skipped, missing, text }`. Emitted after Apply when `confirm` is on.

outputs.name: failed
outputs.description: The resolver failed or the text was refused (`code: 'TOO_LONG'`); the message is also shown with Try again when retryable.

outputs.name: pasting
outputs.description: `true` when a resolve starts, `false` when it ends — done, failed or cancelled.

components.name: Smart Textarea
components.description: A native textarea with inline completion: a suggestion appears in grey after the caret, Tab takes it, Ctrl/Cmd+→ takes a word, Escape dismisses it. Your completer supplies the text — a phrase list on the device, or a model behind your own endpoint — with requests debounced and aborted as the user types on. A ControlValueAccessor and validator with `required` and a character limit.
whenToUse: Replies, notes and descriptions that repeat — support answers, ticket summaries, release notes — where finishing the sentence saves real typing.
You have a completion model and want it in a field that still behaves exactly like a textarea.
For picking people or tags after `@` or `#`, use Mention instead.

examples.title: A phrase list, on the device
examples.description: `svSmartTextareaPhraseCompleter` completes the phrase whose start matches what was just typed — canned replies, snippets, signatures. Nothing is sent.

examples.title: A model behind your own endpoint
examples.description: `svSmartTextareaFetchCompleter` POSTs `{ before, after }` and reads `{ completion }`; the request is aborted the moment the answer cannot be shown. Rejections go to `(completionFailed)` and nothing is shown.

examples.title: Reactive forms
examples.description: Binds with formControl / formControlName / ngModel and reports `required` and `maxlength`; a suggestion is cut to fit `maxLength`.

customization: `value` is a two-way model; `completer`, `enabled`, `debounceMs` (350), `minChars` (3), `contextLength` (2000), `showHint` (the hint line and touch Accept button).
`placeholder`, `rows`, `autosize` + `maxRows`, `maxLength`, `required`, `invalid`, `disabled`, `readonly`, `spellcheck`, `inputId`, `ariaLabel`, `ariaDescribedBy`.
Outputs: `suggestionShown`, `suggestionAccepted` (`{ text, partial }`), `suggestionDismissed`, `completionFailed`. Methods: `focus()`, `requestSuggestion()`, `acceptSuggestion()`, `dismiss()`.
Strings are `smartTextarea…` labels in the `formsPro` namespace, in 12 language packs.
accessibility: A native `<textarea>` with `aria-autocomplete="inline"` while completion is on, and a described-by hint naming the keys: Tab accepts, Escape dismisses, Ctrl/Cmd+Space asks.
Tab accepts only while a suggestion shows; otherwise it moves focus as usual, so the field never traps the keyboard.
Each suggestion is announced once through the live announcer; the ghost text itself is `aria-hidden`.
An Accept button under the suggestion does what Tab does on a touchscreen. IME composition never triggers or accepts a suggestion.
variants: Support Reply — Completion from a Phrase List
Release Update — Mock AI Completer, Word-by-Word Accept
Reactive Forms — Required, a Limit, Read-only & Disabled

inputs.name: contextLength

components.name: Sparkline
components.description: Micro-chart small enough to live in a table cell, list row or stat card. Four encodings — line, area, bar and win/loss — with optional smoothing, last-point and extreme markers, a dashed reference baseline and a pinnable domain. Pure SVG, zero dependencies.
whenToUse: Adding a trend column to a table without giving up a full chart's worth of space.
Showing momentum beside a single number in a stat card or KPI tile.
Summarising a series inside a list row, dropdown or tooltip.
Showing pass/fail history — builds, deploys, uptime checks — with the win/loss variant.

examples.title: In a table row
examples.description: Nothing is measured and no layout is read, so a sparkline per row is safe inside a virtualized table.

examples.title: Win / loss
examples.description: Drops magnitude and shows only direction — the right encoding for binary outcomes like builds or deploys.

examples.title: Comparable rows — the shared-domain mode
examples.description: A column of sparklines each scaled to itself invites exactly the comparison it cannot support: row A rising 2% and row B rising 900% draw the identical shape, side by side, and nothing on the page says otherwise. Compute one range over every row's series and hand the same tuple to all of them. When you do not, the accessible label says so out loud — "scaled to this series alone, so its height is not comparable" — because a reader who cannot see the scale is being invited to compare heights that do not mean the same thing.

examples.title: A sample that was never collected
examples.description: Four policies, and every one of them is a claim about data nobody has. gap (the default) breaks the line and is the only one that invents nothing. skip closes up, which silently rewrites the x axis — a Tuesday the collector never ran renders as a continuous trend from Monday to Wednesday. zero asserts the value was zero, which for a rate or a price is a different statement from "not collected", and it drags the whole domain down with it. connect draws a straight line across. Whichever you pick, the accessible label names it and counts the gaps — being told "12 points" when three of them are holes is the reading a sighted reader gets from the break in the line and a screen-reader user did not.
examples.code:
<!-- null, undefined, NaN and Infinity are all "missing". -->
<sv-sparkline [data]="[10, null, 30, 40]" />
<sv-sparkline [data]="[10, null, 30, 40]" missing="connect" />

examples.title: Target line
examples.description: A dashed rule at a budget or goal. For bar charts it is also the value bars grow from.

customization: Colour comes from `currentColor`, so the chart inherits the text colour around it — wrap it in any `text-*` class to theme it, and dark mode needs no extra work.
`tone` sets that colour from a semantic token: `auto` (direction of travel), `primary`, `positive`, `warning`, `negative` or `neutral`.
`width`, `height`, `strokeWidth` and `barGap` size the drawing box; the viewBox matches, so nothing is scaled or blurred.
`fluid` stretches the chart to its container while keeping `width` as the coordinate space — for a chart spanning a card. Leave it off in a table cell, where a fixed width keeps columns aligned.
`smooth` rounds the line using quadratic segments through point midpoints, which keeps the curve inside the data envelope rather than overshooting a spike the way a cubic spline would.
The geometry is exported (`pointsOf`, `linePathOf`, `areaPathOf`, `barsOf`, `statsOf`, `svSharedDomain`, `toSlots`, `applyMissing`) for building a custom micro-chart on the same maths.
`domain` takes a `[min, max]` tuple for the whole group and wins over `domainMin` / `domainMax`, which stay for pinning one end.
`missing` chooses the gap policy: `gap` (default), `skip`, `zero` or `connect`. A gap keeps its slot, so the break lands where the sample actually is and every later point stays put.
accessibility: The SVG is `role="img"` with a generated summary — for example *"Sparkline, 12 points, trending up 8.7%, from 92 to 100, low 88, high 104"* — so the series is conveyed without sight of the shape.
Pass `ariaLabel` to replace that summary with domain wording.
Pass `ariaHidden` to remove it from the accessibility tree; the `role` is dropped along with the label, so no role-less `aria-label` is left behind for axe to flag.
Colour is never the only carrier: the win/loss variant also positions losses below the axis, and extreme markers differ in fill as well as position.
An empty series renders a sized, `aria-hidden` placeholder so a row does not reflow when data arrives.

The summary states the scale: either the shared range it was drawn against (with a count of any points clamped to the edge) or, when none was given, that the chart is scaled to its own series and its height is not comparable with its neighbours.

Missing samples are counted in the summary along with what was done about them — "3 missing samples, drawn as breaks" — so the hole a sighted reader sees in the line is not invisible to a screen reader.
variants: The Same Picture, Meaning Nothing Like the Same Thing

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the series is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Rendered as a muted dash in the same box, not a card.

inputs.name: data

inputs.description: Pin the bottom of the value range instead of using the series minimum.

inputs.name: domainMax
inputs.description: Pin the top of the value range instead of using the series maximum.

inputs.name: domain
inputs.description: `[min, max]` for the whole group — the shared-domain mode for a table column. A column of sparklines each scaled to itself invites exactly the comparison it cannot support. Row A rising 2% and row B rising 900% draw the identical shape, side by side, and nothing on the page says otherwise. Compute one range with `svSharedDomain()` over every row's series and hand the same tuple to all of them. Takes precedence over `domainMin` / `domainMax`, which stay for pinning one end. When none of the three is set, the scale is per-series and the accessible label says so — because a reader who cannot see that is being invited to compare heights that do not mean the same thing.

inputs.name: missing
inputs.description: What to do with a missing sample.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Drawing style.

inputs.name: width

inputs.name: height
inputs.description: Height of the drawing box in px.

inputs.name: strokeWidth
inputs.description: Line thickness in px.

inputs.name: smooth
inputs.description: Round the line through point midpoints. Ignored by bar variants.

inputs.name: tone
inputs.description: Colour source.

inputs.name: barGap
inputs.description: Gap between bars in px, for `bar` and `winloss`.

Use this for a chart that spans a fluid card; leave it off in a table cell, where a fixed width keeps columns aligned.

inputs.name: showExtremes

inputs.name: baseline
inputs.description: Draw a horizontal rule at this value — a target, budget or zero line.

inputs.name: ariaLabel

inputs.name: ariaHidden
inputs.description: Hide from assistive tech — use when adjacent text already conveys the data.

outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load. Nothing here triggers it.

components.name: Speed Dial / FAB
components.description: Floating action button with up/down/left/right expand directions, a custom action list, pulse animation, tooltip labels and viewport-aware positioning that auto-flips and clamps so the menu never leaves the screen.
whenToUse: Exposing a primary action plus a few related quick actions in a floating button.
Mobile-first or content-heavy screens where a toolbar would crowd the layout.
For a row of always-visible actions, use the Toolbar.

examples.title: Pinned to a corner, clear of other floating UI
examples.description: floating pins the dial and joins the shared floating layer, so Scroll to Top, a host chat launcher, a cookie banner or a bottom nav in the same corner stack instead of overlapping.
examples.code:
<sv-speed-dial [actions]="actions" floating="bottom-right" (actionClick)="run($event)" />

// A host widget the kit does not own registers its own region:
const chat = inject(SvFloatingLayerService).register({ anchor: 'bottom-right', height: 64, order: 5, label: 'chat' });

examples.title: Destructive action with confirmation
examples.description: The first activation arms the item and announces the prompt; the second confirms; Escape or moving away cancels. No window.confirm.

customization: Four expand directions.
Three action styles: default, labeled and mini.
Per-action colour, badge and disabled state.
Solid, high-contrast label chips that stay legible while the page scrolls.
Viewport-aware positioning: measures the panel, flips to the side with room, then shifts it fully on-screen.

Floating layer (`floating`, `floatingOrder`): pins the dial to a corner with `position: fixed`, adds the device safe-area inset, and stacks it with every other registered region — Scroll to Top, affixed blocks, and anything the host registers through `SvFloatingLayerService` (chat launcher, cookie banner, bottom nav). A full-width edge region pushes every corner on its side; `floatingOrder` (default 10) decides who sits nearest the edge. `null` (default) leaves positioning to you.

Confirmation: `destructive` (danger styling + confirmation) and `confirm` (`true` or a custom prompt string, `false` to opt out) per action; `confirmText` localises the default "Confirm: <label>" prompt.

Variant axes: `variant` (default, labeled, mini) and `color` are appearance; `direction`, `tooltip`, `floating` and per-action `confirm` are behavioural modes. Every appearance works with every mode; `mini` with `tooltip=false` leaves only icons, so keep labels meaningful for the accessible name.

Portals and layers: the menu is portalled to `<body>` through the kit's portal host, which carries a locally scoped `.dark`, `data-theme`, `dir` and `lang` from where the dial sits, and takes its z-index from the shared overlay stack — above page chrome, below a dialog opened later. The dial itself, when `floating`, sits in the floating band (z 50), always under overlays. It is not portalled, though: with `floating` set it is `position: fixed`, so an ancestor with `transform`, `filter`, `perspective`, `backdrop-filter`, `contain` or `container-type` becomes its containing block and it pins to that box, not the viewport — mount a floating dial outside such wrappers.

Reduced motion: the pulse ring is removed, and the entrance stagger, icon turn and hover scale are stilled under `prefers-reduced-motion`. Forced colors: the pulse is hidden and the trigger and items get a ButtonText edge, plus a system-coloured focus outline (the focus ring is a box shadow, which forced colors removes).

Browser limits: safe-area insets only apply when the page sets `viewport-fit=cover`; iOS Safari's virtual keyboard does not resize the layout viewport, so a fixed dial can sit under the keyboard while an input is focused — hide it (`@if`) while editing if that matters.
accessibility: Trigger exposes aria-haspopup/aria-expanded/aria-controls; actions live in a labelled `role="menu"`.
Focus moves into the menu on open and returns to the trigger on Escape/select; Arrow keys, Home and End navigate items.
A confirming item keeps focus, is renamed to its prompt, and the prompt is announced assertively. Enter confirms, Escape cancels (a second Escape closes the menu), arrowing away cancels.
Escape is owned by the topmost overlay, so a dialog opened over the dial closes first.
variants: Floating, stacked with Scroll to Top

components.name: Spinner
components.description: Loading indicators in 4 styles (border, dots, pulse, bars), 5 sizes, 7 color variants and an optional fullscreen overlay.
whenToUse: Indicating an indeterminate wait where progress can't be measured.
Inline (button, card) or as a fullscreen overlay during route/data loads.
For content placeholders that preserve layout, use the Skeleton Loader.

Not sure this is the right wait? Compare spinner, skeleton, progress bar, ring and the fullscreen spinner by duration, known progress and blocking in the “Choosing a feedback pattern” guide under Guides.

examples.title: Say how long it usually takes
examples.code:
<!-- One number. It is SHOWN to the user ("about 25 seconds") and it
     derives both escalation thresholds — slow at 1.5x, stuck at 4x — so
     the figure on screen and the moment the spinner admits lateness
     cannot drift apart. The line disappears the instant it stops being
     true. -->
<sv-spinner label="Importing…" [expectedMs]="25000" [labelVisible]="true" />

examples.title: Escalate an indefinite wait
examples.code:
<!-- A spinner is indistinguishable from a failed request, forever. These
     two thresholds are both measured from the moment the spinner appears:
     at 10s it says so, at 45s it offers a way out. Set cancelLabel only
     when (cancelled) can actually stop the work. -->
<sv-spinner
  [overlay]="true"
  label="Importing…"
  [slowAfterMs]="10000"
  [stalledAfterMs]="45000"
  slowMessage="Still importing — large files can take a minute."
  cancelLabel="Stop the import"
  (cancelled)="abortImport()"
  (escalated)="logSlowImport($event)" />

customization: Four animation styles.
Five sizes and seven colors.
Optional fullscreen overlay mode.
`customClass` to extend the wrapper.

Escalation: `[slowAfterMs]` says "this is taking longer than usual", `[stalledAfterMs]` says it looks stuck and can offer a `cancelLabel` button; both messages are overridable, `(escalated)` reports each step, and both are off by default. Shared with the Skeleton Loader — `createWaitEscalation` in `@styloviz/core`.

A stated expectation: `[expectedMs]` renders "about 25 seconds" from the first frame and derives `slow` at 1.5x and `stalled` at 4x, so one number drives the sentence and both timers; an explicit threshold still wins, `expectationMessage` overrides or blanks the wording, and `resolvedSlowAfterMs` / `resolvedStalledAfterMs` report what the component settled on. Figures round up and snap to a five-second grid above ten seconds — understating a wait is the lie that matters, and "about 23 seconds" dresses a guess up as a measurement.

Delayed show and minimum duration: `[showAfterMs]="200"` renders nothing (and announces nothing) until the wait has lasted 200 ms, so a fast response never flashes a spinner; `[minVisibleMs]="400"` keeps one that did appear for at least 400 ms. Bind `[active]="loading()"` and keep the spinner mounted — one the host removes cannot stay for its minimum — and swap your content in on `(visibleChange)` or with `createDelayedVisibility()` from `@styloviz/core`, the same primitive. A delayed overlay spinner takes the stack, scroll lock and inert page only once it shows. Both default to 0: shown at once.
accessibility: Wraps the indicator in a `role="status"` region named by its `aria-label`, and SAYS that label once, politely, through the shared `SvLiveAnnouncer` when it first renders — a status region born with its name is usually never read, so the attribute alone announced nothing. Not on the server, not for the portalled fullscreen surface (moving focus onto it already speaks the name), and escalation messages still speak from inside the region. A blank `label` falls back to "Loading…" and warns in dev mode — a status region with an empty name is announced as nothing at all.

The fullscreen overlay is a real modal surface: it is portalled to `document.body`, registered on the shared overlay stack as blocking (so the rest of the page is `inert`, out of the tab order and the accessibility tree), locks the page scroll, moves focus onto itself (`role="dialog"` + `aria-modal`, named by the label) and restores focus when it closes. Escape does nothing while the wait cannot be cancelled, and triggers the cancel once a stalled wait offers one. `[portal]="false"` keeps the backdrop in place inside the host instead (still stacked and scroll-locked, but the page behind it stays focusable) for a host that queries the backdrop inside the component.
Pair with a visible label for waits over ~1 second so the state is clear to everyone.

The stated expectation rides in the region's accessible name rather than in its content, because a live region announces what CHANGES in it and not what it was born with — so the visible copy is `aria-hidden` and the wait is described once, not twice. That name does not change when the wait escalates; the escalation speaks for itself.

An escalation message is announced from that same region rather than a second one — the region already exists when the text appears, which is what makes the change audible at all. The cancel offer appears only at the stalled stage, so a wait that is merely slow does not invite the user to abandon work that was about to succeed.

Reduced motion: under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the `border` ring keeps turning at a third of the speed — a frozen ring reads as a hang — and `dots`, `pulse` and `bars` stand still as a static icon (a stepped ellipsis, a solid dot, staggered bars).

Non-text contrast (WCAG 1.4.11): every colour variant arc clears 3:1 against its own track and the page in light and dark mode — the tracks are the `-100` tints and the warning arc is `warning-700` for that reason. Under forced colours (Windows High Contrast) the track is `GrayText` and the arc and dots are `Highlight`, so the turning segment never matches its ring.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Size of the spinner.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Color variant.

inputs.name: spinnerStyle
inputs.description: Visual style of the spinner.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Accessible label (also shown visually when labelVisible is true).

inputs.name: labelVisible
inputs.description: Show the label text visually beneath the spinner.

inputs.name: overlay
inputs.description: Fullscreen overlay mode — dims the page behind the spinner.

inputs.name: portal
inputs.description: Portal the fullscreen surface to `<body>` and make the page behind it `inert`. `false` keeps the backdrop in place instead: it renders inside the host, still takes its z-index from the stack and still locks scroll, but the page behind it stays focusable.

inputs.name: active
inputs.description: Whether the wait is in progress. Bind it — `[active]="loading()"` — and keep the spinner mounted when using `showAfterMs` / `minVisibleMs`: a spinner the host removes cannot stay for its minimum.

inputs.name: showAfterMs
inputs.description: Appear only once the wait has lasted this long, in ms — a request that answers in 80 ms then shows nothing instead of a flash of spinner. `0` shows at once.

inputs.name: minVisibleMs
inputs.description: Once shown, stay at least this long, in ms, so a spinner is never yanked away mid-glance. `0` hides with `active`. Watch `(visibleChange)` (or use `createDelayedVisibility` from `@styloviz/core`) to swap the content in at the same moment.

inputs.name: expectedMs
inputs.description: How long this wait usually takes, in ms. `0` = unknown. An escalation is an apology, not an expectation. `slowAfterMs` below only ever speaks once the wait has already gone wrong: it says "longer than usual" without this component ever having said what usual IS. The user's decision — wait, or reload and lose the form — is made in the first second or two, on information the host almost always has and had no way to pass on. Passing it turns a silent animation into a statement: "about 25 seconds". It is also the only number the host should have to pick. Set this and both escalation thresholds derive from it, so the figure the user is SHOWN and the moment the component admits lateness cannot drift apart — which they did by construction when the two were separate inputs, and nothing could catch it. Off by default, like the thresholds: an expectation nobody stated is not one this component may invent.

inputs.name: expectationMessage
inputs.description: Override the generated expectation sentence — for wording, or for a language the generator does not speak. `null` = generate from expectedMs; `''` = state no expectation at all. This does NOT derive the thresholds. Text has no number in it, so a surface that wants both still sets `expectedMs` and overrides the words.

inputs.name: slowAfterMs
inputs.description: Say "this is taking longer than usual" after this many ms. `0` = never. A spinner is indistinguishable from a failed request, forever, and at ninety seconds it is not telling the truth: nothing is happening. The user's only remaining move is to reload the page and lose whatever they had typed — which is what they do. Off by default. Escalating without being asked would put new text under every spinner in every existing layout, and the honest threshold depends entirely on what is being waited for.

inputs.name: stalledAfterMs
inputs.description: Escalate to "this seems to be stuck" after this many ms. `0` = never. Measured from the same start, not from `slowAfterMs`. Thirty seconds means thirty seconds into the wait.

inputs.name: slowMessage
inputs.description: Message shown at the `slow` stage.

inputs.name: stalledMessage
inputs.description: Message shown at the `stalled` stage.

inputs.name: cancelLabel
inputs.description: Label for a cancel button shown once the wait is `stalled`. `null` = none. An output cannot be asked whether anyone is listening, so the offer is an input: a surface that renders "Cancel" and does nothing when it is pressed is worse than one that never offered. Set this only when `(cancelled)` is wired to something that can actually stop the work.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Extra CSS classes merged onto the root wrapper.

outputs.name: visibleChange
outputs.description: Emits whenever the spinner appears (`true`) or leaves (`false`).

outputs.name: cancelled
outputs.description: The user pressed the cancel offer on a stalled wait.

outputs.name: escalated
outputs.description: Fires on each escalation: `'slow'`, then `'stalled'`.

components.name: Split Button
components.description: A primary action button fused to a chevron dropdown of secondary actions — composed from Button, the fused Input Group and Dropdown Menu, not a new control built from scratch.
whenToUse: One dominant action with a small set of closely related variants (e.g. "Deploy" plus "Deploy to staging"/"Deploy preview").
You want the primary action a single click away, with alternates one click further — not a plain Dropdown Menu where every option carries equal weight.
For a set of equally-weighted actions, use a Button Group or a plain Dropdown Menu instead.
components.usage:
<sv-split-button
  label="Deploy"
  [items]="[
    { id: 'staging', label: 'Deploy to staging' },
    { id: 'preview',  label: 'Deploy preview' },
  ]"
  (clicked)="deploy()"
  (itemClick)="onDeployVariant($event)" />

examples.title: Menu as a bottom sheet on phones
examples.description: `sheetOnNarrow` is forwarded to the split button's dropdown menu: below 640px the secondary actions open as a bottom sheet instead of a menu clamped over the button.

examples.title: Grouped secondary actions
examples.code:
<sv-split-button
  label="Export"
  variant="secondary"
  [groups]="[
    { label: 'File', items: [{ id: 'csv', label: 'Export as CSV' }, { id: 'pdf', label: 'Export as PDF' }] },
    { label: 'Share', items: [{ id: 'link', label: 'Copy share link' }] },
  ]"
  (clicked)="exportDefault()"
  (itemClick)="onExportVariant($event)" />

examples.title: Danger action, loading primary
examples.code:
<sv-split-button
  label="Delete"
  variant="danger"
  [loading]="deleting()"
  [items]="[{ id: 'archive', label: 'Archive instead', icon: 'archive' }]"
  (clicked)="delete()"
  (itemClick)="onDeleteVariant($event)" />

customization: Shares Button's `variant` / `btnStyle` / `size` / `shape` across both halves via `variant`, `btnStyle`, `size`, `shape`.
Flat `items` or `groups` (same shape as Dropdown Menu) via `items` / `groups`, with `placement` for the popup side.
`disabled` disables both halves; `loading` shows a loading state on the primary action only — the menu trigger stays interactive so alternates remain reachable mid-operation.
Outputs: `clicked` (primary button), `itemClick` (secondary action id) and `itemSelect` (full item object).
accessibility: The chevron trigger has its own accessible name via `menuAriaLabel` (default "More actions"), independent of the primary button's `label`.
Built on Dropdown Menu, so the popup inherits its `menu`/`menuitem` ARIA roles and full keyboard navigation once opened.
variants: Danger variant, and what loading does to each half
Menu as a Bottom Sheet on Phones

components.name: Splitter / Resizable
components.description: Horizontal and vertical resizable panels with a drag handle, collapsible sides, a two-way splitAt model and optional layout persistence.
whenToUse: Letting users resize two adjacent panels (editor/preview, list/detail, sidebar/content).
You want a draggable, keyboard-resizable divider with min/max bounds.
For fixed layout regions that never resize, plain CSS grid is enough.

examples.title: Save once per gesture
examples.code:
<!-- resizeEnd fires once per drag (released, cancelled or abandoned) and once per
     keyboard / step-button move — the event to persist on. resized fires on every move. -->
<sv-splitter [(splitAt)]="split"
             (resizeStart)="dragging = true"
             (resizeEnd)="dragging = false; savePreference($event)" />

examples.title: Three panes — nest two splitters
examples.description: A splitter has two panels; a three-pane workspace puts a second splitter in the first one's end panel. Give each its own `persistKey`. Keys and drags on the inner divider never move the outer one.
examples.code:
Explorer
Editor
Terminal

customization: Horizontal or vertical split.
Collapsible panels with min/max sizes.
Two-way split position binding.

Set `persistKey` to save the split position + collapsed state to `localStorage` and restore them on load. The stored blob is a versioned envelope stamped `sv-splitter/layout`, so a value written by another component — or by an older release whose shape does not fit — is refused rather than applied, and the panel opens at its default position.
Tunable arrow-key step via `keyboardStep`.

Pixel constraints: `minSizePx` / `maxSizePx` bound the first panel and `minEndSizePx` the second, resolved against the measured container and intersected with the percentage `minSize`/`maxSize` — the stricter wins. When the container cannot fit both pixel minimums, the first panel's wins. The render is clamped without rewriting `splitAt`, so widening the window brings the user's own split back.

Persistence policy: a stored layout that is corrupt, another component's, from a newer release or unmigratable is ignored — the splitter opens at its defaults, emits `restoreRefused` with a user-safe sentence, and does not overwrite that blob until the user changes the layout. Pre-envelope `{ at, collapsed }` blobs are still adopted. A renamed `persistKey` keeps its layout if the old key is listed in `legacyPersistKeys` (migrated once, then removed). `resetLayout()` restores the host's initial split, expands both panels, clears storage and emits `layoutReset`. Other tabs' writes are ignored unless `syncAcrossTabs` is on, in which case a valid one is adopted without being echoed back. Storage is only touched in the browser; on the server nothing is read or written.

Privacy: with `persistKey` set, the only thing written to `localStorage` is a layout envelope — `{ kind: 'sv-splitter/layout', version: 1, state: { at, collapsed } }`, i.e. the split percentage and which panel (if either) is collapsed. It is layout-only: no panel content, no user identifiers and no PII, and nothing leaves the browser. Choose a `persistKey` that does not itself embed a user id or email. The storage glue (SSR guard, legacy keys tried in order, refusal reporting, cross-tab adoption, never echoing back what storage already holds) is the core `svPersistedStore` helper, reusable by any component that keeps a layout.

Scroll roots, containing blocks and portals: nothing is portalled — the collapse buttons are absolutely positioned inside the gutter and overflow into the panels, which each clip their own content (`overflow-hidden`). There is no scroll root of its own: put scrolling content inside a panel. The host is `block h-full min-h-[200px]`, so a vertical split needs an ancestor with a definite height. A drag maps the pointer against the container's `getBoundingClientRect()`, so a `transform: scale()` ancestor is handled, but a rotated one is not supported. No built-in breakpoints: bind `orientation` (and the pixel bounds) to your own media query to stack panels on a phone.

Measurement: the container is observed automatically (`svElementSize`), so pixel bounds re-resolve on resize and a container that is hidden or zero-sized at init gets real bounds the moment it is laid out — no manual call exists or is needed; until then only the percentage bounds apply.

Variant axes: `variant` (default · minimal · thick) and `gutterSize` are appearance only; `orientation` is layout; `collapsible`, `keyboardStep`, `persistKey` / `legacyPersistKeys` / `syncAcrossTabs` and the pixel bounds are behavioural modes. Every appearance works with every mode. Limits: two panels only; collapse applies to one side at a time.

Drag lifecycle: the separator uses Pointer Events with pointer capture, so mouse, touch and pen share one path and the release reaches it even outside the window. A drag ends on release, `pointercancel` (a system gesture or an incoming call), lost capture or the window losing focus — never stuck. Only the primary pointer drags; a second finger is ignored. `touch-action: none` on the separator keeps the browser from claiming the drag as a pan. `(resizeStart)` / `(resizeEnd)` bracket each gesture (a keyboard or step-button move is one too); double-click resets the layout.

RTL: under `dir="rtl"` a horizontal split mirrors — the start panel is on the right — and so do the drag (measured from the right edge with core `svPointerFraction`), ArrowLeft/Right (they move the divider the way the arrow points), the step buttons' arrows and names and the collapse chevrons. `splitAt` stays logical: the start panel's share. A vertical split is unaffected by direction.

Browser limits: `localStorage` is unavailable in some private modes and throws on quota — both are swallowed and the layout simply is not remembered. `inert` needs Chrome 102 / Safari 15.5 / Firefox 112; older engines keep the collapsed panel's content tabbable. Without `ResizeObserver` the pixel bounds resolve only at the last measured size.
accessibility: Labelled `role="separator"` with aria-orientation and aria-valuenow/min/max.

Keyboard resizable: Arrow keys nudge by `keyboardStep`, Home/End jump to min/max. Left/Right follow what the user sees — in RTL ArrowRight moves the divider right, which shrinks the (right-hand) start panel.

Focus after collapse: focus stays on the control that collapsed the panel — the collapse button or the separator (Enter on a collapsible separator collapses and restores the first panel, per the ARIA window-splitter pattern; when a panel is already collapsed — either one — Enter restores that panel, so the layout never jumps to the other side). If focus was inside the panel being collapsed, it moves to the separator first; it never drops to `<body>`.
A collapsed panel is `inert`, so Tab cannot walk into content that is 0px wide.
`aria-valuemin`/`-max`/`-now` report the pixel-resolved range when `minSizePx`/`maxSizePx`/`minEndSizePx` are set, so assistive tech hears the range the keyboard can actually reach.

inputs.name: orientation
inputs.description: Split direction: horizontal or vertical.

inputs.name: splitAt
inputs.description: Split position as a percentage of the first panel (0–100). Two-way bindable.

inputs.name: minSize
inputs.description: Minimum size (%) for the first panel.

inputs.name: maxSize
inputs.description: Maximum size (%) for the first panel.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Visual variant of the gutter.

inputs.name: collapsible
inputs.description: Allow collapsing a panel via the gutter.

inputs.name: gutterSize
inputs.description: Gutter (drag handle) thickness in pixels.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Accessible label for the splitter.

inputs.name: keyboardStep
inputs.description: Percentage the split moves per arrow-key press.

inputs.name: persistKey
inputs.description: When set, the split position and collapsed state are persisted to `localStorage` under this key and restored on load, inside a versioned envelope — see SvSplitterLayoutSnapshot.

inputs.name: legacyPersistKeys
inputs.description: Keys this layout was persisted under by an earlier release of the host. A renamed `persistKey` is a lost layout unless the old key is named here. When nothing is stored under `persistKey`, each of these is tried in order — an unreadable one is reported through `restoreRefused` and skipped, not the end of the search; the first that restores is copied to `persistKey` and removed, so the migration runs once. Refused blobs are left where they are.

inputs.name: syncAcrossTabs
inputs.description: Adopt a layout another tab of the same origin saves under `persistKey` (the `storage` event). Off, other tabs' writes are ignored until the next load — the layout never changes under the user's pointer. A refused or cleared value is always ignored.

inputs.name: minSizePx
inputs.description: Minimum first-panel size in px, resolved against the measured container and combined with `minSize` — the stricter wins. Ignored while the container has no size (hidden, not yet laid out, SSR).

inputs.name: maxSizePx
inputs.description: Maximum first-panel size in px, combined with `maxSize`.

inputs.name: minEndSizePx
inputs.description: Minimum second-panel size in px, so the END panel stays usable too. When the container cannot fit both pixel minimums, the first panel's wins.

inputs.name: soloPanel
inputs.description: Show ONE panel at full size: `'start'` or `'end'`, or `null` for the split. The other panel and the gutter are hidden (`display: none`, so out of the tab order and the accessibility tree) but stay MOUNTED — what they hold, a textarea's undo history, a scroll position, a form's state, survives the switch back. For a write / preview / split toggle; the split position is untouched. Unlike a collapse it leaves no gutter behind.

outputs.name: resized
outputs.description: Emits the first panel's new size as a whole percentage (clamped to the min bounds) on every drag move and keyboard step.

outputs.name: resizeStart
outputs.description: A resize gesture began: a pointer grabbed the separator, or a keyboard / step-button move is about to apply. Carries the split (%) it started from.

outputs.name: resizeEnd
outputs.description: A resize gesture finished — the pointer was released (anywhere, even outside the window), the drag was cancelled (`pointercancel`, lost pointer capture, the window losing focus), or a keyboard / step-button move applied. Carries the settled split (%). This is the event to PERSIST on: it fires once per gesture, where `resized` fires on every move.

outputs.name: restoreRefused
outputs.description: A layout stored under `persistKey` (or a legacy key) could not be applied — corrupt, another component's, from a newer release, or unmigratable — so the splitter opened at its defaults. Carries a user-safe sentence.

outputs.name: layoutReset
outputs.description: `resetLayout()` ran: the split is back at its initial position and the stored layout is gone.

outputs.name: splitAtChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `splitAt` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(splitAt)]`.

components.name: Spotlight Stat Card
components.description: Dark-first KPI card with a gradient hairline border, ambient accent glow, gradient icon token and an inline gradient sparkline.
whenToUse: Dark-themed dashboards where the standard Stat Card looks flat.
A hero KPI row that needs gradient accents and an inline trend sparkline.
Marketing or product pages where the KPI is the focal element.
components.usage:
<sv-spotlight-stat-card
  title="Page Views"
  value="1.24M"
  trend="up"
  [trendPercent]="14.2"
  trendLabel="vs last month"
  accent="violet"
  [sparkline]="series" />

examples.title: Accent colors
examples.description: Six built-in accent themes drive the border, glow, icon and sparkline gradient.
examples.code:
<sv-spotlight-stat-card title="Revenue"   value="$847K" accent="cyan"    [trendPercent]="18.7" [sparkline]="series" />
<sv-spotlight-stat-card title="Customers" value="2,341" accent="emerald" [trendPercent]="5.2"  [sparkline]="series" />

examples.title: Downward trend
examples.description: A down trend renders a rose chip with a descending arrow.
examples.code:
<sv-spotlight-stat-card
  title="Bounce Rate"
  value="42.3"
  suffix="%"
  trend="down"
  [trendPercent]="3.1"
  accent="amber" />

customization: Takes the family's `trendPolarity` and `sparklineDomain`, and abbreviates numbers with the same `svFormatCompact` rule as the free and Pro cards.
Six accents: violet, cyan, emerald, amber, rose, blue.
Gradient border, glow, icon token and sparkline all derive from the accent.
Pass `sparkline` points to render the inline gradient area; omit it to hide the chart.
Name any glyph from the icon library with `icon`.
accessibility: Value, trend and label are real text, not images.
The sparkline is decorative and hidden from assistive tech (`aria-hidden`).
Each instance gets a unique gradient id so multiple cards never collide.
Trend chip color is reinforced with a directional arrow, not color alone.
variants: Spotlight — KPI Row on a dark canvas

components.name: Stack Trace
components.description: A readable error. Pass an `Error` or the text of a stack trace and it shows the name and message, then function, file, line and column for each frame — parsed from V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari) and generic `file:line:col` traces. Runs of library frames (`node_modules`, Node internals, bundler runtimes, native code) fold behind one "Show N library frames" toggle each, so your own frames are on screen; frames can emit `frameClick`; copy takes the original text. `svParseStackTrace()` is exported.
whenToUse: The detail view of an error in a monitoring, logging or support tool.
A developer-facing error page or an admin "job failed" panel.
Use a plain alert for a user-facing error message — a stack trace is for developers.

examples.title: Open a frame in the editor
Decide what counts as library code
The parser on its own

customization: The header paints from the `danger` token; application frames' locations from `primary`; library frames are muted `gray`.
`isLibraryFrame` replaces the default predicate; `frameClickable`, `copyable` and `maxHeight` tune the rest.
`svParseStackTrace`, `svParseStackFrame`, `svIsLibraryFrame` and `svStackFrameLocation` are exported.
All visible strings are `codeBlock` labels in 12 language packs.
accessibility: The trace is a named region; frames are an ordered list named with its frame count.
Each library run's toggle is a button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, and says how many frames it shows or hides.
Clickable frames are real buttons named by their function and location; frames without a file stay text.
Copy confirms through a status message, and says so when the clipboard is unavailable.
Messages and paths render as text — a message containing markup shows the characters.

inputs.name: trace

inputs.name: collapseLibraryFrames
inputs.description: Fold each run of library frames behind a "Show N library frames" toggle.

inputs.name: isLibraryFrame
inputs.description: Decides which frames are library code. The default, `svIsLibraryFrame`, matches `node_modules`, `node:` and `internal/` paths, webpack and Vite runtimes, zone.js, polyfills and native frames.

inputs.name: frameClickable
inputs.description: Render each frame that has a file as a button that emits `frameClick`.

inputs.name: copyable
inputs.description: Show a button that copies the trace as text.

inputs.description: Max height of the frame list, e.g. `'24rem'`; it scrolls past that. `''` for none.

components.name: Stat Card
components.description: KPI metric cards with sparklines, trend chips and four layout variants.
whenToUse: Surfacing a single headline metric with its trend at the top of a dashboard.
You want an inline sparkline and a semantic up/down trend chip.
For many metrics at once, arrange several cards in a Widget Grid.

examples.title: A KPI row on one scale, with a cost that should fall
examples.code:
<!-- one domain for the row: svSharedDomain(cards.map(c => c.series)) -->
<sv-stat-card title="Revenue" [value]="1250000" trend="up" [trendPercent]="8.2" trendLabel="vs last month" [sparkline]="revenue" [sparklineDomain]="rowDomain" />
<sv-stat-card title="Infra cost" [value]="48200" trend="up" [trendPercent]="12" trendLabel="vs last month" trendPolarity="down-is-good" [sparkline]="cost" [sparklineDomain]="rowDomain" />

customization: `trendPolarity` says which direction is good news: `'down-is-good'` for churn, cost or latency paints a fall green and a rise red; `'neutral'` paints any change grey. The arrow and the spoken direction follow `trend` regardless.

Numbers abbreviate from 1,000 up with `svFormatCompact` (`@styloviz/core`) in the locale's compact notation — "2.5M", "-2.5M", "2,5 Mio.", "1.2万" — identically in the free, Pro and Spotlight cards; pass a string to opt out.
Bind one `sparklineDomain` (from `svSharedDomain()` in `@styloviz/sparkline`) to every card in a KPI row so the lines are drawn on one scale.
Four layouts plus optional inline sparkline.
Trend chip colors follow the semantic palette.
Format values with your own pipe before binding.
Set `clickable` on `sv-stat-card-pro` to make the whole card an interactive button that emits `cardClick`.
accessibility: Beside an inline sparkline an sr-only note says whether the line shares a scale with the row ("on a scale shared with the other cards, 0 to 100") or is scaled to the card alone — the line itself is hidden from assistive tech.
Values and trends are real text, not images.
Sufficient contrast across variants and dark mode.
A `clickable` card (Pro) exposes `role="button"`, is focusable, and activates on Enter/Space.
Decorative icons and sparklines are hidden from assistive tech; loading state sets `aria-busy`.
variants: Spotlight — KPI Row on a dark canvas

components.name: Status Page
components.description: A public status / uptime page for a SaaS product: an overall banner derived from the components and active incidents, each component's current state and a 90-day uptime bar with "99.98% uptime over 90 days", active incidents with their update timeline, scheduled maintenance and a day-grouped incident history. Read-only; every state is a word and an icon as well as a colour, and every date and time is formatted with `Intl` in your locale and time zone.
whenToUse: The public status page of a SaaS product, or the "System status" screen of an admin console.
An internal service-health page where each row is a dependency with its own uptime record.
Use `sv-audit-log` for an audit trail with field-level changes, and `sv-timeline` on its own for an activity feed that is not about availability.

examples.title: Components and their uptime
examples.description: One entry per day: a `status`, a measured `percentage`, or both. A day with only a percentage is coloured by fixed thresholds (≥ 99.9 % operational, ≥ 99 % degraded, ≥ 95 % partial outage, below that a major outage). `uptimePercent` passes your monitoring's own figure for the window.

examples.title: An incident with its updates
examples.description: Active incidents (anything not `resolved`) are listed on top, worst impact first; resolved ones move into the history under the day they began. An active incident raises the overall status: minor → degraded, major → partial outage, critical → major outage.

examples.title: A page that refreshes in place
examples.description: Poll your status endpoint and set `live` so a screen reader announces a change in the overall status. Keep `loading` false on the refreshes — it withholds the page and is for the first request only.

examples.title: The same figures elsewhere
examples.code:
import { svOverallStatus, svUptimeSummary, svFormatUptime } from '@styloviz/display';

const overall = svOverallStatus(components, incidents, maintenances); // 'degraded'

customization: Status colours paint from the `accent` (operational), `warning` (degraded, partial outage), `danger` (major outage), `info` (maintenance) and `gray` (no data) tokens, so a theme that remaps them recolours the bars, the banner and the chips.
`days` (1–365) sets the window of the bars; `headingLevel` fits the section headings into your page outline.
Every string comes from the `display` labels (`status*` keys) in 12 language packs — `provideSvLabels(SV_DISPLAY_LABELS_DE)` or the per-instance `labels` input.
`svOverallStatus`, `svStatusFromUptime`, `svUptimeSummary`, `svWorstStatus` and `svFormatUptime` are exported for an e-mail digest or a chat summary that should quote the same figures.
accessibility: Every state is an icon and words beside a colour: the banner says "Partial system outage", a component says "Degraded performance", an incident says "Monitoring" and "Minor impact".

Each uptime bar is one `role="img"` named with the component, the uptime figure and the date range ("API: 99.98% uptime over 90 days, Jul 29, 2026 to Oct 26, 2026"); the days that were not operational are listed after it for a screen reader, and each day has a mouse tooltip.
The overall banner is a `role="status"` live region only when `live` is set, so a refreshing page announces a change and a static one stays quiet.
Sections are labelled regions with real headings at `headingLevel`; incidents and windows are list items with their own headings, and times are `<time datetime>` elements.
An incident's updates are an `sv-timeline` with a feed intent and an accessible name ("Updates on Elevated API error rate").

inputs.name: components
inputs.description: The monitored services, in display order. Rows with no `name` are skipped.

inputs.name: incidents
inputs.description: Incidents, active and resolved, any order. Active ones are listed on top; resolved ones form the history.

inputs.name: maintenances
inputs.description: Planned maintenance windows, any order — listed by start time. `completed` windows are left out.

inputs.name: status
inputs.description: The overall status, when your backend states it. Null derives it: the worst of every component's status, every active incident's impact and any in-progress maintenance.

inputs.name: days
inputs.description: How many days the uptime bars cover, ending on the day of `lastUpdated` (clamped to 1–365).

inputs.name: lastUpdated
inputs.description: When the data was fetched — shown as "Last updated …" and the last day of the uptime bars. Null ends the bars on the latest day any component reports.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the first request is in flight — keep it false on a background refresh.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: The load failed. A string or an `SvDataError`; a non-retryable error hides the retry button.

inputs.name: itemKey
inputs.description: Identity of a component row, a property name or a function.

inputs.name: incidentKey
inputs.description: Identity of an incident.

inputs.name: maintenanceKey
inputs.description: Identity of a maintenance window.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: BCP-47 locale for dates, times and percentages.

inputs.name: timeZone
inputs.description: IANA time zone the times are shown in (and incident days are grouped by), e.g. `'UTC'` or `'Europe/Berlin'`. Null, or a zone `Intl` rejects, uses the viewer's own.

inputs.name: live
inputs.description: Make the overall banner a polite live region (`role="status"`), so a screen reader announces a change when the page refreshes in place. Leave it off for a page that is rendered once — a live region that never changes is noise.

inputs.name: headingLevel
inputs.description: Heading level of the section headings — match your page outline.

inputs.name: labels
inputs.description: Per-instance text, merged over the registry's `display` labels.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: The error state's retry button was pressed — re-run the request.

components.name: Stepper
components.description: 9 variants — eight wizard styles (default, pill, minimal, icon, dot, line, card, progress-bar) plus a non-interactive tracker — all free, in four sizes (xs–lg) and both orientations. The Pro package adds a timeline with a content panel per step, a circular ring, completed-step summaries, linear wizard mode, guard rules and telemetry.
whenToUse: Job: workflow state — renders step buttons and emits step events; it never navigates the page (compare all seven in the “Choosing a navigation pattern” guide under Guides).
Guiding users through a sequential, multi-step process (checkout, onboarding, wizards).
You want progress indication, and — on the Pro package — per-step validation gating.
For non-sequential views, use Tabs; for an overlay walkthrough, a Product Tour.

examples.title: Order status tracker (placed → delivered)
examples.description: variant="tracker" renders a horizontal fulfilment tracker: completed stages fill the rail, the current stage is ringed, each with an icon and timestamp.

examples.title: Cards and a mobile progress bar
examples.description: variant="card" boxes each step (indicator, title, description) and stacks them on a phone; variant="progress-bar" shows the current step over a segmented bar. size="xs" fits a table cell.

examples.title: Timeline with a panel per step (Pro)
examples.description: variant="timeline" renders the current step's <ng-template svStepPanel> under it; next() and previous() go through the gates. A complete step's summary replaces its description.

examples.title: Blocked step → error summary, focus moved
examples.code:
<sv-stepper [items]="steps" [(activeIndex)]="active" [asyncValidation]="true" [announceBlocked]="false"
            (stepChangeRequest)="validate($event)" (stepBlocked)="errors.set([{ fieldId: 'email', label: 'Work email', message: $event.reason }])" />
<!-- autoFocus moves focus to the summary when it appears; it reads the heading and the reason. -->
<sv-form-error-summary [errors]="errors()" heading="This step needs attention" />

customization: Nine variants — default, pill, minimal, icon, dot, line, card, progress-bar and the non-interactive tracker — all included in the free package.
Four sizes (xs · sm · md · lg) and horizontal or vertical orientation; `progressLabel` words the progress bar's "Step {current} of {total}".

Pro adds: the `timeline` variant with an `<ng-template svStepPanel>` per step, the `circular` ring, completed-step `summary` lines with an Edit affordance, linear wizard mode with per-step validation, guard rules and branch telemetry.
accessibility: Rendered as a labelled `list` of `listitem`s; each step is a real `<button>` (announced as a button) that exposes completed/current/disabled state via `aria-current="step"` and `aria-disabled`.
Keyboard reachable via a roving tabindex: the current step is tabbable and Arrow/Home/End move between steps, with optional number hotkeys (`enableHotkeys`).

A refused move is spoken: `stepBlocked` also announces "Cannot go to {step}. {reason}" through the shared live region — the built-in reason (disabled, not validated; Pro: linear, guard) or the host's own `deny('…')` text. Set `[announceBlocked]="false"` when your `(stepBlocked)` handler moves focus to an `sv-form-error-summary`, which speaks for itself.
With `enableHotkeys`, a horizontal stepper's ArrowLeft / ArrowRight mirror under `dir="rtl"` (read from the host), so the arrow always points at the step it moves to.

inputs.name: items
inputs.description: The steps to render (label, optional description, state).

inputs.name: activeIndex
inputs.description: 0-based active step index. Supports two-way binding via `[(activeIndex)]`.

inputs.name: orientation
inputs.description: Layout: horizontal or vertical.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Visual variant — and with it, whether this is a wizard or a tracker. `default`, `pill`, `minimal`, `icon`, `dot` and `line` are WIZARD styles: every step is a `<button>`, and the linear gate, keyboard, `stepClick` and the unsaved prompt are all live. `'tracker'` is a PROGRESS DISPLAY (an order-status strip): it renders a non-interactive `<ol>` with no buttons, so nothing in it can be clicked, focused or arrowed through and `stepClick` / `stepChangeRequest` never fire from it. `'card'` boxes each step (indicator, title, description) and stacks them on a phone; `'progress-bar'` is a segmented bar under the current step's label, for a narrow screen — both are wizard styles. Two axes share this one input — look and interactivity. Choose `tracker` to show where something IS, not to let the user move it; for a wizard's look without its navigation, keep a wizard style and set `interactive=false` instead.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Step size: xs (a table row or a toolbar), sm, md or lg.

inputs.name: progressLabel
inputs.description: The position text the `progress-bar` variant shows — `{current}` and `{total}` are filled in. Translate it here.

inputs.name: mode
inputs.description: Navigation mode: standard sequence, or branch (conditional paths via `activeBranch`).

inputs.name: interactive
inputs.description: Whether users can click steps to navigate.

inputs.name: showDescriptions
inputs.description: Show step descriptions under labels.

inputs.name: showConnectors
inputs.description: Render connectors between steps.

inputs.name: enableHotkeys
inputs.description: Enables advanced keyboard shortcuts for rapid step navigation.

inputs.name: announceBlocked
inputs.description: Announce a refused move (and why) to screen readers through the shared live region. Turn it off when the host already moves focus to its own message on `(stepBlocked)`.

inputs.name: activeBranch
inputs.description: Active branch key used in `mode='branch'`. Supports two-way binding.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Extra CSS classes for the root element.

inputs.name: urlKey
inputs.description: Put the current step's **id** in the URL under this key, so a step can be shared and the back button moves one step back. Needs `provideSvNavLocation()` at the app root.

inputs.name: surfaceId
inputs.description: Names this stepper in the shared navigation-analytics stream, when a page has more than one. Ignored unless `provideSvNavTelemetry()` is wired up.

inputs.name: persistKey
inputs.description: Where `localStorage` keeps this workflow's position, so a reload resumes rather than restarting. Stores the step id and branch only — never the host's form data. Empty = no persistence.

inputs.name: asyncValidation
inputs.description: Ask before moving. With this on, activating a step emits `stepChangeRequest` and nothing happens until the host calls `allow()` or `deny()` — which is what lets a wizard validate the current step against the server before letting the user leave it.

inputs.name: validatingIndex
inputs.description: Index currently being validated, or `-1`. That step shows a spinner and the stepper ignores further activations, so a double-click cannot start two validations.

inputs.name: revisitPolicy
inputs.description: What returning to an earlier step does to the steps after it. See StepperRevisitPolicy. The default, `'preserve'`, invalidates nothing, so a wizard only loses completed steps when it asks for that.

components.name: Stock Chart
components.description: Candles with a range navigator and preset ranges, a volume pane, SMA / EMA / Bollinger overlays and an RSI or MACD pane. Indicators are computed over the whole history and every value is in the table. Pure SVG.
whenToUse: A long price history where the reader needs to zoom into a period without losing where it sits in the whole.
Technical analysis: moving averages, Bollinger bands, RSI or MACD read against the candles they were computed from.
For a short history with no indicators, the Candlestick chart is simpler and has no navigator to explain.

examples.title: The figures without the chart
examples.code:
import { svSma, svRsi, svMacd } from '@styloviz/data';
const rsi = svRsi(closes, 14); // same length as closes, null through the warm-up

customization: `defaultWindow` (sessions in view while `range` is null), `rangePresets` (buttons over the plot; `sessions: 0` is "all") and `showNavigator`.
`overlays`: `sma` / `ema` with a `period`, or `bollinger` with `period` (20) and `multiplier` (2); each takes an optional `color`. Periods are rounded to whole sessions, at least one.
`oscillator`: `rsi` (`period` 14, Wilder) or `macd` (`fast` 12, `slow` 26, `signal` 9).
`showVolume`, `priceScale` (linear or log, with the fallback named), `splits` (back-adjusted before the indicators are computed) and `minSlotWidth` merging, as on the Candlestick chart.
Up and down colours, a currency prefix, plot size.
accessibility: The navigator is three sliders — the window (pans) and its two handles (resize) — each named and with a value text giving the first and last session in view. Arrows step one session, Page Up/Down a tenth of the history, Home/End go to the ends. Pointer drags on the strip do the same jobs.
The candles are ONE tab stop: arrows walk the sessions in view, Home/End jump to the ends, Enter/Space select. Each candle is named with its direction as a word and all four prices.

Every indicator line is named in words in the legend and has its own column in `sv-data-summary-table`, beside the prices, for every session in view. A warm-up cell is blank, never zero — a zero is a price.
The note under the chart says which part of the history is in view, and when an indicator's warm-up reaches into it, where the line begins and why.
Preset buttons are native buttons with `aria-pressed` on the one matching the view.

A Short History, With Its Warm-Up Stated

components.name: Streaming Markdown
components.description: Safe Markdown renderer built for token-by-token output. Renders a parsed token model through Angular bindings — no innerHTML and no bypassSecurityTrust, so untrusted content can never become markup. Headings, lists (incl. tasks), tables with alignment, blockquotes and inline emphasis; fenced code delegates to sv-code-block.
whenToUse: Rendering an LLM response as it streams in, token by token.
Displaying user- or model-authored Markdown where the source is not trusted.
Any place a chat message, changelog entry or docs excerpt is stored as Markdown.

examples.title: Streaming buffer
examples.description: The parser is pure, so re-running it on a growing buffer is correct and cheap.

examples.title: Fenced code with line numbers
examples.description: Fenced blocks render through sv-code-block — highlighting, filename header and copy come for free.

examples.title: Intercepting links
examples.description: linkClick fires with the resolved href — useful for routing citations in-app.

customization: Zero third-party dependencies: a small rule-based parser emits a token model that the template renders through Angular bindings — no `innerHTML`, no `bypassSecurityTrust*`.

Streaming-safe: `parseMarkdown()` is pure, so it can re-run on every token. Unmatched delimiters degrade to literal text and an unterminated fence yields `complete: false` rather than swallowing the document.
Supports ATX headings, paragraphs, fenced code, blockquotes, ordered/unordered lists with `- [x]` tasks and indent depth, pipe tables with alignment, and thematic breaks.
Inline `**strong**`, `*em*`, `` `code` ``, `~~strike~~` and `[text](url)` nest arbitrarily — the template renders the span tree recursively.
Link URLs are scheme-checked at parse time; `javascript:`, `data:` and `vbscript:` are rejected and render as plain text. Accepted links get `rel="noopener noreferrer"`.
Fenced code delegates to `sv-code-block`, so highlighting, the filename header and copy-to-clipboard are inherited; tune it with `codeLineNumbers` and `codeMaxHeight`.
`headingOffset` demotes every heading; `density` switches between two prose scales.
The exported `parseMarkdown()`, `parseInline()` and `safeHref()` helpers are public, so the parser can be reused outside the component.
accessibility: Renders real semantic elements — `<h1>`–`<h6>`, `<ul>`, `<blockquote>`, `<table>` with `<th scope="col">` — so screen readers get the document structure, not a wall of text.
Task-list markers are `role="img"` with a Done / Not done label; decorative bullets and the streaming caret are `aria-hidden`.
Links carry `rel="noopener noreferrer"` and a visible `focus-visible` ring.
Set `ariaLabel` to expose the rendered output as a named `role="region"` when it stands alone.
variants: Fenced Code — Delegated to Code Block

inputs.description: Added to every heading level, so `#` becomes `<h3>` at an offset of 2. Use it to keep document headings from competing with the surrounding page.

inputs.name: completionMessage

A live region updated per token is unusable, which is why this component has never had one — but the silence had its own cost: a screen-reader user got no signal at all that generation had finished, and had to poll the region by hand to find out. The answer is not a quieter live region, it is a DIFFERENT event: `aria-busy` while the text is arriving, and one announcement at the moment it stops. Set to `''` to announce nothing at all.

components.name: Suggestions
components.description: Starter prompts for an empty conversation, or follow-ups under an answer — as a list, a two-column grid or wrapping chips.
whenToUse: The empty state of a chat, where a blank box gives the user nothing to start from.
Follow-up questions under an answer, generated by the model or picked by you.
For a searchable library of saved prompts, use the Prompt Template Library instead.
customization: Three layouts via `layout`: `list` (stacked rows with a description line), `grid` (two columns from `sm`) and `chips` (wrapping pills, label only).
`[max]` shows the first N; `0` — the default — shows them all.
Wire it to a backend with `loading`, `error`, `retry` and `itemKey`: a skeleton while loading, an error with a working retry, and an empty state that says there is nothing to suggest.
Text comes from the `ai` labels (`provideSvLabels({ ai: { … } })`), or per instance through `[labels]`.
Free tier: uses only free icons, and composes into `sv-ai-chat`.
accessibility: A named list of real buttons — every suggestion is one Tab stop and fires on Enter or Space.
A disabled list disables every button, so it is skipped rather than pressed silently.
The icon tile is decorative and hidden from assistive technology; the label carries the meaning.

components.name: Sunburst Chart
components.description: The treemap’s radial sibling on the same `TreemapNode` data: rings by depth, arc angle by share of the parent, click or Enter to zoom into a branch and a centre button to zoom out. Pure SVG.
whenToUse: A hierarchy where the PATH matters as much as the size — cost by team › service › resource, traffic by section › page.
Drilling into one branch at a time; the zoom keeps the parent’s context in the centre.
For comparing many leaves by area across the whole tree, a Treemap packs them more legibly — both take the same data.
customization: `maxDepth` rings (default 3, 1–8).
Colours per node (`color`) or the palette by position; children take a lighter step of their parent’s hue.
`showLabels` and `showLegend` (the first ring).
`size` sets the square, which scales down to fit.
`valuePolicy` — `omit` (default) drops a node whose value cannot be a share and says so under the plot; `reject` refuses the dataset. A zero-value segment has no angle and is counted in the notice.
accessibility: One tab stop with roving focus: Left/Right move around a ring, Down to the first child, Up to the parent, Home/End to the ends; Enter or Space zooms in (or selects a leaf), Escape or Backspace zooms out. A hidden hint describes this to screen readers.
Every segment is named “Label: value (share of parent)”; the chart’s name says where it is zoomed to.
The data table lists every drawn segment with its full path, value, share of parent and share of total — and the chart a11y module can show it on screen.
Zoom animates transform and opacity only, and not at all under reduced motion.
