components.name: Survey (NPS / CSAT)
components.description: An in-app survey: Net Promoter Score (0–10), CSAT (1–5 stars) or one question of your own, as a native radio group with an optional follow-up comment whose prompt follows the NPS band, then a thank-you with an optional follow-up action. As a card, inline, or a floating corner panel. It emits a typed response; saving it is yours.
whenToUse: Measuring loyalty (NPS) or satisfaction (CSAT) inside your SaaS product, admin panel or helpdesk, at the moment the experience happened.
Asking one quick question — "What brought you here?", "What should we build next?" — without sending the user to a separate survey tool.
Use `sv-rating` instead when the score is one field among others in a form you already submit.

examples.title: NPS with a prompt per band
examples.code:
<sv-survey
  kind="nps"
  question="How likely are you to recommend Acme to a friend or colleague?"
  [followUpPrompts]="{ detractor: 'What disappointed you most?', promoter: 'What do you like most?' }"
  (submitted)="save($event)" />

save(response: SvSurveyResponse): void {
  // { kind: 'nps', score: 9, band: 'promoter', comment: 'Fast support' }
  this.api.post('/feedback', response).subscribe();
}

examples.title: CSAT after a support ticket
examples.code: <sv-survey kind="csat" layout="inline" question="How satisfied are you with the help you got?" (submitted)="save($event)" />

examples.title: One question — options or free text
examples.code:
<sv-survey kind="question" question="What brought you here today?" [options]="reasons" (submitted)="save($event)" />

<!-- No options: a free-text answer -->
<sv-survey kind="question" question="What should we build next?" (submitted)="save($event)" />

examples.title: Floating, dismissible, with a follow-up action

customization: Three kinds: `nps` (0–10 number pills, six to a row on a phone), `csat` (1–5 stars from the icon library) and `question` (your own options as pills, or free text when there are none).
Three layouts: `card` (bordered panel), `inline` (no chrome) and `floating` (fixed to a bottom `corner`, slides in; the slide is skipped under reduced motion).
Pills, the submit button and focus rings are painted from the `primary-*` tokens, so a template that remaps primary recolours the survey.
`question`, `description`, `followUpPrompt`, `thanksTitle` and `thanksMessage` replace the default text; `commentMaxLength` caps the comment (1000 by default).
Every string comes from the `forms` labels (`survey*` keys) — `provideSvLabels(SV_FORMS_LABELS_DE)` or the per-instance `labels` input.
Host owns persistence: nothing is stored. `svNpsBand(score)` is exported for reporting on your side.
accessibility: Every scale is native radio inputs in a `<fieldset>` whose `<legend>` is the question, so arrow keys move between answers, Space selects and the question is read on entry — no ARIA widget roles.

NPS radios are named by their number; 0 and 10 are described by "Not likely" and "Very likely". Each CSAT star is named by its level ("Satisfied"), and the chosen level is written beside the stars, so colour never carries the answer alone.
Answer targets are 40 px; every control has a visible focus ring.
Submitting with nothing chosen says "Choose an answer first." in a polite live region, links it to the fieldset with `aria-describedby` and moves focus to the first answer.
After submit, focus moves to the thank-you heading. The survey is a `<section>` named by its question (or the thank-you); `floating` is a region, not a dialog — no focus trap, no inert page.

components.name: Tabs
components.description: 6 visual styles (underline, pills, boxed, lifted, border-card, unstyled), dismissible, icon-only and scrollable tabs with arrows, vertical layout, URL sync, keyboard navigation and lazy panels.
whenToUse: Job: local panels — owns its panels and renders no links; whether the active tab lives in the URL is your decision (compare all seven in the “Choosing a navigation pattern” guide under Guides).
Switching between sibling views of the same context without leaving the page.
Detail panes, settings sections, dashboards with multiple perspectives.
Letting the user dismiss a panel the author permits them to hide (`closable` + `tabClose`) — the author still owns the set.
Not for multi-document or workspace bars where the user opens, closes, reorders and persists tabs — that is a document-tabs pattern, not a configuration of this one.
For a simple value-only toggle with no content panels, use the Segmented Control component instead.

examples.title: Icon-only view switcher
examples.code:
<!-- views: { id: 'grid', label: 'Grid view', icon: 'grid', iconOnly: true }, … -->
<sv-tabs [tabs]="views" [(activeId)]="view" tabsStyle="boxed" size="sm" />

customization: Underline, pills, boxed, lifted, border-card, or unstyled styles.
Horizontal or vertical orientation.
Optional icon, numeric badge, unread dot, and a dismiss (×) affordance per tab via `closable`.

Automatic horizontal scroll for long tab lists — a horizontal tablist scrolls on overflow (e.g. many tabs on a phone) with no scrollbar while the tabs fit, and the selected tab is scrolled into view; `scrollable` keeps tabs at their natural width instead of shrinking to fit first, and adds previous / next arrows while the tabs overflow (`scrollButtons="false"` hides them).
Icon-only tabs: `iconOnly` on a tab with an `icon` draws the icon alone; the label stays its accessible name and hover title.
Lazy-rendered panels.
`findInPage` (default `true`) lets Ctrl+F reach and select inactive mounted panels; set it to `false` for panels that must stay hidden until chosen.
accessibility: Tablist/tab/tabpanel roles with arrow-key navigation (←→/↑↓, Home, End).
Active tab exposes selected state; roving tabindex.
Active panel is focusable (tabindex 0) so keyboard users land in its content.

Dismissible tabs close from the keyboard with Delete or Backspace on the focused tab (announced via `aria-keyshortcuts` and a visually hidden hint). The × is a pointer-only, `aria-hidden` affordance and is not focusable, because the ARIA tablist pattern leaves no valid place for a second focusable control inside a `role="tab"`.
The scroll arrows are pointer-only (`aria-hidden`, out of the tab order) and sit outside the tablist: the arrow keys already move along the strip, and focusing a tab scrolls it into view.
An icon-only tab keeps its label as its accessible name (visually hidden text), so it is announced exactly as a labelled tab.
Under `dir="rtl"` the strip runs right-to-left and ArrowLeft / ArrowRight follow it (read from the host, so a `dir="rtl"` ancestor counts); Home / End and a vertical strip's Up / Down are unchanged.

Find-in-page reaches inactive panels that are mounted (`findInPage`, on by default): they are `hidden="until-found"` where the browser supports it, and a match selects its tab. A never-visited `lazy` panel and every inactive panel under `lazyRetention="destroy"` are not in the DOM, so find-in-page cannot see them — the documented omission. Print prints the active panel only: a tabset is a set of alternative views, not one document.

inputs.name: tabs
inputs.description: Tab definitions in display order.

inputs.name: activeId
inputs.description: ID of the currently active tab. Use `[(activeId)]` for two-way binding.

inputs.name: tabsStyle
inputs.description: Visual style variant.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Size of the tab text and icons.

inputs.name: layout
inputs.description: Layout direction.

inputs.name: fullWidth
inputs.description: Whether tab buttons stretch to fill all available width. Only applicable to the `'horizontal'` layout.

inputs.name: scrollable
inputs.description: Allows the tab list to scroll horizontally instead of wrapping/overflowing when there are more tabs than fit the available width.

inputs.name: scrollButtons
inputs.description: Previous / next arrows at the ends of a horizontal `scrollable` strip, shown while its tabs overflow. They are for the pointer: the arrow keys already move along the strip and scroll the focused tab into view.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Additional CSS classes on the root wrapper.

inputs.name: activation
inputs.description: Whether the arrow keys select the tab they move to (`'automatic'`) or only move focus, leaving Enter/Space to select (`'manual'`). Prefer `'manual'` when a panel costs something to show — `lazy` panels that fetch, heavy charts, anything a keyboard user should not trigger five times on the way past. Leaving it unset resolves to `'automatic'`, and logs a dev-only warning if any tab is `lazy`.

inputs.name: lazyRetention
inputs.description: What happens to a `lazy` panel the user switches away from: `'retain'` keeps it mounted with its state (the long-standing behaviour), `'destroy'` unmounts it and rebuilds it on the next visit. Only `lazy` tabs are affected — a panel that was never deferred is never destroyed. Choose `'destroy'` for panels that must re-read their data on every visit, or hold enough DOM that keeping several alive is the real cost; and know that it discards whatever the user typed.

inputs.name: findInPage
inputs.description: Let browser find-in-page (`Ctrl+F`) reach the text in INACTIVE panels that are mounted, by marking them `hidden="until-found"` where the browser supports it; a match selects its tab. Never-visited `lazy` panels and `lazyRetention="destroy"` panels are not in the DOM and cannot be found.

inputs.name: urlKey
inputs.description: Put the active tab in the URL under this key, so a tab can be shared and survives a refresh. Needs `provideSvNavLocation()` at the app root; give a nested tab strip a different key.

inputs.name: surfaceId
inputs.description: Names this tabset in the shared navigation-analytics stream, when a page has more than one. Ignored unless `provideSvNavTelemetry()` is wired up.

outputs.name: tabClose
outputs.description: Emitted when a closable tab's × is clicked or Delete/Backspace is pressed on it. The tab is NOT removed automatically — remove it from `tabs` yourself.

outputs.name: unresolved
outputs.description: Emitted when `activeId` names a tab this component cannot show. Reports; never corrects, because there is no nearest tab to correct to.

outputs.name: activeIdChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `activeId` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(activeId)]`.

components.name: Tag Input
components.description: 9 multi-select tag-input variants: default (free) plus avatar, grouped, creatable, colors, token limit, async search, inline and overflow (Pro).
whenToUse: Capturing multiple free-form or suggested tokens (tags, recipients, keywords).
You want creatable entries, token limits or async suggestions (Pro).
For a single choice from a list, use Select Dropdown or Autocomplete.

examples.title: Email recipients — per-tag validation
examples.description: `tagValidator` (both tiers) returns a reason for a tag that is not valid: the chip is marked and reads its reason, the input gets `aria-invalid`, a summary under the field names every rejected entry (announced when one arrives), and a form gets `{ invalidTags: { values } }`.
examples.code:
<sv-tag-input-pro variant="creatable" label="To" [tagValidator]="isEmail" [(values)]="to" />

isEmail: TagValidator = (t) => /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(t.value) ? null : 'not an email address';

examples.title: Creatable, saved by the host (Pro)
examples.description: Every created tag emits a typed `createRequest` (label, slug value, idempotency key, resolve/reject). By default the tag is added at once and `reject()` removes it; with `awaitCreate` it waits as a busy pending chip until `resolve()` swaps in the server id.

examples.title: Async search (Pro)
examples.description: queryChange is debounced (asyncDelay); fetch results and feed them back through [asyncOptions]. Async search ships in the Pro package — the tag is `sv-tag-input-pro`.

examples.title: Reactive forms (formControlName)
examples.description: Implements ControlValueAccessor, so it binds to reactive and template-driven forms. The control value is a string[]; formControl.disable() disables the field.

customization: Nine `variant`s (default, with-avatar, grouped, creatable, with-colors, token-limit, async-search, inline, overflow) in three `size`s. The free `sv-tag-input` is the default variant; the other eight are `sv-tag-input-pro`.
Provide `options`; add `label`, `hint`, `errorMessage`, `required`. Pro adds `groups`, a `maxTags` cap and async suggestions (`asyncOptions` + `asyncDelay`).
Two-way bind `[(values)]` (string[]) or use a reactive control (CVA); react to `tagsChange` (Pro: `queryChange`). Fixed-position dropdown escapes overflow containers.
accessibility: Correct ARIA combobox: `role="combobox"` sits on the `<input>` with `aria-expanded`, `aria-haspopup`, `aria-controls` and `aria-activedescendant`; the popup is a `role="listbox"` of `role="option"` rows (headers, loading and "no results" are presentational).
All option ids are generated per instance, so multiple tag fields on one page never collide; the input is named via `label` → `placeholder`.
Keyboard: arrows highlight, Enter adds, Backspace removes the last token; every chip exposes a labelled Remove button.
Implements ControlValueAccessor — works with `[(ngModel)]`, `[formControl]` and `formControlName`; `formControl.disable()` disables the field.

inputs.name: values
inputs.description: Current tags (two-way).

inputs.name: options
inputs.description: Suggestion options offered as the user types.

inputs.name: compareWith
inputs.description: What "the same tag" means. Defaults to strict equality on `value`. Set it when your ids are not byte-identical across the wire (`U1` vs `u1`), so the field still de-duplicates and resolves them.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Field size: sm, md or lg.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Field label.

inputs.name: placeholder
inputs.description: Placeholder shown in the input.

inputs.name: hint
inputs.description: Helper text shown below the field.

inputs.name: tagValidator
inputs.description: Check each selected tag — the email-recipients case. A tag the validator rejects stays (the user can see and fix it) but its chip is marked, the reason is read out with it, a summary appears under the field, the input reports `aria-invalid`, and a form gets `{ invalidTags }`.

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: Error message; sets the field to an error state when present.

inputs.name: serverError
inputs.description: A validation failure reported by the **server** — the 422 that comes back after submit, not something the client could have known. It is a separate input from `errorMessage` because it has a different lifetime, not because it needs a second way to show a string. A server error is a statement about *the value that was submitted*: the moment the user edits the field it stops being true, and this input expires itself rather than sitting there telling someone their new email is already taken. `errorMessage` has no such expiry — it is the host's to clear. While live it outranks `errorMessage`: it is the more specific fact, and it is the one the user has not seen yet. Typed structurally rather than as `SvDataError` so this stays dependency free — an `SvDataError` satisfies it unchanged.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disable the field.

inputs.name: required

inputs.name: values

inputs.name: options

inputs.name: compareWith
inputs.description: What "the same tag" means. Defaults to strict equality on `value`. Set it when your ids are not byte-identical across the wire — a backend that returns `'U1'` where the form holds `'u1'` — so the field still selects, de-duplicates and resolves them. It compares values, not options. The value is what the form holds and what a server sends back; the option may not exist yet when a value arrives (see `unresolvedTags`). A comparator over options would be uncallable in exactly the case that needs it.

inputs.name: groups

inputs.name: serverError
inputs.description: A validation failure reported by the **server** — the 422 that comes back after submit, not something the client could have known. It is a separate input from `errorMessage` because it has a different lifetime, not because it needs a second way to show a string. A server error is a statement about *the value that was submitted*: the moment the user edits the field it stops being true, and this input expires itself rather than sitting there telling someone their new email is already taken. `errorMessage` has no such expiry — it is the host's to clear. While live it outranks `errorMessage`: it is the more specific fact, and it is the one the user has not seen yet. Typed structurally rather than as `SvDataError` so this stays dependency free — an `SvDataError` satisfies it unchanged.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disables all interactions.

inputs.name: required
inputs.description: Shows a required asterisk next to the label.

inputs.name: maxTags
inputs.description: Maximum number of tags that can be selected (0 = unlimited). The token-limit variant displays a visual progress counter.

inputs.name: asyncDelay
inputs.description: Debounce delay in ms before `queryChange` is emitted for async-search. The parent component is expected to populate `asyncOptions` in response.

inputs.name: asyncOptions
inputs.description: Options fed by the parent for the async-search variant. Update this whenever you receive results for the current query.

inputs.name: debounceMs
inputs.description: Delay before `queryChange` fires, in ms. Spelled the same way as every other picker in the kit; left at 0, `asyncDelay` (400) applies.

inputs.name: serverSide
inputs.description: Fetch options from the server in **any** variant, not just `async-search`. The supplied options are shown exactly as given.

inputs.name: minChars

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the host is fetching. Merged with the component's own in-flight state, so a real backend and the built-in delay render identically.

inputs.name: stale
inputs.description: The results on screen answer an **older** query — a newer request is still in flight. Blanking the panel on the second is the most jarring thing a picker can do; showing the old list with no indication is a quiet lie. outputs.name: retry

outputs.name: queryChange

outputs.name: createRequest

outputs.name: valuesChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `values` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(values)]`.

components.name: Terminal
components.description: A terminal for logs and for typing. Feed it an append-only `lines` stream (a build, a deploy, an agent's tool run) and it renders the ANSI colour subset — SGR 30–37, 90–97 and bold — as styled spans from the kit's tokens, never as markup; follows new output only while you are at the bottom, pausing with a "jump to latest" button and a count when you scroll up; copies the whole scrollback as plain text; and keeps the newest `maxLines`. Add a command registry and it becomes a shell with history, Tab completion and a real `<input>` prompt — and nothing typed is ever evaluated.
whenToUse: Showing CI, deploy or job output as it streams in, with the colours the tools already print.
Showing an AI agent's shell or tool runs live in an ops console.
A "try it" shell on a developer landing page, alongside ordinary links.
Use `sv-code-block variant="terminal"` for a short, fixed transcript inside documentation.

examples.title: Stream a log
examples.description: Append to the array as output arrives; a shorter array is a new run and clears the screen. `info` lines are notes the host adds that no process printed.

examples.title: A shell with commands
examples.description: Handlers are functions you write; input is looked up in the registry by name and never evaluated. Output can carry ANSI colour.

examples.title: The parts, outside the component

customization: Line kinds: `command`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `exit`, `info` — each coloured from the `gray`, `danger`, `warning` and `info` tokens; ANSI colours map onto `danger`, `accent`, `warning`, `primary`, `brand`, `info` and `gray`, one step darker in light mode.
`ansi="false"` strips every escape sequence and colours by kind only.
`autoScroll`, `copyable`, `chrome`, `title`, `minHeight`, `maxHeight`, `maxLines` and `typeIntro` tune the frame; `interactive="false"` removes the prompt.
All visible strings are `codeBlock` labels in 12 language packs.
`svParseAnsi`, `svAnsiPlainText` and `svIsScrolledToEnd` are exported for your own log views.
accessibility: The scrollback is a named `role="log"` with `aria-live="polite"` (or `off`), so new lines are announced once rather than the whole session re-read; it takes focus so a keyboard can scroll a paused log.
Autoscroll never moves the reader: scrolling up pauses it, and a labelled "jump to latest" button (with the count of new lines) resumes it.
The prompt is a labelled native `<input>`, so dictation, IME composition and assistive technology work; Tab moves on whenever there is nothing to complete.
Copy confirms through a status message — and says so when the clipboard is unavailable, instead of claiming a copy that did not happen.
Colour is never the only signal: errors are `stderr` lines, notes are `info` lines in italics, and the text of every line is plain text.

inputs.name: commands
inputs.description: The command registry. Anything not in here does not run.

inputs.name: intro
inputs.description: Lines printed before the visitor's first keystroke.

inputs.name: prompt
inputs.description: Prompt string, e.g. `visitor@styloviz:~$`.

inputs.name: inputLabel
inputs.description: Accessible label for the prompt input.

inputs.name: maxHeight
inputs.description: Max height of the scrollback.

inputs.name: minHeight
inputs.description: Minimum height of the scrollback. For a hero, where the terminal is a design element as much as a control: sized to its content, a five-line intro renders as a small box with the column's remaining height empty beneath it. A floor makes it read as a window that happens to be mostly unused, which is what a real one looks like before you type.

inputs.name: maxLines
inputs.description: Scrollback cap, in lines. A cap, not virtualisation. A session someone actually types is a few hundred lines at the outside; carrying a virtual scroller for a case that does not occur costs more than it saves. The oldest lines drop.

inputs.name: chrome
inputs.description: Show the window chrome (three dots + title).

inputs.name: title
inputs.description: Title in the chrome bar.

inputs.name: typeIntro
inputs.description: Type the intro out character by character. Ignored under `prefers-reduced-motion`, where the intro prints at once.

inputs.name: typeSpeedMs
inputs.description: Milliseconds per character while typing the intro.

inputs.name: lines
inputs.description: Output the host owns — a build log, a deploy stream, an agent's tool run. APPEND-ONLY. Lines added to the end are printed as they arrive, after whatever is already on screen. A SHORTER array means a new run: the screen clears and the new array prints from the top. Pass a new array each time (signals do), never a mutated one. While this is non-empty the intro prints at once rather than typing, so a log is never held back behind an animation.

inputs.name: interactive
inputs.description: Show the prompt. `false` makes a read-only log viewer: no input, no history, no click-to-focus — `[lines]` and `intro` are all it shows.

inputs.name: ansi
inputs.description: Honour the ANSI colour subset in line text: SGR 0 / 1 / 22 / 39, 30–37 and 90–97. Other sequences (cursor moves, erase, OSC titles) are always removed. `stderr` keeps its own colour — an escape code cannot paint an error green — but may still be bold. `false` strips every sequence and colours by `kind` only.

inputs.name: autoScroll
inputs.description: Follow new output to the bottom — but only while the reader is already there. Scrolling up pauses it and shows "jump to latest"; `false` never scrolls on its own (submitting a command still does).

inputs.name: copyable
inputs.description: Show a button that copies the whole scrollback as plain text, escape codes removed.

inputs.name: live
inputs.description: How the log announces new lines. `polite` (the `role="log"` default) reads each line as it arrives; `off` is for a fast stream a screen reader could never keep up with — the reader moves into the log to read it.

components.name: Text Field
components.description: Single- and multi-line inputs with validation states, icons, addons, hints and character counting.
whenToUse: Collecting a single line of free-form text, email, password or number.
You need built-in label, hint, validation and counter wiring instead of a bare <input>.
Switch to `multiline` for short paragraphs; use the Rich Text Editor for formatted content.
components.usage:
<sv-input-field
  label="Email"
  type="email"
  placeholder="you@example.com"
  hint="We'll never share your email."
  [(value)]="email" />

examples.title: Autosizing textarea
examples.description: `autosize` (with `multiline`) grows the textarea with its text — `field-sizing: content` where supported, measured in WebKit and Firefox, including for values a form writes; `maxRows` caps it.

examples.title: Clearable
examples.description: `clearable` adds a real, labelled clear button while the field holds text; it empties the value, notifies the form and returns focus to the field. `(cleared)` fires after. Prefix/suffix addons (`leadingAddon`, `trailingAddon`) work alongside it.

examples.title: Validation state
examples.description: Drive the field with state + errorMessage for inline validation.
examples.code:
<sv-input-field
  label="Username"
  state="error"
  errorMessage="That username is taken."
  [(value)]="username" />

examples.title: Addons & icons
examples.description: Leading icon, trailing addon and a character counter.

examples.title: Native constraints & autofill
examples.description: Pass-through native attributes for real validation and better mobile keyboards. pattern, minLength, min/max/step feed the built-in Validator.

examples.title: Reactive forms (CVA + Validator)
examples.description: Works with formControlName; required/minLength/pattern surface as control errors and disable() disables the native control.

customization: Set `type` (text, email, password, number…) or `multiline` for a textarea; pick a `variant` (default, filled, flushed; Pro adds floating) and `size`.
Drive validation with `state`, `errorMessage` and `successMessage`, or let the built-in Validator enforce `required`, `minLength`, `maxLength` and `pattern`.
Tune native behaviour with `autocomplete`, `inputMode`, `min` / `max` / `step`, `spellcheck` and `autofocus`.
Add `leadingIcon` / `trailingIcon`, `leadingAddon` / `trailingAddon` and `maxLength` counter; listen to `focused`, `blurred` and `submitted` (Enter).
accessibility: A stable id is generated automatically, so the `<label for>` association and `aria-describedby` work even when no `inputId` is supplied.
Hint, error and success text are linked via `aria-describedby`; `aria-invalid` and `aria-required` reflect state, and errors use `role="alert"`.
The password show/hide toggle is keyboard reachable with `aria-pressed`; the character counter announces politely via `aria-live`.
Supports `disabled` and `readonly` with correct semantics — programmatic `formControl.disable()` disables the native control too.

inputs.name: serverError
inputs.description: A validation failure reported by the **server** — the 422 that comes back after submit, not something the client could have known. It is a separate input from `errorMessage` because it has a different lifetime, not because it needs a second way to show a string. A server error is a statement about *the value that was submitted*: the moment the user edits the field it stops being true, and this input expires itself rather than sitting there telling someone their new email is already taken. `errorMessage` has no such expiry — it is the host's to clear. While live it outranks `errorMessage`: it is the more specific fact, and it is the one the user has not seen yet. Typed structurally rather than as `SvDataError` so this stays dependency free — an `SvDataError` satisfies it unchanged.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible name for the control, for the case where there is no visible label. A placeholder is not an accessible name. components.name: Thread List
components.description: A searchable conversation history grouped by recency — pinned, today, yesterday, the last seven days, older — with rename, pin and delete per row.
whenToUse: The history rail of a chat app — `sv-ai-chat`’s full-page layout uses it.
Any list of past sessions a user returns to by title and date.
customization: `groupBy`: `recency` or `none` (one flat list).
`[actions]` turns on row actions; delete takes two presses, the second confirming.
The async contract: `loading`, `error`, `retry`, `itemKey`, and two empties — no conversations at all, and none matching the search.
`[now]` fixes the clock for grouping and time labels (tests, screenshots).
Text comes from the `aiChatPro` labels, or per instance through `[labels]`.
accessibility: A `nav` landmark with one list per group, each labelled by its heading; the open thread carries `aria-current`.
Row actions appear on hover and are always reachable by keyboard and touch; each names the conversation it acts on.
The rename box takes focus, commits on Enter and cancels on Escape.

components.name: Thumbnail Card
components.description: Media card with a configurable image position (top/left/right), four aspect ratios, gradient overlay, badge and content/action projection slots.
whenToUse: Presenting media-led items in a grid: articles, products, videos, files.
You want a consistent image + title + meta card with optional badge/overlay.
For dense rows without imagery, a List View is more compact.
components.usage:
<sv-thumbnail-card
  image="/cover.jpg"
  alt="Cover"
  title="Annual report"
  subtitle="2025"
  badge="New"
  (cardClick)="open()" />

examples.title: Horizontal media card
examples.code:
<sv-thumbnail-card
  image="/thumb.jpg"
  alt="Preview"
  title="Quarterly review"
  subtitle="12 min read"
  imagePosition="left"
  aspectRatio="4/3"
  [hoverable]="true" />

examples.title: Premium variant — full-bleed cinematic card
examples.description: cardVariant="premium" renders an edge-to-edge image with a dark gradient scrim and inline title/subtitle overlay.
examples.code:
<sv-thumbnail-card
  cardVariant="premium"
  image="/hero.jpg"
  alt="Feature"
  title="Design systems at scale"
  subtitle="8 min read"
  badge="Featured"
  aspectRatio="16/9"
  (cardClick)="open()" />

examples.title: Product variant — price, rating & action footer
examples.description: cardVariant="product" renders a commerce card: star rating, price with an optional compare-at + discount badge, and an add-to-cart footer.
examples.code:
<sv-thumbnail-card
  cardVariant="product"
  image="/product.jpg"
  alt="Aurora headphones"
  title="Aurora Wireless Headphones"
  [price]="199"
  [compareAt]="249"
  [rating]="4.5"
  [reviewCount]="128"
  badge="Sale"
  aspectRatio="1/1"
  (action)="addToCart()" />

examples.title: One target per card, and it has to exist
examples.description: The rule is one sentence: a card has exactly ONE primary target — the title, stretched over the whole card by a ::after overlay — and everything else interactive sits above it on z-10. That is what keeps a nested Add to cart clickable inside a clickable card without nesting one control in another, which is invalid HTML and unusable by keyboard. The corollary: a card with no title has no target, so cardClick cannot fire, and a hover lift would promise a click that does nothing. cardLabel gives a titleless card a real target with a name only assistive tech sees; without either, the card is not interactive and does not look it.
examples.code:
<!-- Titleless: the name comes from cardLabel. -->
<sv-thumbnail-card
  image="/gallery-cover.jpg"
  alt="Aurora over a fjord"
  cardLabel="Open the Tromsø gallery"
  (cardClick)="open()" />

<!-- A nested action goes in the slot, which is already on z-10. -->
<sv-thumbnail-card image="/a.jpg" alt="" title="Q3 report" href="/reports/q3">
  <button svThumbnailActions type="button" (click)="pin()">Pin</button>
</sv-thumbnail-card>

examples.title: When the picture is not there
examples.description: Three different reasons, and they are not interchangeable. A card with no image is a design choice; a card whose image FAILED is a fault — the photo exists and could not be fetched — and rendering the same grey glyph for both told the reader this item simply has no picture. A third, loading, is neither, and an empty frame reads as the first. The failure state re-arms on a new src, so retrying is just handing the card a different URL.

customization: `focalPoint` (`{ x, y }`, each 0–1) anchors the cover crop in every variant, so a portrait's face or a product's label stays in frame at any aspect ratio; the hover zoom grows from the same point.
Position the image with `imagePosition` and pick an `aspectRatio`.
Add a `badge` with `badgeColor`, optional `overlay` gradient and `hoverable` lift.
Switch `cardVariant` to `premium` for a full-bleed cinematic card with a gradient scrim and overlaid title/subtitle, or keep the `default` bordered layout.
Project custom body and action content into the card slots; set `href` to navigate or handle `cardClick`.
Switch `cardVariant` to `product` for a commerce card with a star rating, price (with compare-at + discount badge) and an add-to-cart action footer.
`cardLabel` names the whole-card target on a card with no visible title; `hoverable` paints no pointer cursor on a card that has no target at all.
`loading` renders a neutral placeholder while you fetch the image, and a failed `src` renders a distinct "Image unavailable" state rather than the no-image glyph.
accessibility: Set `href` and the title becomes a real anchor (keyboard-native); without it the title is a button emitting `cardClick`.
A stretched-link overlay makes the whole card clickable while projected actions/links stay independently reachable above it — one control is never nested inside another.

A card with no visible title takes its accessible name from `cardLabel`, given to a screen reader only; a card with neither renders no target and no pointer cursor, so it does not advertise a press it cannot deliver.
A failed image is announced as "Image unavailable" rather than falling back to the same placeholder a card with no picture uses.
Focus moves a ring around the whole card; images require descriptive `alt`.
variants: One Target Per Card, and Three Kinds of No Picture

components.name: Tiles Layout
components.description: Responsive CSS Grid container for arbitrary tiles — auto-fill or fixed columns, configurable gap and minimum column width, an optional uniform aspect ratio and masonry progressive enhancement.
whenToUse: Laying out a gallery, dashboard or bento grid of arbitrary tile content.
You want auto-fitting columns or a fixed count without hand-writing grid CSS.
For a data-bound list of cards, render them inside the tiles container.

examples.title: What masonry does to reading order — and whether you even got it
examples.description: Masonry does not reorder anything: the markup, the tab order and the screen-reader order are already correct, and it is the VISUAL order that diverges. No amount of ARIA fixes that, because there is nothing wrong for ARIA to describe. Grid masonry is the harsher case of the two — CSS multi-column at least has a describable mapping (column one holds 1, 2, 3; the first visual row is 1, 4, 7), whereas grid masonry puts each item in the shortest track, so where item N lands depends on the heights of items 1…N−1 and the mapping cannot be stated at all. Which is why the answer is to point at the plain grid rather than to describe the divergence. The second thing the note can tell you is for you, not the reader: grid-template-rows: masonry ships almost nowhere, so [masonry]="true" usually produces an ordinary grid, and the note says so.
examples.code:
<sv-tiles [masonry]="true"> … </sv-tiles>

<!-- Order genuinely does not matter here — a wall of unrelated thumbnails. -->
<sv-tiles [masonry]="true" [showLayoutNote]="false"> … </sv-tiles>

<!-- masonryState() is 'off' | 'applied' | 'unsupported',
     and the grid carries it as data-sv-masonry. -->

customization: Switch between auto-fill and a fixed `columns` count; tune `gap` and `minColumnWidth`.
Apply a uniform `aspect` ratio to every tile via one input.
Opt into CSS `masonry` where the browser supports it — `masonryState()` reports `off`, `applied` or `unsupported`, and the grid publishes it as `data-sv-masonry`.
`showLayoutNote` suppresses the reading-order note for a tile set whose order carries no meaning.
accessibility: Unlabelled, it is a presentational layout container with no role. Give it `ariaLabel` and it becomes a named `group`, which is valid around any content; set `role="list"` only when every tile is `role="listitem"` — dev mode names the first tile that is not.
Reading order follows DOM order; keep tiles in a logical sequence for screen readers.

When masonry is genuinely in force, the divergence between reading order and visual order is **stated** rather than papered over: the markup is already correct, so there is nothing for ARIA to fix, and the note points at the plain grid for cases where order matters.
The note never claims a divergence that is not happening — in a browser that drops the property it says the opposite, that reading order and visual order agree.
Give interactive tiles their own roles, names and focus states.

inputs.description: Show the reading-order note when masonry is actually in force.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible label for the grid region. When set, the grid also exposes an ARIA role (`role`, default `group`) so assistive tech announces it.

inputs.name: role
inputs.description: ARIA role for the grid element, applied only when `ariaLabel` is set. `group` is valid around any content; use `list` for a collection a screen reader should count, and mark every tile `role="listitem"`.

components.name: Time Picker
components.description: 12h/24h scroll-column time picker with hour/minute/second wheels, AM/PM selector, Now button and 3 sizes.
whenToUse: Selecting a time of day with hour/minute (and optional second) precision.
You want scroll-column wheels and a "Now" shortcut.
Pair with a Date Picker when you need a full timestamp.

examples.title: Locale day periods and a minute step
examples.description: On a 12-hour clock `locale` (default: the kit locale) picks the day periods from `Intl` — 午前/午後 written first in Japanese, a. m./p. m. in Spanish — on the buttons, the trigger and the typed field, which parses them back. `minuteStep` offers minutes on a step and snaps typed minutes down to it.

examples.title: Type the time instead of scrolling to it
examples.description: The panel opens with a text field focused, so the keyboard path to any time is Tab, Enter, type, Enter. It accepts 14:30, 14.30, 1430, 2:30 PM, 2:30pm and the same forms in Arabic-Indic, Bengali or fullwidth digits. Set [typed]="false" to remove the field; the columns remain.
examples.code:
<!-- on by default -->
<sv-time-picker format="24h" [(ngModel)]="time" />

<!-- wheels only -->
<sv-time-picker [typed]="false" [(ngModel)]="time" />

customization: 12-hour or 24-hour mode with optional seconds, plus min/max bounds and a "Now" shortcut.

The value is a wall-clock `HH:mm` (or `HH:mm:ss`) string — not an instant, and not zoned. Pair it with the Date Picker's `YYYY-MM-DD` calendar date through `svComposeDateTime` when you need a real timestamp.
Three sizes; the trigger shows the selected time with a chevron and is named via `label`.
Two-way bind `[(value)]` or a reactive control (CVA); listen to `(changed)`.

`typed` (default `true`) puts a text field at the top of the panel and focuses it on open. It parses `14:30`, `14.30`, `1430`, `143015`, `2:30 PM`, `2:30pm` and the same forms written in Arabic-Indic, Bengali, Devanagari or fullwidth digits, plus day-period markers in Arabic, Japanese and Korean. It commits on Enter and on blur — never mid-keystroke, because `1` and `14` are both valid times on the way to `14:30`.
`locale` (12-hour day periods from `Intl`, in the locale's own position) and `minuteStep` (a stepped minute column; typed and Now times snap down to the step, then into `min`/`max`).
accessibility: The trigger is named by `label` (announced with the current value) and exposes `aria-expanded` / `aria-haspopup`.
The popover is a non-modal `role="dialog"`; columns are buttons reachable by keyboard, and the selected time updates the value live.

Each column is a single tab stop on its selected cell, with Up/Down by one, PageUp/PageDown by five, and Home/End to the ends — clamping at the ends rather than wrapping, and stepping over cells disabled by `min`/`max` rather than landing on one (a disabled button cannot take focus, which would strand focus on the body with the panel still open).
A refused typed time sets `aria-invalid` on the field and turns its hint into a `role="alert"` carrying the accepted format, so the correction is announced with the complaint.
Implements ControlValueAccessor — works with `[(ngModel)]`, `[formControl]` and `formControlName`; `formControl.disable()` disables the trigger.

components.name: Timeline
components.description: 9 variations: horizontal, alternate zigzag, numbered stepper, check stepper, activity feed, status tracker, rich card, date-grouped and interactive (clickable rows).
whenToUse: Showing a sequence of events over time: history, activity, status changes.
You want per-item icons/colors and optional date grouping.
For an interactive multi-step process, use the Stepper.

examples.title: Status / Progress Tracker
examples.description: displayMode="status" (or dotStyle="check" with activeIndex) turns the timeline into an order/onboarding progress tracker with complete / active / pending steps.

examples.title: What the list means, separately from what it looks like
examples.description: A stepper is not a feed. `displayMode` is an appearance choice; `intent` is what the list means, so the shape of the dot never decides what a screen reader is told: a process says aria-current="step", a chronology says "true", and a feed says nothing at all, because a log of events has no position to be at. It also names the list — "Timeline", "Progress tracker", "Activity feed". The default, auto, infers it (feed from displayMode="feed", process from "status" or a ticked/numbered dotStyle, chronology otherwise); an inferred chronology with an active item says aria-current="true", and each list is named after its intent. Set intent explicitly to pin the semantics.
examples.code:
<!-- A process, drawn with plain dots, that still announces as one. -->
<sv-timeline [items]="steps" intent="process" [activeIndex]="2" />

<!-- A log. Nothing in it is "current". -->
<sv-timeline [items]="events" intent="feed" />

examples.title: Collapsing a long history
examples.description: A long history is not a list, it is a wall. `collapseAfter` renders the first N items in the host's order and a "Show 45 more entries" control that names the count; `expanded` is two-way so a host can persist it. It applies to every layout, including `groupByDate` — a date group whose items are all collapsed is not drawn until the reader expands.

customization: Vertical, horizontal or alternating layouts.
Per-item icon, color and rich content.
Group by date for activity feeds.
`displayMode="status"` renders a Status / Progress Tracker — drive it with `activeIndex` (items before → complete, at → active, after → pending) or per-item `itemStatus`.
Rich-card CTAs emit `actionClick` (rendered as a link when `actionUrl` is set, otherwise a button).
`displayMode="interactive"` makes whole rows clickable — emits `itemClick` and highlights `selectedId` (two-way bindable).

`intent` (`chronology` / `process` / `feed`, default `auto`) is what the list MEANS, separate from what it looks like. It sets the list's accessible name ("Timeline" / "Progress tracker" / "Activity feed") and what `aria-current` says. `auto` infers it from `displayMode` and `dotStyle`; an inferred chronology with an active item says `aria-current="true"` and each list takes its intent's name — set `intent` to pin it.
`collapseAfter` (default `0`, off) shows the first N items and a count-naming "Show N more entries" control; `expanded` is two-way. Works in every layout, including `groupByDate`.

`showVariantIcon` (default `false`) draws a tick / cross / triangle / "i" inside `success` / `error` / `warning` / `info` dots that have no `icon` of their own, so the state is a shape as well as a hue.
Time-zone policy: `groupDate` is a label, never parsed. Consecutive items sharing it are grouped; resolve the day in the zone you want displayed before passing it.
accessibility: Ordered list semantics preserve sequence — an `<ol>` of `<li>`s, so the sequence is the DOM order and needs no off-screen table alongside it.

The dot has a text equivalent, so a failed deploy and a successful one do not differ by hue alone (WCAG 1.4.1): a coloured dot is `role="img"` named "Error", "Success" and so on, and the variants that carry no meaning stay silent.

Name the list with `ariaLabel` when a page has more than one. Without it a release feed and an audit log are both "Timeline" in a landmark list. In the date-grouped layout each group's list is that name plus its date ("Deploy log, Today").
Icons are decorative; text carries the meaning.
Stepper modes expose each step's state (Completed / Current / Pending) to screen readers and mark the active step with `aria-current="step"`.
The pulsing ring on an active step stops under `prefers-reduced-motion` (`motion-reduce:animate-none`); the dot itself stays, because it is the state.

`intent` decides what the current item is announced as, not the shape of the dot: a process drawn with plain dots still announces its step. A `process` says `step`, a `chronology` says `true`, and a `feed` says nothing at all — a log of events is not somewhere you are partway through.
CTA controls carry a descriptive label combining the action and the item title.

Interactive rows (`displayMode="interactive"`) are keyboard-focusable `role="button"` controls inside the list items — Enter/Space activate, and the selected row is marked `aria-pressed` — so the list keeps its semantics while every row is operable without a mouse.
