components.name: Toast
components.description: Imperative toast stack with 4 variants, 6 anchor positions, action callbacks and an auto-dismiss timer.
whenToUse: Confirming a completed action transiently without interrupting the flow.
Non-blocking feedback: "Saved", "Copied", "Email sent".
For persistent status use an Alert Banner; for decisions, a Confirm Dialog.

Not sure this is the right outcome surface? Compare toast, banner, result, empty state, notification center and modal by severity, persistence and whether the user can correct it in the “Choosing a feedback pattern” guide under Guides.

examples.title: With an action
One toast for an async action
A retry loop that fails eleven times
A toast that is about the PAGE, not the action

customization: Six anchor positions and four variants.
Action buttons and auto-dismiss duration.
Driven imperatively via ToastService.

Deduplication, on by default: a repeat refreshes the toast that is already up, increments a `×n` badge and restarts its countdown, instead of filling a bounded stack with eleven copies of one failure. It keeps its place and its id, so the caller's handle still works and a screen reader is not read the same sentence twice. Key it yourself with `dedupeKey` (or `null` to opt out).

Route scope: a toast survives navigation by default, and `{ scope: 'route' }` marks one as belonging to the page it was raised on. `provideSvOverlayRouteClose()` (from `@styloviz/layout`) drops those and only those on `NavigationEnd`; `ToastService.navigated()` is the router-agnostic call behind it, for an app on a different router.

A bounded stack: `maxVisible` (validated — anything below 1 is 1, `Infinity` means no cap) shows the newest toasts and a "+N more" line counts the older ones held back; they stay alive and slide back into view as newer ones go. A toast raised while the pointer or focus is on the stack is paused on arrival, and a keyed replacement (`Saving…` then `Saved` on one `dedupeKey`) is announced — only an identical repeat is silent.

`[portal]="true"` moves the region into a `<body>` portal. Use it when toasts carry actions and your app opens modals: a modal makes the page behind it `inert`, and `inert` is inherited, so a region inside the app shell can still be heard (speech goes through the shared announcer) but its Undo button cannot be pressed until the dialog closes. Portalled, the region is a `<body>` child the overlay stack keeps live. Off by default because it moves the region out of the host element.

`toast.promise(work, { loading, success, error }, opts?)`: one toast for an async action. It shows `loading` with a spinner (`pending: true`, `aria-busy`), persists and is not dismissible until the work settles, then turns into the success or error toast in place — same id, no repeat count — and is announced again. `success` and `error` may be functions of the result. `opts.duration` sets how long the outcome stays (default 4 s, 6 s for an error). Returns the work promise, so you still await the result and handle the rejection.

Phones: the stack keeps `max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-*))` from each edge, so it clears the notch, the rounded corners and the home indicator (add `viewport-fit=cover` to your viewport meta), and a bottom stack is lifted above the virtual keyboard while one is up, so a toast raised by a form Save is not hidden by the keyboard that form raised.
accessibility: One shared live region announces every toast (`SvLiveAnnouncer`) — assertively for `error`, politely for the rest, including `warning`.

A toast is not a live region of its own: a region inserted with its text already inside it is what AT is least likely to read, and it would take its region away with it seconds later, mid-sentence. The stack container stays `role="region"` + `aria-label="Notifications"`, so a screen reader user can navigate to a toast and press its action.
Auto-dismiss pauses while the pointer OR keyboard focus is over the stack — both, separately — and resumes only when neither holds (WCAG 2.2.1); actions are keyboard reachable before dismiss.

inputs.name: position
inputs.description: Where the stack is anchored on screen.

inputs.name: maxVisible
inputs.description: Maximum number of toasts visible simultaneously.

inputs.name: portal
inputs.description: Move the region to `<body>` so it stays usable above a modal. `inert` is inherited and cannot be undone by a descendant. A modal makes the page behind it inert, and a host mounted inside the app shell is part of that page: its toasts are still announced (speech goes through the shared announcer) but an "Undo" button on one cannot be pressed until the dialog closes. Portalled, the region is a `<body>` child the stack keeps live at any depth. Off by default because it moves the region's DOM (and its `data-sv-toast-*` hooks) out of the host.

components.name: Toggle Switch
components.description: Accessible toggle for boolean settings in multiple sizes, colors and label positions.
whenToUse: Toggling a single setting that takes effect immediately (no Save needed).
The choice is binary and the default is meaningful — e.g. notifications on/off.

Use a Checkbox instead whenever the change only lands on submit — a form field, a terms acceptance, a row selection, or anything a Cancel button is expected to undo. A switch promises "this is on now", so putting one inside a form with a Save button makes a promise the form then breaks; and if the user closes the dialog, nothing tells them which of the two things they saw was true.

Use a Checkbox instead when the action needs confirming. A switch cannot ask "are you sure" without contradicting itself: it has already moved by the time the dialog opens, and a cancelled confirmation leaves it to move back on its own — which is indistinguishable from a failed save.
components.usage:
<sv-toggle-switch
  label="Email notifications"
  description="Get notified when something needs your attention."
  [(checked)]="notifications" />

examples.title: Reactive forms + required
examples.description: Works with formControlName via ControlValueAccessor; required sets aria-required and the description is linked for assistive tech.
examples.code:
<sv-toggle-switch
  formControlName="acceptTerms"
  label="I accept the terms"
  description="You must accept to continue."
  [required]="true" />

examples.title: A setting that has to reach a server
examples.description: A switch that silently flips back three seconds later is the defining trust failure of a settings screen. The switch moves first — waiting for the round-trip reads as broken — so it owes the host a way back. `(toggleRequest)` carries an idempotency key and a guarded `rollback()`, and `[pending]` is the lock that makes the rollback unambiguous: with two writes outstanding there is no single previous state to return to. `(toggled)` still fires for hosts that need neither.
examples.code:
<sv-toggle-switch
  label="Two-factor authentication"
  [checked]="twoFactor()"
  [pending]="saving()"
  [error]="failure()"
  (toggleRequest)="save($event)" />

save(e: SvToggleChange): void {
  this.saving.set(true);
  this.api.setTwoFactor(e.checked, e.requestKey).subscribe({
    next:  () => this.saving.set(false),
    error: () => { e.rollback(); this.failure.set('Could not save that.'); this.saving.set(false); },
  });
}

examples.title: Pending is not loading
examples.description: They wear the same spinner and mean opposite things. `loading` says *we do not know what this switch is* — a settings screen that rendered before its settings arrived, so dimming it is honest. `pending` says *we know exactly what the user asked for, it is already drawn, and the server has not agreed yet* — so it spins without dimming, because fading a value the user just chose reads as "this did not take".
examples.code:
<!-- The value has not arrived. Nothing on screen is trustworthy yet. -->
<sv-toggle-switch label="Email digest" [loading]="settings.isLoading()" />

<!-- The value is the user's own choice, and the write is out. -->
<sv-toggle-switch label="Email digest" [checked]="digest()" [pending]="saving()" />

examples.title: A lock that says why
examples.description: A disabled switch tells the user "not you, not now" and nothing else, leaving them to guess between "not on your plan", "your admin turned this off" and "this is broken" — three different next actions, and only the host knows which applies. `lockReason` locks the control, renders the reason and points `aria-describedby` at it, and the switch stays in the tab order so the readers most likely to need the explanation can reach it.
examples.code:
<sv-toggle-switch
  label="Single sign-on"
  [checked]="true"
  lockReason="Enforced by your organization" />

customization: Set `size` (xs, sm, md, lg) and `variant` (primary, success, warning, danger, neutral) for the active color.
Place the label with `labelPosition` (right, left, top, hidden), add a `description` line and inline `onLabel` / `offLabel` track text.
Show inline `onIcon` / `offIcon` icons inside the thumb; toggle `disabled`, `loading` and `required`.

Two-way bind with `[(checked)]` or bind a reactive control; listen to `(toggled)` for the new boolean, or `(toggleRequest)` for a `{ checked, requestKey, rollback }` payload when a server has to agree.
`pending` locks the switch while a write is in flight without dimming it; `lockReason` locks it and says why.
accessibility: Uses `role="switch"` with `aria-checked`; operable with Space/Enter and a visible focus ring.
The visible `label` is associated via `<label for>`, so clicking the text toggles the switch; a unique id is generated automatically when `inputId` is omitted.
The accessible name comes from `aria-labelledby` (visible label) or `ariaLabel` (hidden); `description` is linked with `aria-describedby`.

`required` sets `aria-required`; `loading` and `pending` both set `aria-busy`; `disabled`, `pending`, `lockReason` and a programmatic `formControl.disable()` all set `aria-disabled` and block interaction.

A `lockReason` is rendered as text and linked with `aria-describedby`, and the switch keeps `tabindex="0"` — a lock explained only in a tooltip, or on an unfocusable control, is unreachable by the people most likely to need it.
variants: Async settings — pending, revert, and a lock that says why

inputs.name: checked
inputs.description: Current on/off state. Use `[(checked)]` for two-way binding.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Visible label text.

inputs.name: description
inputs.description: Smaller descriptor line beneath the label.

inputs.name: labelPosition
inputs.description: Position of the label relative to the track.

inputs.name: onLabel
inputs.description: Text shown inside the track when ON. Keep ≤ 3 characters for `md` size, fewer for smaller sizes.

inputs.name: offLabel
inputs.description: Text shown inside the track when OFF.

inputs.name: onIcon
inputs.description: Icon-library NAME rendered inside the thumb when the toggle is ON — e.g. `'check'`. Omit to show a plain thumb.

inputs.name: offIcon
inputs.description: Icon-library NAME rendered inside the thumb when the toggle is OFF — e.g. `'close'`. Was `offIconPath`.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Size of the toggle track and thumb.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Active-state color variant.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disable interaction.

inputs.name: required
inputs.description: Mark the control as required (sets `aria-required`).

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: The switch's own value is not known yet — a settings screen that rendered before its settings arrived. Shows a spinner in the thumb and blocks interaction.

inputs.name: pending
inputs.description: The user's change is applied on screen and the write is in flight. Why this is not `loading`: They are opposite states wearing the same spinner. `loading` means *we do not know what this switch is* — there is nothing on screen to trust yet. `pending` means *we know exactly what the user asked for, it is already drawn, and the server has not agreed yet*. Collapsing the two costs the host the only lock that makes `rollback()` unambiguous: with two writes outstanding there is no single previous state to return to, so the older handle would silently discard the newer change. Bind it for the whole round-trip and clear it in both branches.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: The write failed. Why this is not `serverError`: They are different facts about different things, and using one for the other is a real bug rather than a naming preference. `serverError` is the field-error contract: *the server rejected this VALUE*, and it self-expires on the next change because a rejection stops describing a value the moment the value moves. A failed write is *the server never recorded the change* — and reverting it **is** a change, so routing it through `serverError` would clear the message in the same tick the rollback ran. The user would see the switch move back and be told nothing, which is the precise failure this whole contract exists to prevent. Accepts an `SvDataError` or a plain string. Roll the value back as well — a message beside a switch still showing the state that failed to save is worse than either on its own.

inputs.name: lockReason
inputs.description: Why this switch cannot be changed. Non-empty locks the control and renders the reason, which `aria-describedby` also points at. Distinct from `disabled`, deliberately. A disabled switch is a dead end: it tells the user they may not, and nothing else, so they are left to guess between "not on your plan", "your admin turned this off" and "this is broken". Those need different next actions, and only the host knows which one applies.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: `aria-label` override — required when `labelPosition === 'hidden'` so screen readers still announce the control's purpose.

inputs.name: inputId
inputs.description: id forwarded to the hidden `<input>` for `<label for="">` use.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Additional CSS classes on the root wrapper element.

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: Client-side validation message.

inputs.name: serverError
inputs.description: A rejection reported by the server about this value. Self-expiring.

outputs.name: toggled
outputs.description: Emits the new boolean state after every toggle.

outputs.name: toggleRequest
outputs.description: The same toggle, carrying what a server write needs: an idempotency key and a guarded way back. Additive, not a replacement — `toggled` still fires, and a switch that only writes to local state has no use for either of these. Both are emitted for one interaction, in this order.

outputs.name: checkedChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `checked` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(checked)]`.

components.name: Tool Call Card
components.description: Inspector for the tool / function calls an agent makes. 4 variants: compact one-line pills, expanded disclosure, streaming (arguments filling in) and error (message, stack trace and retry) — with per-call latency and token attribution, and recursive sub-calls.
whenToUse: Showing what an assistant actually did while producing an answer.
Debugging an agent run — which tool was called, with what, and how long it took.
Surfacing a failed tool call with enough context for the user to retry it.
Rendering a plan that fans out into sub-calls.

examples.title: Compact pills under a message
examples.description: Dense read-only rows that do not steal attention from the answer.

examples.title: Retry a failed call
examples.description: Expose a Retry button and re-run the tool through your own runtime.

examples.title: Streaming arguments
examples.description: A running call auto-expands and renders a caret while its arguments arrive.

examples.title: Deep fan-out and large payloads
examples.description: Sub-calls past two levels wait behind "Show N nested calls"; a result over 4,000 characters truncates with Show all and Download.

customization: Five failure causes, not one error state: `failure: 'transport' | 'tool' | 'policy' | 'timeout' | 'cancelled'`. Each renders its own chip label, its own meaning and its own recovery line, because three of the five are not the tool's fault and the reader's next move differs in every one. Leave it unset and the card renders the generic **Failed** state it always has — an undeclared cause is never guessed at, since blaming the tool for a network fault sends the reader to the wrong owner.
A `policy` refusal is offered **no retry at all**, even with `[retryable]` on: it was refused for a reason a second press does not change, and the recovery line says what would actually help.

`idempotent: false` grows a warning beside the retry — except on a `transport` failure, which never reached the tool: nothing ran, so there is nothing to duplicate. The case it exists for is a non-idempotent tool that *timed out* — 'charge the card' may have charged, may not have, and the button could charge it again. The warning is attached to the control (`aria-describedby`, and folded into the button's label) rather than replacing it: the reader may need to retry, they just have to know what they are risking. It renders directly under the header, so a collapsed card shows it too, and only where a Retry is actually offered — never on a success, a policy refusal or a card with `retryable` off.

Redaction, from the pack-wide policy: arguments, results, the error message and the stack trace are masked per `provideSvAiPrivacy({ patterns })`, in the expanded panes and in the compact inline summary, with one note per call saying something is hidden rather than one per pane. An error is where a key leaks by accident — a failing client echoes the request it made. Copy is not gated here because there is no copy control to gate — both code blocks render headerless, and the header is where copying lives.
Four variants: `compact` (one-line pills), `expanded` (disclosure, the default), `stream` (running calls auto-open with a caret) and `error` (message, stack trace and retry).

Arguments and results render through `sv-code-block`, so JSON is highlighted and scrollable — and nothing is injected as HTML. The blocks render headerless, so the card offers no copy control of its own (see the redaction note).

Sub-calls in `children` render recursively with depth-capped indentation; the header shows the child count. `[maxDepth]` (default `SV_TOOL_CALL_MAX_DEPTH`, 4) caps how many nested levels render without asking: past it a call's sub-calls wait behind a "Show N nested calls" disclosure that counts every hidden call, and each further level asks again, so an agent that fans out recursively cannot flood the chat. `0` renders every level.

`[maxPaneChars]` (default `SV_TOOL_CALL_PANE_CHAR_CAP`, 10,000) caps how much of an argument or result pane is highlighted. A longer pane says "Showing the first 10,000 of 152,340 characters." with **Show all** and **Download** — the download is the pane as shown, so a value the privacy policy masked stays masked in the file, and `(paneDownloaded)` reports it. `0` renders every character.
Per-call `durationMs` and `tokens` render as header chips, with a total across a stack of calls; hide them with `showTiming`.
Emits `retry` (the failed call) and `toggled` (call plus new expanded state) so a host can drive a real runtime.
Supply one call via `call` or many via `calls` — `calls` wins when both are set.
Status colours, `language` and `paneMaxHeight` are all inputs; icons come from `@styloviz/icons`.
accessibility: Each expandable card is a real `<button>` with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` pointing at its panel; a call with nothing to reveal renders no button at all.
The card stack is a `role="list"` / `role="listitem"` structure with an accessible name from `ariaLabel`.
An in-flight call exposes its status chip as `role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"`, so a screen reader hears the call complete.
The Retry button carries an explicit `aria-label` naming the tool, since the visible label is just "Retry".
Status glyphs are decorative and `aria-hidden`; the status word beside them carries the meaning.

Past `maxDepth`, "Show N nested calls" is a `button` with `aria-expanded` (and `aria-controls` once the list exists); a truncated pane's Show all is `aria-pressed`, and its Download button names the pane and the tool ("Download Result of search_orders").

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the data is being fetched.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse`.

inputs.name: call
inputs.description: A single call. Ignored when `calls` is non-empty. Set `failure` on an errored call (`transport`, `tool`, `policy`, `timeout` or `cancelled`) to render its cause, meaning and recovery path in place of the generic Failed chip; left unset, the generic state renders.

inputs.name: calls
inputs.description: Several calls, rendered as a stack. Takes precedence over `call`.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Layout preset.

inputs.name: defaultExpanded
inputs.description: Expand every card on first render.

inputs.name: showTiming
inputs.description: Show the duration and token chips.

inputs.name: retryable
inputs.description: Show a Retry button on failed calls. Never offered on a `policy` refusal. A call with `idempotent: false` gets a duplicate-action warning beside its Retry (louder on a `timeout`), except on a `transport` failure, which never reached the tool.

inputs.name: language
inputs.description: Language that `args` and `result` are highlighted as.

inputs.name: paneMaxHeight
inputs.description: Max height of the argument / result panes, as a CSS length.

inputs.name: ariaLabel
inputs.description: Accessible label for the list of calls.

inputs.name: maxDepth
inputs.description: Nesting levels below the top that render without asking. Sub-calls past it collapse behind a "Show N nested calls" button (each level asks again), so an agent that fans out recursively cannot flood the surface. `0` renders every level.

inputs.name: maxPaneChars
inputs.description: Characters of arguments or result rendered before the pane truncates, with "Show all" and "Download" for the rest. The download is the text as shown — masked per the privacy policy. `0` renders every character.

inputs.name: locale
inputs.description: Locale for the character counts in the truncation notice.

inputs.name: openedIds
inputs.description: Call ids the user opened (two-way). A `model` so a host can restore or persist which calls were open. The variant's own default (`defaultExpanded`, a running streamed call) still applies to calls not listed here.

inputs.name: depthRevealedIds
inputs.description: Ids of calls whose sub-calls past `maxDepth` the reader asked to see. A `model` so a host can restore or persist what was revealed.

inputs.name: fullPaneKeys
inputs.description: `<callId>:<pane>` keys (`pane` is `arguments` or `result`) the reader asked to see in full past `maxPaneChars`. A `model` so a host can restore it.

outputs.name: retryLoad
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed load. Named `retryLoad` because this component already publishes `retry` for re-running a single item — stealing that name would silently change what existing handlers receive.

outputs.name: retry
outputs.description: Emits the failed call the user asked to re-run.

outputs.name: toggled
outputs.description: Emits whenever a card is expanded or collapsed.

outputs.name: paneDownloaded
outputs.description: Emits after a pane was downloaded, with the call, the pane and the file name.

outputs.name: openedIdsChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `openedIds` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(openedIds)]`.

outputs.name: depthRevealedIdsChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `depthRevealedIds` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(depthRevealedIds)]`.

outputs.name: fullPaneKeysChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `fullPaneKeys` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(fullPaneKeys)]`.

components.name: Toolbar
components.description: 5 visual variants (default, glass, bordered, elevated, ghost) and 3 sizes, with grouped action buttons, separators and an actionClick output.
whenToUse: Hosting a row of actions above content: editors, tables, document views.
You want grouped icon buttons with separators, toggle state and keyboard navigation.
For a floating single primary action, use the Speed Dial.

examples.title: Overflow menu
examples.code:
<!-- Actions that do not fit move into a "More" menu, from the end of the list -->
<sv-toolbar [actions]="actions" overflow="menu" overflowLabel="More editing actions" (actionClick)="run($event)" />

examples.title: Pending actions and shortcuts

customization: Five visual variants incl. a chrome-less `ghost` for embedding in an existing card or header.
Three sizes: sm / md / lg.
Grouped actions with separators.
Toggle buttons with two-way `activeIds`.
Per-action color accents: primary, danger, success.

Action metadata: `ToolbarAction.pending` (aria-busy + spinner + inert click, the per-action twin of `busyIds`) and `ToolbarAction.shortcut` (an `sv-kbd` chord; exposed as `aria-keyshortcuts` and drawn with `sv-kbd` in an `sv-tooltip` that replaces the native `title`, and in the overflow-menu row). A sequence such as `g i` is drawn but gets no `aria-keyshortcuts`, because a space there means "alternatives". `svToolbarAriaShortcut()` is exported for hosts that want the same mapping.
Responsive: an action-heavy toolbar scrolls horizontally when it can't fit (no scrollbar while it does), so it never overflows the viewport on small screens.

Overflow menu mode: `overflow="menu"` measures the width the parent allows and moves the trailing actions into a "More" menu button (`overflowLabel` names it). Order the actions by importance — the end of the list overflows first. The default is `overflow="scroll"`.

Variant axes: `variant`, `size` and each action's `variant` are APPEARANCE and combine freely. `overflow`, `sticky`, toggles (`activeIds`) and `busyIds` are BEHAVIOURAL modes. Known limits: in `overflow="menu"` the host becomes `display: block` to measure its parent; a `sticky` toolbar's overflow menu is a body portal that re-anchors on scroll but does not itself stick; `loading` replaces the strip, so there is nothing to overflow.

Floating layer (`floatingAnchor`): a `sticky` or host-fixed toolbar can register its strip as an occupied region — usually `'top'` or `'bottom'` — so Scroll to Top, a floating Speed Dial and host regions on that side stack clear of it. Opt-in because the toolbar cannot tell where the host's CSS puts it; `null` (default) registers nothing.
accessibility: Exposes a labelled `role="toolbar"` with labelled buttons; toggles report `aria-pressed`.

Forced colors: focus is a box-shadow ring, which forced colors removes, so every action, the More button and every menu item also draws a system-coloured focus OUTLINE in that mode only. An active or pressed tool keeps a Highlight border.

Overflow menu layering: the menu takes its z-index from the shared overlay stack (above page chrome, below a dialog opened from it), handles Escape only while it is the topmost overlay, and treats a click inside a surface opened above it as inside. If the menu item holding focus is removed or turns busy while the menu is open, focus moves to the item now in its place, else the one before it, else the menu itself; if the menu empties, to the toolbar's tab stop — never `<body>`.
Single tab stop with roving tabindex; Arrow keys, Home and End move between buttons (ARIA toolbar pattern). The tab stop follows a click too, so Tab returns to the action last used.

Orientation and RTL policy: the toolbar is horizontal only. Left/Right follow what the user sees — under `dir="rtl"` the strip mirrors, so ArrowLeft moves to the NEXT action — while Up/Down always mean next/previous and Home/End first/last. Menu rows align to the inline start.
Roving focus is scoped to each toolbar's own host, so two toolbars sharing action ids never steal focus from each other.

Focus after change: when the action holding the tab stop is disabled or removed, the stop moves to its successor (the action now in its place, else the one before it). If that action held keyboard focus, focus moves there too; with nothing focusable left it goes to the toolbar itself — never `<body>`. A toolbar the user has already left does not pull focus back.

Overflow menu: the More button is part of the roving tab stop and exposes `aria-haspopup="menu"` / `aria-expanded`; Down or Enter opens it on the first item, Up on the last. Items are `menuitem` (toggles are `menuitemcheckbox` with `aria-checked`); Arrow keys, Home and End move, Escape closes and returns focus to More, Tab closes and continues past the toolbar.
Action ids must be unique: a duplicate logs a dev-mode warning, because `actionClick` emits the id and the host could not tell the two apart.

inputs.name: groups
inputs.description: Grouped actions rendered with separators between groups.

inputs.name: actions
inputs.description: Flat action list (alternative to `groups`).

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Toolbar size: sm, md or lg.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Visual variant: default, glass, bordered, elevated or ghost.

inputs.name: label
inputs.description: Accessible label for the toolbar region.

inputs.name: sticky
inputs.description: Stick the toolbar to the top while scrolling.

inputs.name: floatingAnchor
inputs.description: Opt in to the shared floating layer: register the toolbar strip as an occupied region on this edge or corner, so kit controls there (Scroll to Top, a floating Speed Dial) and host regions stack clear of it. For a `sticky` toolbar, or one the host pins `position: fixed` — the component cannot tell where the host's CSS puts it, so it never guesses. Registers at `SV_FLOATING_ORDER.edge` (nearest the edge). `null` registers nothing and the rendered output is unchanged.

inputs.name: overflow
inputs.description: What happens to actions that do not fit: `scroll` keeps them inline in a horizontally scrolling strip; `menu` measures the available width and moves the trailing actions into a keyboard-accessible "More" menu (a body-portal `role="menu"`). In `menu` mode the host element becomes `display: block` so it can measure the width its parent allows.

inputs.name: overflowLabel
inputs.description: Accessible name (and tooltip) of the "More" button and its menu.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while the action set is being fetched. A toolbar whose actions depend on the user's permissions is fetched, not hard-coded.

inputs.name: loadError
inputs.description: The definition fetch failed — the toolbar has no actions to show. Separate from `error`, which is a failure of an action the user just TRIGGERED. The two need opposite affordances: a failed action is retried by clicking that action again, while a failed load has nothing left to click. Collapsing them into one input gave the action strip a "Try again" button that could not know which action to re-run.

inputs.name: busyIds
inputs.description: Ids of actions with a request in flight. Those controls disable and show a busy state, so a double-click cannot fire the same request twice — the most common way an action button creates duplicate records.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Failure from the last action. Rendered above the control group; nothing is removed from view, so the user can see what state things are in.

inputs.name: activeIds
inputs.description: Pre-seeded set of active toggle IDs. Two-way bindable.

outputs.name: retryLoad
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed definition fetch. Named `retryLoad`, matching `sv-agent-task-queue`: on a component where `error` already means something else, the load states carry the `…Load` spelling rather than stealing a name that is already taken.

outputs.name: actionClick
outputs.description: Emitted with the id of the clicked action.

outputs.name: activeIdsChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `activeIds` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(activeIds)]`.

components.name: Tooltip
components.description: Hover/click/focus/long-press tooltip with 12 placements, rich title · description · keys content, nine looks, tooltip groups, a controlled open, anchors and three animations — and a Pro twin that can be hovered, focused and follows the cursor.
whenToUse: Revealing a short, supplementary hint on hover/focus of a control.
Explaining icon-only buttons or truncated labels.
For rich, interactive content use a Popover (a hint with one link in it is `sv-tooltip-pro` with `[interactive]`); for persistent info, inline text.

examples.title: Inside a table cell or card — portalled by default
Explaining a disabled control
examples.code:
<!-- A natively disabled button fires no pointer events and takes no focus,
     so a plain tooltip on it never appears. The preset takes the dead
     control out of hit-testing and gives the wrapper the tab stop.
     Prefer aria-disabled="true" when the control is yours - it needs none of
     this. Never use the preset around an ENABLED control. -->
<sv-tooltip text="Only admins can delete projects" [forDisabledControl]="true">
  <button disabled>Delete</button>
</sv-tooltip>

customization: Twelve placements (`top`, `top-start` … `right-end`; `start`/`end` mirror in RTL), nine looks (dark · light · primary · danger · success · warning · inverted · glass · value) and three sizes (sm · md · lg).

Rich content: a `title` above the text, `kbd` keys, an `icon`, a `status` dot, or your own markup in a `[svTooltipContent]` template; `[arrow]` toggles the pointer and `animation` is `fade` · `scale` · `shift`.

`[svTooltipGroup]` on a toolbar: the first tooltip waits for `groupDelay`, the next one along shows at once (within `skipDelay`), and only one is open at a time. `[open]` controls it from outside; `[anchor]` points it at another element or a viewport point.

Hover, click or focus triggers — and on a pointer that cannot hover, a `hover` tooltip becomes tap-to-toggle by itself, with the show delay skipped and a press anywhere else dismissing it (`touch="hold"` makes it a long-press instead, `touch="off"` leaves it out on touch). A `focus` or `click` trigger is left alone.
Configurable show/hide delay.
`customClass` on the bubble; `visibleChange` output.

The bubble renders in a `<body>` portal positioned by measurement (the default; `[portal]="false"` keeps it in place) — the same arithmetic Popover and Dropdown Menu use. It escapes an `overflow: hidden` ancestor (every table cell, card and scroll area), flips with `[flip]`, is clamped to the viewport, keeps its arrow over the trigger when clamped, and re-anchors on scroll of any ancestor.
A portalled tooltip paints in the ambient tooltip band, so it clears a dialog it appears inside — and it never becomes the surface Escape closes.

`[forDisabledControl]="true"` — the disabled-control preset: the projected control gets `pointer-events: none` so hover and tap land on the wrapper, and the wrapper becomes a tab stop described by the tooltip from the start (Enter/Space toggle a `click` tooltip there). Dev mode warns when the projected content is not actually disabled.

Pro (`sv-tooltip-pro`): `[interactive]` keeps the bubble open while the pointer is on it (after `hideDelay`) or focus is inside, so links in it work and Tab from the trigger goes in; `[followCursor]` makes it ride with the pointer over a chart or a timeline.
accessibility: Shows on keyboard focus, not just hover, and emits `visibleChange` on every transition.
Associated via aria-describedby; dismissible with Esc.

It works on touch, which a hover tooltip does not — worse, it half-works: mobile browsers synthesise `mouseenter` on tap, so the tap meant to activate the trigger raises the tooltip over the control just pressed, and with no `mouseleave` coming it stays there. Where hovering is unavailable the tooltip switches to tap-to-toggle, skips the delay (a tap is deliberate), and dismisses on a press elsewhere — there is no `mouseleave` on a finger and no Escape key on a phone. It follows a pointer that changes mid-session, because a convertible laptop folds.
Forced colours: every bubble — the glass one included — keeps a `CanvasText` edge, because forced colours repaint its fill as Canvas and remove its ring.

inputs.name: text
inputs.description: Tooltip text content.

inputs.name: position
inputs.description: Position relative to the trigger.

inputs.name: variant
inputs.description: Color variant.

inputs.name: size
inputs.description: Size — controls font and padding.

inputs.name: trigger
inputs.description: What triggers the tooltip.

inputs.name: maxWidth
inputs.description: Max width of the tooltip bubble (px); the text wraps at it. `null` keeps the bubble on one line however long the text is.

inputs.name: delay
inputs.description: Delay before showing (ms).

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Whether the tooltip is disabled.

inputs.name: customClass
inputs.description: Extra CSS classes merged onto the tooltip bubble.

inputs.name: portal
inputs.description: Render the bubble in a `<body>` portal, positioned by measurement — on by default. The in-place bubble clips: an absolutely positioned child is clipped by any ancestor with `overflow: hidden` — every table cell, card and scroll area in a dashboard — and it is placed by CSS classes alone, so it cannot see the viewport edge. The portal moves the bubble to the end of `<body>` and positions it with `svPositionAnchored` (the arithmetic Popover and Dropdown Menu use): it escapes the clip, flips when it does not fit, and is clamped to the viewport. `[portal]="false"` keeps the bubble inside the trigger wrapper, for a host that styles it by its position in the DOM. It was the default in earlier versions.

inputs.name: flip
inputs.description: Flip to the opposite side when the preferred one does not fit. Only meaningful when portalled (the default) — the in-place path has no measurement to decide with.

inputs.name: offset
inputs.description: Gap between trigger and bubble, in px, when portalled. Matches the `mb-2` / `mt-2` the in-place path uses, so `[portal]="false"` does not move the bubble.

inputs.name: fullWidth
inputs.description: Stretch the trigger wrapper to the width of its container. The wrapper is `inline-flex` by default, which is right for a word, an icon or a button — it hugs whatever it wraps. It is wrong the moment the trigger is a card in a grid or flex row: the wrapper becomes the track item and shrinks to its content, so the card does not fill its cell. Set this to lay the wrapper out as a full-width block instead.

inputs.name: forDisabledControl
inputs.description: Make the tooltip work over a control the browser has `disabled`. A disabled control fires no pointer events and takes no focus, so the tooltip explaining WHY it is disabled is the one tooltip in the kit that could never appear — and it is also the one users most need. The browser does not dispatch mouse events whose target is a disabled form control, so nothing reaches this wrapper either; and the control is out of the tab order, so the keyboard path is gone as well. What this does is two lines and both are necessary: the projected content gets `pointer-events: none`, which takes the disabled control out of hit-testing so hover and tap land on the WRAPPER; and the wrapper takes `tabindex="0"`, so the explanation is reachable by keyboard at all. `aria-describedby` already lives on the wrapper, so a screen-reader user who lands there hears the reason. Prefer `aria-disabled="true"` over `disabled` and you need none of this. A control marked `aria-disabled` stays focusable and keeps firing pointer events — it is announced as unavailable, your handler ignores the click, and every tooltip path works untouched. This preset is for the control you cannot change: a third-party component, or markup that is not yours. Do NOT set it around an ENABLED control. `pointer-events: none` applies to whatever is projected, so the control's own clicks stop working. Dev mode warns when the projected content does not look disabled.

inputs.name: title
inputs.description: A bold first line above `text`, which becomes the description.

inputs.name: kbd
inputs.description: Keys to show on the bubble's end — a shortcut, drawn with `sv-kbd`.

inputs.name: arrow
inputs.description: Draw the arrow pointing at the trigger.

inputs.name: icon
inputs.description: An icon before the content — a `@styloviz/icons` name.

inputs.name: status
inputs.description: A coloured status dot before the content.

inputs.name: open
inputs.description: Controlled visibility (two-way). Unbound, the tooltip shows and hides on its trigger. Bound, the trigger only REQUESTS — through `openChange` — and the bubble follows `open`, so a host can drive it: a slider showing its value while dragging, a guided tour.

inputs.name: anchor

components.name: Transcript
components.description: A speech transcript: speaker-labelled segments with timestamps, interim (still-changing) text drawn apart from final text, the line under the playhead highlighted, timestamps that seek a linked player, search with highlighted and counted matches, and copy / download as plain text or WebVTT. Live mode announces each new final line politely — never interim text — and follows the latest line until the reader scrolls up. Loading, error, empty and no-results states.
whenToUse: Call recordings in a helpdesk or CRM, meeting notes, interview and podcast transcripts, voicemail.
Live captions or dictation where interim results must be shown without being announced.
For a short voice turn with a mic button and level, use the Voice Assistant; for the recording itself, the Media Player.

examples.title: A call recording with a linked player
examples.description: `player` takes anything with `seek(seconds)` — `sv-media-player` itself. A timestamp seeks it (and plays, unless `playOnSeek` is off) and emits `seek`; `currentTime` highlights the line playing and keeps it in view inside the list.
examples.code:
<sv-transcript
  [segments]="segments"
  [speakers]="[{ id: 'agent', name: 'Maya' }, { id: 'caller', name: 'Jordan Lee', tone: 'accent' }]"
  [player]="player"
  [currentTime]="time()" />

examples.title: Live transcription from a streaming service
examples.description: Each result replaces the segment with the same id; `final: false` marks interim text. In `live` mode only a line's first final version is announced.

examples.title: Search and export
examples.description: `query` is two-way and settles after `debounceMs`; `filterOnSearch` hides lines that do not match. `exportFormats` picks the download buttons; `copied` / `exported` report exactly what was written.

examples.title: Export without the component
examples.description: The serialisers are plain functions — for a server job or a "send transcript" email.

customization: `showTimestamps`, `showSpeakers`, `collapseSpeakers` (name once per turn), `maxHeight` (a CSS length or `none`), `searchable`, `copyable`, `exportFormats` and `exportFilename`.
Speaker tones (`primary`, `accent`, `info`, `warning`, `danger`, `gray`) are theme tokens with `dark:` pairs; unset, speakers take them in turn.
`copy()`, `download(format)` and `jumpToLatest()` drive it from code; `svTranscriptToText`, `svTranscriptToVtt`, `svActiveSegmentIndex` and `svTranscriptParts` are exported.
Every string comes from the `display` labels (`transcript*` keys) in 12 language packs, or the per-instance `labels` input.
On paper the list prints in full (no scroll cap) and the toolbar is hidden.
accessibility: A labelled region with an ordered list of lines. Each timestamp is a button named "Play from 0:05, Jordan Lee" (or "Go to …" with no player); a line that continues a speaker's turn hides the name visually but still says it to a screen reader.
The line under the playhead has `aria-current="time"` and "now playing"; it is scrolled into view inside the list, never by scrolling the page.

In `live` mode a polite live region reads each new FINAL line once ("Jordan Lee: …"); interim text is marked "(still transcribing)" and never announced, because it changes several times a second. The list itself is not a live region.
Search is a `role="search"` box with a polite match count; Enter / Shift+Enter step matches and Escape clears. Matches are `<mark>`; the current one has a ring as well as a colour.
Copy reports its result in a status message and confirms only when the clipboard accepted the text.
The kit builds this without `@angular/aria`, which it does not depend on in 2.0.
variants: States — Loading, Error, Empty & No Results

inputs.description: A player to seek when a timestamp is pressed — `sv-media-player` fits, or anything with `seek(seconds)`.

components.name: Transfer / Dual List
components.description: Dual-list transfer widget for moving items between a source and target panel, with per-panel search, check-all and move-all controls, and rows you can drag from one panel to the other.
whenToUse: Moving items between two explicit lists: assign members, pick columns, build playlists.
You want per-panel search and move-all / check-all controls.
For ordering within one list, use the Drag-and-Drop List.

examples.title: Persisting a move, and putting it back
Drag between the lists
examples.description: On by default. A drop runs the same move as the arrow button, so one `(transferChange)` handler covers buttons, keys and drag. A ticked row carries every ticked row of its list; an unticked row moves alone.
examples.code:
<sv-transfer
  [sourceItems]="backlog()"
  [targetItems]="sprint()"
  sourceTitle="Backlog"
  targetTitle="Sprint 14"
  (transferChange)="onTransfer($event)" />

<!-- Checkboxes and arrows only: -->
<sv-transfer [draggable]="false" [sourceItems]="backlog()" [targetItems]="sprint()" />

examples.title: A pane that loads from the server

customization: Label each side with `sourceTitle` / `targetTitle`.
Enable `searchable` for per-panel filtering.
Read moved items from the `transferChange` event; replacing the `sourceItems`/`targetItems` set re-initialises the panels while in-progress moves survive unrelated re-renders.
For a pane too large to hold in memory, set `serverSide` and drive it from `sourceSearchChange` (debounced by `debounceMs`) plus `loadingSource` / `sourceError`.
`sourceChecked` / `targetChecked` are two-way, so a host can preselect a saved set or drive its own move control.
`moveError` accepts a bare string or a structured `SvDataError`, and renders above both panes rather than replacing either.

Rows drag to the other panel by default (native HTML5 drag and drop): dragging a ticked row carries every ticked row of that list, dragging an unticked row carries just that row, and a drop back on the same list does nothing. Set `[draggable]="false"` to keep only the checkboxes and arrow buttons.
accessibility: Keyboard at scale: each pane is ONE tab stop over its item checkboxes: ↑/↓/Home/End, PageUp/PageDown (ten items, clamped) and typeahead over labels move within the pane, while ←/→ keep their meaning — move the checked items across. Documented ceiling: 2,000 items in a pane, past which a dev-mode warning fires.
Each panel is a labelled group of individually-named checkboxes; the header check-all reflects a tri-state (indeterminate) when partially selected.

The check-all box **names its own scope** — "Select all 2 matching in Available" while a search is running, "Select all 5,000 in Available" when it is not — so the contract is legible before the click rather than inferable after it.
Move buttons are labelled with the count and the keyboard shortcut ("Move 2 selected to Selected. Right arrow."); the arrow glyphs are hidden from assistive tech.

Right and Left arrow move the ticked items from inside the list, and Ctrl/⌘ with them moves everything shown — so a keyboard user never has to tab out to the control column between the panes and back for each item. Space and Enter are left to the checkbox under the cursor.

A polite live region announces each transfer, and the same sentence is **rendered** under the panes — a move that skipped something has to say so to everyone, and the most likely reading of an item that stayed put is that the click missed. "Move undone." on a rollback, so the jump is not silent.
While `saving`, the move buttons carry `aria-busy="true"` — in flight, not merely switched off.
A failed move is announced through `role="alert"` above both panes.

Dragging is a pointer shortcut, never the only way: every drop is a move the checkboxes plus the arrow buttons (or ←/→ inside a list) make with a keyboard or single taps, which is the WCAG 2.5.7 alternative to the drag. A drop is announced and summarised exactly like a button move, disabled items and a disabled or saving component cannot be dragged, and the panel under the pointer shows a visible drop-target ring.

A selection the current search is hiding is disclosed in the pane header — "2 more selected, hidden by this search — a move takes 4 in total" — because ticks survive a search, and without it the header reads "all selected" over the visible rows while a move takes every hidden one too.
variants: Persisting a Move, and Putting It Back

inputs.name: targetItems

inputs.name: targetTitle

inputs.description: Show per-panel search fields.

inputs.name: disabled
inputs.description: Disabled state — no interactions possible.

inputs.name: draggable
inputs.description: Let rows be dragged to the other list (native HTML5 drag and drop). A drop performs exactly the move the arrow buttons do — same `transferChange`, same `saving` lock, same `rollback()`. The checkboxes and arrow buttons stay as the keyboard and single-pointer path (WCAG 2.5.7).

inputs.name: serverSide
inputs.description: Let the server do the searching. The supplied items are shown exactly as given — client-side search can only ever look at the page already loaded.

inputs.name: debounceMs
inputs.description: Delay before a search event fires, in ms. `0` emits immediately.

inputs.name: loadingSource
inputs.description: True while the source pane is being fetched.

inputs.name: loadingTarget
inputs.description: True while the target pane is being fetched.

inputs.name: sourceError
inputs.description: Failure loading the source pane, rendered in its place.

inputs.name: targetError
inputs.description: Failure loading the target pane, rendered in its place.

inputs.name: saving
inputs.description: True while a move is being written. Every move button and every tick stops responding, so a second move cannot race the first and leave `rollback()` holding an arrangement that predates it.

inputs.name: moveError
inputs.description: The last MOVE failed, shown above both panes. Spelled `moveError` rather than `error` because `sourceError` and `targetError` are already here and mean something else: *that pane would not load*. Those replace a pane and offer a retry, because a failed fetch leaves nothing to press. A failed move leaves both panes full and the buttons where they were, so it is reported and not retryable — you retry by pressing the arrow again. Overloading one input with both meanings is what the split exists to stop.

inputs.name: sourceChecked
inputs.description: Which source-pane items are ticked (two-way). A `model` because it is the state the two transfer buttons act on, so a host driving the component — preselecting a saved set, or enabling its own "move" control — has to be able to both write it and watch it. Held in a plain signal it was readable only from inside the template.

inputs.name: targetChecked
inputs.description: Which target-pane items are ticked (two-way). Same reasoning as sourceChecked.

outputs.description: Emitted whenever items are transferred.

outputs.name: sourceSearchChange
outputs.description: The source pane's search term changed — fetch matching items. Debounced.

outputs.name: targetSearchChange
outputs.description: The target pane's search term changed — fetch matching items. Debounced.

outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed source load.

outputs.name: retryTarget
outputs.description: The host should re-run the failed target load.

outputs.description: Emits the new `sourceChecked` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(sourceChecked)]`.

outputs.name: targetCheckedChange
outputs.description: Emits the new `targetChecked` whenever it changes — the output half of `[(targetChecked)]`.

components.name: Tree Select
components.description: Hierarchical picker in a body-portalled tree panel: single or multi-select, an ancestor-preserving filter with debounced server search, full keyboard control through aria-activedescendant, ControlValueAccessor support, and the loading / error / empty states inside the panel.
whenToUse: Picking one node out of a hierarchy the user already thinks of as a tree — folders, org units, categories.
A taxonomy too deep for a flat select but too shallow to need a full page.
For a strictly level-by-level walk (country → state → city), the Cascader reads better; for browsing rather than picking, use the Tree View.

examples.title: Bottom sheet on phones
examples.description: Below 640px the tree opens as a bottom sheet (`createSheetMode`): full width, safe-area padded, riding the virtual keyboard. Off by default.

examples.title: Lazy branches
examples.description: Mark an unfetched branch `children: []`. `loadChildren` runs once per branch on first expand, gets an `AbortSignal` that fires if the branch is collapsed mid-load, and a branch that failed is retried on the next expand.

customization: Single or multiple selection.
Leaf-only or any-node selection.
Filter box, local or server-side, with a configurable debounce.
Three trigger sizes, clearable, disabled.
accessibility: The trigger is a `button` with `aria-haspopup="tree"`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`; the panel is a `role="tree"` with `aria-multiselectable` in multi mode.
Every row is a `role="treeitem"` carrying `aria-level`, `aria-posinset`, `aria-setsize`, `aria-selected` and — only where it can open — `aria-expanded`.
Keyboard: ↑/↓ move, →/← expand, collapse or jump to the parent, Enter/Space select, Escape closes. DOM focus stays in the filter box and the active row is published through `aria-activedescendant`.
variants: Lazy Tree — Load Branches on Expand

inputs.name: options
inputs.description: The tree to pick from.

inputs.name: loadChildren
inputs.type: ((node: TreeSelectNode, signal?: AbortSignal) => Promise<readonly TreeSelectNode[]>) | null
inputs.description: Fetch a branch's children the first time it is expanded. For a tree you cannot fetch whole — a permissions tree, a file browser — instead of fetching everything up front and feeding it in. The signature takes an `AbortSignal` because a branch the user has navigated away from must be cancellable — the same rule as `sv-cascader`, and both use `svKeyedRequestGuard`. Honour it: a tree browsed quickly opens and abandons branches faster than they return. It is called once per branch. A node that has been loaded is not asked again, and a node that FAILED is retried when the user expands it again — a failed branch that could never be retried would be a dead end with no way out but a page reload. Mark an unloaded branch with `children: []`. With a loader bound, an empty `children` array is a branch whose contents have not been fetched: it renders a chevron, `aria-expanded`, and expands (rather than selects) on click. A node with no `children` property at all is a leaf. Once loaded, a branch that came back empty is shown as a leaf.

inputs.name: loading
inputs.description: True while `options` are being fetched.

inputs.name: stale
inputs.description: The results on screen answer an **older** query — a newer request is still in flight. Distinct from `loading`, which cannot separate the two cases it covers: the first fetch (nothing on screen — show a skeleton) and a refinement of results already visible (keep them, and say they are provisional). Blanking the panel on the second is the most jarring thing a picker can do; showing the old list with no indication is a quiet lie. Bind `svSuggestController(...).stale` from `@styloviz/data`, or `createRequestGuard().stale` from `@styloviz/core`. The results dim and report `aria-busy` while staying fully interactive.

inputs.name: error
inputs.description: Load failure. Use `toSvDataError()` from `@styloviz/core` to normalize an `HttpErrorResponse` and get sensible retry behaviour.

inputs.name: emptyMessage
inputs.description: Copy for the no-data state.

inputs.name: checkedValues

components.name: Tree View / Table
components.description: 8 variants: collapsible tree, file explorer, tri-state checkboxes, org chart, tree table, searchable, drag & drop reordering and lazy load. Lazy loading, the tree-table columns and drag & drop reordering are Pro (`sv-tree-view-pro`); the free component renders the nodes you give it. Both draw as an indented list or, with `layout="org"`, as a top-down org chart of boxes joined by connector lines.
whenToUse: Browsing hierarchical data: file systems, categories, org charts, nested menus.
You need expand/collapse. Tri-state checkbox selection and lazy loading of branches are Pro — the free component is a single-select tree and has no checked state at all.
Free renders every node you pass, so give it a set you are happy to hold in memory — for a very large tree (tens of thousands of nodes) you want Pro’s `lazyLoad`.

The size contract, stated rather than left to be discovered: neither component virtualizes, so every VISIBLE row is a DOM node. The flatten is not the limit — 200,000 rows flatten and search without throwing — but the render is. Keep visible rows in the low thousands and lazy-load or collapse below that. A single wide branch flattens too: no level is spread into a function call, so there is no engine argument cap (~65k in JavaScriptCore, ~124k in V8) to hit.
For picking one path from a hierarchy in a form, use the Cascader.

An org chart people can read at a glance: `layout="org"` draws the same tree top-down, each parent centred over its children. Reach for it when the shape of the hierarchy is the point (reporting lines, a team structure); keep the list layout when people search or scan names (a file tree, a settings menu).

examples.title: Org chart — boxes and connectors
examples.code:
<!-- role → the line under the name, department → the chip -->
<sv-tree-view layout="org" ariaLabel="Leadership team" [nodes]="people" (nodeSelect)="open($event)" />

people: TreeNode[] = [
  { id: 'ceo', label: 'Sarah Chen', role: 'CEO', department: 'Executive', expanded: true,
    children: [
      { id: 'cto', label: 'Marcus Reid', role: 'CTO', department: 'Engineering' },
      { id: 'cfo', label: 'Aisha Patel', role: 'CFO', department: 'Finance' },
    ] },
];

examples.title: Org chart with presence and report counts (Pro)
Saving a move, and putting it back (Pro)
A lazy branch that fails, or comes back empty (Pro)

<sv-tree-view-pro
  variant="lazy"
  [nodes]="nodes()"
  [loadingNodeIds]="loading()"
  [nodeErrors]="errors()"
  emptyBranchText="No members"
  (lazyLoad)="load($event)" />

// errors() is a Map of node id to a message or an SvDataError. The id-only

customization: Tree, tree-table or org-chart presentations.

**`layout`: `'list'` (default) or `'org'`.** The org layout draws each node as a box — initials or the node's `icon`, `label`, `role` on the line beneath, `department` as a chip, `badge` in the corner (Pro's `org-chart` variant adds the avatar photo, presence dot and `reports` count) — with each parent centred over its children, even sibling spacing and orthogonal connector lines drawn as CSS borders on logical sides, so RTL mirrors. A collapsed box shows how many direct children are folded under it. Wider than its container, the chart scrolls sideways inside its own labelled region; on paper the region lets go so the chart prints. `showLines` applies to the list; the org layout always draws its connectors. On Pro, `tree-table` and `draggable` stay lists (a table and a drop target need rows) and say so in dev mode.
Tri-state selection and lazy loading (both Pro, `variant="checkbox"` / `variant="lazy"`).

**Selection propagation, stated rather than left to be discovered.** Down: ticking a branch ticks every **enabled** descendant; a disabled node and its subtree keep the state they had, in both directions. Up: a branch is ticked once every enabled child is, `indeterminate` while only some are, and a branch whose children are all disabled behaves as a leaf — its box stands for the branch alone. A ticked branch also cascades to children that arrive later, so a lazy folder ticked before its load still means "everything in here" once the files show up, and `checkedChange` re-fires with them.
Drag & drop reordering with custom columns (Pro).

Keyboard reordering on the Pro draggable variant: Ctrl/Cmd + ↑/↓ reorder among siblings, Ctrl/Cmd + → indents under the sibling above, Ctrl/Cmd + ← lifts the node out to after its parent. Both inputs go through one apply path, so `(nodeMoved)` carries the same `requestKey` and `rollback()` either way.
Per-branch async state on the Pro lazy variant: `loadingNodeIds`, `nodeErrors` and `emptyBranchText` describe one branch each, independently of the whole-tree `loading`/`error`.
accessibility: Keyboard at scale: the tree is ONE tab stop — expand chevrons and checkboxes leave the tab order; →/← expand, collapse and retry a failed branch, Space ticks a row in the checkbox variant, and the tree-table variant roves its row headers. ↑/↓/Home/End, PageUp/PageDown (ten rows, clamped) and typeahead over labels. Documented ceiling: 2,000 visible rows, past which a dev-mode warning suggests lazy children.
Focus after a mutation: when the host removes the focused node through `nodes`, focus moves to the row now at its position, then the one before it, then the tree — never `<body>`.
WAI-ARIA `tree`/`treeitem` roles with `aria-level`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-selected` state.

`aria-selected` is published only when `selectable` is true. A display-only tree that reports `aria-selected="false"` on every row announces a selection model that does not exist, and a listener can only discover that by pressing Enter and getting nothing.

Reordering has full keyboard parity on the draggable variant, because `dragstart` fires for a pointer and for nothing else: a tree whose whole purpose is rearranging a hierarchy could be read by a keyboard user and not changed by one. Ctrl/Cmd + ↑/↓/→/← express exactly what a drop can, and the row publishes them in `aria-keyshortcuts` so the gesture is discoverable rather than folklore.

A move is announced in an assertive live region — "main.ts moved to position 2 of 3 under src." A reorder is the one gesture whose entire result is off-screen: the row keeps its own name and only its POSITION changes, so without this a keypress had no reported outcome. The position is in the sentence, which is also what makes two consecutive moves differ, and a rejected save announces the put-back for the same reason.

Focus follows the moved node rather than the position it left, and the re-focus lands after the render: moving a row detaches and re-inserts its element, so focusing it any earlier dropped the user out of the tree with no way to press the shortcut again.

A lazy branch’s state is on the expand control itself, not only in the note beside it — "Loading Team", "Retry loading Other — Request timed out", "Collapse Team, empty". The control is what the arrow keys land on; the notes are `aria-hidden` so the row is not read twice.

The ARIA model per variant, stated rather than left to be discovered: `default`, `file-explorer`, `checkbox`, `org-chart`, `searchable`, `draggable` and `lazy` are all `role="tree"` with `treeitem` rows; `tree-table` is a real `<table>` with an `sr-only` `<caption>` and `scope="row"`/`scope="col"` headers.

The `tree-table` variant is deliberately NOT `role="treegrid"`. A treegrid promises cell-level arrow navigation, and this one navigates by row — claiming the role without the keyboard model behind it strands a user pressing → in a cell that will never move. A plain table with correct headers is the honest description.

Already a semantic structure, so it publishes no off-screen summary table — a second copy would read every node twice. The `tree-table` variant is a real table with a caption and `scope` headers, and its row header carries the branch and repeats it as you move across the data columns, because otherwise "24 MB" arrives attached to nothing.
Name the tree with `ariaLabel`. An unnamed `role="tree"` announces as "tree" and nothing more, which is unhelpful on any page with two of them.
Full keyboard navigation: ↑/↓ move, →/← expand/collapse or move to child/parent, Home/End jump, Enter/Space select — via a roving tabindex so the tree is a single tab stop.

A disabled row is disabled to the cascade too: ticking its parent does not tick it, so a row the user could not select never arrives in `checkedChange`. One locked child does not stop its branch from completing either: the roll-up reads the enabled children, so a folder with a read-only file in it can still be ticked.
Checkboxes are individually labelled; search highlighting keeps the underlying text intact.

The org layout is the SAME tree, not a second widget: `role="tree"`, each box a `treeitem` with `aria-level`, `aria-setsize`, `aria-posinset`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-selected`, and its children in a nested `role="group"`. The keys keep their WAI-ARIA tree meanings even though the picture runs top-down — ↓/↑ walk the boxes depth-first, → opens a box or steps to its first child, ← closes it or climbs to the parent, Home/End/typeahead as in the list. No 2-D grid is invented: a screen-reader user hears "tree", and the keys do what the role promised.

Each org box is named explicitly from what it shows ("Sarah Chen, Chief Executive Officer, Executive" — plus presence and report count on Pro). The `<li>` that is the treeitem also holds its children, so a name taken from content would read out the whole department under every manager.
The org chart scrolls inside a focusable `role="region"` named by `ariaLabel` (or "Org chart"), so a wide company scrolls the chart rather than the page, and keyboard users can scroll it too.

A Branch That Fails, and One That Is Empty
Org Chart — Connector Layout with Presence

examples.title: A layout that does not move

customization: Four visual variants.
Nested / hierarchical data support.
Custom color mapping per node.

`tileOrder` chooses between largest-first packing (`value`, the default, which keeps tiles closest to square) and the order of the `nodes` array (`input`, which keeps a tile where the reader last saw it).
A branch that contains itself is cut before anything walks the tree, and the cut is named under the plot with the path that reaches the loop.

`valuePolicy` decides what happens to a node this chart cannot lay out — a negative, `NaN` or `Infinity`. Tile area is `value / total`, so an unplottable node distorts the area of every sibling. `omit` (default) drops it and discloses the count; `reject` refuses the dataset. `clamp` is not offered: a tile clamped to 0 has zero area, which is a tile that is not there — an invisible outcome cannot be a disclosure.
accessibility: The SVG is a `role="group"` with a generated summary (override via `ariaLabel`) — `group`, not `img`, because every tile is a tab stop.

Tile AREA is the value, and the small tiles are exactly the ones whose labels do not fit — so the alternative is the only place their numbers exist at all. `sv-data-summary-table` gives every tile its value and share, and adds a "Share of" column for nested data so a child's share of its own parent is not mistaken for its share of the whole.
Every tile is keyboard-focusable with a label/value `aria-label`; hover/focus highlights the tile and Enter/Space emits `tileSelect`. Adequate contrast for tile labels.
A cut branch is named under the plot too, with the path down to the loop, so a truncated hierarchy is never mistaken for a shallow one.

A dropped node is named in the rendered output under the plot — how many, and their real values — not only in `console.warn`. A tile that is simply absent is indistinguishable from a tile that was never in the data, so the count is the only thing that tells a reader the map is of a subset.

inputs.name: valuePolicy
inputs.description: What to do with a tile this chart cannot plot — a negative value, `NaN`, `Infinity`. Area is the encoding, and there is no negative area; worse, the tile's own subtree sum is the denominator for its children, so one bad weight makes a whole level's tiles overlap rather than merely misdraw. - `omit` (default) — drop it wherever it appears in the tree, and disclose the count. Percentages are then of the tiles that remain. - `reject` — refuse the tree and show the error state. `clamp` is not available: a zero-value tile has zero area, so there is no rectangle left to mark. Asking for it warns in dev and omits instead.

components.name: Voice Assistant
components.description: A voice turn with a level meter driven by measured amplitude, interim-vs-final transcript rendering, and barge-in as a real transition. 3 variants: button, transcript and call.
whenToUse: A voice input surface where the user needs to know whether the microphone is actually being heard.
A live transcript where the recogniser emits interim guesses that must not read as settled text.
A call-style turn where the user has to be able to interrupt the assistant mid-sentence.
customization: `[ambientLevels]` — the first second of capture, measured while nobody is talking — calibrates the silence threshold from the room. `SV_SILENCE_LEVEL` (0.04) is a guess about a quiet office: in a car, a café or a warehouse the ambient floor sits above it, so every frame reads as speech, the auto-stop never fires and the meter claims to hear a user who has not spoken. Derived from the 90th percentile of ambient rather than the mean (the mean sits under most of the room) and never from the maximum, so one cough cannot deafen the assistant for the session.

The calibrated threshold is **capped at 0.35** and floored at 0.02. The cap is the important one: a café calibration would otherwise climb above ordinary speech and the assistant would stop hearing anybody at all — a worse failure than the one calibration fixes, and one the user cannot diagnose. When the cap is doing the deciding the component says so and tells the user to move somewhere quieter.

`[consentRequired]` with two-way `[(consent)]` (`unknown` / `granted` / `declined`) gates capture behind an explicit 'this records your voice' prompt. The browser's microphone permission is not consent — it asks whether the page may use the microphone, not whether the user agrees to being transcribed, stored or sent to a third-party model. The gate is enforced in `dispatch`, the one entry point, so no control or host call routes around it, and it blocks `start` only: stop, interrupt and reset always work, because a gate that trapped a live microphone would be the opposite of what it is for.

A **Recording** indicator (`role='status'`) shows whenever the microphone is open, in every variant, with no host opt-in. An indicator that appears only when somebody remembered to ask for it is not an indicator.

Redaction, from the pack-wide policy: transcript segments AND the settled-text footer are masked — they are two renderings of the same words, so masking one would leave the secret six lines below where it was hidden. `copy: false` withdraws the footer entirely, because it exists to be selected and copied. People dictate what they cannot type one-handed: a card number read off the card, an address, a patient identifier. The mask covers every string that reaches the DOM, not only visible text: each segment's `aria-label` (what a screen reader reads instead of the text) and the settled-character count are built from the masked text too. The policy's `reveal` and `telemetry` flags are not read here, because there is nothing for them to govern: the component offers no unmask control and emits no analytics, and none of its outputs (`action`, `silenceDetected`, `retry`, `turnChange`, `consentChange`) carries transcript text. Telemetry of the transcript is therefore the host's own code, and the host should consult `svAiPrivacy().telemetry` there.
`levels` (measured amplitude, 0–1) and `transcript` are inputs defaulting to empty; import `DEMO_LEVELS` / `DEMO_TRANSCRIPT` for a demo.
Three layouts via `variant`: `button` (the control and meter alone), `transcript` (plus the folded transcript) and `call` (plus interrupt and hang-up).
The turn is a state machine — `idle`, `listening`, `thinking`, `speaking`, `denied` — driven by `start` / `stop` / `interrupt` / `reset`. `denied` is terminal until `reset`.
`SV_SILENCE_LEVEL` (0.04, not zero) is the amplitude floor: a live microphone in a quiet room reads a non-zero noise floor, so a `> 0` test calls silence speech forever.
The meter draws a 6 % floor while capturing, so a live-but-silent microphone is visibly live rather than indistinguishable from a dead one.
`SV_LOW_CONFIDENCE` (0.6) flags settled text the recogniser was unsure about — never interim text, which is already drawn as provisional.

`[lowConfidence]` (default `SV_LOW_CONFIDENCE`, 0.6, still exported) is the recogniser confidence below which a settled segment is marked uncertain — the “?” chip and the spoken “unsure” both follow it. Confidence scales are vendor-specific, so tune it to your recogniser; `0` turns the marker off.
accessibility: The meter is `role="img"` with an accessible name stating whether input is being heard, not only drawn.
A denied microphone gets a written explanation of where the browser hid the permission, not a dead-end "unavailable".
The turn label and hint are text; the control reports what pressing it will do.

inputs.description: True while the session is being set up.
